title: test(artifact): run internal/artifact tests in parallel
body:
Runs 197 isolated `internal/artifact` top-level tests in parallel to shorten an
I/O-bound CI package. Five tests that change process-wide state or measure
process-wide allocations remain serial, and subtests are unchanged.

The change only affects test scheduling, not assertions or fixtures.
Parallelism uses more memory and can become slower at very high concurrency
because the fixtures compete for filesystem writes.

title: ci: run NilAway package lints concurrently
body:
Runs up to four per-package NilAway checks at once while keeping the existing
CPU and memory caps for each process. `NILAWAY_JOBS` remains configurable and
rejects zero or invalid values so concurrency stays bounded.

Each check writes to separate temporary output, which is printed in package
order after the run. Output no longer streams, but all packages are checked
before the target reports failure.

title: feat(import): support Google Takeout Gemini Apps activity exports
body:
Adds `agentsview import --type gemini-apps` support for Google Takeout Gemini Apps activity exports. Whole-hour numeric zones could be interpreted as UTC when the timestamp matcher accepted only the `GMT` prefix after the numeric form failed, so the import could persist a valid-looking record with the wrong instant and stable session ID.

The importer admits Gemini Apps records by their document structure and compatibility grammar, skips non-prompt activity, and emits each compatible `Prompted` activity as one stable plain-text message. It keeps visible text from inline and preformatted code, including spaces, tabs, line breaks, and authored backticks, without treating HTML presentation as speaker roles or generating Markdown delimiters. The parser now consumes each complete timestamp zone token and validates it once at the existing Gemini Apps zone authority. It accepts the existing named zones plus complete `GMT±H`, `GMT±HH`, `GMT±H:MM`, and `GMT±HH:MM` forms, with omitted minutes treated as zero. Malformed and unsupported complete tokens fail before import callbacks, while canonical UTC timestamps continue to drive timestamp-local stable IDs.

Unsupported locale or timestamp grammar fails before callbacks, while unrelated Takeout products are ignored and valid Gemini records in the same archive remain importable. The import-only provider, shared persistence, reimport identity, FTS handling, CLI dispatch, and Gemini CLI behavior remain unchanged. Browser upload, HTTP, schema, sync, remote transfer, frontend import UI, and raw archive handling are out of scope.

Closes #1295

title: fix(sync): bound OpenCode background work to the changed session batch
body:
Recurring OpenCode work is scheduled per root, so its cost follows the container instead of what actually moved. Any write to the shared database breaks the freshness trust that lets a pass skip unchanged sessions; the next pass rebuilds the per-session digest over every message and part row, and each watcher batch that advances a session's update time re-parses that session's entire history. OpenCode publishes a durable event journal recording which sessions changed and which finished changing. This makes that journal the unit of scheduling: with 5,000 stored sessions and one changed, the recurring pass previously evaluated all 5,000 sessions to skip 4,999, while the journal drain reads one row and returns one session identity.

What this changes:

- A bounded change-feed capability, declared by the provider and unsupported by default, reads a fixed window of journal rows and returns session identities, continuation state, and an audit reason. Row metadata is read for every candidate and payload only for the small settlement-bearing types, with the size predicate in SQL so an oversized row is never materialized. A session becomes ready when an assistant message update carries a completion timestamp, and only a part update returns it to pending, because ordinary message and session updates routinely trail a completed turn. (internal/parser/opencode_change_feed.go, internal/parser/capabilities.go)
- Feed eligibility is schema provenance rather than table presence, since the journal tables exist in forks that never write them; anything else falls through to existing behavior. (internal/parser/opencode_provider.go, internal/parser/sqlite_container_state.go)
- Deletion never appears in the feed's output: deleting a session cascades its event history away without a tombstone, so removal keeps converging through existing verification and the audit. Cursor anchors span multiple sessions so an ordinary deletion cannot erase every witness, and a changed file identity, schema generation, or rewound row id forces one audit. (internal/parser/opencode_change_feed.go, internal/parser/sqlite_file_identity_unix.go, internal/parser/sqlite_file_identity_windows.go)
- Scheduling moves behind one keyed worker built from the existing per-key scheduler. It holds one active pass per coverage unit, unions escalating reasons so a later ordinary event cannot downgrade them, measures degraded intervals from completion with backoff, and commits a checkpoint only after the archive write for that pass succeeded. (internal/sync/opencode_coverage_worker.go, internal/sync/keyed_schedule.go)
- The engine resolves journal identities through its existing source-lookup contract, with archive ownership batch-loaded per pass; the feed itself returns no source paths and performs no filesystem walk. (internal/sync/opencode_coverage_coordinator.go, internal/sync/engine.go, internal/db/sessions.go)
- Archive-scale reconciliation becomes reachable only through a sealed runner held by startup and the audit worker; watcher callbacks, degraded polling, and retries hold a bounded executor that can request recovery through a deduplicated audit lane but cannot run it inline. The grouped polling path now requires a named provider instead of treating an empty one as an unscoped pass. (internal/sync/coverage_executor.go, internal/sync/engine.go, cmd/agentsview/main.go, cmd/agentsview/unwatched_poll.go)
- The portable watch backend owns missing recursive roots' lifecycle the way the macOS backend already does: the watch activates when the directory appears, files created in the handoff window are covered by the existing bounded created-subtree scan, and the storage coverage unit is emitted from the plan rather than from directory existence, so a pending root never blocks fallback polling behind a missing probe. This closes the runtime-creation gap disclosed in #1318, where a storage tree created after startup got no live coverage until restart or the daily audit. (internal/sync/watch_backend_fsnotify.go, internal/sync/watch_backend.go)

Session lineage and termination classification are unchanged, and providers without the capability construct no adapter. Journal checkpoints are in-memory, so a restart rebaselines under startup reconciliation. Pure-SQLite OpenCode roots remain in the startup and daily audit scope when storage is absent, while poll-path deletion detection for admitted containers still defers to the daily audit.

Based on #1318; the diff collapses to this change alone when it lands.

Closes #1208

title: feat(recall): inspect extraction progress
body:
Recall’s aggregate coverage counts do not identify which sessions are blocked or explain extraction failures. This adds a read-only progress drilldown to the Recall page with generation-scoped pending, partial, and failed rows, source-session links, unit progress, error details, retry timing, localized state filters, and bounded cursor pagination.

The endpoint reads directly from persisted extraction state, so existing archives remain inspectable without a configured extraction manager. The surface deliberately excludes retry, run, activation, and retirement actions; those model-work and corpus-lifecycle controls remain separate follow-ups.

title: Session upload derives session identity from the uploaded filename, letting a basename collision silently replace an archived session's messages
body:
**Observed on:** `agentsview v0.39.0` (commit `627a8afa`, built 2026-07-27), daemon on `127.0.0.1:8080`.

---

## Summary

`POST /api/v1/sessions/upload` takes the session's identity from the **uploaded
filename**, ignoring the `sessionId` recorded inside the transcript. Because the
resulting basename is the archive's primary key, uploading an unrelated file whose
basename collides with an existing session **replaces that session's messages**, with
an `HTTP 200` and no warning.

In one measured case a single POST reduced an archived session from 96 messages to 24.

## Reproduction

A 326-line Claude Code transcript was copied and its internal session UUID rewritten to
a fresh value, so no pre-existing record was involved. The same content was then
uploaded under different filenames.

| Step | Uploaded basename | `sessionId` inside file | Response `session_id` | Response `messages` | Archived `message_count` for `344e9899…` |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | `344e9899….jsonl` (326 lines) | `344e9899…` | `344e9899…` | 96 | 96 |
| 2 | `344e9899….jsonl` (first 100 lines) | `344e9899…` | `344e9899…` | 24 | **24 — 72 messages gone** |
| 3 | `344e9899….jsonl` (full again) | `344e9899…` | `344e9899…` | 96 | 96 |
| 4 | `renamed-truncated-copy.jsonl` (100 lines) | `344e9899…` | **`renamed-truncated-copy`** | 24 | 96 (untouched) |
| 5 | `zzz-unrelated-name.jsonl` (326 lines) | `344e9899…` | **`zzz-unrelated-name`** | 96 | 96 (untouched) |

Steps 4 and 5 isolate the variable: identical bytes produced three distinct archive
records, each keyed to its filename. Step 2 is the destructive case.

Requests were sent with `-H "Origin: http://127.0.0.1:8080"`, which is required — the
example curl in `docs/usage.md:1176-1179` returns `403` as written when remote access
is disabled. That is a separate, smaller documentation issue.

## Why this is a problem rather than a quirk

The failure needs no malice and no unusual input:

- **Recovered or archived transcripts frequently have altered basenames** —
  `session-copy-2.jsonl`, `foo.jsonl.bak.jsonl`, timestamped variants. Uploading those
  as-is mints archive records under identifiers that match nothing, dedupe against
  nothing, and cannot be retrieved by the session's real ID.
- **Basename collisions are reachable from an ordinary recursive walk.** Claude Code
  session directories contain `subagents/` subdirectories; two genuinely different
  sessions sharing a basename collapse into one record, and whichever uploads second
  destroys the first's messages.
- **The response is indistinguishable from success.** `{"session_id": …, "messages":
  24, "sessions": 1}` with `HTTP 200` looks identical whether 24 messages were added or
  96 were replaced by 24.

## Contradiction with documented invariants

- `docs/contributing.md:85-88` — "Preserve the project's cross-cutting contracts: Treat
  the SQLite archive as persistent user data. Schema and parser changes must preserve
  existing sessions through the migration and resync paths…"
- `docs/configuration.md:930-932` — "Sessions already in the archive are preserved (the
  SQLite database is a persistent archive); remove unwanted existing sessions
  explicitly with `agentsview prune`."

Step 2 removed 72 messages with no `prune` and no acknowledgement. The endpoint itself
appears exactly once across the 27 files in `docs/` (the example at `usage.md:1178`),
and that section states no replace-versus-merge semantics — so the behavior is not
documented either way, and the invariants above are the only stated contract it can be
measured against.

The changelog suggests transcript-rewrite handling is already treated as a correctness
domain: `changelog.md:227` replays replaced JSONL segments "instead of treating
same-length splices as append-only transcript growth", and `changelog.md:501` reparses
in-place rewrites "so same-length edits no longer leave stale stored messages." This
looks like an unhandled case in that same area rather than a deliberate design.

## Relationship to #128

This is the same class as #128 ("Upload handler should return 409 for excluded/trashed
sessions"), which fixed a case where `saveSessionToDB` returned `nil` for an excluded
session and the handler replied `200`, "giving the caller no indication the upload was
rejected."

That was the silent-**skip** case. This is the silent-**replace** case: the handler
replies `200` while the archive loses messages the caller never asked to remove. The
remedy there was to make the outcome visible to the caller through a distinct status
code; the same reasoning applies here.

## Suggested direction

Derive session identity from the transcript's own `sessionId` rather than the uploaded
filename, and treat a message-count regression on an existing session as something the
caller must opt into rather than a silent default.

## What this fix would NOT achieve

Stating these plainly because each is a real limit, and a fix presented without them
would be overclaiming:

1. **It does not settle multi-session files.** The response's `sessions` field can
   exceed 1 when one file parses into forked or resumed branches, so "the transcript's
   `sessionId`" is not always singular. Any fix has to define which ID wins, or key on
   each parsed session separately.
2. **It does not repair existing records.** Sessions already stored under
   filename-derived identifiers stay as-is; correcting them is a migration question,
   and skipping that leaves archives with duplicates that the new logic will not merge.
3. **It does not make every shortening wrong.** A transcript legitimately rewritten
   shorter should still be able to update its record — `changelog.md:501` shows
   in-place rewrites are a real scenario. Blanket-refusing shorter uploads would break
   that. The problem is silence, not shortening.
4. **A client-side workaround protects only clients that know about it.** Renaming
   uploads to `<sessionId>.jsonl` before POSTing avoids the hazard for one caller and
   leaves the documented curl in `usage.md` as hazardous as before.
5. **It does not address the concurrent-writer race.** Even with identity fixed, a
   check-then-upload sequence from any client can be overtaken by a sync writing the
   same session. Only server-side enforcement closes that.

## Second, smaller issue observed in the same session

`agentsview export sessions --all` combined with `--date-from` and/or `--date-to`
returned **0 records** for each of three non-overlapping windows spanning the full data
range, while the identical command without date flags returned 8,010. Worth filing
separately; recorded here so it is not lost.

## Provenance

All probe records were created under a dedicated `zz_truncation_probe` project and
deleted afterward via `DELETE /api/v1/sessions/<id>`; no real session was involved at
any point. Happy to supply the exact transcript or re-run any step.

title: test(artifact): serialize deadline-bound drain test
body:
The unsettled-queue full-export test has a 30-second context to catch real stalls, but it also performs repeated real SQLite and Docbank writes. Since the artifact suite was parallelized, shared-runner contention can consume that deadline even while export progresses, failing both plain and race jobs at different write sites.

Keep this single deadline-bound integration test in the serial phase. Its real-store coverage, behavioral assertions, and hang guard remain intact; other artifact tests remain parallel and production behavior is unchanged.

title: ci: reduce Windows Go test critical path
body:
Windows Go tests became the CI critical path after redundant Linux work was removed. Recent successful jobs spend nearly all of their wall time inside the Go test command, with real SQLite fixture setup and the CGo-heavy DuckDB package competing for four runner cores; adding broad `t.Parallel` calls would increase contention without addressing that work.

The suite now constructs high-cardinality SQLite fixtures transactionally while preserving the production triggers, scale comparisons, and 1,024-row claim boundary they protect. The ordinary database suite deterministically verifies the closed-writer fallback, while the concurrent close/reopen stress case remains in the existing Linux race job. On Windows, DuckDB runs on an independent runner and the main package set avoids verbose log I/O, allowing both long test groups to advance concurrently.

This trades additional Windows runner-minutes for a shorter required-check critical path. The principal review points are the package split in `.github/workflows/ci.yml`, the deterministic/race coverage split in `internal/db`, and the transaction-backed fixtures in `internal/artifact`, `internal/parser`, and `internal/sync`.

title: ci: path-filter docker.yml and ci-macos-main.yml push triggers
body:
## Summary

Docs-only and other unrelated pushes to `main` no longer rebuild and publish the Docker image or occupy the self-hosted macOS runner. Each workflow now runs only when a changed file can affect its output.

## Design

- The Docker workflow watches the backend, frontend, Go module files, container inputs, and its own workflow file.
- The macOS workflow watches Go code, module files, the golden fixtures used by its tests, and its own workflow file. Frontend changes are intentionally excluded because this job does not build the frontend.
- Release tags still build the Docker image because GitHub does not apply path filters to tag pushes.
- Manual Docker builds remain available through `workflow_dispatch`.

title: Kimi Work undercounts tool-call usage and leaves k2d6-agent unpriced
body:
## Summary

AgentsView v0.40.0 discovers Kimi Work sessions, but it undercounts token usage
for Kimi Work model steps whose persisted event order is:

```text
step.begin -> [content.part...] -> tool.call -> tool.result -> step.end
```

The same artifacts also report the explicit model alias `k2d6-agent`, which is
currently left unpriced even though it identifies the K2.6 model era.

This is a correctness issue in the newly released Kimi Work support rather than
a discovery problem.

## Environment

- AgentsView: v0.40.0, commit `a2cebf55`
- Kimi Code wire protocol: 1.4
- Kimi Work source root:
  `%APPDATA%\kimi-desktop\daimon-share\daimon\runtime\kimi-code\home\sessions`

## Storage and usage source

Kimi Work embeds the Kimi Code runtime. User conversations are stored as:

```text
sessions/
  wd_<workspace>_<hash>/
    conv-<id>/
      state.json
      agents/
        main/wire.jsonl
        agent-*/wire.jsonl
```

Sibling `ctitle-*`, `sklsum-*`, and `dvlt-*` sessions are internal runtime
work and should remain excluded.

The canonical usage data is in `wire.jsonl`, not the desktop LevelDB stores.
Each model step persists both:

- `context.append_loop_event` with `event.type = "step.end"` and
  `event.usage`
- a following `usage.record` with the same usage values

The fields are:

```json
{
  "inputOther": 100,
  "output": 20,
  "inputCacheRead": 300,
  "inputCacheCreation": 0
}
```

Only one of the duplicate sources should be counted.

## Reproduction

An anonymized minimal event sequence is:

```jsonl
{"type":"turn.prompt","input":[{"type":"text","text":"run a tool"}],"time":1785720000000}
{"type":"context.append_loop_event","event":{"type":"step.begin","uuid":"step-1"},"time":1785720000001}
{"type":"context.append_loop_event","event":{"type":"tool.call","toolCallId":"call-1","name":"Shell","args":{}},"time":1785720000002}
{"type":"context.append_loop_event","event":{"type":"tool.result","toolCallId":"call-1","result":{"output":"ok","isError":false}},"time":1785720000003}
{"type":"context.append_loop_event","event":{"type":"step.end","uuid":"step-1","finishReason":"tool_use","usage":{"inputOther":100,"output":20,"inputCacheRead":300,"inputCacheCreation":0}},"time":1785720000004}
{"type":"usage.record","model":"k3-agent","usage":{"inputOther":100,"output":20,"inputCacheRead":300,"inputCacheCreation":0},"usageScope":"turn","time":1785720000004}
```

Sync the transcript and query `agentsview usage daily --agent kimi-work
--breakdown`.

## Observed behavior

`tool.result` flushes the pending assistant tool-call message before
`step.end` is processed. `step.end` then stores usage in an empty pending turn,
and `flushAssistantTurn` discards it because there is no remaining content or
tool call. The following `usage.record` also cannot attach the usage because
the last parsed message is the user-role tool result.

With the synthetic fixture above, the expected uncached input, output, and
cache-read counts are 100, 20, and 300. The parser emits no per-message usage
for that tool step, so those values do not reach daily usage. Reordering the
same fixture to place `step.end` before `tool.result` makes the values appear.

Separately, setting the fixture's reported model to `k2d6-agent` leaves it with
zero rates instead of resolving it to the canonical K2.6 pricing model.

## Expected behavior

- Usage is attached to the assistant model step regardless of whether
  `step.end` appears before or after its `tool.result` records.
- Multiple tool results from one step attach the step usage exactly once.
- The duplicate following `usage.record` does not double-count the same step.
- `k2d6-agent` resolves to the canonical K2.6 pricing model.
- Daily totals match the sum of one canonical usage record per model step.

## Suggested implementation

Track the assistant message flushed by `tool.result` as the pending usage
target for the current native Kimi Code step. When `step.end` arrives with no
pending assistant content, attach its model, stop reason, and normalized token
usage to that message. Let `usage.record` use the same target only as a fallback
when `step.end` did not carry usage, while retaining the existing no-double-
count guard.

Add parser regression coverage for both event orders, including multiple tool
calls/results, and add pricing coverage for the explicit `k2d6-agent` alias.

## Format provenance note

The existing Kimi Work evidence entry should be updated to record the observed
protocol-1.4 `tool.result`-before-`step.end` ordering and that `usage.record`
duplicates the native `step.end.usage` values.

title: Fix Kimi Work tool-step usage and K2.6 pricing
body:
Fixes #1337.

Kimi Code protocol 1.4 tool steps can persist tool results before the trailing step-end usage record. Preserve the flushed assistant tool-call message as the usage target so step-end or usage.record fallback populates token data exactly once.

Also canonicalize Kimi Work's explicit k2d6-agent model alias to the existing K2.6 pricing row across SQLite, PostgreSQL, and DuckDB, and bump the parser data version so existing sessions are repaired on resync.

Review focus: the post-tool-result state transition in internal/parser/kimi.go and DuckDB SQL parity for fixed aliases.

title: docs: publish the 0.40.0 release documentation
body:
The 0.40.0 release adds the Data workspace, Recall corpus browser, reporting exports, machine-labeled sources, new providers, and chart palettes, so the public documentation now reflects those released surfaces and their operational boundaries. Artifact folder transport is explicitly presented as an early manual, trusted-folder workflow rather than a complete synchronization service.

The release pages, configuration guides, contributor acknowledgements, and generated captures now follow the shipped source. The screenshot reducer remains compatible with pre-0.40 archives, and the generated-assets branch carries the new Data, Recall, palette, and refreshed machine-label images.

Exercising the PostgreSQL capture exposed a startup failure on affected PostgreSQL minors when the automation audit sliced compressed multibyte text. The audit now takes explicit UTF-8 byte prefixes, matching its classifier contract and avoiding the server bug without requiring operators to upgrade PostgreSQL first. Reviewers should focus on `docs/changelog.md`, `docs/artifact-sync.md`, the screenshot scenarios, and `internal/postgres/automated_audit.go`.

title: feat(parser): add Goose session support
body:
Adds support for [Goose](https://goose-docs.ai/): local Goose sessions now appear in AgentsView alongside other agents. Resolves #1315.

## How it works

Goose stores all conversations in a single SQLite database (`sessions.db` with `sessions`, `messages`, and `usage_ledger` tables) rather than one file per session. The integration follows the DB-backed provider pattern:

- **Discovery** streams session metadata from the database and gives each session a virtual source path (`sessions.db#<sessionID>`). Default locations (`~/.local/share/goose/sessions/`, `%APPDATA%\Block\goose\sessions\` on Windows) are searched automatically; `GOOSE_PATH_ROOT` and `goose_dirs` override them.
- **Watching** uses bounded row cursors over the three tables, so an update only processes the newly inserted rows, not the whole database. Watermarks are captured before discovery so no rows fall between discovery and the watcher.
- **Reconciliation** (periodic) handles what cursors can't: metadata-only edits, row deletions, and cursor retreats, detected via per-session content fingerprints. Schema changes or a replaced/uninitialized database fall back to full discovery. If the database disappears, archived sessions are preserved rather than tombstoned.

## Parsing

The parser extracts visible user/assistant text, thinking markers, images, tool calls/results (paired via Goose IDs), confirmation prompts, and system notifications from `content_json`; messages hidden with `userVisible=false` are skipped. Session metadata carries the Goose title, working directory, project, model, timestamps, and native session ID, and `parent_session_id` maps to AgentsView's subagent relationship.

## Usage and cost

Token usage comes from `usage_ledger` rows, imported as request-scoped `goose-request` events so they flow through SQLite, PostgreSQL, and DuckDB reporting. Cost provenance is preserved (provider-reported vs. estimated vs. carried-forward), and rows without costs still contribute tokens. Older schemas without a ledger fall back to the accumulated counters on the session row. `session usage goose:<id>` can sync a session on demand via provider-authoritative lookup.

## Limitations

- Ledger rows can't be attributed to individual messages (Goose keeps no stable message ordinal), so usage attaches at the session level.
- Image blocks import as `[Image]` markers without payloads; unknown content block types are ignored.
- Validated against a real schema-version-15 database. Older `sessions` schemas are tolerated via optional-column fallbacks; a `messages` table missing referenced columns fails discovery with a clear error rather than enumerating sessions that can never parse.

## Where to look

- `internal/parser/goose.go`, `goose_provider.go` — schema compatibility, extraction, discovery, watcher cursors
- `internal/sync/engine.go` — DB-backed sync, reconciliation, freshness
- `internal/db|postgres|duckdb` usage files — request-scoped reporting and pricing
- `internal/parser/goose_test.go`, `internal/sync/goose_integration_test.go` — parsing, bounded watcher work, reconciliation, tombstones

title: docs: prepare the 0.40.1 release
body:
v0.40.1 needs a narrow release boundary for two correctness fixes that landed after v0.40.0. Kimi Work protocol 1.4 can persist tool results before trailing usage, which previously left affected tool turns without usage and could price explicit `k2d6-agent` reports incorrectly. PostgreSQL servers on affected minor releases could also fail their startup audit when compressed multibyte text was sliced by the database.

This promotes those fixes from Unreleased into dated 0.40.1 notes and credits their contributors. Internal CI path filters and documentation-only changes since v0.40.0 are intentionally absent from the user-facing notes. AgentsView derives its version from the Git tag, so no checked-in binary version changes in this PR; after merge, `v0.40.1` should be tagged from `main`.

title: feat(usage): add JSON output to usage statusline
body:
`usage statusline` is the only reporting command in the `usage` group without
the shared `--format`/`--json` pair, so anything consuming it has to read the
human line. The budget example in `docs/token-usage.md` does exactly that:

```bash
today=$(agentsview usage statusline --offline --no-sync | tr -dc '0-9.')
```

That strips every non-digit, so it only works while the line happens to carry
no other digit. `--agent` is echoed into the line verbatim, so `--agent gpt-4`
already turns `$6.42 today (gpt-4)` into `6.424`, and any later change to the
format breaks it the same way. It fails by returning a plausible wrong number
rather than an error, which is the worst failure mode for a spend guard.

This registers the existing `registerFormatFlags`/`outputFormat` pair on
`statusline` and emits the same facts the human line carries, nothing more:

```json
{
  "date": "2026-08-04",
  "cost": { "microdollars": 9610000 },
  "agent": "claude"
}
```

`cost` stays a `money.Money` rather than a float of dollars, following the
type's documented role as the sole machine-readable representation of a
monetary value, so the documented threshold check becomes exact integer
arithmetic. `agent` is omitted when no filter was applied.

Two design notes, in case either should go the other way:

- The payload is deliberately unversioned, alongside the other small CLI
  payloads (`projects`, `health`, `skills list`); `usage daily` stays the
  versioned contract surface for this group.
- The key is `cost`, matching `ModelBreakdown.Cost`, rather than `totalCost`
  as in `usage daily`'s totals. Either is defensible; `cost` reads better on a
  payload that only ever carries one figure.

The same section's other scripting examples read `.totals.totalCost`, which is
also a money object, so they printed `{"microdollars": N}` into a `printf`.
They now read `.microdollars` and divide, which is the same class of fix. The
JSON *output* samples further up the guide still show pre-money floats; those
are a larger doc pass and are left alone here.

Tradeoff: this deliberately does not move budget thresholds or notifications
into the tool. The scripting recipe stays where the policy lives; it just gets
an input that cannot silently drift. The human line is untouched, so existing
prompts and tmux status lines are unaffected.

Related to #1185, which asked for a built-in guardrail; this is the smaller
composable piece of it.

Reviewers: `newUsageStatuslineCommand` in `cmd/agentsview/cli.go` for the flag
wiring, `usageStatuslineReport` in `cmd/agentsview/usage.go` for the payload
shape, and the updated budget example in `docs/token-usage.md`.

title: refactor(storage): establish canonical Bun schema and DuckDB dialect
body:
SQLite, PostgreSQL, and DuckDB previously evolved independent schema and query foundations, so parity depended on duplicated declarations and backend-specific plumbing. This first stack layer establishes one Bun model registry, guarded backend handles, and a dedicated DuckDB dialect while converging SQLite and PostgreSQL in place under their existing serialization boundaries.

Stamped schemas now validate structural, index, and trigger drift without repair; expensive row invariants remain limited to one-time convergence. Shared timestamps preserve the shipped SQLite empty sentinel and RFC3339Nano text contract, and Quack rejects direct driver arguments that would otherwise be discarded.

Direct database/sql access remains limited to lifecycle, connection-local, transport, and compatibility seams. DuckDB remains a disposable mirror, while narrowly scoped FTS and vector behavior stays adapter-specific. Stack 1 of 6.

<sup>generated by a clanker</sup>

title: refactor(storage): consolidate common store behavior through Bun
body:
The concrete stores separately implemented sessions, project identity, curation, Recall, usage, and analytics, so fixes had to be repeated and snapshot semantics could drift. This layer makes the guarded BunStore the owner of those common behaviors while leaving adapters responsible for lifecycle and genuine engine capabilities.

Composite session pages, sidebars, message hydration, and timing reads now use replay-safe consistent views. Signal and trend analytics stream transcript content in bounded batches, and the dead PostgreSQL usage renderer is removed. Shared contracts preserve filtering, ordering, hydration, reduction, and supported mutations across real SQLite, PostgreSQL, and DuckDB stores. Stack 2 of 6.

<sup>generated by a clanker</sup>

title: refactor(storage): isolate dialect search behind Bun capabilities
body:
Full-text and vector candidate retrieval legitimately differs by engine, but hydration, visibility, filtering, deduplication, and public pagination should not. This layer narrows dialect-specific search to capability adapters and moves the observable search pipeline into the shared Bun store.

DuckDB tool-content search now uses canonical session and message-ordinal identity instead of disposable physical row IDs. Timestamp ordering and portable search choices are supplied through narrow adapter hooks, while engine-specific relevance ranks remain allowed where the engines expose genuinely different semantics. Stack 3 of 6.

<sup>generated by a clanker</sup>

title: refactor(storage): route canonical writes through Bun
body:
Independent archive, PostgreSQL replication, and DuckDB mirror writers manually projected overlapping schemas, which made column ownership and transaction semantics vulnerable to drift. This layer routes canonical session, pricing, cursor, identity, and dependent writes through Bun transactions and the shared model registry.

PostgreSQL ownership serialization uses collision-resistant full-digest keys, SQLite pricing uses the canonical Bun writer and pricing contract, and usage-event snapshots order mixed-offset timestamps chronologically. Operational synchronization metadata and backend lifecycle remain adapter-owned. Stack 4 of 6.

<sup>generated by a clanker</sup>

title: refactor(storage): complete unified Bun storage cutover
body:
Shared reads and writes still left a legacy query renderer, concrete adapter shadows, and several identity, vector, unit-range, and usage paths outside the Bun ownership boundary. This fifth layer removes those alternate paths and completes the shared Bun storage cutover.

Bun owns the common schema and public store behavior. Dialect-specific SQL remains allowed behind the documented closed seams for lifecycle, schema convergence, synchronization metadata, timestamp ordering, capability probes, FTS, and vectors. Observable usage dollar values remain unchanged under the cross-backend pricing and usage contracts, providing contract-verified dollar parity rather than relying on a one-off output comparison. Stack 5 of 6.

title: feat(parser): add TraeX (TRAE CLI 2.0) as a first-class agent
body:
TRAE CLI 2.0 (`traex`) is a closed-source fork of codex-rs. It writes rollout
JSONL that is field-for-field the Codex shape into `~/.trae/cli/sessions`,
including the subagent `session_meta`, `token_count` records, and a sibling
`history.jsonl` at the same position relative to the sessions root. Until now
the only way to index it was to declare that root as a `codex` source, which
gives the sessions the wrong agent and an ID prefix whose one-click resume
command (`codex resume <id>`) cannot resume them.

This adds `traex` as its own agent, served by the Codex provider through a
relabel hook — the same shape `opencode_provider.go` already uses to serve
Kilo, MiMoCode, and Icodemate from one implementation. Parsing, discovery,
fingerprinting, and JSONL-tail incremental appends are shared; only the agent
label and the `traex:` ID prefix differ. `internal/parser/traex.go` is the
whole fork-specific surface and is the first place to look.

The relabel covers more than Kilo's does. Besides the session ID, parent, and
source-session ID, the Codex parser stamps `codex:` onto the
`SubagentSessionID` of tool calls and their result events, so a partial
relabel would leave a TraeX parent pointing at `codex:<uuid>` rows the
`traex:` namespace never stores. The provider's incremental path returns
appended messages with no session, so the hook takes `(*ParsedSession,
[]ParsedMessage)` and treats a nil session as that path.

Discovery keys are now agent-scoped (`CodexSourceKey` takes an agent). Both
agents name files by UUID, so a shared key would let one agent's session
resolve to the other's file.

In `internal/sync`, the branches that describe the *format* — same-UUID
duplicate resolution, dated-over-flat layout preference, reconciliation
identity, the incremental `file_mtime` basis, and the parse-diff raced guard —
move behind a new `isCodexFormatAgent` predicate. The branches that describe
Codex's *out-of-band files* stay keyed to `parser.AgentCodex` alone, because
TraeX writes neither: there is no `session_index.jsonl` sidecar (so no title
backfill, no index-driven cache invalidation, and no index watch or changed-path
fan-out), and no `s3://.../raw/codex/...` archive convention, so a `traex` root
that looks like an S3 URI is skipped rather than imported under Codex's
identity. That split is the main thing worth reviewing.

Two consequences of having no index file are worth stating. Titles come from
the rollout head only, so a TraeX session never picks up a renamed thread name.
And `~/.trae/cli` is not watched shallowly, unlike `~/.codex`, since the only
reason to watch it would be the index file and the directory otherwise holds
constantly-rewritten SQLite WALs.

Evidence for the format is observational and documented as `no-public-source`
in the format inventory: TRAE CLI ships only as a binary, and neither Trae's
product site nor the public `Trae-AI/Trae` repository publishes a session
schema. A de-identified rollout with subagent spawn/wait records is kept as a
fixture.

Switching an existing installation from the `codex`-source workaround to
`agent = "traex"` is not handled: the stored rows are keyed by file path, so
the old `codex:<uuid>` rows would satisfy the freshness skips and the new rows
would never be written. A full resync into a fresh database is the intended
path.

title: embeddings build treats HTTP 429 as fatal instead of backing off, stranding a large build
body:
`embeddings build` aborts the entire run when the embedding endpoint returns HTTP 429, rather than backing off and continuing.

```
Embedded 28085 documents (29056 chunks), skipped 0, stale 0
fatal: encode batch at 0: [vector.embeddings] status 429: {"detail":"You have
exceeded the project's Tokens Per Minute (TPM) rate limit of 3,000,000 tokens
per minute for voyage-4-large. In the minute before this request, you used
2,982,224 tokens. See our documentation for ways to avoid or increase the
project rate limits on the dashboard."}
```

That was 28,085 of 142,161 documents on a first full build over an existing archive.

Progress is durable, so re-running resumes where it stopped — but a large first build then needs an external retry loop wrapped around the command, and each attempt simply runs until it saturates the quota and dies again.

429 is the one error a provider tells you exactly how to handle: Voyage documents the cap and reports how much of it was consumed. Backing off and retrying, or pacing requests to stay under the ceiling, seems strictly better than aborting the run — especially because a first-time build over a large archive is precisely the case that will hit it.

This looks like the same shape as #1272: a recoverable per-batch condition ending the whole build instead of being handled and carried past.

## Environment

- v0.40.1 (commit 9ef48912)
- Provider: Voyage, `voyage-4-large` at 1024 dimensions
- Store: `messages`, first full build of ~142k documents

## Workaround

Setting `concurrency = 2` on the server block slows how quickly the ceiling is reached, but does not remove the failure — it only makes it take longer to arrive.

title: feat(parser): add Prime Agent session support
body:
Prime Agent sessions now appear in AgentsView as Prime Agent sessions. AgentsView finds them in Prime Agent’s session folder, reads their messages, model, times, and token use, and shows Prime Agent in settings and filters.

Prime Agent can add child-agent token use to an earlier assistant message after it first writes the transcript. AgentsView now picks up those later changes during a full sync and updates the stored messages, token totals, and cost.

AgentsView checks a saved transcript path before it uses that path for a session lookup. If the file now belongs to a different session, AgentsView finds the transcript whose header has the requested session ID. It also stores sessions with parentSession as forks, so top-level reports do not count the same session lineage twice.

I installed Prime Agent v0.7.0, signed in with Codex, ran a real prompt, and parsed the saved transcript. The result had the correct provider, model, messages, times, token use, and cost.

This support is based on the flat file layout used by Prime Agent v0.7.0. A future Prime Agent format change might need a parser update. The included data migration repairs old Pi-family cache-write token totals in existing AgentsView archives.

The main areas to review are Prime Agent session discovery, session lookup, parent and fork links, child-agent token accounting, archive updates after a later sync, and the Prime Agent name and settings in the frontend.

title: fix(opencode): keep the session container off the recursive watch budget
body:
OpenCode's SQLite container, its WAL, and its storage archive share one recursive watch unit over the configured root, so the live container draws on the same shared recursive budget as the archive. A root reached after that budget is spent registers no native watch at all, and exhaustion inside the root's own walk marks the container's coverage degraded along with the archive's.

This separates each OpenCode-family root into a shallow container unit covering the database and its WAL and a recursive unit at `<root>/storage`. A shallow watch never draws on the recursive budget, so the container's coverage no longer depends on the archive's size. The split applies only where it is representable: a root with no storage directory keeps the single recursive unit, because naming an absent watch root would plan a polling obligation probed on a path that may never appear, and a probe that cannot be satisfied defers every other obligation on the same configured dir. A symlinked root also keeps it, since the daemon refuses to watch a recursive root through a symlink and gates the configured dir's reconciliation on the link target instead.

A native watch shared by overlapping roots is now charged to the shared budget once. `RecursiveWatchResult.Watched` still counts the directories a root covers; `Allocated` counts the watches a registration installed, and registration subtracts that. Reuse is settled before the budget check, so a root whose directories are already watched registers cleanly against an exhausted budget and records its ownership, and reclaiming a shared watch returns one budget slot rather than one per root that walked it.

Two units share one configured root and the engine dispatches every changed path once per emitted watch root, so `unitScopeAllows` scopes classification to the units of the root that owns the path; without it a WAL write would run the shared container's whole session listing twice. Configured roots can nest, so the deepest one containing the path owns it, and a virtual member path resolves to its physical container before the check. The container unit still claims storage paths: whether the storage unit exists is a filesystem fact, while the engine resolves each provider's watch roots once and reuses that set, so deferring would leave a storage tree created afterwards claimed by nothing. That costs one repeated source lookup per storage event, which the engine's per-pass source set discards; the database fan-out cannot double, because a storage watch root never contains the database or its WAL.

This PR stands alone and supersedes PR #1318, whose conditional storage-unit split covered the same provider topology. Portable lifecycle ownership of a missing watch root is not attempted here. The bounded parser feed that motivated PR #1331 is abandoned rather than shipped: OpenCode exposes no producer-owned cross-drain journal cursor, so that work was closed and this slice is the salvage.

Refs #1208

title: embeddings build can construct a batch that exceeds the provider's per-request token cap, then retries it unchanged forever
body:
Batch composition counts documents, but the provider caps a request by *tokens*. Because each input is truncated to the model context, the worst case for a batch is `batch_size × model_context`, which can exceed the per-request cap. When it does, the same batch is rebuilt identically on every retry, so the build cannot advance past it.

Distinct from #1353: that one is about a 429 (a rate limit that clears with time). This is a 400 that never clears, because nothing about the request changes between attempts.

## What happened

Backfilling ~142k documents with `voyage-4-large` @ 1024. Voyage caps a single request at 120,000 tokens and truncates each input to the model context (32,000 tokens).

Three runs, three different `batch_size` values, same failure:

```
# batch_size unset (default)
status 400: The max allowed tokens per submitted batch is 120000.
Your batch has 147910 tokens after truncation.  TOO_MANY_TOKENS_IN_BATCH

# batch_size = 16
Your batch has 121625 tokens after truncation.

# batch_size = 4
Your batch has 128000 tokens after truncation.
```

The third is the tell: **128,000 is exactly 4 × 32,000.** A batch of four inputs, each truncated to the model context, lands precisely on the theoretical maximum — and 8,000 tokens over the cap.

So the safe bound is arithmetic, not tuning: the largest `batch_size` that *cannot* exceed 120,000 with a 32,000-token context is **3** (96,000). Anything above that can fail depending on the documents that happen to land together, which makes it look intermittent and content-dependent while actually being deterministic per batch.

## Why it strands the build

Batch composition is deterministic, so a rejected batch is rebuilt identically next time. The scheduler burns its retries on a request that cannot succeed and stops:

```
embed scheduler: build failed: encode document ...: status 400 ... TOO_MANY_TOKENS_IN_BATCH
embed scheduler: retry limit reached; deferring until new work
```

`deferring until new work` is the part that hurts on a backfill: there is no new work coming, so progress simply halts with a large `missing` count and no indication that it is permanent rather than slow. Combined with #1353, a long build has two independent ways to stop early and look merely slow.

## Suggested fix

Bound batch construction by an estimated token budget rather than a document count — cap at `min(batch_size, floor(request_cap / model_context))`, or accumulate estimated tokens and cut the batch when the next input would cross the cap.

Failing that, treat `TOO_MANY_TOKENS_IN_BATCH` as retryable-with-adjustment: on a 400 of this shape, halve the batch and retry rather than replaying the identical request. Splitting is always possible here, since a single input is already bounded by the model context.

A validation-time warning would also have saved the whole investigation: if `batch_size × model_context > request_cap`, say so at config load, when the answer is cheap.

## Workaround

`batch_size = 3` in the server block. The extra round trips cost nothing in practice, because on a large build the per-minute token budget is the real throughput gate, not request count.

--- ### Mermaid configuration APIs allow prototype pollution [CVE-2026-71438](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-71438) / [GHSA-c4c3-pg64-4m4v](https://redirect.github.com/advisories/GHSA-c4c3-pg64-4m4v)
More information #### Details ##### Summary Mermaid's configuration setters (`mermaid.initialize`, `mermaidAPI.setConfig`, and `mermaidAPI.updateSiteConfig`) merge the caller-supplied configuration object into Mermaid's internal config using the `assignWithDepth` deep-merge helper that is vulnerable to prototype pollution. Because these APIs are intended to receive **trusted** configuration supplied by the application integrating Mermaid, Mermaid assesses the practical risk as **low**. The vulnerability is only reachable if an application forwards attacker-controlled data directly into one of these configuration entry points, which is outside their documented usage. User-controlled configuration (e.g. configuration in diagram code using `%%{init: {}}%%` or YAML frontmatter) are already protected from prototype pollution. ##### Patches This has been patched in https://github.com/mermaid-js/mermaid/commit/2cd6dcf735533b323507e3e889ffdea870540b43 and released in [Mermaid v11.16.1](https://redirect.github.com/mermaid-js/mermaid/releases/tag/mermaid%4011.16.1). title: fix(deps): update dependency dompurify to v3.4.13 [security]
body:
This PR contains the following updates: | Package | Change | [Age](https://docs.renovatebot.com/merge-confidence/) | [Confidence](https://docs.renovatebot.com/merge-confidence/) | |---|---|---|---| | [dompurify](https://redirect.github.com/cure53/DOMPurify) | [`3.4.12` → `3.4.13`](https://renovatebot.com/diffs/npm/dompurify/3.4.12/3.4.13) | ![age](https://developer.mend.io/api/mc/badges/age/npm/dompurify/3.4.13?slim=true) | ![confidence](https://developer.mend.io/api/mc/badges/confidence/npm/dompurify/3.4.12/3.4.13?slim=true) | --- ### DOMPurify: IN_PLACE hook removal leaves a detached subtree executable, causing XSS [GHSA-55q2-fjhq-7xh7](https://redirect.github.com/advisories/GHSA-55q2-fjhq-7xh7)
More information #### Details ##### Summary During `IN_PLACE` sanitization, a hook that removes an element can leave that element's detached descendants executable. A descendant image can retain its attacker-provided `onload` handler and fire after `sanitize()` returns, even though the returned root is clean and the image remains disconnected from the document. ##### Details In DOMPurify 3.4.12, `_sanitizeElements()` in `src/purify.ts:1862-1904` runs the `beforeSanitizeElements` or `uponSanitizeElement` hook and returns immediately when the hook detached the current node. The return does not call `_neutralizeSubtree(currentNode)`. The detached subtree is not added to `DOMPurify.removed`, so the post-walk `IN_PLACE` neutralization cannot reach it. If the browser queued a resource event while the application constructed the detached dirty root, a descendant can therefore retain its handler and execute after sanitization. The hook only rejects the containing element and does not add or approve the event handler. DOMPurify's ordinary removal path de-arms the same queued event; only the hook-detachment early return skips the existing subtree neutralization. ##### PoC Load the published `dompurify@3.4.12` `dist/purify.js` before this script in Chromium: ```html
not fired
``` `sanitize()` returns with no handler execution and the returned root contains only the safe `div`. After the event loop advances, the original image remains disconnected but its retained `onload` changes the page to `XSS after sanitize`. As the claim-matched control, use the same detached input with `ALLOWED_TAGS: ['div', '#text']` and no hook. DOMPurify's ordinary removal path removes the original image's handler, the returned root is still `
safe
`, and the marker does not fire. ##### Impact In an application that uses `IN_PLACE` with the documented element-removal hook pattern, an attacker who can supply HTML can execute JavaScript in the integrating application's origin after the application sanitizes and renders that content. The required non-default configuration is `IN_PLACE` plus a hook that removes a containing element. The hook does not add or approve the event handler, and the dirty root never needs to be connected before sanitization. ##### Suggested fix Reuse the existing `_neutralizeSubtree(currentNode)` helper before returning from both hook-detachment branches in `_sanitizeElements()`. Add regressions for `beforeSanitizeElements` and `uponSanitizeElement` that retain a reference to a descendant resource element and verify that its event handler is removed after the hook detaches its ancestor. #### Severity - CVSS Score: 5.1 / 10 (Medium) - Vector String: `CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:N/PR:L/UI:P/VC:N/VI:N/VA:N/SC:L/SI:L/SA:N` #### References - [https://github.com/cure53/DOMPurify/security/advisories/GHSA-55q2-fjhq-7xh7](https://redirect.github.com/cure53/DOMPurify/security/advisories/GHSA-55q2-fjhq-7xh7) - [https://github.com/cure53/DOMPurify/pull/1557](https://redirect.github.com/cure53/DOMPurify/pull/1557) - [https://github.com/cure53/DOMPurify/commit/3067f7746769](https://redirect.github.com/cure53/DOMPurify/commit/3067f7746769) - [https://github.com/cure53/DOMPurify](https://redirect.github.com/cure53/DOMPurify) - [https://github.com/cure53/DOMPurify/releases/tag/3.4.13](https://redirect.github.com/cure53/DOMPurify/releases/tag/3.4.13) This data is provided by [OSV](https://osv.dev/vulnerability/GHSA-55q2-fjhq-7xh7) and the [GitHub Advisory Database](https://redirect.github.com/github/advisory-database) ([CC-BY 4.0](https://redirect.github.com/github/advisory-database/blob/main/LICENSE.md)).

title: feat(recall): manage extraction generations
body:
Recall already showed extraction status, but operators still had to leave the browser to promote a completed generation, recover a retired configured generation, or retire an abandoned build. This PR closes that operational gap without exposing model execution or unsafe force controls.

- Adds confirmed **Activate** actions for the configured generation whenever it is not active, including recovery after a configuration revert.
- Allows **Retire** only for non-current building generations; the active corpus cannot be force-retired through the UI.
- Serializes lifecycle changes against extraction passes and returns actionable conflicts instead of racing corpus updates.
- Reports maintenance windows as retryable HTTP 503 responses with `Retry-After`.
- Refreshes semantic indexing after the served Recall corpus changes.
- Capability-gates and localizes the controls across supported languages.

Practical result: operators can inspect extraction state and safely maintain the served Recall corpus from one page. Starting extraction and force retirement remain intentionally outside this surface.

Review focus: lifecycle safety in `internal/recall/extract/manager.go`, HTTP behavior in `internal/server/recall.go`, and action visibility and confirmation in `frontend/src/lib/components/recall/RecallPage.svelte`.

title: Complete Bun writes and bound fresh-sync memory
body:
Archive sync and repairs now keep Bun execution and transaction guards through full-session writes, incremental updates, attached scratch publication, usage caches, and PostgreSQL metadata operations. A staged import commits its session, tool results, usage, signals, and parser checkpoint together. SQLite-only result identity metadata survives replacements without entering portable mirror schemas.

Usage queries stream ordered rows into Go aggregation instead of retaining the complete input. Token interpretation, pricing, snapshot selection, and billing remain in Go. Shared queries retain date overlap and Unicode search behavior across backends. SQLite string formatting preserves internal raw-byte identities and copies text between quotes without rune-by-rune conversion.

Fresh-sync writes use a 1 MiB estimated payload per statement while preserving transaction boundaries and whole oversized rows. This limits transient formatted SQL buffers. The local corpus comparison and remaining allocation tradeoff are recorded in docs/internal/bun-usage-performance.md; external BenchDB measurements remain the acceptance check for its distinct machine and corpus.

The combined stack preserves upstream reasoning effort, archive-content policies, image offloading, installation identity adoption, CJK full-text search, schema-4 joint reporting, activity categories, and Codex streaming and checkpoint behavior and advances archive data version to 109. Review the shared session-batch transaction, scratch publication, canonical result metadata, and SQLite literal formatter. Existing archives retain the rebuild and recovery procedure in docs/internal/storage-upgrade.md.

DuckDB pushes share a per-mirror process lock through probing, checkpointing, and replacement, preventing a concurrent push from leaving an old WAL for the rebuilt mirror. Session upserts reuse cached archive-column metadata throughout the write path.

CJK index checks and tokenization use the search transaction, avoiding a second reader connection or nested archive lock while reopen is waiting.

title: test(parser): shorten posit-assistant fixture paths for Windows
body:
The posit-assistant testdata tree used full-length placeholder IDs: a 24-character workspace hash and 36-character UUIDs for the main conversation, its subagent, and the default-workspace conversation. The deepest fixture file sat 178 characters below the repository root. When the repository is checked out as a submodule under a deep CI workspace prefix on Windows, the absolute path exceeded the 260-character MAX_PATH limit and broke the clone.

The fixture directories now use truncated IDs (a1b2c3d4, 11111111, 22222222, 33333333), capping the deepest path at 106 characters. The matching ID references inside conversation.json, index.json, and the test constants are updated in step. The parser's IsValidSessionID only requires alphanumeric, dash, or underscore names, so discovery, find-by-ID, changed-path classification, and parent-linkage behavior are unchanged; a comment on the test constants records why the IDs are short so they are not restored to full UUIDs later.

Reviewers should look at the constants and comment at the top of internal/parser/posit_assistant_provider_test.go and the renamed tree under internal/parser/testdata/posit-assistant/workspaces/. The tradeoff is that fixture names are no longer format-realistic UUIDs; the parser does not validate UUID shape, so no covered behavior depends on it. The grok-build fixtures are now the longest paths in the repository at 144 characters relative and remain untouched here.

title: feat(amp): record per-inference token usage and model
body:
Amp thread exports include per-inference usage and timestamps, but AgentsView previously ignored them. Exported Amp sessions now show model-specific token use, cost, and accurate daily attribution.

- Records each inference’s model, timestamp, input/output tokens, and cache buckets.
- Preserves Anthropic-family semantics and treats OpenAI-family cache-creation tokens as uncached input to avoid inflated cost.
- Reprocesses existing Amp sessions with data version 84 and documents the format evidence.

This reads complete thread documents already on disk; it does not fetch server-side threads. Amp exports also omit subagent usage, so those tokens remain unavailable.

Review focus: `internal/parser/amp.go`, `internal/parser/amp_provider.go`, and the Amp fixtures in `internal/parser/amp_test.go`.

title: fix(sync): stop probing macOS protected folders during discovery
body:
Closes #1364.

## Problem

On first open, the macOS app asked for access to Documents, Downloads, and Dropbox. The app requests no special entitlements — the prompts came from background sync reading files inside those folders:

- Every session's recorded working directory gets probed for git info (repo root, remote, branch).
- The first sync probes every session in the archive at once.
- macOS shows one consent prompt per protected folder that any session ever ran in.

## Fix

- New path classifier decides, before touching anything: **safe**, **protected** (Documents, Downloads, Desktop, Movies, Music, Pictures, iCloud Drive, cloud folders like Dropbox), or **automount** (`/home`, `/net`).
- Protected paths are not probed. Sessions there are still ingested, listed, and searchable — they just show a path-based name with no git remote, worktree, or branch info.
- Every probe checks the classifier first: git-root walks, gitfile targets, metadata files (`HEAD`, `config`, `commondir`), deleted-session recovery, and stored snapshot roots.
- The classifier follows symlinks and `..` in real traversal order, folds case, and recognizes the `/System/Volumes/Data` firmlink spelling — without itself entering protected folders or waking automountd.
- Custom autofs mounts from the host's mount table (e.g. `/corp/home`) count as automount too.
- Passive discovery never runs the `git` binary: git follows config-derived paths (`[include] path`) that no vetting can constrain. All git-layout resolution is filesystem-local; rare layouts only git could resolve now get path-based names.

## Opting back in

- Set `scan_protected_paths = true` in `config.toml` to restore full git info for code kept in protected folders. macOS prompts once per folder.
- The opt-in never allows automount probing (that would cause CPU churn, not a prompt).
- Applies to sessions parsed after the change; run `agentsview sync --full` to refresh existing ones.

## Known limits

- The protected-folder list is fixed; a cloud app that mounts a folder directly in `$HOME` (outside `~/Library/CloudStorage`) would still prompt.
- An old-style real `~/Dropbox` folder (not cloud-mounted) loses git info it didn't have to; the opt-in restores it.

## Where to look

- `internal/export/project_identity.go` — the classifier
- `internal/sync/engine.go` — identity capture gates
- `internal/parser/project.go` — project-name extraction gates

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

title: feat(recall): organize generated insights and quality
body:
- Recall now groups durable corpus entries and saved model-written reports under one URL-backed workspace, so users no longer have to infer how two kinds of reusable context relate.
- Generated insights expose their complete session scope before execution, preserve that scope across tab changes, and retain deep links plus export, publish, retry, and delete workflows.
- Deterministic recommendations and evidence move to Quality, making the model-written versus measured-data boundary explicit; the former `/insights` route is a clean break and falls through to Sessions.
- Read-only backends keep access to saved generated reports while hiding the unsupported corpus, and the public docs now describe both surfaces and their privacy boundary.

title: fix(frontend): keep root sessions landing unfiltered
body:
A bare local visit should show the unfiltered Sessions landing page, but the remembered filter state was being applied immediately and could be written back during refresh or session-detail navigation. That made the root URL surprising and risked erasing the user’s saved Sessions preference.

This change treats the root path as an unfiltered landing state while preserving the saved preference. Explicit filter URLs remain authoritative, direct or provenance-preserving navigation to bare /sessions can restore the remembered view, and opening a session from the root does not overwrite the preference when the detail view refreshes or closes. The task-specific design artifacts have also been removed now that the behavior is implemented.

The full frontend suite passes in serialized single-worker mode. The default parallel runner is resource-sensitive in this environment and previously timed out in an unrelated Playwright-config test; that focused test passes independently.

title: feat(recall): review extracted entries from the corpus
body:
Machine-extracted Recall entries can now be approved or archived from their expanded Corpus row. Approval requires valid provenance and marks an entry human-reviewed. Archive asks for confirmation, marks it human-rejected, and removes it from the served corpus. Extraction generation changes preserve both decisions.

Review actions use guarded transactions and return conflicts for stale or repeated decisions. Local row updates preserve pagination and scroll position. This change excludes editing, bulk review, and undo.

Writable archives remove the old review-state constraint when present and convert legacy Recall search indexes to FTS5, preserving entries, evidence, and row identities. Index conversion also runs when the entry schema is already current. Existing FTS5 indexes are retained. Read-only archives use the existing text fallback when legacy indexes cannot run ranked entry search; read-only backends continue to reject mutations.

Review focus: archive migration and review transactions in `internal/db`, HTTP error mapping in `internal/server/huma_routes_recall.go`, and row updates in `RecallCorpusPanel.svelte`.

title: Zed threads.db without parent_id fails the entire sync pass
body:
### agentsview version

agentsview v0.40.1 (commit 9ef48912, built 2026-08-04T11:33:50Z)

### Install method

Other / not sure: `uv tool install agentsview`

### OS / platform

openSUSE Tumbleweed 20250809 (x86_64)

### Which agent and version

Zed 1.14.2, with a `threads.db` retained from an older Zed installation. The problem also reproduces with the synthetic five-column database below.

### Which model(s)

n/a

### What happened, and what did you expect

A Zed `threads/threads.db` whose `threads` table predates the `parent_id` column makes the entire AgentsView sync pass fail:

```text
sync error: listing zed thread metas: no such column: parent_id
```

The sync worker reports one failed session and exits nonzero, even when the legacy database is empty:

```json
{"result":{"status":"failed","synced":0,"skipped":0,"failed":1,"discoveryComplete":true,"stats":{"total_sessions":1,"synced":0,"skipped":0,"failed":1}}}
```

This also makes daemon startup report an incomplete initial sync and retry it periodically. Other provider sessions may be processed, but the pass is never authoritative.

I expected an empty or legacy Zed database not to fail the whole cross-provider sync. AgentsView could either read compatible legacy columns using defaults or skip an unsupported empty database with a useful diagnostic. The documentation does not appear to specify a minimum Zed schema or version.

The current parser queries `parent_id` unconditionally. The integration fixture only covers the modern schema containing `parent_id`, `folder_paths`, `folder_paths_order`, and `created_at`.

Related history: #610 introduced Zed support and #884 migrated the SQLite/container providers. I found no issue or open PR covering legacy Zed schemas or this exact error.

A local workaround is to back up the database and apply Zed's additive schema migrations, but AgentsView should not require users to modify an agent-owned database.

### Sample session file or snippet

This empty SQLite schema is sufficient to reproduce the problem; no session content is needed:

```sql
CREATE TABLE threads (
  id TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
  summary TEXT NOT NULL,
  updated_at TEXT NOT NULL,
  data_type TEXT NOT NULL,
  data BLOB NOT NULL
);
```

### Steps to reproduce

```sh
workdir="$PWD/agentsview-zed-legacy-repro"
mkdir -p \
  "$workdir/user/.local/share/zed/threads" \
  "$workdir/user/.config" \
  "$workdir/data" \
  "$workdir/tmp"

sqlite3 "$workdir/user/.local/share/zed/threads/threads.db" <<'SQL'
CREATE TABLE threads (
  id TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
  summary TEXT NOT NULL,
  updated_at TEXT NOT NULL,
  data_type TEXT NOT NULL,
  data BLOB NOT NULL
);
SQL

HOME="$workdir/user" \
XDG_DATA_HOME="$workdir/user/.local/share" \
XDG_CONFIG_HOME="$workdir/user/.config" \
AGENTSVIEW_DATA_DIR="$workdir/data" \
ZED_DIR="$workdir/user/.local/share/zed" \
TMPDIR="$workdir/tmp" \
agentsview sync-worker --mode=sync
```

The command exits 1. `$workdir/data/debug.log` contains:

```text
discovered 1 files (... 1 zed ...) in 1ms
sync error: listing zed thread metas: no such column: parent_id
```

title: feat: add proactive cross-chat issue review

Adds a local-first Issue Review workflow for recurring failures, blockers, slow tools, repeated work, and remediation opportunities across scoped sessions. title: fix(parser): trim replayed prefix of backgrounded Claude sessions
body:
Fixes #1370.

Backgrounding a Claude Code session (left-arrow picker, Ctrl+B, `/background`) copies the whole conversation into a new transcript with a new session id and no back-reference. agentsview ingested both files as unrelated sessions: the conversation showed up twice in the sidebar and its usage was counted twice.

Verified against controlled reproductions and the Claude Code 2.1.226 bundle: copied lines are byte-identical except a rewritten `sessionId` and an injected `sessionKind:"bg"`; only uuid-bearing chain entries are replayed; the marker is process-derived, so ordinary interactive forks carry none.

## Fix (`internal/parser/claude_lineage.go`)

- A bg-marked transcript finds the same-directory sibling that shares its root uuid and covers the longest prefix — its nearest ancestor — drops that replayed prefix, and links to it as a `continuation` (nested in the sidebar).
- Chains trim link by link. A candidate that strictly contains the fork is its descendant and never wins; exact-equal twins pick a deterministic direction by stem.
- A fork with no content of its own is excluded; a prompt queued at handoff counts as content.
- Everything ambiguous fails open (no trim, no link): unmarked manual forks, missing or divergent siblings, branches at the replay boundary. Worst case is the status-quo duplicate.
- Data version 83 re-parses existing archives to repair old duplicates.

## Limits

- Root-to-root matching only: sessions compacted before backgrounding stay duplicated for now.
- Lineage reads on-disk state at parse time; a sibling appearing after a fork was stored is picked up at the next resync.
- Only the local Claude provider participates; uploads, Cowork, Qoder, subagents, and s3 sources are untouched.

title: Reduce idle CPU and let users turn off unused providers
body:
agentsview now keeps normal watch-triggered PostgreSQL pushes limited to the
sessions and roots that changed. Watcher and timer triggers enter one serialized
work queue, so a periodic catch-up scan cannot be replaced by pending scoped
work. Lost or ambiguous watcher events still expand to validated recovery scope,
and interval recovery still performs full discovery so unwatched changes cannot
remain stale.

Settings lists every local session provider and lets users disable filesystem
sources they do not use. The selection is applied when local sync engines,
watchers, polling, and activity scanning start, so those processes must restart
after a change. It does not affect HTTP or SSH remote imports or any export
path. Existing archived sessions remain searchable and exportable. During
archive rebuilds, shared provider identities such as Codebuff and Freebuff are
protected together. RemoteSyncExcluded remains the separate remote-export
safety boundary.

HTTP remote sync rejects missing or mismatched protocol versions before targets
or archive data are exchanged. Directory-scoped and safe curated exports use
manifest-based delta transfer; sanitized exports retain their explicit
full-archive path.

Daemon push requests can use only paths under startup-configured provider and
watch roots. Network and device paths are rejected before filesystem access.
Server-backed settings mutations run through one first-in, first-out queue so
older full responses cannot replace newer settings state. Failed saves appear
in a shared danger flash, while provider toggles also restore the previous
confirmed selection.

Gemini no longer loads project metadata when no Gemini sessions exist.

title: Feature request: official compaction/compression story for large sessions.db (tool results dominate)
body:
### Problem / motivation

`sessions.db` grows linearly with tool-result content and there is currently no non-destructive official way to reclaim space:

- On a normal Codex-heavy machine: 888 sessions / 534k messages / ~396k tool calls produce a ~7.0 GiB `sessions.db`.
- The largest consumers are `tool_calls.result_content` (~3.07 GB) and `tool_result_events.content` (~3.04 GB). These store the same output twice for the same call.
- Bash output alone is ~2.4 GB; `view_image` results add ~0.58 GB of base64 image payloads.
- `result_content_blocked_categories` only controls future ingestion; it does not shrink an existing archive.
- `agentsview prune` deletes the original JSONL session files as well as DB rows, and it does not `VACUUM` the SQLite file, so the on-disk DB may stay large even after pruning. (There is an internal `db.Vacuum()` helper but no exposed command.)
- SQLite files do not shrink by themselves after DELETEs.

### Proposed solution

A first-class storage-maintenance story that does not require deleting source transcripts:

1. `agentsview db compact` (or similar) that VACUUMs / rebuilds the archive and reports before/after sizes.
2. A non-destructive rebuild path that re-parses source JSONL and applies `result_content_blocked_categories` to existing sessions (`agentsview sync --full` already rebuilds; it would be helpful for that path to be the documented way to reclaim space).
3. Consider storing tool results once instead of duplicating the same content in `tool_calls.result_content` and `tool_result_events.content`.
4. Optionally support transparent compression for the large text columns (for example zstd), or at least leave a documented extension point for ZIPVFS/sqlite-zstd-style VFS/row compression.

### Alternatives considered

- `result_content_blocked_categories = ["Bash"]` plus `agentsview sync --full`: works for new/rebuildable data, but requires understanding that a full resync is the only retroactive path.
- `agentsview prune --before ...` + manual `VACUUM`: works, but deletes source JSONL files and is not discoverable as a size-reclaim flow.
- Using ZIPVFS (commercial) or sqlite-zstd externally: not currently integrated and would need official support to be safe with the daemon/writer model.

title: fix(vector): recover invalid Ollama embeddings on CPU
body:
Repeated Ollama Metal embedding requests can return zero-norm or non-finite vectors even when prompt caching and slot reuse are disabled. Keeping embeddings permanently on CPU avoids the corruption but is too slow for normal indexing.

This adds an explicit per-server `ollama_cpu_fallback` recovery path. Metal remains primary and receives the configured retries; after the final invalid response, AgentsView preserves valid vectors, sends only invalid inputs through Ollama native `/api/embed` route with `num_gpu = 0` and immediate unload, strictly validates the result, and gates matching fallback-enabled encoders during the runner transition. Gate waits honor cancellation, and URL derivation preserves escaped proxy paths and query parameters.

The option is disabled by default, requires an Ollama endpoint ending in `/v1`, and is transport-only, so enabling it neither changes the generation fingerprint nor rebuilds the index. Coordination is process-local and keyed by the exact derived native URL; aliases, mixed opt-ins, and external Ollama clients remain outside that boundary.

title: fix(parser): exclude replayed Codex subagent usage
body:
Codex subagent rollouts can begin with a re-stamped copy of the parent transcript, including historical `token_count` events. Agentsview treated that copied prefix as fresh child work, which duplicated cost and attributed old usage to the child creation hour.

This change extends the existing Codex fork replay gate to subagents only after the copied parent `session_meta` positively identifies a replay prefix. It drops parent turns until the first child-owned UUIDv7 `turn_id`. Direct child-only transcripts remain unchanged. Incremental parsing preserves an active replay boundary across offsets and requests an authoritative replacement of the current child when copied metadata first appears after a saved offset; the parent remains untouched.
