title: A single incremental sync makes the embedding refresh read about 900 MB of the archive, even when only a few hundred messages changed
body:
### agentsview version

`main` at d0395b50 (v0.42.0 plus two docs commits); the same code is in v0.41.1.

### Install method

Built from source

### OS / platform

Linux x86_64 (Debian-based), 31 GB RAM

### Which agent and version

Not agent-specific; observed with a mixed Claude Code / Codex archive of 1,637 sessions (12.7 GB `sessions.db`, 1.2 GB `vectors.db`)

### Which model(s)

Not applicable

### What happened, and what did you expect

## Scope

This is one of three independent causes behind a daemon whose memory footprint tracks the archive size instead of the change rate; the other two are filed separately: #1585 (glibc retention of freed SQLite memory) and #1586 (tool-result content stored twice). This issue covers the largest and most frequent one: the read amplification of the after-sync embedding refresh. Per incremental sync it reads roughly 900 MB of database pages that are never touched again, against a measured UI working set of about 85 MB.

## What happened

With `[vector] enabled = true` and `[vector.embed] run_after_sync = true`, every sync completion schedules an embedding refresh 30 s later, and that refresh reads the entire message corpus twice, regardless of how much changed.

Measured with `posix_fadvise(DONTNEED)` on the database files followed by `fincore` sampling every 5 s: a 7-message incremental append to one live session was followed, about 35 s later, by `sessions.db` going from 2 MB to 640 MB resident and `vectors.db` from 0 to 275 MB, with no API requests in the window. The pattern reproduced on two independent runs. cgroup `memory.stat` reported all of it as `inactive_file`; over a day this accumulates to several GB of page cache that nothing ever touches again. For comparison, replaying the real UI request mix from the same day (session detail, usage, children, messages, projects, stats, usage summary, search) had a file working set of 72 MB of `sessions.db` plus 11 MB of the usage cache.

Two queries are responsible:

1. `DB.ScanEmbeddableUnits` (`internal/db/messages.go`) carries a `since` watermark, but `optionalSinceClause` wraps the column in a function:

   ```sql
   AND (NULLIF(s.ended_at, '') IS NULL OR datetime(NULLIF(s.ended_at, '')) >= datetime(?))
   ```

   The query is `FROM messages m JOIN sessions s ... ORDER BY m.session_id, m.ordinal`, so on the real archive the plan is:

   ```
   SCAN m USING INDEX idx_messages_session_ordinal
   SEARCH s USING INDEX sqlite_autoindex_sessions_1 (id=?)
   ```

   It scans all 693,237 messages and reads every `content` column, then filters each row through the sessions probe. Only 550 messages in 8 sessions were newer than the watermark at the time: a 1,260x overshoot, and it accounts for the 640 MB (the `messages` table is 384 MB plus indexes).

2. `Index.countPending` (`internal/vector/build.go`) runs `SELECT content FROM <docs> d WHERE NOT EXISTS (...)` and splits every document's content in Go just to compute the progress-bar denominator. That reads the whole 228 MB `vector_messages` table on every refresh and accounts for the 275 MB.

## Expected behavior

The cost of an after-sync refresh should be proportional to what changed. Driving the scan from `sessions` with a sargable predicate on `ended_at` (it is already an RFC 3339 string, so a plain comparison works; the `NULL` case can be a separate branch) and then reading messages through `idx_messages_session_ordinal` for those few sessions turns the plan into a handful of SEARCHes. `countPending` can count rows via the `stamps`/`docs` anti-join on `doc_key` and `content_hash` without fetching content; the chunk count is only used for progress reporting.

Neither change touches the stored format or the embedding output.

### Sample session file or snippet

```text
20:51:15 incremental claude <session>: 10 new message(s)
20:51:50 incremental claude <session>: 7 new message(s)
                    sessions.db   vectors.db   (fincore RES)
20:51:44               1.8M           0
20:51:54             647.3M       264.3M
20:52:04             637.9M       274.0M
```

### Steps to reproduce

1. Enable `[vector]` with `run_after_sync = true` on an archive with a few hundred thousand messages.
2. Evict the database files from the page cache (`vmtouch -e` or `posix_fadvise(DONTNEED)`) and watch `fincore` on `sessions.db` and `vectors.db`.
3. Let one small incremental sync happen; about 30 s later both files become hundreds of MB resident.
4. `EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN` on the `ScanEmbeddableUnits` query with a recent `since` value shows `SCAN m USING INDEX idx_messages_session_ordinal`.

### Checklist

- [x] I searched existing issues
- [x] I removed secrets and private data from any attached session files

title: The daemon's memory keeps growing past 1 GB because glibc holds on to memory that SQLite has already freed
body:
### agentsview version

`main` at d0395b50 (also v0.41.1 and v0.42.0)

### Install method

Built from source (Linux, glibc malloc, `mattn/go-sqlite3`)

### OS / platform

Linux x86_64 (Debian-based), 31 GB RAM, glibc 2.x

### Which agent and version

Not agent-specific

### Which model(s)

Not applicable

### What happened, and what did you expect

## Scope

One of three independent causes of a daemon footprint that tracks archive size instead of change rate; see #1584 (after-sync embedding refresh reads the whole corpus) and #1586 (tool-result text stored twice).

## What happened

The serve daemon's RSS ratchets upward and never comes back down: 233 MB right after startup, 448 MB after 40 minutes, 1.18 GB after 22 hours on the previous build, with the same archive and no growth in the data it serves.

Splitting RSS by mapping (`/proc/PID/smaps`) shows the Go side is not the problem. `runServe` already installs `debug.SetMemoryLimit(256 MiB)` and the `[anon: Go: heap]` mappings hold about 33 MB. The growth is entirely in unnamed anonymous regions at `0x7f..`, i.e. glibc malloc arenas used by the cgo SQLite driver: 331 MB at the 448 MB sample, against a theoretical SQLite page-cache ceiling of about 110 MB (4 archive readers, the writers, 4 usage-cache connections and 2 vector connections at `_cache_size = -8192`).

The mechanism is glibc's, not SQLite's: with about 20 threads each cgo call lands in a per-thread arena, freed chunks stay in the arena, and fragmentation across arenas means the high-water mark of every transient (usage rollups with `temp_store=MEMORY`, large queries, full parses) is retained forever. A reference-bit measurement (`clear_refs` + `Referenced`) over a two-minute idle window confirmed that after the fix below the remaining anonymous memory is 85 to 90% hot, so the retained portion was purely cold.

## A/B measurement

Same binary, same archive, same load (five rounds of the usage summary, top sessions, comparison, session list and usage endpoints), only the allocator policy changed through the systemd unit:

| | default glibc | `MALLOC_ARENA_MAX=2` + `MALLOC_TRIM_THRESHOLD_=1048576` |
|---|---|---|
| RSS after startup (anon) | 293 MB (237) | 166 MB (111) |
| RSS after 3 load rounds (anon) | 356 MB (300), stays | 157 MB (101), flat |
| `usage/summary` latency | 0.5 to 0.8 s | 0.47 to 0.77 s |

## Expected behavior

The daemon's resident memory should follow its working set, not the high-water mark of past transients. The two-line allocator policy above achieves that with no measurable latency cost; the equivalent in code is `mallopt(M_ARENA_MAX, 2)` and `mallopt(M_TRIM_THRESHOLD, 1<<20)` at serve startup (Linux/glibc only), or a `malloc_trim(0)` next to the existing `debug.FreeOSMemory()` in the end-of-pass scavenge. Documenting the environment variables would already help operators on small machines.

### Sample session file or snippet

```text
RSS by mapping (448 MB sample):
  [unnamed anon 0x7b..]        331 MB   <- glibc arenas (SQLite via cgo)
  agentsview binary text        36 MB
  [anon: Go: heap]              33 MB
  [heap]                        12 MB
  [anon: Go: immortal metadata]  9 MB
```

### Steps to reproduce

1. Run `agentsview serve` on Linux against a multi-GB archive and note RSS after startup.
2. Exercise the usage endpoints or let a few syncs happen; watch RSS climb and never return.
3. Restart with `MALLOC_ARENA_MAX=2 MALLOC_TRIM_THRESHOLD_=1048576` in the environment; RSS stays flat under the same load.

### Checklist

- [x] I searched existing issues
- [x] I removed secrets and private data from any attached session files

title: About 5 GB of a 12.7 GB archive is tool output that is stored twice
body:
### agentsview version

`main` at d0395b50 (schema data_version 96)

### Install method

Built from source

### OS / platform

Linux x86_64

### Which agent and version

Mixed archive: Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, zcode; 1,637 sessions

### Which model(s)

Not applicable

### What happened, and what did you expect

## Scope

One of three independent causes of a daemon footprint that tracks archive size instead of change rate; see #1584 (after-sync embedding refresh reads the whole corpus) and #1585 (glibc retention of freed SQLite memory).

## What happened

A 12.7 GB `sessions.db` holds 170 MB of conversation text. Measured with `dbstat` and `SUM(LENGTH(...))`:

| table | size | rows | of which |
|---|---|---|---|
| `tool_calls` | 6,053 MB | 545,069 | `result_content` 5,341 MB, `input_json` 340 MB |
| `tool_result_events` | 5,533 MB | 463,378 | `content` 5,232 MB |
| `messages` | 384 MB | 693,095 | `content` 170 MB, `thinking_text` 16 MB |
| indexes, FTS, signals | about 700 MB | | |

Only 23 of the 545,069 tool calls have more than one result event. For every other call, `tool_calls.result_content` (the summary produced by `SummarizeToolResultEvents`) is byte-for-byte the single event's `content`, so about 5.2 GB, 41% of the archive, is the same text stored twice. Tool output is 83% of the file; conversation text is 1.3%.

Every cost that scales with archive size inherits the amplification: page cache pressure (a full resync streams 13 GB through the cache), resync duration, backup size, and the full-parse re-read paths.

## Expected behavior

`result_content` should be derived, not stored, when it equals the single event's content: leave it NULL and read it from `tool_result_events` through the existing `(session_id, tool_call_message_ordinal, call_index)` key, keeping `result_content_length` so list views need no join, and store the summary only for the few calls whose events differ. That removes 5.2 GB with one data_version bump; per-call reads add one indexed lookup. A follow-up could compress `tool_result_events.content` at rest (tool output is highly repetitive) and would take the remaining 5.2 GB to roughly a quarter, but the deduplication alone is the simple, large win.

### Sample session file or snippet

```sql
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM (
  SELECT session_id, tool_call_message_ordinal, call_index, COUNT(*) c
  FROM tool_result_events GROUP BY 1,2,3 HAVING c > 1);   -- 23
SELECT SUM(LENGTH(result_content))/1048576 FROM tool_calls;         -- 5341
SELECT SUM(LENGTH(content))/1048576 FROM tool_result_events;        -- 5232
```

### Steps to reproduce

1. Open any sizeable archive read-only and run the three queries above.
2. Compare with `SELECT name, SUM(pgsize)/1048576 FROM dbstat GROUP BY name`.

### Checklist

- [x] I searched existing issues
- [x] I removed secrets and private data from any attached session files

title: perf(serve): cap glibc malloc arenas in the serve daemon
body:
The serve daemon's RSS ratchets from about 230 MB after startup to over 1 GB after a day even though its working set does not grow. The Go heap is already bounded by the 256 MiB soft limit `applyServeMemoryLimit` installs and holds about 33 MB; the growth is entirely glibc malloc arenas used by the cgo SQLite driver. With roughly 20 threads each cgo call lands in a per-thread arena, freed chunks stay resident, and fragmentation across arenas retains the high-water mark of every transient (usage rollups, large queries, full parses).

On Linux with cgo, `runServe` now calls `mallopt(M_ARENA_MAX, 2)` and `mallopt(M_TRIM_THRESHOLD, 1 MiB)` right after the Go memory limit. The change is three new files under cmd/agentsview, one line in runServe, and a short docs section; it is independent of every other open PR. An operator who already set `MALLOC_ARENA_MAX` or `MALLOC_TRIM_THRESHOLD_` keeps that value for that knob, since glibc has applied it before `main` runs; the decision lives in a pure-Go function with a table-driven test. Other platforms and non-cgo builds get a no-op. Only the daemon is tuned: one-shot commands exit before fragmentation accumulates, and the resync worker child returns everything on exit, so capping its arenas would only serialize its parse workers.

Measured on the same binary and archive under an identical load of usage and session endpoints: RSS after three load rounds went from 356 MB and still climbing to 157 MB and flat, with no measurable change in `usage/summary` latency (0.5 to 0.8 s before, 0.47 to 0.77 s after). All release and Docker builds are glibc (Debian bookworm), so the `linux && cgo` constraint covers them; musl would compile the stub.

Measured after deploying this build (no MALLOC_* variables in the environment, so the in-code policy is what ran): RSS went from 191 MB to 208 MB across three rounds of the same usage and session load and then stayed there, against 293 MB to 356 MB and still climbing on the same binary without the change.

Closes #1585

title: perf(vector): make the after-sync embedding refresh read only what changed
body:
With `[vector] enabled` and `run_after_sync = true`, every sync completion schedules an embedding refresh that read the whole message corpus twice, however little had changed. On a 693k-message archive one seven-message append was followed by about 640 MB of `sessions.db` and 275 MB of `vectors.db` being pulled into the page cache, all of it cold afterwards, against a measured UI working set of about 85 MB. Two queries were responsible.

`ScanEmbeddableUnits` has a `since` watermark, but the predicate lived on the joined `sessions` row behind a `datetime()` call, so SQLite drove the scan from `messages` (`SCAN m USING INDEX idx_messages_session_ordinal`) and read every row's content before discarding it; only 550 messages in 8 sessions were newer than the watermark. The restriction is now a session-id `IN` subquery that repeats the caller's `deleted_at` and automated-scope filters, so the small `sessions` table becomes the outer loop and messages are fetched with `SEARCH m ... (session_id=?)` on the same index, which also keeps the `(session_id, ordinal)` order the reducer relies on without a temp sort. The `since` comparison semantics, the `NULL ended_at` handling, and the empty-`since` full scan are unchanged. On the real archive the plan is now `SEARCH m USING INDEX idx_messages_session_ordinal (session_id=?)` with a bloom-filtered list subquery over `sessions`, and the equivalent count query drops from 0.50 s to 0.10 s while returning the identical 1,090 rows.

`countPending` selected `content` for every mirror document to evaluate the stamp anti-join and then split each one in Go to size the progress bar. The mirror DDL gains a `(doc_key, content_hash)` covering index on the docs tables, and the pending set is resolved in a materialized CTE through that index before content is read only for the survivors; the generation coverage query in `index.go` shares the anti-join and benefits from the same index. The index is additive and `prepareMirrorSchema` replays the DDL on every write-path open, so existing `vectors.db` files gain it on their next build; bumping `MirrorSchemaVersion` would instead drop the mirror state and re-embed the corpus for what is only an index. One consequence: a read-only open never runs DDL, so `embeddings status` against a store that has not been rebuilt yet keeps the old plan until the next build.

Reviewers should look at `sinceSessionScopeClause` and `embeddableUnitsQuery` in `internal/db/messages.go`, and `pendingContentQuery` plus the DDL change in `internal/vector`. The new tests pin the emitted unit sequence, the stream order and watermark across since/automated combinations, and assert the query plans directly (no `SCAN` of messages when `since` is set, covering-index anti-join for pending documents).

Measured after deploying this build against the same 693k-message archive: with the database files evicted from the page cache, a 90 s window containing a dozen incremental syncs (two live sessions appending) left 5 to 9 MB of sessions.db and 0 bytes of vectors.db resident. The identical experiment on the previous build pulled 640 MB of sessions.db and 275 MB of vectors.db into the cache about 30 s after a single seven-message append.

End-to-end effect: the dashboard queries the app runs on a cold open are page-cache bound, taking 0.3 to 1.6 s warm but 2 to 18 s once the archive has been evicted. Before this change the embedding refresh evicted it every 30 s of activity by streaming 900 MB of unrelated pages through the cache, so an interactive session kept landing in the cold regime; after it the archive's working set stays resident (5 to 9 MB touched per sync) and the warm numbers are the steady state.

Closes #1584

title: perf(db): stop storing tool-result summaries their single event repeats
body:
On a 12.7 GB archive, `tool_calls.result_content` held 5,341 MB and `tool_result_events.content` 5,232 MB. Only 23 of 545,069 calls had more than one result event; for every other call the summary produced by `SummarizeToolResultEvents` was byte for byte the single event's content, so about 5.2 GB (41% of the file) was the same text stored twice. Tool output was 83% of the archive and conversation text 1.3%, and every cost that scales with archive size (page cache pressure, resync duration, backups, full re-read paths) inherited the amplification.

A summary is now dropped when the call has exactly one result event whose content equals it. `result_content_length` still records the summary's size, so an empty column with a non-zero length is the signal that the text lives in the event; multi-event calls, single-event calls whose summary differs, and blocked categories store exactly what they did before. The rule, the write-side helper, the read-side refill and the SQL fallback expression live together in `internal/db/tool_result_dedup.go`.

Write sites: `resolveToolCalls` in `internal/db/messages.go` (the choke point for full sync, incremental inserts, session batch and import) and `applyToolCallSubagentLinkTx` (a linked result carries no events of its own, so it checks the stored ones; without this an incremental pass would re-inflate the column). The PostgreSQL and DuckDB push paths apply the same rule so their tool-call fingerprints keep matching SQLite and sessions are not re-pushed forever.

Read sites: the refill happens once in `attachToolCallsWithQuerier`, which covers the HTTP API and its JSON shape, HTML and Markdown export, MCP, resume, secret scanning and redaction with no per-consumer change; the PostgreSQL and DuckDB stores and the artifact wire decoder refill the same way. `buildRecallEvidenceWindow` reads the column in SQL and uses `ToolCallResultContentSQL`, a fallback to the single event's content guarded on `result_content_length > 0`. `SearchSession` on SQLite and PostgreSQL now also matches `tool_result_events.content`, closing a parity gap with DuckDB that the change would otherwise have made load-bearing. Content search already suppressed `result_content` for calls with events and matches the event rows; the fingerprint and digest readers deliberately keep comparing raw stored state on both sides, and the orphan-copy path copies rows verbatim, so sessions whose source files are gone keep their old rows and still read back correctly.

`dataVersion` moves to 97 so existing archives shed the duplicates on their next resync. Reviewers should start with `tool_result_dedup.go` and `resolveToolCalls`, then the refill in `attachToolCallsWithQuerier`. The PostgreSQL integration suite (`make test-postgres`, all pgtest cases in `internal/postgres` and `internal/activity`) passes against a PG16 container with these changes; on that side they are the push-side dedup, the read-boundary refill and the added event join in `SearchSession`. One consequence worth knowing: the artifact wire format now carries the deduplicated column and refills on decode, so a third party reading raw artifact JSON rather than decoding it sees an empty `result_content` on those calls next to the event that holds the text.

Measured after deploying this build: the data-version resync took 577 s (1,550 sessions written, 58 orphans copied, FTS and usage indexes rebuilt), sessions.db went from 12.4 GB to 7.10 GB, and a query for single-event calls whose stored summary still equals the event content returns 0 rows. The API output is unchanged: in the first 60 messages of the largest Codex session, 45 of 46 tool calls carry a result and every one is derived from its single event.

End-to-end effect, measured by running the previous release and this build one at a time on the same machine against the same session sources (each with its own archive built from those sources) and timing the dashboard queries the app fires on a cold open, with the archive evicted from the page cache: `analytics/summary` 11.5 s before, 2.2 s after; `analytics/skills` 18.0 s before, 1.6 s after; `analytics/activity` 2.0 s before, 1.4 s after. The queries are unchanged; the rows they scan carry 5 GB less text. With a warm cache both builds answer in 0.3 to 1.6 s, so the gain shows up whenever the working set has been pushed out, which the background scans in #1584 did every 30 s before that fix.

Closes #1586

title: The usage rollup gives up and returns 500 whenever any session is being written during its build
body:
### agentsview version

`main` at d0395b50 (also v0.41.1 and v0.42.0)

### Install method

Built from source

### OS / platform

Linux x86_64

### Which agent and version

Not agent-specific; reproduced with two live sessions (one Claude Code, one Codex) appending every few seconds

### Which model(s)

Not applicable

### What happened, and what did you expect

## What happened

Whenever the archive is being written to at a steady rate, the usage rollup gives up and the usage page fails.

- At every daemon start, `usage cache backfill: usage cache backfill could not stabilize after 3 attempts: building usage rollups during backfill: usage cache source archive changed during rollup build` while live sessions are syncing, even though the same backfill succeeds a few seconds later when the archive happens to be quiet.
- Right after a data-version resync, `/api/v1/usage/summary` returned HTTP 500 for 18.3 s and then again for 13.6 s (`usage summary error: usage cache source archive changed during rollup build`), then 200 in 6.6 s, then 200 in 0.47 s. Nothing was wrong with the data; the two live sessions were appending every five seconds while the rollup was being rebuilt.

The mechanism is in `usage_rollup.go` (`recheck`) and `usage_cache_consumers.go`: a rollup build captures the source versions of every session in scope, builds the rollups across several transactions and two database files, then re-reads the versions and aborts with `errUsageCacheSourceChanged` if any of them moved. The caller retries at most `usageFillMaxAttempts` (3) times with no backoff and no fallback, so a build that takes longer than the interval between appends to any session in scope can never complete. This is a livelock, not a race: nobody computes anything wrong, the work just never finishes. And when it gives up, the request fails even though a complete rollup built seconds earlier is sitting in the cache.

Two things compound here. The validation granularity is the whole snapshot (every session the summary covers) while the change granularity is one append to one session, so an unrelated live session vetoes the entire summary. And the failure policy is abandonment: three attempts, then an error to the user, instead of serving the last complete result.

## Expected behavior

The cache is already organized per session (per-session facts with source versions), so the natural fix is to keep the layers apart:

1. Per-session facts are filled independently: one append only invalidates and refills that session's rows.
2. Any step that reads the archive does so inside one read transaction. In WAL mode that is a consistent snapshot for the whole step, so there is nothing to re-check afterwards. The only cost is that the WAL cannot be checkpointed past that snapshot while the read is open, which is seconds.
3. The rollup aggregates only committed per-session facts from the cache and never reads the archive. Then "source archive changed during rollup build" cannot happen by construction; sessions written during the build are picked up by their own notification fill and appear in the next summary.

With that layering the recheck and the three-attempt loop can be deleted rather than tuned. If a stopgap is wanted first, serving the previous complete rollup when a rebuild is invalidated would already turn the 500 into a slightly stale 200.

### Sample session file or snippet

```text
22:37:34 resync: rebuild usage indexes: 8.985s
22:38:02 usage cache backfill: covered 1649 sessions (0 deleted), built 2028 daily rows ...
22:38:22 usage summary error: usage cache source archive changed during rollup build

curl /api/v1/usage/summary:  500 18.3s,  500 13.6s,  200 6.6s,  200 0.47s
```

### Steps to reproduce

1. Have one or two sessions appending to their transcripts every few seconds (any live agent session does this).
2. Restart the daemon, or trigger a resync, so the usage cache has to rebuild.
3. Request `/api/v1/usage/summary` during the rebuild; observe 500s until the writes happen to pause long enough for one build to pass its recheck.

### Checklist

- [x] I searched existing issues
- [x] I removed secrets and private data from any attached session files

title: fix(db): stop live archive writes from vetoing the usage rollup
body:
Usage summaries now complete while live sessions continue writing to the
archive. Previously, one session changing during a multi-session build could
invalidate the whole request and make the usage endpoint return an error after
its retry limit.

Fact extraction now reads each session's facts and source version from one
archive snapshot. The cache install compares its current revision with the
revision observed before extraction. If another fill installed different facts
first, only the sessions that lost that race are extracted again. Source
fingerprints remain equality checks because they are not ordered versions.

Rollup builds stay on the usage-cache side of the archive boundary. Under the
cache write lock, each install verifies that its facts and source still match
the committed cached session. Readers require the exact rollup write sequence
that they verified, so a late build cannot look current merely because it wrote
last. An older Cursor build cannot replace one that already includes newer
events, and a session deleted during a rollup retry is skipped without aborting
the background cache pass.

The branch also streams recall evidence JSON directly into SHA-256. This
preserves the digest while avoiding the full temporary evidence buffer that
caused the allocation benchmark to vary after the rebase.

The concurrency-sensitive paths are `fillSessionsDetached` and
`installSpoolBatch` in `internal/db/usage_cache_fill.go`, plus `ensureAttempt`
and `installUsageRollupBuilds` in `internal/db/usage_rollup.go`.

Closes #1590

title: Antigravity CLI parser splits Gemini 3.7 Flash usage between gemini-3.7-flash-high and gemini-3.7-flash-exp-b
body:
### agentsview version
`agentsview v0.42.0 (commit ff8fb4e8, built 2026-09-01T19:37:06Z)`

### Install method
Homebrew cask

### OS / platform
macOS 27.0 (arm64)

### Which agent and version
Antigravity CLI (agy) 1.1.24

### Which model(s)
`gemini-3.7-flash-high` / `gemini-3.7-flash-exp-b`

### What happened, and what did you expect
When using Antigravity CLI (`agy`) with `Gemini 3.7 Flash (High)`, AgentsView usage analytics splits the usage between two separate model rows:
1. `gemini-3.7-flash-high`
2. `gemini-3.7-flash-exp-b`

Expected behavior:
All usage events and step models should be unified under `gemini-3.7-flash-high`.

### Root Cause
In `internal/parser/antigravity.go` (added in #1461):
```go
func resolveAntigravityGenerationModel(data []byte, executorModel string) string {
    generationModel, hasDisplayLabel := extractAntigravityGenerationModel(data)
    if hasDisplayLabel || executorModel == "" {
        return generationModel
    }
    if antigravityBaseModel(executorModel) == generationModel {
        return executorModel
    }
    return generationModel
}

func antigravityBaseModel(model string) string {
    for _, suffix := range []string{"-low", "-medium", "-high"} {
        if base, ok := strings.CutSuffix(model, suffix); ok {
            return base
        }
    }
    return model
}
```
- In recent Antigravity CLI versions, Google's Cloud Code backend returns `gemini-3.7-flash-exp-b` in `gen_metadata` field 19 (an internal experimental serving variant identifier), while `executor_metadata` field 28 contains `gemini-3.7-flash-high`.
- `antigravityBaseModel("gemini-3.7-flash-high")` yields `"gemini-3.7-flash"`.
- Because `"gemini-3.7-flash"` != `"gemini-3.7-flash-exp-b"`, `resolveAntigravityGenerationModel` fails to match the base model slug. Consequently, the executor model is not applied, and the raw wire identifier `gemini-3.7-flash-exp-b` leaks into the usage events.

### Suggested Fix
Update `antigravityBaseModel` or normalize `generationModel` to handle `-exp` / `-exp-b` variant suffixes, e.g.:
```go
func antigravityBaseModel(model string) string {
    for _, suffix := range []string{"-low", "-medium", "-high", "-exp-b", "-exp"} {
        if base, ok := strings.CutSuffix(model, suffix); ok {
            return base
        }
    }
    return model
}
```
And check if `antigravityBaseModel(executorModel) == antigravityBaseModel(generationModel)`.

### Steps to reproduce
1. Use Antigravity CLI (`agy`) with model `gemini-3.7-flash-high`.
2. Run a few prompts and open `agentsview`.
3. Check the Models / Usage dashboard: observe both `gemini-3.7-flash-high` and `gemini-3.7-flash-exp-b` listed.

### Checklist
- [x] I searched existing issues
- [x] I removed secrets and private data from any attached session files

title: fix(parser): preserve Antigravity CLI effort for experimental serving variants
body:
Antigravity CLI 1.1.24 can store an experimental serving identifier such as `gemini-3.7-flash-exp-b` in generation metadata while the covering executor metadata records the effort-qualified product model, such as `gemini-3.7-flash-high`. The parser previously required the generation value to equal the executor's base slug, so the serving identifier leaked into usage events and split one model's dashboard accounting.

This change applies the executor range to both SQLite `gen_metadata` and preferred `.trajectory.json` sidecar generations. It recognizes only the observed `-exp-b` serving suffix when matching generation metadata to a covering executor range. Complete display labels and explicitly effort-qualified generation models remain authoritative, unmatched or missing executors preserve the raw generation model, and steps outside every declared executor range are not guessed. Existing archived rows are reparsed through data version 98 so historical message and usage records receive the correction.

The Antigravity format inventory now pins the official CLI 1.1.24 release and records the observed field 19 variant. Generic `-exp` and hypothetical serving suffixes remain distinct until evidence supports normalizing them.

The shared model-resolution and executor-range behavior is in `internal/parser/antigravity.go`; sidecar attribution is in `internal/parser/antigravity_cli.go`; regression coverage is in `internal/parser/antigravity_test.go`. The archive reparse boundary is in `internal/db/db.go`, and provenance is documented in `docs/internal/session-format-sources.md`.

Closes #1593.

title: fix(sync): bound full-sync memory without fragmenting writes
body:
Full sync now bounds parsed data at both ownership stages without turning parser
backpressure into small SQLite transactions. AgentsView v0.42.0 could admit all
eight workers during archive-scale passes, retain their completed results
alongside the pending 100-session batch, and kept flushed pointer entries live
in reused collector arrays.

The final design uses a 128 MiB weighted budget for active and queued parses and
a separate 512 MiB estimate for completed results waiting to be written. The
collector releases parse admission when it takes ownership, flushes before the
pending estimate would cross its limit, and clears pointer-bearing arrays after
each write. Unknown-size and oversized sources run conservatively. Incremental
sync keeps its existing lease-through-write policy.

## Measured tradeoff

An isolated production-scale workload on a generic 16 GB Linux machine produced
these aggregate results:

| Measurement           | v0.42.0 A |   v0.42.0 B | Candidate |
| --------------------- | --------: | ----------: | --------: |
| Worker elapsed        | 530.861 s |   603.099 s | 569.777 s |
| Peak Go heap          | 735.3 MiB |   684.0 MiB | 617.5 MiB |
| Peak worker RSS       | 978.3 MiB | 1,017.3 MiB | 815.6 MiB |
| Peak worker anonymous | 925.3 MiB |   964.7 MiB | 762.4 MiB |
| Final Go heap         |  71.8 MiB |    75.5 MiB |  52.0 MiB |

Against the midpoint of the bracketing baselines, elapsed time changed by
+0.49%, peak heap fell 13.0%, and peak worker anonymous memory fell 19.3%. The
candidate completed and sealed the fresh archive. Its total cgroup peak remained
file-cache dominated and exceeded the benchmark harness's 8 GiB aggregate gate;
this change addresses process retention and does not claim that separate harness
metric as fixed.

The main review surface is the collector ownership handoff in
`collectAndBatchWithOptions`: archive-scale passes release active admission when
the result enters the separately bounded pending batch, while ordinary
incremental collectors continue holding each lease through its write.

title: Recall: setting Session agent filter fails insight generation with huma required-property error
body:
### agentsview version

agentsview v0.42.0 (commit ff8fb4e8, built 2026-09-01T19:48:29Z)

### Install method

GitHub release binary (via scoop, r-bucket)

### OS / platform

Windows 11 Pro (10.0.26200)

### Which agent and version

n/a (unrelated to a specific coding agent's session data)

### Which model(s)

n/a

### What happened, and what did you expect

On the Recall page, "Generated insights" tab, I set "Session agent" to `Claude` while leaving the template at "Model and Cost" and generator at "Codex", then clicked Generate. It failed immediately with:

```
expected required property automated_scope to be present (body.filters: map[agent:claude]); expected required property include_one_shot to be present (body.filters: map[agent:claude]); expected required property timezone to be present (body.filters: map[agent:claude])
```

I expected the generation to run with just the agent filter applied, the same way it does when "Session agent" is left unset.

### Steps to reproduce

1. Open Recall → Generated insights.
2. Leave Session scope at "No automated", Template at "Model and Cost".
3. Set "Session agent" to any agent (e.g. Claude).
4. Click Generate.
5. Observe the "Generation error" panel with the message above.

### What I'm seeing in the code

I'm not fully sure this is the right read, please correct me if I'm missing something server-side.

`insights.svelte.ts` builds the `filters` payload only from the session-agent picker, with nothing else set:

https://github.com/kenn-io/agentsview/blob/f88fab198b6fe60204d9e35b05e52fbf4ba1fbb9/frontend/src/lib/stores/insights.svelte.ts#L195-L197

```ts
sessionFilters: this.type === "llm_canned" && this.sessionAgent
  ? { agent: this.sessionAgent }
  : undefined,
```

On the server, `CannedSessionFilters` declares `timezone`, `include_one_shot`, and `automated_scope` without `omitempty`:

https://github.com/kenn-io/agentsview/blob/f88fab198b6fe60204d9e35b05e52fbf4ba1fbb9/internal/insight/canned.go#L119-L128

```go
type CannedSessionFilters struct {
	Timezone        string `json:"timezone"`
	Machine         string `json:"machine,omitempty"`
	Agent           string `json:"agent,omitempty"`
	Termination     string `json:"termination,omitempty"`
	MinUserMessages int    `json:"min_user_messages,omitempty"`
	IncludeOneShot  bool   `json:"include_one_shot"`
	AutomatedScope  string `json:"automated_scope"`
	ActiveSince     string `json:"active_since,omitempty"`
}
```

It looks like huma turns those three fields into required JSON-schema properties and rejects the request body before the handler runs, since the error text matches huma's schema-validation format rather than an application-level message.

There's also a `normalizeCannedSessionFilters` helper that looks like it was written to backfill exactly these fields from the top-level request when `filters` is present but incomplete:

https://github.com/kenn-io/agentsview/blob/f88fab198b6fe60204d9e35b05e52fbf4ba1fbb9/internal/server/insights.go#L56-L77

If that's right, the huma-level required-property check on `CannedSessionFilters` happens earlier than that normalization and never lets a partial `filters` object reach it, which would explain why sending just `{agent: ...}` fails while omitting `filters` entirely (and using the top-level `agent` field instead) works fine.

### Sample session file or snippet

n/a — not a parse/render bug, this is a request payload rejected before it reaches any session data.

### Checklist

- [x] I searched existing issues
- [x] I removed secrets and private data from any attached session files

title: feat(usage): add smooth, lines and bars styles to Cost Over Time
body:
The Cost Over Time chart on the Usage page now has a style toggle with Smooth, Lines and Bars. The issue asked for stepped areas, and an earlier version of this PR drew them. Gapped bars give the same exact reading of each day and match the Activity timeline, and smooth areas read trends better, so the toggle offers those instead.

title: Stream and skim layouts hide per-message token counts, timing, and timestamps
Windows Sync CI job hangs inside a SQLite cgo call until the package timeout
body:
## Symptom

The `Go Test (windows-latest, Sync)` CI job intermittently hits the 20-minute package timeout in `internal/sync`. Each time, one test is blocked inside a single cgo call into SQLite that never returns. Every other lane on the same commit passes, and the job passes on re-run.

## Occurrences

| Date | Branch | Run | Hung test | Blocked call |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 2026-08-27 | `main` @ 1940e41f1 | https://github.com/kenn-io/agentsview/actions/runs/33072104713/job/98516726190 | `TestOpenCodeFullPassSkipsAfterWatcherPassParse` | `sqlite3_step` inside a `Row.Scan` |
| 2026-09-02 | PR #1573 @ a707264d9 | https://github.com/kenn-io/agentsview/actions/runs/33698490860/job/100472437600 | `TestResyncAllMixedOpenCodeRootsKeepsSQLiteFallback` | `sqlite3_close_v2` while closing the writer pool of the replacement archive at the end of `resyncBuildLocked` |

Both runs used `windows-latest`, Go 1.27.0, and `github.com/mattn/go-sqlite3` v1.14.50.

## What the goroutine dump shows

In the 2026-09-02 run only eight goroutines were alive when the timeout fired: the test runner, the hung test, one parallel test waiting on `t.Parallel`, and the `database/sql` helper goroutines. The hung test's stack is:

```
github.com/mattn/go-sqlite3._Cfunc_sqlite3_close_v2
github.com/mattn/go-sqlite3.(*SQLiteConn).Close
database/sql.(*driverConn).finalClose
database/sql.(*DB).Close
go.kenn.io/agentsview/internal/db.(*DB).CloseContext   internal/db/db.go:4539
go.kenn.io/agentsview/internal/db.(*DB).Close
go.kenn.io/agentsview/internal/sync.(*Engine).resyncBuildLocked   internal/sync/engine.go:3663
go.kenn.io/agentsview/internal/sync.(*Engine).resyncAllWithOptionsLocked
go.kenn.io/agentsview/internal/sync.(*Engine).ResyncAll
```

No other goroutine was in a cgo call, so this is not a Go-side lock order problem between two connections. The SQLite call itself does not come back.

The 2026-08-27 run has the same shape with `sqlite3_step` instead of `sqlite3_close_v2`.

## Why the existing close guard does not help

`CloseContext` bounds connection draining with `closeDrainTimeout`, but the drain runs after `pool.Close()` returns. The blocked call is the synchronous close of the writer connection inside `pool.Close()`, so no timeout in the repository covers it. The same is true for a blocked `sqlite3_step`.

## Open questions

- Whether the hang is inside SQLite's Windows VFS (for example a file handle held by another process on the runner, such as antivirus, during WAL cleanup at close) or inside go-sqlite3.
- Whether the sync tests leave a second handle open on the replacement archive or its WAL at the moment of close on Windows.
- Whether running the affected tests with `-v` and a per-test timeout would capture which SQLite file the call was operating on.

## Not in scope

This is not caused by the usage-cache retirement change in #1573. The sync package never opens a usage-cache generation, and the dump contains no usage-cache, lease, or flock frames.

title: test(ci): stabilize capture and Windows process timing
body:
Capture integration tests now keep the normal 15-second finalization budget,
with outer watchdogs beyond that boundary. The disappearing-source test
synchronizes at the persisted-source hook instead of polling the manifest, so
slow SQLite setup no longer exhausts an artificially short test deadline before
the `source_unavailable` assertion. The signal test likewise allows
race-instrumented shutdown to complete within the real operation budget.

Docs script tests retry only Windows `STATUS_DLL_INIT_FAILED` (`0xC0000142`)
when launching Bash. Every other nonzero exit remains single-attempt, so script
and assertion failures are not masked.

The capture failures reproduced locally under heavy contention with the old
short deadlines and passed repeated normal and race-instrumented runs after the
change. [Default-branch CI run 5035](https://github.com/kenn-io/agentsview/actions/runs/33702150659),
the next run after 5034, also completed successfully.

title: fix(sync): preserve bulk parse parallelism
body:
Full sync now keeps all eight parser workers available for medium-sized session
files while retaining explicit memory bounds. The 128 MiB active budget
introduced in #1595 charged each source at four times its on-disk size, so eight
roughly 6 MiB sources exceeded the budget and only five could parse
concurrently. In an isolated parse-heavy benchmark, that raised median elapsed
time from 165.1 ms to 255.2 ms.

This raises the active and queued parse capacity to 256 MiB while leaving the
completed pending-result limit at 512 MiB. The two explicit stage bounds
therefore total 768 MiB; conservative handling for unknown and oversized
sources and the existing collector batching remain unchanged. The same
benchmark completed in 153.6 ms, and a count-based invariant now protects
eight-worker admission for 6 MiB sources.

title: fix(insights): accept partial canned session filters
body:
Recall's Generated insights flow currently rejects a session-agent filter before generation because the HTTP request schema reuses a fully normalized aggregate type. Huma requires timezone, include_one_shot, and automated_scope inside filters even though the server already fills those values from the top-level request or defaults.

This adds an optional request-only filter shape, normalizes it once at the server boundary, and passes the normalized value through analytics, usage, Coach selection, aggregate serialization, and cache-key construction. The aggregate filter type keeps its required fields, so normalized prompts and cache inputs remain stable. The existing browser request shape stays unchanged.

The partial payload and error came from cderv's report: https://github.com/kenn-io/agentsview/issues/1596

Closes #1596

title: fix(recall): bound vector overfetch
body:
Selective hybrid recall queries can exceed sqlite-vec's 4,096-result KNN limit when a project, cwd, or current-cwd filter matches a small share of the archive, turning a normal short result into HTTP 500.

This bounds vector candidate expansion at the backend's supported window and returns the snapshot-validated filtered page available at that boundary. Expansion below the ceiling, lexical ranking, reciprocal-rank fusion, and existing recall filter semantics remain unchanged.

Closes #1565

title: fix(vector): reload Ollama Metal before CPU fallback
body:
Ollama can enter a state where embedding requests return zero vectors until its model runner unloads. AgentsView previously sent invalid inputs directly to CPU, which could leave a long-running CPU fallback doing work that a fresh Metal runner could handle.

Recovery now stays under the existing endpoint-wide gate. AgentsView unloads the affected Metal runner, confirms its removal through Ollama's process API, retries only the invalid inputs on fresh Metal, and uses `num_gpu: 0` only if Metal recovery fails. Valid vectors from the original batch remain unchanged.

<sup>generated by a clanker</sup>

title: Block visibility has no switch for system boundary cards
body:
The transcript renders session continuation, session resume, request
interrupted, task notification, and stop hook feedback as their own compact
boundary cards, but the Block Visibility menu has no entry for them. The menu
lists five categories (User, Assistant, Thinking, Tool, Code) and none of them
names this family.

The cards are not unfiltered, though. The Claude parser keeps these rows on
role `user` so analytics do not count them as assistant replies, and
`hasVisibleSegments` decides visibility from that role, so they are filtered as
if they were ordinary user messages. Turning off **User messages** hides every
boundary card along with the real prompts, and there is no way to hide only the
cards. On a session with many background agents, the task notification cards
crowd the transcript and the only way to get rid of them also removes the
prompts you are reading around them.

A second, smaller problem sits in the same code path. `hasVisibleSegments`
parses the boundary message's body to decide visibility, but the card renders
only a label and a one-line preview. A card whose body parses into no text
segment, such as stop hook feedback that is entirely a fenced block, disappears
when **Code blocks** is turned off, which nothing in the card's own rendering
would suggest.

Steps to reproduce:

1. Open a Claude session that contains a task notification.
2. Open the funnel menu in the message viewer header.
3. Nothing there controls the "Task notification" card.
4. Turn off **User messages**. The card disappears together with every real
   user prompt.

Expected: the boundary cards are their own visibility category, independent of
the user-message toggle.

title: feat(frontend): let readers hide system boundary cards
body:
Closes #1605.

Session continuation, resume, interrupted-request, task notification, and stop
hook feedback render as their own boundary cards, but the block-visibility menu
had no switch for them. They were filtered as ordinary user messages, because
the Claude parser keeps these rows on role `user` so analytics do not count
them as assistant replies. Turning off "User messages" hid every boundary card
as a side effect, and nothing could hide only the cards.

A `system` block type now covers the whole family. Both surfaces that expose
block visibility iterate `ALL_BLOCK_TYPES`, so the header dropdown and the
Appearance settings pick it up together, and the `Record<BlockType, ...>` label
and colour maps make a missing entry a type error rather than a silent gap.

`hasVisibleSegments` now short-circuits on boundary messages and asks about
`system` alone. That also fixes a smaller bug: the old path parsed the card's
body even though the card renders only a label and a one-line preview, so a
card whose body held no text segment vanished when "Code blocks" was hidden.
`MessageList` renders through the same `isSystemBoundaryMessage` predicate the
filter uses, so the two cannot drift apart.

The stored filter payload needed a format change. It listed the visible types,
so a newly added type is absent from every payload already on disk and would
have been read back as one the reader had hidden: anyone who had ever touched a
block filter would have lost their boundary cards on upgrade, with a stray
count on the funnel badge. The payload now lists hidden types, and a legacy
array is migrated against the vocabulary the writing build could name. Any
block type added later stays visible by default without another migration.

Reviewers should look at `parseHiddenBlocks` in `ui.svelte.ts` for the
migration, and at the short-circuit in `hasVisibleSegments` for the filtering
change.

title: feat(rawderive): add hosted parse worker foundation
body:
Adds a worker library for deriving sessions from retained raw captures. Workers verify manifest and object digests, reconstruct a read-only source tree, reuse provider parsing, and hand results to an atomic projection sink. PostgreSQL leases fence job completion to the current source generation.

Replay preserves provider inputs: SQLite snapshots use immutable reads, Codex retains alias-home title precedence and replay parents across configured directories, and Claude and Evener retain their lineage companions. Growing transcripts reuse captured prefixes. Hosted skill names come from recorded paths without reading worker-local frontmatter or cached local names.

Changing sources no longer stop an audit; full audits report skipped captures as incomplete so the watcher retries. Unchanged Claude sniff checks reuse filesystem evidence, and idle job cleanup excludes future retries.

Runtime activation and PostgreSQL session projection remain pending, so hosted browsing still requires `pg push`. The implemented capture-to-parser boundary has been exercised with Claude and WAL-mode ZCode inputs using PostgreSQL job leases and a recording projection sink.

Existing least-privilege raw-sync roles need `SELECT` and `UPDATE` on `raw_ingest_jobs`. Startup names missing requirements; grants are documented in the hosted raw-sync and PostgreSQL sync guides.

Rollout to existing raw-sync deployments still needs a compatibility decision: stricter validation rejects stored case-colliding paths, and an upload committed remotely but not bound locally before upgrading can retry indefinitely with a different manifest ID after modification times are added.

Refs #1352

title: Top Skills analytics is empty for Pi sessions (skill inference never runs)
body:
Top Skills analytics is empty for Pi sessions (skill inference never runs)

## Background

The "Top Skills" analytics panel and its underlying skill-usage data are
empty for Pi coding agent sessions. Skill attribution relies on every
parser populating `ParsedToolCall.SkillName`, but the Pi parser never
does, so Pi tool calls never count toward Top Skills.

Root cause: the `toolCall` branch in `parsePiAssistantMessage`
(`internal/parser/pi.go:473`) sets only `ToolUseID`, `ToolName`,
`Category`, and `InputJSON`. It never runs skill inference. Every other
parser does:

- Codex (`internal/parser/codex.go:529`) calls
  `inferCodexSkillNameWithBase(name, inputJSON, b.cwd)`.
- Cursor (`internal/parser/cursor.go:258`) and Kimi
  (`internal/parser/kimi.go:350`) call `inferToolSkillName`.
- Claude JSONL (`internal/parser/content.go:87-96`) reads
  `input.skill`/`input.name` for the Skill tool, then falls back to
  `inferToolSkillName`.

Pi has no dedicated skill tool: a native skill load is emitted as an
ordinary `read` tool call whose `path` argument points at the skill's
`SKILL.md` (Pi resolves skills from many roots: `~/.pi/agent/skills`,
project `.pi/skills`, `.agents/skills`, package `skills/`, `--skill
<path>`), or, in newer OMP builds, at a `skill://<name>` URI. The
existing read-file heuristic in `internal/parser/skill_inference.go`
would attribute the `SKILL.md` reads (Pi's tool name `read` and
`path`/`file_path` argument keys already match its matchers), but it is
never invoked from the Pi parser.

This is the same gap #1040 identified for OpenCode (fixed by #1041 and
#1042); Pi was simply never given the same treatment.

## Evidence

From a live Pi session (786 Pi sessions in a production archive): Pi
tool inputs regularly carry unattributed skill paths, e.g.

```json
{"path": "/home/geert/Code/personal/pi-my-rifle-ext/skills/engineering/implement-plan/SKILL.md"}
```

These inflate the Read tool count and leave the Skills dimension empty
for Pi.

For reference, codeburn solved the identical problem for Pi in
`src/providers/pi.ts` (`skillLoadName`, their issue #588): it matches
`read` calls whose path ends in `SKILL.md` and takes the parent
directory as the skill name, plus a `skill://<name>` URI arm.

## Acceptance Criteria

## Must

- [ ] Pi `read` tool calls whose path points at a `SKILL.md` are
      attributed a skill name (parent directory of the SKILL.md) so they
      count toward Top Skills.
- [ ] Pi tool calls carrying a `skill://<name>` URI are attributed the
      URI's skill name.
- [ ] Pi `bash` tool calls that cat/sed/grep a `SKILL.md` are attributed
      via the existing shell-command heuristic (matches the OpenCode and
      Codex treatment).
- [ ] Relative `SKILL.md` paths in Pi tool calls resolve against the
      session cwd (already parsed at `internal/parser/pi.go:81` and
      stored on the session).
- [ ] Resyncing existing Pi sessions populates skill usage without
      losing any session data.
- [ ] A unit test covers a Pi tool call inferring a skill name.

title: fix(parser): attribute skill names for Pi skill loads
body:
Top Skills analytics is empty for Pi sessions because the Pi parser never
populates `ParsedToolCall.SkillName`. Pi has no dedicated skill tool: a
native skill load is emitted as an ordinary `read` tool call whose path
points at the skill's `SKILL.md` (resolved from many roots:
`~/.pi/agent/skills`, project `.pi/skills`, `.agents/skills`, package
`skills/`, `--skill <path>`), or, in newer OMP builds, at a
`skill://<name>` URI. Without attribution these calls inflate the Read
tool count and leave the Skills dimension empty.

This mirrors the OpenCode gap fixed in #1040/#1041/#1042, applied to the
Pi parser.

## What the code does now

`parsePiAssistantMessage` receives the session working directory (already
parsed from the session header) and runs a new `inferPiSkillName` helper
on every tool call. Attribution is additive: every call that does not
look like a skill load keeps an empty `SkillName`, exactly as before.

The helper attributes three shapes:

- `skill://<name>` URIs are scanned from the input JSON and reduced to
  the URI's first path segment, so `skill://create-plan/SKILL.md`
  attributes `create-plan`.
- Read calls whose `path`/`file_path` value ends in `SKILL.md` resolve
  through the shared inference helpers. Pi's read input carries no
  cwd/workdir key, so the session working directory is tried first and
  relative `SKILL.md` paths resolve against it; this mirrors
  `inferOpenCodeSkillName`.
- Shell commands route through the existing Codex shell-command
  heuristic (`inferCodexSkillNameWithBase`) with the session working
  directory as the fallback base, the same way the Codex and OpenCode
  parsers thread their session cwd.

`dataVersion` is bumped to 97 so existing Pi sessions re-parse on the
next sync and backfill skill attribution. The resync is the standard
non-destructive rebuild: no session data is lost.

## Limits

- The URI scan is a substring scan of the raw input JSON, so a skill
  name containing JSON-escaped or control characters would truncate.
  Real skill names are plain identifiers, so this is not expected in
  practice.
- A URI extraction win means a `read` of a path that is *also* a
  SKILL.md path but arrives with a `skill://` URI inside another field
  attributes from the URI. Both routes describe the same skill load, so
  the attribution is the same in practice.

## Where to look

- `inferPiSkillName` / `piSkillURISkillName` in `internal/parser/pi.go`
- Data-version bump in `internal/db/db.go`
- Table-driven tests in `internal/parser/pi_skill_inference_test.go`
  covering SKILL.md reads (absolute, tilde, relative-to-cwd,
  frontmatter-named), `skill://` URIs (path form, bare form, other
  fields, query suffix, empty-name fallthrough), shell commands
  (cat/grep/sed, relative paths, non-skill commands), and a
  session-level fixture test asserting non-skill reads stay
  unattributed.

Fixes #1608

title: Correct generated API collection types and retire duplicate wire contracts
body:
### Problem / motivation

The frontend currently has two partially overlapping sources of truth for API response shapes:

- generated models in `frontend/src/lib/api/generated/`;
- handwritten models in `frontend/src/lib/api/types/`.

The handwritten models predate the generated client. Many are still more useful than their generated equivalents because the OpenAPI output and TypeScript generator lose two independent parts of the collection contract:

- the element type, producing `any[]`; and
- accurate nullability, often producing `any[] | null` even when a successful response always encodes an array.

The reverse problem is possible too: a schema can describe a collection as required and non-null when a request handler intentionally accepts an omitted or null value and normalizes it. The goal should be accurate nullability in both directions, based on observable HTTP behavior, rather than applying `nullable:"false"` indiscriminately.

Several stores currently work around these deficiencies by calling a generated service and then casting its response through `as unknown as` to an independently maintained handwritten type. That prevents TypeScript from checking whether the response type generated from OpenAPI is compatible with the type the UI actually consumes.

As a motivating example, `GET /api/v1/usage/summary` has four top-level collection fields:

- `daily`;
- `projectTotals`;
- `modelTotals`;
- `agentTotals`.

All successful storage-backed implementations currently return non-null arrays, including when there is no usage:

```json
{
  "daily": [],
  "projectTotals": [],
  "modelTotals": [],
  "agentTotals": []
}
```

SQLite constructs a non-nil empty daily slice and has a test protecting that invariant. PostgreSQL and DuckDB also normalize empty daily results to non-nil slices. The server's conversion helpers allocate empty slices for the other three fields.

Huma nevertheless describes these properties as nullable arrays in OpenAPI:

```json
{
  "type": ["array", "null"]
}
```

The generated `UsageSummaryResponse` therefore declares the fields as `any[] | null`. The frontend also has a handwritten `UsageSummaryResponse` which declares precise, non-null collection types. The usage store calls the generated service but historically asserted that its result was the handwritten type, bypassing any compatibility check between them.

This produced a plausible code-review finding about a possible `summary.daily.length` crash, even though investigation found that `daily: null` is not reachable from the current server. The generated type accurately reflects the overly permissive schema, while the handwritten type more accurately reflects current runtime behavior.

Usage is not the only area with this pattern. Generated models such as `DbAnalyticsSummary`, `DbSessionActivityResponse`, `DbSessionTiming`, and `InsightsResponse` also contain untyped or nullable collections. Handwritten files such as `analytics.ts`, `session-activity.ts`, `timing.ts`, and `insights.ts` restore concrete element types, stronger nullability guarantees, or both.

This creates several risks:

- server changes can regenerate the client successfully while leaving the handwritten model stale;
- incorrect nullability, renamed fields, and changed response shapes can be hidden from TypeScript;
- tests can construct fixtures that satisfy a handwritten model but are not representative of a real API response;
- similarly named generated and handwritten models make it unclear which one defines the wire contract; and
- generated-type deficiencies accumulate because casts make them easy to work around rather than correct at the schema boundary.

Collection item typing and collection nullability must be verified separately. A field can have a concrete item type but incorrect nullability, or correct nullability while still being generated as `any[]`. Both cases weaken the contract, and each needs evidence from the handler and its serialized HTTP response.

Generated output can be completely fresh while remaining semantically inaccurate,[^1] and an unchecked cast can prevent the frontend from noticing future generated-contract changes. Issue #1596 illustrates the complementary nullability failure: an OpenAPI request schema can be stricter than the handler's intended normalization behavior. A freshness check cannot determine whether a collection should be optional, nullable, or always present.

Handwritten types are still appropriate for genuine frontend domain models, such as normalized data, derived UI state, or values combined from multiple endpoints. Those models should have names distinct from wire-response models and should be produced by explicit, typed adapters whose inputs are generated API types.

[^1]: #977 covers keeping the committed generated client in sync with OpenAPI; this issue concerns whether that schema accurately describes the server contract.


### Proposed solution


1. Audit generated-service call sites that replace response types through `as unknown as`, including stores for usage, analytics, sessions, messages, insights, and synchronization.
2. Classify the corresponding handwritten types as duplicate wire contracts, workarounds for deficient generated models, or intentional frontend domain/view models.
3. Correct Huma/OpenAPI schemas that produce untyped collections or inaccurate collection nullability. For each request and response collection:
   - emit the concrete element schema instead of `any[]`;
   - determine independently whether the field is required, optional, or nullable;
   - verify the decision against actual HTTP serialization and normalization behavior; and
   - use `nullable:"false"` only where the server guarantees a JSON array.
4. Regenerate the client and confirm both properties of each corrected field: its element type and its nullability.
5. Use generated response types directly wherever they adequately describe the API.
6. For intentional domain models, use a distinct name and an explicit typed API-to-domain adapter instead of `as unknown as`.
7. Add HTTP-level contract tests for important empty, omitted, null, and populated collection cases on which the generated frontend types depend.
8. Remove duplicate handwritten wire types as their generated equivalents become precise enough.

The usage summary can serve as the first migration:

1. Mark the four top-level response slices as non-null in the Huma schema, following the existing `nullable:"false"` convention.
2. Ensure each slice has its concrete entry schema rather than an untyped array.
3. Regenerate the client and verify both the element types and the absence of `| null`.
4. Add an HTTP-level test proving that an empty usage response encodes the fields as `[]`.
5. Remove the unchecked usage-summary cast and use the generated response type directly.
6. Audit nested usage arrays separately because some breakdown fields may legitimately be absent, null, or empty when breakdowns are disabled.

The implementation is complete when:

- generated service responses are not replaced with independently maintained wire types through `as unknown as`;
- corrected OpenAPI collection fields have concrete element schemas;
- corrected OpenAPI collection fields accurately distinguish required, optional, nullable, and non-null behavior;
- nullability decisions are supported by HTTP-level tests for representative empty, omitted, null, and populated cases;
- OpenAPI accurately describes the usage summary's top-level collections as concrete, non-null arrays;
- an empty usage response encodes its top-level collections as JSON arrays;
- generated usage collections have concrete element types rather than `any`;
- handwritten API types are either removed or clearly identified as frontend domain models with explicit typed adapters; and
- generated-client freshness checks continue to pass and protect the resulting contracts.

### Alternatives considered

1. **Keep the handwritten response types and unchecked assertions.** This preserves the frontend's current precision, but it leaves two independent contracts that can drift and prevents TypeScript from checking generated responses at the API boundary.
2. **Normalize every generated nullable collection in the frontend.** This is appropriate when `null` is genuinely part of the API contract or when adapting an external boundary, but it would hide inaccurate schemas such as the usage summary's `daily: null` case and encourage tests for states the server does not emit.
3. **Replace every handwritten type with the generated type immediately.** This removes duplication, but it would spread `any[] | null` through application state, discard useful domain distinctions, and force consumers to defend against unsupported null states before the schemas are corrected.
4. **Rely on generated-client freshness checks.** Freshness proves that committed output matches the current OpenAPI document; it does not prove that collection item types or nullability match the handler's runtime behavior.
5. **Mark all collection fields non-null.** This would improve some response types, including the usage summary, but would be incorrect for optional request collections and for response fields where absence or null has defined semantics. Nullability should be established per field with HTTP-level evidence.

title: Add first-class configuration for alternate Claude and Codex homes
body:
## Problem / motivation

Some tools run Claude Code or Codex with a separate home directory for each instance. t3code does this when `homePath` is set. Without `homePath`, its native sessions land in the standard directories that agentsview already discovers and parses. With `homePath`, those sessions move outside the defaults and users must know and configure the exact low-level session directory by hand.

[PR #1496](https://github.com/kenn-io/agentsview/pull/1496) tried to cover this case with a dedicated t3code parser over its SQLite projections. The discussion identified a more general direction:

- [Why a separate parser may be unnecessary](https://github.com/kenn-io/agentsview/pull/1496#issuecomment-5397598974)
- [How t3code's custom `homePath` escapes default discovery](https://github.com/kenn-io/agentsview/pull/1496#issuecomment-5402080475)
- [Preference for easier alternate-home configuration](https://github.com/kenn-io/agentsview/pull/1496#issuecomment-5417148437)

## Proposed solution

Add a first-class way to register one or more alternate homes for the existing Claude Code and Codex providers.

For each configured home, agentsview should:

- derive the provider's native session directory, such as Claude's `projects/` or Codex's `sessions/`;
- pass that directory through the existing discovery, watcher, sync, and parser paths;
- deduplicate it against default roots, environment overrides, explicit provider directories, and `[[session_sources]]`;
- expose the setting through the normal configuration surface and document a t3code `homePath` example.

This should solve the t3code case without adding a t3code-specific parser. Database-only t3code metadata, including its own titles, project grouping, and soft-delete state, is outside this issue. Session names should come from the native Claude or Codex naming mechanisms when available.

## Alternatives considered

Users can configure the underlying Claude or Codex session directory directly today, but that requires knowing how each agent maps a home directory to its on-disk session layout.

The dedicated parser in #1496 recovers t3code-specific database metadata, but it duplicates parsing for sessions already stored in native Claude or Codex formats and adds provider-specific sync behavior.
