`search_sessions` now accepts optional `date_from` and `date_to` values in `YYYY-MM-DD` format. They match the inclusive session-activity date rules used by `list_sessions` and `search_content`; omitting either bound leaves that side unrestricted. The filters apply before pagination through the daemon API and SQLite, PostgreSQL, and DuckDB.

MCP descriptions now recommend hybrid or semantic content search for questions about prior work when a vector index is configured, with keyword and exact-text guidance when those modes are unavailable. Search defaults remain unchanged.

title: fix(usage): restore click-to-hide model attribution
body:
Clicking a model in the Usage attribution treemap, side rail, or list now hides it and leaves the other models visible. These clicks had reused the header model picker's inclusion toggle, which isolated the clicked model instead.

Attribution now uses a separate model-exclusion action. The header picker keeps its selection behavior, the active chart range stays in place, and hidden models survive refreshes and shared URLs. Clear Filters restores all models. The main behavior change is in the usage store, with URL restoration handled by UsagePage.

title: Focused mode treats task notifications as new turns
body:
Follow-up to #1605.

Focused mode decides that a new turn starts at every row with role `user`.
The Claude parser keeps task notifications and stop hook feedback on that role
so analytics do not count them as assistant replies, but those rows arrive
mid-turn while the assistant is still working on the same prompt. Each one
therefore ends the current turn: the assistant text right before it is promoted
to a "final answer", and any narration that a tool call had followed is dropped
outright.

On a session that drives several background agents this defeats the mode. One
real Claude transcript with 29 user prompts and 50 task notifications rendered
145 items in focused mode, most of them notification cards and one-line
"still waiting for the remaining agents" status updates, which is exactly the
intermediate material focused mode exists to strip. Turning off the System
boundaries block does not help, because the role check runs before the
visibility check and the boundary side effect has already happened.

Steps to reproduce:

1. Open a Claude session in which the assistant spawns background agents and
   receives several `<task-notification>` rows before replying.
2. Switch the transcript to Focused.
3. The transcript shows every notification card plus one short assistant
   line before each of them, instead of the prompt and the final answer.

Expected: task notifications and stop hook feedback count as part of the turn
they interrupt. Interruptions, continuations, resumes, and queued commands
should still end the turn.

title: fix(frontend): keep task notifications inside their turn in focused mode
body:
Closes #1650.

Focused mode ended a turn at every row with role `user`. The Claude parser
keeps task notifications and stop hook feedback on that role so analytics do
not count them as assistant replies, but they arrive mid-turn while the
assistant is still working. Each one split the exchange, promoted the "still
waiting" status line before it to a final answer, and dropped any narration
that a tool call had followed. A session driven by background agents came out
as a wall of notification cards and one-line progress updates: one real
transcript rendered 145 focused items for 29 prompts.

`filterDisplayItemsByTranscriptMode` now drops those two subtypes as
intermediate work, the way it already drops tool groups. Interruptions,
continuations, resumes, and queued commands still end the turn, since each of
them really does. Normal mode is unchanged and still renders the cards, where
the System boundaries block toggle from #1606 governs them. The exported HTML
needs no change: `focusedExportOrdinals` already skips every system row
before its boundary logic runs.

The same transcript now renders 53 focused items: its 29 prompts, 23 final
answers, and one interruption. Reviewers should look at the new
`isMidTurnSystemMessage` check at the top of the loop and at the four cases
added to `transcript-mode.test.ts`, including the one that pins an
interruption as a boundary so the rule is not widened by accident.

title: Lifecycles for various commands are tangled
body:
### agentsview version

v0.42.0

### Install method

GitHub release binary

### OS / platform

fedora 43

### Which agent and version

N/A

### Which model(s)

N/A

### What happened, and what did you expect

# `sync` starts daemon, which starts sync, resulting in collision
```
$ agentsview serve stop; ./agentsview sync

Stopped agentsview (pid 1212).

Preparing sync...
Running sync via daemon...
fatal: daemon sync: daemon sync error: {"error":"sync already in progress"}
```
This was the first command I ran, and this is what I got. 

My 3c: 
1. `sync` should either refuse to run if the daemon isn't running
2. or, it should join/pend/block on in-flight sync. It should not treat it as an error.

Related: #1082

# `daemon start` starts web server
```
$ agentsview serve stop; ./agentsview daemon start; ./agentsview serve
Stopped agentsview (pid 1406).

Starting agentsview (pid 1471)...
  log: /root/.agentsview/serve.log
  opening database (0s)
agentsview running at http://127.0.0.1:8080 (pid 1471)

agentsview already running at http://127.0.0.1:8080 (pid 1471)
```

My 3c: 
1. if you consider daemon and serve to be separate components, their lifecycles should be controlled independently. That means if one requires the other, and it hasn't been started, you get an error.
2. if one requires the other, independent control over lifecycle should be exposed.

# Stopping web server shuts down daemon
```
$ agentsview daemon start;  ./agentsview serve stop;  ./agentsview daemon stop
Starting agentsview (pid 1674)...
  log: /root/.agentsview/serve.log
  opening database (0s)
agentsview running at http://127.0.0.1:8080 (pid 1674)
Stopped agentsview (pid 1674).
agentsview daemon is not running.
```
My 3c:
1. This is the same issue as the previous but in the opposite direction. You have separate sub-commands for managing web server and daemon lifecycles independently, but their lifecycles are tied together in the code. This is incoherent. Should users think of agentsview as made up of daemon+server, or just "running an application"?

title: Arguing about arguments
body:
### agentsview version

v0.42.0

### Install method

GitHub release binary

### OS / platform

Fedora 43

### Which agent and version

N/A

### Which model(s)

N/A

### What happened, and what did you expect

# --public-port is really --tls-port

`--public-port` has little if anything to do with --public-url. It's role is to set the HTTPS port when `-proxy caddy` is used. I think it's poorly named. My 3c is that the argument name should tie it to --proxy-*, not to --public-*.

# consistency in argument naming

Why  name `-host` this way, but  `--proxy-bind-host` this way?

shouldn't it be either 
`--bind-host` and  `--proxy-bind-host`
OR 
`--host` and  `--proxy-host`
?


# [Rant Warning] What is --public-url *really* for?

The help says:
```
   --public-url string                   Public URL to trust and open for hostname or proxy access
```
"To trust and open" is a rather strange brew. 

It seems like  `--public-url`  conflates two somewhat unrelated things, and I'm not sure is either needed or makes sense:
1. It's a singleton duplicate of --public-origin - and thus not strictly needed
2. It Instructs agentsview what url to point the launched browser at. For this, it's poorly named.
3. It identifies the "primary url" you expect the app to be accessible from to non-local users, and logs it. But agentsview can't verify that address works since it doesn't control it. So what's the point of logging it as "public"?
what is the value of a "--print-this-value-on start" option?

For me,  printing out "public at https://0.0.0.0:9999", suggests that agentsview is listening at that address, which isn't the case at all. 

Printing out whitelisted origins can be helpful. But since agentsview has not visibility into routing at those hosts, it  shouldn't present them as its "public" facing url.

I also struggle to see when it would make sense to launch a browser to a public url which differs from the backend url. That either means
1.  you're not local and so can't launch a browser, or
2. you're local and can simply access the backend server directly.

So... what is this option for? Why does it mix Origin whitelisting, with browser launching, with reverse-proxies and network routing outside its control?

title: fix(usage): unify model picker and chart visibility
body:
The Usage model picker now controls visibility: checked models are shown, unchecked models are hidden. Clicking an attribution tile unchecks that model, and checking it in the picker restores it without changing the other models. Select all and Deselect all use the same visibility state.

This completes the restore path missed in #1649. Hidden models now seed the picker even when they are absent from a filtered response, including on fresh URLs and reloads. The time-series chart also uses the same exclusions while displaying cached range data.

Usage now stores and shares only `exclude_model` filters. Its former inclusion-only `model` links and saved selections no longer restrict the view. Analytics and API model filters are unchanged. The behavior is concentrated in the usage store and UsagePage; page-level coverage exercises chart clicks, picker restoration, and bulk actions through the real store and mocked API responses.

title: fix(sync): reserve in-place progress for terminals
body:
When you run `agentsview sync` with stdout or stderr redirected to a pipe, file, or CI log, AgentsView now emits readable output. Incremental sync keeps its final summary. Full resync and remote sync keep phase and completion lines. Interactive terminals retain live counters and line clearing.

The bug came from progress renderers writing carriage-return and `ESC[K` control sequences to every output writer. The fix checks the actual destination before using in-place rendering, then preserves existing summaries, timings, hints, `Synced` and `Skipped` results, failure reporting, and startup progress updates. The issue report measured about 700 KB of retained refresh frames for a 6,600-session sync.

Closes #1645

title: fix(codex): link guardian review sessions to their parents
body:
Codex guardian review sessions now appear under the thread that spawned them, so the sidebar, `session list`, and `session search` keep those rollouts with their parent. The parser uses Codex's structural `source.subagent` marker when it reads the top level `parent_thread_id`, while older files with `thread_source: "subagent"` continue to link.

The parser data version moves to 100, which sends existing source files through the archive's normal reparse path and repairs rows that were stored as roots. The issue reproduction and producer format evidence came from @gabe97330's report in https://github.com/kenn-io/agentsview/issues/1644.

Closes #1644

title: fix(cli): clarify listener and browser URL settings
body:
Server startup now labels the listening address and browser URL separately, so a configured URL no longer reads as a claim of public reachability. `--public-url` rejects wildcard bind addresses such as `0.0.0.0` and `::`, with guidance to use the bind flags instead.

Help and remote-access docs distinguish backend and Caddy listeners, the browser URL, and trust-only origins. They correct the Caddy bind default to loopback and explain how explicit URL ports, `--public-port`, and the 8443 default interact.

The existing flag names remain: `--public-url` still selects a browser destination and trusted origin, while `--public-port` applies to managed Caddy in both HTTP and HTTPS modes.

Closes #1653.

title: fix(cli): clarify server lifecycle and wait for busy sync
body:
Local-only incremental sync now waits with visible status when the daemon is busy, then runs its requested pass. Canceling the wait leaves the existing work running. Only contention before a sync starts is retried; actual sync failures still surface immediately. Other API callers retain prompt rejection unless they opt into waiting.

CLI help, the README, and command guides explain that daemon and serve manage the same process, which provides the web UI, API, sync, and file watchers. Sync prints the server URL and stop command, and the docs show how to run once without leaving a server behind.

The waiting message covers the normal daemon's local-only incremental path. Full resync, configured remote sync, and servers started with --no-sync retain their existing wait behavior.

Fixes #1652.

title: fix(parser): preserve Cursor legacy tool results
body:
Legacy Cursor text transcripts now retain nonempty `[Tool result]` bodies as ordered anonymous events on the latest preceding tool call in the same assistant block. Results without a preceding call and empty bodies are omitted. Indented `user:` and `assistant:` lines stay in tool output instead of starting extra messages. The existing call summary selects the last nonempty anonymous result.

Data version 102 makes unchanged, available source files eligible for reparsing, so previously archived sessions gain the output on their next sync. Incremental S3 sync also checks stale parser versions, so an old object modification time does not prevent recovery. Current S3 sources still follow the modification-time cutoff. Cursor also declares its result-event capability.

The parser keeps its existing indentation convention: a nonempty unindented line ends a result body and becomes assistant prose. `docs/internal/session-format-sources.md` records the live-inspection report in #1627 and its limits; the available references contain no raw legacy excerpt that verifies indentation. JSONL parsing is unchanged.

Refs #1627

title: feat(parser): support Open Code Review sessions
body:
Open Code Review sessions now appear in AgentsView from `.opencodereview/sessions`, with review metadata, thinking, tool results, structured review comments, recorded token usage, and resume links. The new provider supports custom session directories and replaces parsed sessions when appended tool results update earlier calls.

The parser counts new user turns from main and plan requests, excludes auxiliary prompts, and avoids replaying compressed history. It treats `task_done` as a control signal and separates uncached input from cached tokens for pricing. Upstream fallback or proxy usage records can omit whether prompt totals include cached tokens; those records may undercount. The pinned format evidence and limitations are recorded in `docs/internal/session-format-sources.md`.

Closes #1612

title: feat(parser): add Tau session support
body:
Adds Tau as a native file provider so AgentsView can browse and search sessions under `~/.tau/sessions/`, with session names, working directories, thinking, tools, models, and recorded token usage. Tau sessions use an amber accent in the frontend.

Discovery excludes the metadata-only `index.jsonl`. The parser follows the latest `leaf` through the entry tree and replaces the stored transcript when the active branch changes, removing abandoned messages and usage. Ordinary session IDs come from filenames; default sessions remain scoped to their project directory and canonical configured root. Token accounting counts the total `cacheWrite` once and uses catalog pricing instead of Tau's stored cost object.

The parser renders separate branch-summary and compaction entries. It skips messages with roles `bashExecution` (user-run shell commands), `custom`, `branchSummary`, and `compactionSummary`, and does not synchronize index metadata or convert legacy Tau v1 sessions. The format evidence document links the pinned upstream source and records these limits. The issue reproduction always uses the checked-in sanitized fixture.

Closes #1634

title: fix(parser): use Cursor turn timestamps instead of file mtime for session times
body:
Cursor transcripts now retain user turn times when the source includes the leading `<timestamp>` metadata tag. AgentsView parses the explicit UTC offset at minute precision, stores zero seconds, and derives session bounds from the earliest and latest usable user turns. Transcripts without a usable tag keep their file modification time, and the latest user turn remains a lower bound because Cursor provides no assistant completion time. Existing Cursor sessions reparse to receive the corrected values.

The parser recognizes the tag only in the Cursor user metadata position immediately before `<user_query>`. Ordinary timestamp XML outside that position remains in message content. Incomplete or unusable leading candidates keep the existing `<user_query>` extraction with an empty timestamp. The shared Grok user-query behavior remains unchanged.

This change follows prateek's report in issue #1627. The legacy transcript fixture is constructed and sanitized because the issue does not include a loadable transcript artifact. Its tag values follow the observed Cursor grammar.

Refs #1627

title: feat(db): add tool-result image retention and db strip --images
body:
`agentsview db strip --images` removes supported inline image payloads from archived tool results while preserving surrounding text, event identity, and original source files. Project and date filters also reach trashed and source-missing sessions. Each changed session is rescanned for secrets in the same transaction so detections and their offsets match the remaining content. Run `agentsview db compact` afterward to reclaim SQLite free pages; content savings and disk reclamation are reported separately.

Set `tool_result_images = "drop"` in `config.toml` to apply the same policy to future writes. This is a TOML-only setting; desktop Settings and the settings API do not expose it. The default `keep` preserves existing provider decoding. Supported Codex image arrays become structured placeholders with media type and decoded byte size, displayed alongside their text in the UI.

Large Codex imports project events before scratch storage, and late results preserve raw digests before projection so replay deduplication remains stable. Combined summaries strip both labeled and anonymous sections, including summaries rebuilt from older events. Full resync projects only copied archived sessions; freshly parsed sessions are already projected. Review the staged sink and incremental result writer for these storage boundaries. Windows sync tests are split across two exhaustive jobs to fit the existing 20-minute timeout.

Closes #1622

title: feat(parser): read Cursor CLI store.db transcripts
body:
Cursor CLI sessions now gain assistant reasoning and producer timestamps from matching `~/.cursor/chats/<workspace>/<agent-id>/store.db` files while keeping the transcript's session identity. Previously, AgentsView read only the text or JSONL transcript under `~/.cursor/projects`.

The provider reads the database and its WAL in one read-only transaction, follows only the tree selected by `latestRootBlobId`, and aligns decoded turns with transcript messages. The composite fingerprint detects store changes even when the transcript is unchanged.

Chats directory scan failures and readable stores with missing required tables or columns, or unsupported metadata or blob structure leave transcripts available for initial import and later updates, with a warning. A failed scan retains usable cached store locations and retries on the next discovery pass. Database open/read errors remain retryable source errors that preserve existing archive content. Temporary path-access failures retain cached stores and newly observed store candidates for retry, and store fingerprint failures prevent freshness skips.

Format evidence is limited to one installed Cursor CLI capture. Native tool-call/result joining, store-only discovery, encrypted payloads, and cross-version field stability remain outside this change. Store enrichment is local and automatically associates chats only with a resolved `.cursor/projects` root. Custom roots such as `.cursor/archive` remain transcript-only. The chats directory stays outside remote, SSH, and S3 transfer targets. Store and WAL events map back to the transcript, and shared-memory events are ignored by the provider.

Refs #1627

title: fix(daemon): self-heal an orphaned startup-state lock
body:
On some setups, if the app crashes while starting up, it gets stuck forever saying "startup is still in progress" and can never launch again you have to manually delete startup-state.json to fix it. That's because it only checks if the start lock is held, not whether the process that's supposedly holding it is actually still alive.

Fixed it to check the recorded pid before trusting the lock if that process is dead, it clears the stale state automatically instead of getting stuck. Added tests for both cases (dead pid clears it, live pid still blocks correctly).

Closes #1558

title: perf(activity): speed up reports on large archives
body:
Activity reports no longer read historical tool-result payloads for every session while finding sessions in the selected period. SQLite and PostgreSQL now use a partial index on session and timestamp for completed or errored tool-execution events. The existing report query still includes completions that outlive session end metadata.

On an isolated large-archive snapshot, the same HTTP report took 60.1 seconds before indexing, 4.06 seconds on the first request afterward, and 0.44 seconds on a repeated request after reopening. The report data was unchanged.

Existing SQLite archives receive the index on their next writable open. PostgreSQL schema setup and the push readiness check install it for existing mirrors. Building the index requires a one-time scan and can delay that startup; SQLite logs the wait. The index does not require a session resync. Reviewers should focus on the partial-index predicates and the PostgreSQL push upgrade path.

title: ci: right-size Namespace runners, share build caches, and remove benchmark gate
body:
Linux and Windows CI use Namespace runners for pushes and pull requests. Lint, integration, docs/scripts, and Windows Go/Rust unit jobs use 4 CPUs; Linux full Go/race, frontend, E2E, and desktop packaging use 8 CPUs. CI has 14 jobs: docs and scripts share a job, Windows Capture/Database/Parser share setup, and the complete Windows Sync suite runs in one job. macOS, ARM, and the Ubuntu 22.04 release AppImage baseline retain their existing runners.

Namespace jobs use local Go, npm, Rust, and Playwright caches instead of duplicate GitHub cache transfers. The desktop composite opts into Namespace caching only for Namespace runners. GitHub Go-cache uploads are limited to GitHub-hosted desktop runners so self-hosted jobs do not archive their shared caches during cleanup. Runner profiles are configured externally with Restricted access and cache writes limited to main. SQLite header preparation and private Windows temporary directories cover differences in the Namespace images; timing-sensitive test fixtures use deterministic inputs. Sidebar E2E assertions wait before navigation and teardown.

The benchmark gate workflows are removed so benchmark ratios no longer block pull requests. Local benchmark comparisons and deterministic work-count tests remain available.

title: fix: honor remote project discovery policy in OpenHands
body:
OpenHands sessions imported from another machine now derive project names from their recorded paths without inspecting those directories on the receiving machine. Previously, OpenHands dropped the existing import policy and could pick up an unrelated local repository or probe a network-backed path. Local sessions keep their normal Git project discovery.

This is the focused OpenHands follow-up to #1638. Imported sessions may use the recorded directory name instead of a repository name discovered on the receiving machine.

title: test(parser): stabilize Evener fingerprint checks
body:
Stabilizes three Evener fingerprint tests that could fail when rapid file updates shared filesystem timestamps. The metadata rewrite now waits for a distinct change time while preserving size and modification time. The replacement parent and each parent-metadata revision receive explicitly different modification times.

The existing digest, content-hash, and parsed-history assertions remain intact. This changes only test setup.

title: Show reasoning effort alongside model in session breadcrumb
body: The session breadcrumb's model badge (the `model-badge` span after the cost) shows the model name but not the reasoning effort level. For sessions where the agent uses a configurable effort (e.g. `xhigh`, `high`, `medium`, `low`), the badge should display both, like `gpt-5.6-luna xhigh` or `claude-opus-4-6 medium` instead of just the model name. ## How the model badge works today The breadcrumb reads `mainModel` from the messages store (`messages.svelte.ts:30`), which calls `computeMainModel()` (`utils/model.ts`). That function iterates all assistant messages and picks the most frequently used `message.model` string by count, with alphabetical tie-breaking. The per-message `model` field is populated by the backend parser. For pi-family agents (Claude Code, Codex), `pi.go:523` reads `gjson.Get(line, "message.model")` from the JSONL transcript. The `Message` interface (`api/types/core.ts:151`) has a `model: string` field but no reasoning effort field. The model badge renders at `SessionBreadcrumb.svelte:1077`: ```svelte {#if mainModel} {mainModel} {/if} ``` ## What needs to happen Reasoning effort should appear next to the model, using the same resolution method. Since `computeMainModel` picks the model from the last (most frequent) assistant message, the effort level should follow the same logic, either: 1. Derive a `mainReasoningEffort` from messages the same way `mainModel` is derived (most frequent effort among assistant messages that match the main model), or 2. Pair model + effort as a composite key so they're resolved together The backend parsers would need to extract reasoning effort from the transcript JSONL (if present in the source data) and expose it on the `Message` or as a separate per-message field. The frontend `Message` type and the `model-badge` rendering would then include it. The breadcrumb already has limited horizontal space, so the effort label should be compact (the raw string like `xhigh` or `high`, not a verbose label).

title: fix(docker): reuse base-image build tools and certificates
body:
Removes Debian package downloads from the Docker build, where mirror requests were exhausting the 90-second timeout. The Go Bookworm base already supplies the compilers and CA certificates; the runtime image now copies that CA bundle from the build stage.

Removes the unused mirror lists. Base images, application compilation, entrypoint, and runner configuration are unchanged.

title: Add an option to render unknown XML blocks as preformatted text
body:
Diffs inside unknown XML-style prompt tags render as Markdown lists and headings in the session viewer. @thibaudcolas reported this while testing Open Code Review in https://github.com/kenn-io/agentsview/pull/1660#issuecomment-5583286507 I reproduced it through the shared `renderMarkdown` function with this input: ```text diff --git a/example.py b/example.py --- a/example.py +++ b/example.py @@ -1,2 +1 @@ - # FIXME: replace this - old_value + new_value ``` The output contains lists and an `

` for the deleted comment. Replacing the wrapper with `` or `` produces the same result. Any provider that supplies this text can hit the issue. `frontend/src/lib/utils/markdown.ts` preserves unknown tags as escaped text, but it tokenizes the enclosed content as Markdown first. The relevant renderer code is identical at PR #1660's head and main commit `c34055661f2deb35facf9f53485fa46e878b376d`. Following @mariusvniekerk's suggestion, add a display preference to render unknown XML blocks as preformatted text, including their tags. Keep current rendering as the default, since some prompts intentionally put Markdown inside those tags. Recognize complete blocks before Markdown tokenization, preserve whitespace, and include the preference in the render cache key. Existing HTML sanitization, shell wrappers, code fences and inline code need to retain their behavior. This follows the tag-preservation work in https://github.com/kenn-io/agentsview/pull/892 and belongs in the shared renderer. Parser output can remain unchanged.

title: Keep long agent names distinguishable in the session sidebar
body: Long agent names lose their distinguishing text in the session sidebar. @thibaudcolas reported that OpenCode and Open Code Review are hard to tell apart while testing PR #1660. Screenshot from the original report: Source: https://github.com/kenn-io/agentsview/pull/1660#issuecomment-5583286507 `frontend/src/lib/components/sidebar/SessionItem.svelte` applies `max-width: 52px`, `white-space: nowrap`, `overflow: hidden` and `text-overflow: ellipsis` to every `.agent-tag`. Custom agent labels use the same element, so this also affects other long names. The rule is identical at PR #1660's head and main commit `c34055661f2deb35facf9f53485fa46e878b376d`. To reproduce, view OpenCode and Open Code Review sessions together in the sidebar using PR #1660's build. Compare their displayed labels with the full provider names. Other sufficiently long provider or custom labels reach the same width limit. Let agent names use available row space so users can distinguish them while scanning sessions. Check narrow sidebar widths and rows with other metadata. Expose the full name when truncation remains necessary, though a tooltip alone would still require hovering to distinguish sessions. This is a shared sidebar layout issue and can be handled separately from the Open Code Review parser.

title: test: make embedding scheduler retry coverage deterministic
body:
Stabilizes three embedding scheduler regression tests for pending backstop requests. Their notifications raced with automatic retries: a notification delivered after recovery could trigger an unrelated build and fail an exact-count assertion on a slow runner.

The tests now let retries run without extra notifications under Go 1.27's [synctest.Sleep](https://pkg.go.dev/testing/synctest@go1.27.0#Sleep), which advances fake time and waits for goroutines to settle. Coverage still checks retry counts, preservation of the backstop request through collisions and failures, and clearing it after recovery.

This changes only test timing, not scheduler behavior.

title: hermes: ended_at is null for in-progress sessions, so an active conversation always shows its start time and never sorts to the top
body:
### Summary

For the `hermes` provider, `ended_at` is only populated once a session closes. Every other provider I have loaded keeps `ended_at` moving with the newest message while the session is still running. Because the UI uses `ended_at` as the "last activity" timestamp for relative times and for ordering the session list, a hermes conversation that is actively in progress permanently displays its **start** time and never rises in the list.

The practical effect is that the one session you are talking in right now is the one that looks stalest.

### Version

`agentsview v0.42.0 (commit ff8fb4e8, built 2026-09-01T19:35:44Z)`, running `serve` in a container and reading a hermes archive (`state.db` + `sessions/`) mounted read-only.

### Evidence

Both of these sessions were open and receiving messages at the moment `GET /api/v1/sessions` was called:

```
agent   id                        ended_at                    started_at
claude  windows~c7f26306-...      2026-09-08T21:02:33.290Z    2026-09-08T19:39:52.498Z
hermes  hermes:20260908_103923_…  null                        2026-09-08T14:39:23.417Z
```

The Claude Code row carries an `ended_at` that tracks the latest message even though the session has not ended. The hermes row has `null`, so the UI falls back to `started_at` and renders "6h ago" while `message_count` climbs correctly (I watched it go 33 → 46 → 53 over a few minutes).

`session get` on the hermes session agrees:

```
Name:          Start a conversation
Started At:    2026-09-08T14:39:23.417868137Z
Ended At:      -
Messages:      5/31
```

Closed hermes sessions are fine — they all show sensible relative times — so the bug is specific to sessions still in progress.

### Expected

An in-progress hermes session should sort and display by its most recent message, the same way the JSONL-backed providers behave. Whether that means populating `ended_at` from `max(message timestamp)` while the session is open, or having the UI fall back to the newest message rather than `started_at`, is a design call — but the two providers should not disagree.

### Reproduce

1. Point agentsview at a hermes archive (`HERMES_SESSIONS_DIR` covering `state.db` and `sessions/`).
2. Start a conversation in hermes and leave it open.
3. Send messages to it and let agentsview sync.
4. `GET /api/v1/sessions` — the hermes row's `message_count` increases while `ended_at` stays `null`, and the UI keeps showing the session's start age.

### Workaround

`ended_at: null` turns out to be a usable "still open" marker, so filtering for it and sorting by `started_at` descending finds the live conversation. That is obviously not something a UI user can do.

title: cursor-ide: one NULL cursorDiskKV value fails every sync worker pass (jsontext: unexpected EOF)
body:
### Summary

A single row in Cursor's `state.vscdb` whose `value` is SQL `NULL` makes the cursor-ide parser fail, and that one failure marks the entire startup sync worker pass as failed — on every pass, forever. The daemon keeps serving and other providers keep indexing, but the console shows `fatal: sync worker startup: failed` at every start and the log fills at roughly one error every five seconds.

### Version

`agentsview v0.42.0 (commit ff8fb4e8, built 2026-09-01T19:35:44Z)`, Windows, daemon started as `serve --background --no-browser`.

### Symptom

```
2026/09/07 19:52:35 sync error: decoding cursor IDE composer 1bf6b690-…: jsontext: unexpected EOF
… repeated every ~5s …
ERROR: startup sync worker ran but did not complete: startup worker pass reported failed (surfacing incomplete pass; not re-syncing in process)
```

13,734 occurrences of that line accumulated in `debug.log` over about 20 hours. On the console, mixed into the startup banner:

```
  332/332 sessions (100%) · 43 messages   fatal: sync worker startup: failed
```

### Root cause

The offending record is not corrupt or truncated — the value is `NULL`. Reading `%APPDATA%\Cursor\User\globalStorage\state.vscdb` directly:

```
table = cursorDiskKV
key   = composerData:1bf6b690-2756-4be9-8cfd-033354f0e040
value = NULL
```

Handing that nil byte slice to the JSON decoder produces exactly `unexpected EOF`.

It is not a one-off. That database had **64 rows with a NULL value** out of 2,189 in `cursorDiskKV` — 2 `composerData:` keys and 62 `bubbleId:` keys. Only the first is ever logged, because the pass gives up there.

I have not established what leaves the NULLs behind; the database had not been written since February and Cursor was no longer installed on the machine, so they look like rows Cursor orphaned rather than anything agentsview did.

### Expected

A NULL or empty value for one key should be skipped (ideally counted, the way parser anomalies already are) rather than failing the whole worker pass. As it stands, one dead row in an unused editor's leftover database permanently reports every sync as failed.

### Reproduce

Insert a NULL-valued `composerData:` row into `cursorDiskKV` in a `state.vscdb` under a cursor-ide root and start the daemon.

### Workaround

Either delete the NULL rows:

```sql
DELETE FROM cursorDiskKV WHERE value IS NULL;
```

or remove the cursor-ide root entirely. I did the latter (the editor was uninstalled). Immediately afterwards the discovery line came back clean and the errors stopped:

```
watcher error: remove invalidated native watch "…\Cursor\User\globalStorage": GetFileAttributes: The system cannot find the file specified.
discovered 328 files (313 claude, 0 codex, 2 copilot, 0 cursor, 11 vscode-copilot, …) in 76ms
```

Zero `sync error` lines and zero worker-pass failures since. Note there is no per-provider disable switch in v0.42.0, so deleting the data directory was the only way to opt out of the cursor-ide root.

Adjacent to #1515, which covers cursor-ide sessions in `cursorDiskKV` not being discovered; this one is about a single bad row there taking down the whole pass.

title: feat(sessions): show reasoning effort beside the model
body:
The session breadcrumb now shows recorded reasoning effort beside the model for Claude Code and Codex sessions. The header chooses the most common model, then the most common effort among assistant messages using that model, with alphabetical tie-breaking. Sessions without recorded effort keep the model-only label. The optional field is preserved through parsing, storage, mirrors, artifacts, API responses, and sync comparisons.

Existing archives perform a full session resync on upgrade to populate effort from source transcripts. This can take time for large archives. Sessions whose source files are gone remain in the archive with their existing data.

The responsive header changes apply to all sessions. Compact metadata now starts at 900px instead of 760px: timestamps, session IDs, and the usage breakdown are hidden at 900px or narrower. At 640px or narrower, the agent badge is also hidden and spacing is reduced. The model label can truncate while the effort token and session actions remain visible.

![Session breadcrumb with recorded reasoning effort](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rodboev/agentsview/screenshots/agentsview-1670-after.png)

Closes #1670

title: fix(sidebar): let agent names use available row width
body:
Long agent names use more of the session sidebar, so OpenCode and Open Code Review remain distinguishable while you scan rows. Names that still need truncation show their full label in a tooltip on hover.

`SessionItem.svelte` capped every agent label at 52px even when the sidebar had more room. This change lets the label use a bounded share of the row while preserving the flexible session title, machine metadata, entrypoint resolution and suppression, row actions, and responsive sidebar limits. Long entrypoint badges stay on one line and ellipsize within that bound.

The reproduction came from @thibaudcolas while testing https://github.com/kenn-io/agentsview/pull/1660#issuecomment-5583286507.

Closes #1673

title: fix(frontend): add preformatted rendering for unknown XML blocks (#1672)
body:
Selecting "Render unknown XML blocks as preformatted text" in Appearance settings makes complete unknown XML blocks display as literal preformatted text with their opening and closing tags, so diff text keeps its literal lines. The default renderer keeps its current behavior for prompts that intentionally use Markdown inside unknown tags.

This adds a browser-local preference, passes it through all six shared Markdown consumers, recognizes complete blocks before Markdown tokenization, preserves whitespace inside the block, and includes the preference in the renderer cache key. The block scanner keeps Markdown prose, known HTML, inline code, fenced code, and mismatched tags on their existing paths, including malformed nested blocks whose inner tags close first. Existing HTML sanitization, shell wrappers, asset links, and parser output remain unchanged. The current workaround requires the provider text to include a fenced code block, which stored provider output cannot add after capture.

The shared behavior lives in `markdown.ts`, with the preference in `ui.svelte.ts` and the control in Appearance settings. The reproduction came from a user report on Discord and @thibaudcolas's report on https://github.com/kenn-io/agentsview/pull/1660; https://github.com/kenn-io/agentsview/pull/892 supplies the existing custom XML tag preservation path.

The enabled session view renders the issue fixture as an XML block using the active app background, text color, and border. Regular code blocks keep their existing palette.

![Unknown XML in the light theme](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rodboev/agentsview/0363bf22c9a54900a1dcefb83dca70042561f51c/docs/review/1679-xml-light.png)

![Unknown XML in the dark theme](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rodboev/agentsview/0363bf22c9a54900a1dcefb83dca70042561f51c/docs/review/1679-xml-dark.png)

Closes #1672

title: fix(identity): preserve local history when adopting installation IDs
body:
Keep local session history together across updates, restarts, and hostname changes. AgentsView owns the existing plain ID file, `telemetry-install-id`, and creates it even with telemetry disabled; PostHog consumes that ID. The display label defaults to the current hostname or an explicit `local_machine_name`. Creating an identity does not force a config rewrite.

Upgrade moves the archive's recorded local sessions, worktree rules, and project/source metadata to the installation ID in one transaction. Session IDs, content, and curation stay intact. Adopted hostnames remain aliases for saved filters, URLs, and generated insights. Read handlers use the shared filter resolver without rewriting request URLs.

Unknown hostname keys remain untouched and are logged once; startup continues. Operators can inspect them with `db adopt-machine --list` and explicitly adopt history they own. Matching labels never prove ownership. Conflicting worktree rules still require reconciliation, and retired hostnames no longer grant artifact export ownership.

Local `session_sources` entries must omit `machine`; remove any old hostname setting. PostgreSQL republishes adopted history incrementally and accepts alias updates; in a shared mirror, the latest push wins a hostname-alias collision. DuckDB rebuilds once when its default machine key changes. Label edits take effect after a daemon restart and the next mirror push. Copying the data directory copies its identity; deleting the ID file creates a new installation without automatically claiming the previous one's history.

title: feat(config): add Pi home support and structured agent directories
body:
Pi sessions are now discovered from `PI_CODING_AGENT_DIR` and `PI_CODING_AGENT_SESSION_DIR`, locally and over SSH. `PI_DIR` retains priority, and discovery handles both flat session directories and the default project-grouped layout.

Directory configuration now uses `[agents.<id>]` tables. Locally discovered providers accept `dirs`; Claude, Codex, and Pi also accept additive `homes`. Settings edits those home lists using the same shared configuration path.

Normal startup converts existing top-level directory and home keys once, replacing the config file atomically. Read-only commands convert in memory. Conflicting old and new entries produce an error without rewriting the file. Conversion preserves unrelated settings but rewrites TOML formatting and comments. Review `internal/config/agent_directories.go` for conversion and persistence behavior.

Closes #1681

title: fix(copilot): report output without shutdown summaries
body:
Completed Copilot responses now contribute their known output tokens even when no shutdown summary exists. Output already covered by a shutdown stays suppressed, while responses after a resumed session's last shutdown remain counted. Input, cache, and reasoning usage are not invented.

This is the first replacement for #1626. It contains only transcript parsing and the data-version refresh; observed store usage and shared-store performance follow in dependent PRs.

Merge order: #1683, then #1684, then #1685.

title: fix(copilot): import observed request usage without double counting
body:
Copilot sessions now import observed per-call tokens from session-store.db, so usage can appear before shutdown. Each row receives request-level catalog pricing without requiring a transcript message ordinal. The latest shutdown reported cost remains authoritative.

A failed earlier store insert can coexist with a later successful row. Overlapping transcript output contributes only its positive per-model excess over store output; a recovered row replaces that excess without double counting. This remains a lower bound when extra store-only calls mask missing output, and it cannot recover missing input or request bands.

This is the second replacement for #1626. The dependent performance PR bounds refresh work for the shared store.

Merge order: #1683, then #1684, then #1685.

title: perf(copilot): refresh shared-store usage without rereading transcripts
body:
A Copilot store update now rereads usage payloads only for sessions whose latest row ID changed. Unchanged transcript hashes are reused across provider instances and engine restarts. Shared database timestamps affect freshness, not session timestamps.

The producer leaves sessions.updated_at unchanged when inserting usage, so the refresh uses the producer's session-and-row-ID index. Startup builds the store hashes once. Runtime updates follow appends and latest-row removal; historical edits below an unchanged maximum ID wait for a new engine or CLI sync. Missing or incomplete usage schemas are cached as empty usage for the current SQLite state, so metadata-only writes leave unchanged sessions skipped. Unreadable store markers and operational read failures remain retryable.

title: fix(parser): import OpenCode 2.0 sessions and preserve upgrade history
body:
OpenCode 2.0 stores conversations in `session_message` projections, and the released beta moves session metadata to `session_v2`. Import those layouts so beta conversations appear with their text, reasoning, tools, results, and token usage.

Preserve history when earlier CLI messages and API projections share a session, and keep unmigrated sessions visible during upgrades. Prefer migrated projections and use OpenCode's migration marker to prevent deleted beta sessions from reappearing through retained legacy rows. Include terminal idle timestamps in session duration and freshness, retain attachment-only prompts, and mark completed compactions as context boundaries. Inline text attachments retain their content; binary and URI-only attachments retain named placeholders.

Captured workflows from GitHub beta 19381 and OpenCode 1.18.25 back the parser fixtures, alongside a simulator for projection updates and sync behavior. The exact `2.0.0-beta.7` label in the issue remains unverified. Data version 104 makes existing imports eligible for correction without another producer write. The format provenance document records the pinned upstream sources and observed upgrade behavior.

Closes #1642.

title: Idle serve daemon burns most of a machine's CPU: the usage-cache backfill re-reads every installed rollup row for each 256-session batch
body:
### agentsview version

agentsview v0.42.0 (commit ff8fb4e8, built 2026-09-01T19:37:16Z), and still present on `main` at 988c7406.

### Install method

Built from source

### OS / platform

Ubuntu 24.04.4 LTS (x86_64), 24 cores

### Which agent and version

n/a (usage cache / serve daemon)

### Which model(s)

n/a

### What happened, and what did you expect

On a large archive the serve daemon sits at eight to nine cores with no clients connected and startup sync long finished. Expected an idle daemon to be idle.

The cost is the usage-cache backfill. `readUsageRollupInstalls` in `internal/db/usage_rollup.go` filters only on `timezone_key`:

```sql
FROM usage_rollup_timezones tz JOIN usage_rollup_installs i
  ON i.timezone_id = tz.id WHERE tz.timezone_key = ?
```

A backfill pass correctly narrows each batch to 256 sessions and calls `Ensure` per batch, but that read is unscoped, so every batch materializes *all* installed rows into four maps and discards them — twice per batch whenever anything is stale. The pass is therefore quadratic in archive size.

Measured on a 128,343-session archive with 141,454 installed rollup rows: one daemon lifetime spent 3,161 CPU-seconds and 27,798 GC cycles, nearly all of it in a five-and-a-half-minute window that ended when the backfill gave up with `could not stabilize after 3 attempts`. The allocation profile attributed 57% of allocation to `readUsageRollupInstalls` alone. Each of the 502 batches read 141,454 rows to verify 256. Against the 256 MiB soft memory limit the serve daemon sets for itself, that allocation rate is what turns a slow pass into sustained garbage collection.

The archive's cache had not finished a backfill in three days, so it was being rebuilt from scratch and abandoned on every daemon start.

Query plan for the read today:

```
SCAN i
```

### Steps to reproduce

1. Build an archive large enough that installed rollup rows greatly outnumber a 256-session batch (this was 128,343 sessions / 141,454 installed rows; the effect scales with the ratio, so it shows up well below that).
2. Start `agentsview serve` and leave it with no clients connected.
3. Watch CPU during the usage-cache backfill, or take a heap profile and look at the share of allocation under `readUsageRollupInstalls`.

Scoping the read to the sessions a snapshot can actually consult turns the scan into one seek per batched session against the unique `(timezone_id, session_id)` index — 257 rows instead of 141,454 per batch, plan `SEARCH i USING COVERING INDEX (timezone_id=? AND session_id=?)`. Rebuilt against the same archive, the pass completes in 4 minutes 6 seconds for 1,349 CPU-seconds and 14,397 GC cycles, and `readUsageRollupInstalls` falls to 0.6% of allocation. That was the difference between never finishing and finishing on this archive.

I have that change ready with a regression test and will open a PR against this issue.

### Checklist

- [x] I searched existing issues
- [x] I removed secrets and private data from any attached session files

title: fix(db): scope usage rollup install reads to the snapshot
body:
On a large archive the serve daemon burned most of a machine's CPU with no clients connected and startup sync long finished. Measured on a 24-core machine against a 128,343-session archive with 141,454 installed rollup rows, one daemon lifetime spent 3,161 CPU-seconds and 27,798 GC cycles, nearly all of it inside a five-and-a-half-minute window that ended when the backfill gave up with `could not stabilize after 3 attempts` — eight to nine cores sustained, of which the allocation profile attributed 57% to `readUsageRollupInstalls` alone. That read filtered only on `timezone_key`, so although a backfill pass correctly narrows each batch to 256 sessions and calls `Ensure` per batch, each of the 502 batches materialized all 141,454 installed rows into four maps and discarded them, twice per batch whenever anything was stale. The pass is quadratic in archive size, and against the 256 MiB soft memory limit the serve daemon sets for itself, that allocation rate is what turns a slow pass into sustained garbage collection.

This scopes the read to the sessions a snapshot can actually consult, binding them and the cursor row through the package's existing `maxSQLVars` and `inPlaceholders` seam. The unique `(timezone_id, session_id)` index turns the table scan into one seek per batched session, so a batched verification materializes 257 rows instead of 141,454 and the plan changes from `SCAN i` to `SEARCH i USING COVERING INDEX (timezone_id=? AND session_id=?)`.

Iterating `Versions` alone is sufficient because `Sessions` and `Versions` are appended one-for-one at capture, filtered by the same predicate in `dropDeleted`, reordered together, and sliced together per batch. Snapshots above the bind limit — the whole-archive verification at the end of a pass, and the foreground usage read — keep the unscoped query, which returns a superset of the same rows; that is safe because `installs` is only ever indexed by key and is never ranged over. Rollup contents, install revisions, staleness semantics, batch size, and the retry policy are unchanged, and no schema or column changes are involved, so the PostgreSQL and DuckDB paths need no matching update.

Reviewers should look at the bind gate in `readUsageRollupInstalls`, which reserves one parameter for the timezone predicate, and at `internal/db/usage_rollup_lifecycle_test.go`, where a real-database regression proves a batched verification does not materialize an installed session outside its batch.

Rebuilt and run against that same archive, the pass now completes in 4 minutes 6 seconds for 1,349 CPU-seconds and 14,397 GC cycles, and `readUsageRollupInstalls` falls to 0.6% of allocation; the remaining 63.5% is `loadUsageRollupFacts` building the rollups, which is linear and one-time. That archive's cache had not finished a backfill in three days, so it was being rebuilt from scratch and abandoned on every daemon start. This change does not alter how often a pass restarts — on an archive whose transcripts are appended continuously, a pass can still exhaust its three attempts against `errUsageCacheSourceChanged` — it just loses far less work each time, which on this archive was the difference between never finishing and finishing.


Closes #1688

title: fix(pricing): correct Codex costs on Amazon Bedrock
body:
Fix missing or incorrect cost estimates for Codex sessions using GPT-5.4, GPT-5.6 Luna, GPT-5.6 Terra, or GPT-6 Astra through Amazon Bedrock.

These sessions report names such as `openai.gpt-6-astra`. Agentsview now uses Bedrock prices for those exact names, wherever they are reported. Direct OpenAI names such as `gpt-6-astra` continue to use their own pricing lookup.

Use historical Bedrock prices when available, so older Luna and Terra sessions use the prices from before the July 30 cut. Include Astra's Bedrock prices in the app so costs are available before an online price refresh. Recalculate cached usage totals with the corrected pricing.

Keep custom price overrides, regional prices such as GovCloud, and the model names shown in usage breakdowns.

title: fix(parser): skip NULL cursorDiskKV values instead of failing the cursor-ide pass
body:
A Cursor IDE database with an empty `cursorDiskKV` row no longer fails the sync worker pass. One such row used to abort the whole parse with `jsontext: unexpected EOF`, dropping every other conversation and reporting `sync worker startup: failed` at each start, with no in-app fix.

A SQL `NULL` scans into a nil byte slice and a zero-length blob into an empty one, and neither is `sql.ErrNoRows`, so both reached the JSON decoder. The composer and bubble readers now treat a row holding no bytes as absent rather than malformed; a row with even one byte still fails loudly.

A composer with no bytes yields no result, and its session moves to the recoverable source-missing state with its transcript intact. A bubble with no bytes becomes one transcript gap, flagged truncated so the engine still refuses to drop an archived message.

The guard covers both `NULL` and empty blobs, since an empty value hits the identical error with the identical reach. It adds no anomaly counter, because that branch also covers a bubble row that never existed, so counting there would move a published number for databases with no empty rows.

Closes #1676

title: fix(parser): keep Hermes session activity timestamps current
body:
Hermes sessions imported from `state.db` now advance their last-activity time as messages arrive instead of staying at their start time until Hermes closes the session.

The parser reconciles the selected transcript's end time, the recorded `ended_at`, and the newest state message timestamp. A message advances the end time only when it is newer than both the existing end time and `started_at`. This covers stale JSON snapshots and close times that precede newer messages through both archive and per-session imports, using already loaded rows without extra queries.

Open sessions can now carry an end time, as Hermes JSON transcripts already do. Timing stops labeling them as running, and Recall's “has not ended” check no longer blocks them. Usage event timestamps still follow the recorded end or start time, so daily usage attribution remains a separate follow-up.

Closes #1675

title: feat(settings): add tool-result image retention control
body:
Open Settings, choose Archive content, and pick Keep or Drop for tool-result images. Drop makes ingestion store a readable `agentsview_image` placeholder carrying the media type, decoded byte size, and any hash the source block already provided, in place of a base64 payload. The `tool_result_images` key previously existed only in `config.toml`, with no read or write surface above it.

![Archive content settings panel with Keep and Drop options for tool-result images](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rodboev/agentsview/screenshots/agentsview-1622-6-after.png)

The field goes on `GET` and `PUT /api/v1/settings` as a `keep`/`drop` enum beside `chart_palette` rather than under `/api/v1/config`, which holds a multi-field composite needing cross-field validation and a write-only secret whose read is a derived boolean. A single validated enum belongs with the other settings scalars, and `config.SaveSettings` already accepted and validated this exact patch key. The enum tag rejects an out-of-range value before the handler runs, so the stored selection is untouched, and a write persists the documented spelling.

The selection applies to the daemon's own ingestion after a restart, the same way `disabled_agents` and the remote-access toggle already behave, and the panel says so. Projection stays a write-time property, so stored sessions render exactly as before and switching back to Keep does not restore payloads a previous Drop removed. `agentsview db strip --images` remains the way to project rows that are already stored, and nothing under `internal/db` or `internal/sync` changes.

Refs #1622

title: feat(data): add tool-result image cleanup endpoints and panel
body:
Open Settings, choose Tool-result images, and click Preview to see how many stored tool results still hold inline image payloads, broken down by project with stored and decoded byte totals. Removing them replaces each payload with a readable placeholder. Until now `agentsview db strip --images` was the only way to do this, so it was out of reach for anyone not running the CLI.

![Tool-result images settings panel showing a preview broken down by project](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rodboev/agentsview/screenshots/agentsview-1622-7-after.png)

Two routes carry it under `/api/v1/data`: `strip-images/preview` reports the selection without writing, and `strip-images` performs it. Both accept an optional project substring and a `YYYY-MM-DD` bound on session end. The apply route requires `confirmed: true` in the body and returns 400 otherwise, so a bare POST cannot destroy stored content, and the panel pairs that with a dialog stating the rewrite cannot be undone. Both routes are localhost-only and reject a remote backend the same way archive compaction already does; preview also works against a read-only archive, and only the apply requires a writable one.

The apply route uses a new `tryArchiveWrite` helper rather than the existing `serializeArchiveWrite`. `serializeArchiveWrite` blocks until the engine's exclusive lock frees, which suits background scheduled work but leaves a user waiting behind a running sync pass. `tryArchiveWrite` calls `engine.TryRunExclusive` and returns 409 immediately when the lock is held, matching the foreground compact runner the daemon already injects. The five existing `serializeArchiveWrite` call sites are untouched. Removal rewrites stored rows in place, so the archive file keeps its size until `agentsview db compact` runs, which the panel states.

Refs #1718

title: Use the shared calendar picker for the tool-result image cleanup date bound
body: The tool-result image cleanup panel in #1694 takes its `Ended before` bound as a free-text field with a `YYYY-MM-DD` placeholder: You have to know the format before you type, a typo only surfaces as a 400 from the server after you click Preview, and there is nothing to tell you which dates would actually select anything. Every other date input in agentsview hands you a calendar instead. The activity, analytics, quality, trends and usage pages, the recall insights panel and the shared refresh control all go through `RangePicker.svelte`, a thin wrapper over kit-ui's `DateRangePicker`, whose Calendar and Custom tabs are a real grid. The cleanup panel is the odd one out. ## Proposed solution Swap the text input for kit-ui's `Calendar`, which the package already exports (`src/lib/index.ts:10`) alongside the `DateRangePicker` the app uses today. It fits the existing contract without touching the backend: - `onpick` hands back a `YYYY-MM-DD` string, which is exactly what `POST /api/v1/data/strip-images` and its preview route already accept, so `stripImagesTarget`'s `time.Parse("2006-01-02")` check and its 400 stay as they are. - `maxDate` set to today removes a bound that can only ever select nothing. - All eight of its nav labels already have translated keys in all six catalogues, passed through at `RangePicker.svelte:82-89`: `shared_range_previous_period`, `shared_range_next_period`, `shared_range_previous_year`, `shared_range_next_year`, `shared_range_previous_years`, `shared_range_next_years`, `shared_range_choose_month` and `shared_range_choose_year`. So the change adds no new strings to translate. A single-date bound is what the filter means, so `Calendar` rather than `DateRangePicker` looks like the right primitive here. Keeping the typed value as the bound state and letting the calendar write into it would also leave the field paste-able. This makes more sense than using the `RangePicker` from the landing page directly, since the cleanup filter has no start, and if we used it we'd need a wrapper for a one-sided mode with a single consumer.

title: feat(db): add db migrate --images to move tool-result images into the asset store
body:
`agentsview db migrate --images` moves retained inline tool-result images out of `sessions.db` and into the assets directory beside it, leaving a reference in their place. The database rows lose the inline payload at once; `db compact` can reclaim the resulting free pages.

Before/after:

| ![Tool output before migration, showing a base64 data URI inline in the stored result](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rodboev/agentsview/screenshots/agentsview-1622-2-before.png) | ![The same tool output after migration, rendering the image from the asset store](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rodboev/agentsview/screenshots/agentsview-1622-2-after.png) |
| --- | --- |

Each eligible payload is written to the content-addressed store chat import already uses. An existing object is reused only when its byte count and SHA-256 digest match. A missing or corrupt object is replaced before the row changes. The `input_image` block becomes an `agentsview_image` placeholder carrying an `image_ref` and a markdown image. The file lands through a rename before its referencing row commits.

If that session transaction fails, complete assets remain unreferenced on disk. A matching retry reuses them; there is no automatic orphan cleanup. Both migrate and strip report sessions that committed before a later failure.

JPEG assets now use `.jpg` filenames, including `.jpeg` files copied from chat exports. Existing `asset://<hash>.jpeg` references still resolve, but re-importing an export with those files can store a second copy under `.jpg`.

Migration changes rows already stored locally. A later keep-mode reparse or full resync can restore inline payloads from provider source files. The existing `tool_result_images = "drop"` policy continues to remove supported inline images during future ingestion and resync. A separate mirror or serving host needs the matching assets directory.

Only four passive media types are migrated. The image renders in formatted mode when every sibling block is text. Under `require_auth`, the asset request remains protected. `db strip --images` remains the broader removal command.

Refs #1622

title: Persist appearance preferences
body:
### Problem / motivation

First, thanks for the wonderful tool, it's been a mainstay for a while now!

Second, I find myself constantly re-adjusting the text size option to be 120% rather than the default 100% and it doesn't appear that I can persist this in the `config.toml` file. It's worth noting that if I make the size change in the settings menu, then it persists, but if I do it from the little status bar at the bottom, then it doesn't and that the two compound each other if adjusted simultaneously.

### Proposed solution

The ability to be able to persist appearance options like text size among the others available.

### Alternatives considered

Maybe there's an alternative here that I'm not privvy to, but even for the sake of being portable across multiple machines, a configuration option would seem to make sense.

title: chore(release): remove repository release automation
body:
Remove the CLI/PyPI, desktop/updater, and container publication workflows, along with the local release/tagging scripts, their release-health checks, and the obsolete setup guide. Version tags and main-branch commits no longer start publication jobs in this repository.

Normal CI, desktop artifact builds, the wheel builder, Docker inputs, local build targets, installer scripts, and updater behavior remain unchanged. Existing releases and download URLs are untouched.

Hold this draft until the publication handoff is complete, including development image updates and outstanding runs of the old workflows.

title: Flaky pricing refresh test times out on loaded Windows runners
body:
`TestRunPeriodicPricingRefreshFetchesAfterRecentAttempt` in `cmd/agentsview/pricing_schedule_test.go` fails intermittently on the Windows CI job. It failed on main at 71ade856a4154cecdddb846d56a51ed590fb1db4 in `Go Test (windows-latest)`, while the same code had passed the same job on the PR beforehand.

```
--- FAIL: TestRunPeriodicPricingRefreshFetchesAfterRecentAttempt (1.85s)
    pricing_schedule_test.go:87:
        	Error Trace:	D:/a/agentsview/agentsview/cmd/agentsview/pricing_schedule_test.go:87
        	Error:      	Condition never satisfied
        	Test:       	TestRunPeriodicPricingRefreshFetchesAfterRecentAttempt
```

## Cause

Line 87 waits for the refresh to store the fixture's model, with a one second budget:

```go
ticks <- time.Now()
require.Eventually(t, func() bool {
	price, err := database.GetModelPricing("scheduled-model")
	return err == nil && price != nil
}, time.Second, time.Millisecond)
```

One second is not enough when the runner is starved for CPU. The Windows leg runs on `namespace-profile-windows-4cpu`, and the step hands one `go test` invocation every package except the five SQLite-heavy ones, so binaries compete for those four cores.

The rest of the file already accounts for this. `pricingResyncTestTimeout` at line 21 exists for exactly this reason:

```go
// Resync may spend up to five seconds draining SQLite connections before a
// swap, and the surrounding work can take longer on loaded Windows runners.
const pricingResyncTestTimeout = 30 * time.Second
```

Seven `require.Eventually` calls from line 138 down already use it. Five do not: lines 83, 90, 295, 301, and 306.

## Reproduction

On Windows, pin the test binary to a single core so it contends for one core the way the CI runner's packages contend for four:

```
go test -tags fts5 -c -o av.test.exe ./cmd/agentsview
# run av.test.exe with ProcessorAffinity = 1 and GOMAXPROCS=1
av.test.exe -test.run TestRunPeriodicPricingRefreshFetchesAfterRecentAttempt -test.count=60
```

13 of 60 iterations failed, with output matching CI. Unpinned on a 16 core machine the same test takes about 100ms and never fails, which is why this only shows up on the shared Windows runner.

## Suggested fix

Use `pricingResyncTestTimeout` at the five remaining call sites and widen the constant's comment, since it would no longer be resync-specific. With that change, 60 of 60 iterations passed under the same pinned conditions.

Longer term these are a job for `testing/synctest`, which `embed_scheduler_test.go` and `raw_sync_test.go` in the same package already use. A budget is still a guess about runner speed; `synctest.Wait()` returns exactly when the refresh goroutine parks back on its select. The open question is whether the SQLite handle's cgo startup goroutines ever reach durably blocked inside a bubble.

title: test(pricing): use the shared wait budget for pricing schedule tests
body:
This raises the wait for a flaky pricing refresh test, and the four like it in the same file, to the 30 second budget the file's other seven waits already use.

`TestRunPeriodicPricingRefreshFetchesAfterRecentAttempt` gave a goroutine one second to be scheduled and finish, which a loaded 4-vCPU Windows runner misses, timing out in 13 of 60 runs pinned to one core and none of 60 at thirty seconds.

Closes #1700

title: Roadmap: deterministic timing tests with testing/synctest
body:
Go tests across the tree wait on concurrent work by giving it a fixed budget and polling until the budget runs out. Roughly 260 such waits exist today. A budget is a guess about how fast the machine is, so on a loaded Windows runner the slow ones fail and the failure has nothing to do with the change under test. `testing/synctest` replaces the guess with a synchronization point. This issue tracks the direction so each focused pull request can stay reviewable without losing the larger context.

## Outcomes

- Tests that wait on in-process work finish when the work finishes, with no budget to tune and no dependence on how many cores the runner has free.
- Tests that genuinely depend on the operating system keep an explicit budget, and the budget is visible at the call site rather than hidden in a per-file constant.
- The Windows job stops contributing timing failures that are unrelated to the code being tested.
- New budgets do not quietly reappear as the tree grows.

## Delivery sequence

1. Convert `cmd/agentsview`. The package already uses synctest in several files, so the pattern needs no introduction, and its database-backed tests prove the approach against the storage layer.
   PR: #1708
2. Convert `internal/sync`, excluding the filesystem watcher tests. Largest concentration of waits in the tree, and the watchers sit on the other side of the boundary below.
   PR: #1709
3. Convert the remaining packages. Smaller and more uniform than the first two.
   PR: #1710
4. Clear the budgets that survive conversion and add a check that fails on a new bare one. Ship together since the check holds only once nothing is left to climb back from.
   PR: #1727, merged 2026-09-11

Conversions land per package. One pull request per call site is the wrong unit at this count.

## Design constraints

- The boundary is where a goroutine parks, not which package it lives in. A wait converts when every goroutine it depends on either runs to completion or parks on a Go channel, mutex, or timer.
- A goroutine that stays parked on an operating system event source for the life of a test cannot be bubbled, and a bubble containing one never finishes. Filesystem watchers and the FSEvents tests are that shape and keep budgets.
- SQLite through cgo works inside a bubble, so database-backed tests are convertible.
- Conversions change tests only. Production code and behavior stay as they are.
- A converted test must fail for the same reasons it failed before. Removing a budget removes a class of false failures, never a real assertion.

## Adjacent

- #1700 and #1701: one instance of the class, addressed by raising that file's budget. Step 1 stacks on #1701 and converts that file with the rest of the package.
- Playwright flakes on the e2e job are a separate source with a separate fix, tracked on their own.

title: refactor(poller): share background job scheduling
body:
Claude usage collection will also require polling. This moves pricing refresh
onto a shared scheduler so both jobs can use the same timing and retry behavior.

Jobs are configured at startup, with jitter, cooldown, capped retry backoff,
Retry-After support, and manual triggering. Pricing remains the only job; it
refreshes at startup and serializes writes with resync. State stays in memory,
with no new configuration, API routes, or tables.

Failed pricing refreshes now retry after 1.5, 3, 6, and 12 hours before reaching
the usual 24-hour interval, with up to five minutes of jitter. Previously,
failures waited for the next daily tick. Shutdown waits for pricing work to
finish, including any pending sync/resync lock wait.

Two CI test expectations also match current session URLs and Windows temporary
paths.

Review `internal/poller` and `cmd/agentsview/pricing_schedule.go`.

title: feat(usage): browser notifications when a rate-limit window drops below a threshold
body:
Stacked on #1704. Until that merges, this diff includes its commits; the notifications work itself is the commits from `feat(usage): add rate-limit threshold browser notifications` onward.

Once rate-limit windows are on the Usage page, the obvious next want is to be told before one runs out. This adds a Notifications panel under Settings with a "Rate limits" card. You pick a remaining-percentage threshold on a slider from 0 to 25, and when any tracked window drops below it the browser posts a notification naming the account, the window and what is left. A second checkbox fires again when a window reaches zero, so you can hear about it going low and then about it being gone. Each source, meaning each vendor and account pair that has snapshots, can be turned off individually.

Permission is only requested when you flip the enable switch. Nothing prompts on page load, and if the browser has already denied notifications the panel says so instead of trying again.

State lives in `localStorage`. A settings record holds the threshold, the exhausted flag and the per-source mutes. A separate notified record remembers which stage has already fired for each window key of vendor, account, limit id, plan type and window kind, and clears when the window resets so the next cycle can notify again. Windows that never report a reset time re-arm once their usage recovers instead. Both records sync across open tabs through the `storage` event so two tabs do not each post the same notification.

The runner is a small store that reacts to the rate-limit store's current snapshots, evaluates them against the settings and asks a notifier abstraction to post. The abstraction exists so a desktop shell can plug in its own delivery, which is the follow-up PR. All labels are composed through Paraglide in the six locales, and the strings are vendor-neutral so a new vendor's windows appear without new copy.

Reviewers should start with `frontend/src/lib/utils/rateLimitAlerts.ts`, which is the pure evaluation logic, then the settings store and the runner. The test file for the evaluation logic is the largest file in the diff; it drives the stage machine through threshold, exhausted, reset and recovery transitions for both vendors.

title: feat(desktop): deliver rate-limit notifications natively in the Tauri app
body:
Stacked on #1705, which is stacked on #1704. The desktop-specific work is the commits from `feat(desktop): deliver rate-limit notifications via tauri-plugin-notification` onward.

The Tauri desktop app loads the same frontend inside a webview, where the browser Notification API is not what a user sees as a system notification. This adds `tauri-plugin-notification` to the shell and a `DesktopNotifier` on the frontend that the notifications runner selects when `window.__TAURI__` is present, so a rate-limit alert arrives as a native macOS, Windows or Linux notification instead of a webview one.

Permission handling differs by platform in ways worth knowing. The plugin's Windows shim reports permission as denied before anything has been asked, so the desktop path requests permission whenever it is not already granted rather than only when the state is undecided. Reading permission can also reject on some platforms; the notifier catches that, logs it and reports undecided so the enable flow does not get stuck, and the runner retries the read without prompting on each poll while the user has notifications enabled but not yet granted. The browser path keeps its narrower behavior of asking only when the state is undecided.

The capability file grants the notification permission to the main window only. Locale strings for the permission states were made platform-neutral, since the same copy is shown in both the browser and the desktop shell.

Reviewers should look at `frontend/src/lib/utils/notifier.ts` for the two notifier implementations and the platform gate, `desktop/src-tauri/src/lib.rs` and `capabilities/default.json` for the shell wiring, and the runner change that retries the permission read.

title: fix(pricing): price Ollama Cloud model tags at the base model rate
body:
Fix $0.00 cost estimates for OpenCode turns served through Ollama Cloud, such as Kimi K2.7 Code reported as `kimi-k2.7-code:cloud`.

OpenCode records the model key from the user's provider config verbatim, so an Ollama-backed provider yields Ollama tags (`kimi-k2.7-code:cloud`, `gpt-oss:120b-cloud`). No catalog row carries that tag, so every step of the pricing ladder failed and the tokens were counted but unpriced, while the same model reported without the tag priced normally. Ollama bills its cloud models per token at the upstream model's published rate (its pricing page lists `kimi-k2.7-code` at $0.95 / $0.19 / $4.00, matching the Moonshot row in GenAI Prices), so the untagged catalog row is the right estimate.

`PricingResolver.ResolveAt` now retries the untagged name once the whole ladder has failed on the tagged name. `pricing.OllamaCloudBaseModel` strips a `:cloud` tag or a `-cloud` suffix from a size tag and nothing else: local tags (`:27b-mlx`, `:latest`, `:31b`) stay unpriced because a locally served model has no per-token price, a size in the tag is kept because size changes the rate, and a catalogued cloud row (LiteLLM's `ollama/gpt-oss:120b-cloud`) or a custom rate for the tagged name still wins. The reported name remains the priced model in usage breakdowns; the matched pattern names the row used.

The usage cache format version moves to 12 so cached rollups rebuild with the corrected resolution, since the pricing digest hashes only catalog rows and cannot detect a resolver change. This does not populate `provider_id` for OpenCode messages; OpenCode's `providerID` is the user's own config key rather than a catalog provider, and the model tag is the reliable signal.

Reviewers should look at `ResolveAt` in `internal/export/pricing.go`, `OllamaCloudBaseModel` in `internal/pricing/normalize.go`, and the embedded-catalog test that reproduces the original report.
