title: feat(usage): estimated energy mode alongside cost and tokens
body:
This adds a third mode to the Usage page's Cost/Tokens picker: Energy. It switches the summary cards, the cost/time chart, the attribution panel and treemap, top sessions, the pairwise comparison, and the session-detail usage breakdown to an estimated watt-hour figure for the same rows, computed at read time across SQLite, DuckDB, and PostgreSQL. Top sessions can now be ranked by energy the same way it already ranks by cost or tokens. A figure that includes usage with no published rate for its model is marked with a trailing asterisk instead of quietly reading as a smaller, complete number. A Settings > Preferences panel lets a user pick which point on the estimate's low/mid/high band the app reports. A small marker next to every energy figure explains what it means on hover.

No vendor publishes a real "Wh per token" number, so the estimator leans on something that does exist: list price. Anthropic and OpenAI both charge less for cache reads and more for output than for a plain input token, and those ratios already track how expensive each token type is to serve. Two outside attempts at estimating Claude's energy use lean on the same assumption. That is reassuring, not proof; list price also carries margin and demand that energy draw does not.

The estimator has three steps, all in `internal/energy`. First, a small committed dataset of published energy measurements (an Epoch estimate for ChatGPT, Google's own Gemini disclosure, two independent third-party Claude estimators, and a couple of GPU benchmark papers) gets normalized onto one scale, watt-hours per million output tokens, using each row's own input/output price ratio to fold input tokens into an output-token-equivalent count. Second, those normalized points get a weighted least-squares fit in log-log space, output-token price against output-token energy, so a vendor's list price converts into a watt-hour figure. A vendor with three or more calibration rows of its own gets its own fit; everyone else falls back to the pooled fit across every vendor. Third, a session or usage row's token counts by type get converted into an output-token-equivalent using the model's own price ratios, then multiplied by the fitted watt-hour rate for that model.

The result is not presented as precise. The low and high scenarios come from the fit's own residual spread rather than a hand-picked multiplier, and both the doc and the in-app estimate marker say plainly that this is anchored on a handful of measurements and carries something like 2x uncertainty either way. A model with no catalog price gets no energy figure, the same way it gets no cost figure today. An operator can override the fitted rate for a specific model in config.toml if they have a better number for their own deployment.

Reasoning and thinking tokens from Claude and Codex are already counted inside output tokens by those providers, so the estimator does not add a separate term for them; this is checked against the evidence already tracked in `docs/internal/session-format-sources.md`. One thing worth flagging for review: a late pass re-checked every calibration source against what it actually said, rather than against an earlier summary of it, and that changed the pooled fit's price sensitivity from roughly 0.49 to roughly 0.22. The methodology doc and its generated tables reflect the corrected numbers, so they are worth reading next to the code rather than skimmed.

For the model itself, start with `internal/energy/fit.go` and `calibration.go`, then `internal/energy/estimate.go` for how a token mix becomes a watt-hour number, and `docs/internal/energy-model.md` for the worked examples and full source list. On the read path, `internal/db/energy.go`, `internal/duckdb/energy.go`, and `internal/postgres/energy.go` each wire the same estimator into their existing cost computation rather than growing a parallel cache.

There is one exception to the read-time-only rule, and it is deliberate. The usage-facts rollup gains a single column, `energy_billable_output_tokens`, and `usageCacheFormatVersion` moves from 11 to 12 in `internal/db/usage_cache_schema.go`. A reasoning-only row can have zero output tokens and nonzero reasoning tokens, and the cost pipeline already falls back to the reasoning count for that case. The energy estimate needs the same fallback applied per fact, before facts merge into a rollup row. Once two facts are summed, the merged counters no longer say which fact was reasoning-only, so recomputing the fallback at read time from the sums gets the wrong answer for exactly the sessions where it matters. Storing the per-fact value is the only way to keep it correct. The cost of the bump is a one-time cold rebuild of the usage cache on the first read after upgrading. The cache is a disposable sibling database, the SQLite archive is untouched, and nothing is lost, but on an archive with tens of thousands of sessions that first Usage page load can take several seconds to a couple of minutes before it is warm again. A handful of correctness details live in that same layer, all worth a close look: the scenario a user picks in Settings can change while a usage read is already in flight on another goroutine, so every backend now builds one estimator up front per request and guards the underlying config with a lock; `duckdb serve` previously ignored a configured scenario or override entirely and always estimated at mid, which is now fixed the same way the SQLite and PostgreSQL servers already worked; the per-model override and vendor-family lookup now key on the pricing catalog's matched pattern rather than whatever model name the cost resolver happened to return, since the two can diverge after alias handling and a mismatch would make a correctly written override silently do nothing; and a row whose output tokens are zero but reasoning tokens are not (an edge case the cost pipeline already has a fallback for) now estimates at the reasoning-token count instead of reading as exactly zero energy for work that genuinely happened. A session that delegates to Claude Task-tool subagents now folds their energy into the parent session's total the same way it already folds in their cost, in `internal/service/session_usage_subagents.go`; that combining logic predates energy and previously dropped it entirely for any session with delegated work. On the frontend, `frontend/src/lib/energy.ts` holds the formatting and the TV-equivalence wording, and `EnergyEstimateMark.svelte` is the one component every energy figure on the page shares for its tooltip.

One known gap: the scenario picker in Settings does not currently propagate to a Usage page tab that was already open before the change, so a second tab can keep showing figures from the old scenario until it is reloaded. Fixing that properly means either the backend pushing a change notification or the frontend polling for one, and neither felt worth the added complexity for a preference a user sets once and rarely revisits. Reviewers should treat this as accepted for now rather than something the PR tries to hide.

title: feat(export): add combined project, model and agent reporting
body:
Reporting exports can preserve project, model and agent relationships at a chosen time resolution. Separate breakdowns cannot answer questions such as "how much did this model cost on this project?" Opt-in reporting schema 4 supplies those combined facts without session identifiers, messages or tool content.

- Hour, day and digest exports accept repeatable `--project-key` selection and `--bucket`, such as `1m`, `5m` or `15m`. Any positive whole-minute duration that divides an hour is valid. Five minutes remains the default; v4 documents declare `bucket_seconds`. Schema 3 remains the default and keeps its existing bytes and digests. Versions 1 and 2 are no longer supported.
- Activity and usage cells share the Activity classification: interactive, subagent, or automated, with subagents taking precedence over the automation flag, including sessions whose usage falls after their activity range. Bucket duration does not change the inactivity gap cap or accounting rules. Usage deduplication and cost allocation precede project selection. Standalone usage remains unattributed, including when a real session has an empty project label. Known costs retain their pricing provenance; unknown pricing remains visible.
- Each hour contains a complete replacement set. Scope, resolution and cells participate in its digest, so corrections and resolution changes replace old facts instead of adding another charge. Finer precision does not require more frequent uploads. Device bucket peaks tighten concurrency bounds, but do not establish exact selected or cross-device concurrency.

The synthetic SQLite benchmark compares one- and five-minute exports with overlapping sessions, model switches and two project counts. This adds aggregation and payload cost, not incremental history discovery: digest screening still computes full day exports.

The timeout-response test uses virtual time and waits for its handler to finish, removing its dependence on host scheduling.

title: fix(parser): apply Claude queue links incrementally
body:
## Summary

- Apply Claude queue and progress subagent links incrementally.
- Preserve deterministic ordering and existing first-link precedence.
- Keep link-only appends on the incremental sync path.

## Why

Active Claude sessions append queue and progress events. Replacing the stored session for each event repeatedly parses large JSONL files and drives sustained CPU use.

## Tests

- go test ./internal/parser -count=1
- focused incremental sync tests for Claude queue and progress links
- focused database incremental-link tests
- go vet ./internal/parser

title: fix(activity): separate interactive, subagent, and automated activity
body:
Activity now separates interactive conversations, subagents, and automated sessions across counts, concurrency, minutes, costs, and session badges. The timeline has three aligned tracks with independent scales and peaks; the headline peak counts interactive conversations. Subagents take precedence over the automation flag when assigning a category.

Activity JSON schema 8 and hourly/day/digest schema 3 expose the same categories and independent peaks. Reporting exports now accept only schema 3. Integrations pinned to versions 1 or 2 must update and refresh their saved digests.

The shared aggregation serves SQLite, PostgreSQL, and DuckDB. Combined usage and cost totals remain unchanged, and automation filters still use each session's automation flag. Existing relationship metadata supplies the classification, so archives need no migration or reclassification.

title: fix(parser): validate DeepSeek Harness v0 provenance ranges
body:
DeepSeek Harness version-0 sessions accept compressed `sourceEventSeqs` while retaining strict validation. Each entry may be a non-negative safe integer or an inclusive `[start, end]` range, including mixed arrays such as `[1, [3, 9], 12]`. `[[138, 144]]` represents seven sequences. Invalid members, malformed ranges, overlapping or unordered ranges, and expansions exceeding the owning event sequence produce a parse error when the log is committed. The parser validates lineage without allocating an unused expanded list.

The known-event map now matches upstream's complete frozen version-0 inventory, including `model/selection`, delivery tracking, subagent model policy, and team events. The provenance entry is reverified against `56c4c3e47c195ff5edbfe3d307bdef81f3de348b` and links to the frozen codec, event inventory, and envelope rules.

This remains a version-0 parser. It retains `assistant/chunk`, `tool/code-dispatch*`, and `start`/`end` surface replacements. Versions 1–3, their migrations, newer event semantics such as `system/message` and `assistant/attempt`, and model-selection reasoning-effort import require separate work.

title: Project extraction costs 12% of resync time rescanning directories per session
body:
Project extraction burns 12% of full-resync wall time rescanning directories it already scanned. On a 5.4 GB archive that is 19.3s of a 156s resync, and caching the result by working directory removes all of it.

The cost comes from resolving the git repository root once per parsed session with no reuse between sessions. When the recorded working directory no longer exists, `findGitRepoRoot` climbs to the first surviving ancestor and hands it to `repoRootFromSiblings`, which reads the whole directory and stats `<child>/.git` for every child. Sessions recorded in git worktrees that have since been deleted all land on the same few surviving ancestors, and each one pays for the full scan again.

Memoize the resolution by recorded working directory and reuse it for the rest of the pass. A sync pass already carries per-run state, so the cache can belong to the pass rather than the process, which keeps a long-running daemon from serving a stale root after a repository moves. Whether a process-lifetime cache is acceptable instead is a maintainer call; the measurement below used one to establish the ceiling.

Mechanism, at `internal/parser/project.go`:

- `findGitRepoRoot` (line 652) stats the recorded cwd. A missing cwd sets `cwdMissing` and the function walks up to the first ancestor that exists.
- `repoRootFromSiblings` (line 744) then calls `os.ReadDir` on that ancestor and, for every child directory, runs `probeGitfileTarget` and `statGitEntry` against `<child>/.git`, reading gitfile contents for the ones that qualify.
- Both run per session, on every parse, with no cache. Two sessions from two deleted worktrees under the same parent repeat the identical scan.

Environment: `main` at 514c875770f00a5e55ee8d8508a988fb4bd9d55f, built with `-tags fts5` and CGO on, Go 1.27.0, Windows 11, archive and rebuild both on the same local NVMe volume, 61 GB RAM.

Reproduction and measurement: a 5.4 GB `sessions.db` at `user_version = 96` upgraded to `dataVersion = 107`, 6740 sessions and 252k messages rebuilt from local Claude, Codex, OpenCode and MiMoCode sources. The CPU profile of that upgrade (`--cpuprofile`, 217s wall, 356.9 CPU-seconds) attributes 34.3s to `findGitRepoRoot`, of which 33.7s is `repoRootFromSiblings`, or 9.6% of sync CPU. A second profile on a later run reproduced it at 31.6s of 270.7.

Adding a memo keyed on the recorded cwd and rerunning `sync --full` against the same warmed archive:

| Build | Run 1 | Run 2 | Mean |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `main` | 158.2s | 153.9s | 156.1s |
| `main` plus the memo | 138.7s | 134.9s | 136.8s |

The engine's own phase totals show the write phase unchanged at roughly 61s across both builds, so the whole saving lands in the parse workers.

The same scan runs on every incremental sync, not only on resync, so the cost scales with how many sessions a pass parses rather than with the upgrade itself.

title: feat(claude): track Claude Code rate-limit windows per account via oauth/usage
body:
Stacked on #1703 and #1704. This PR's own commit is the last one on the branch, `feat(claude): track Claude Code rate-limit windows per account via oauth/usage`; everything below it belongs to those two PRs.

Adds a background poller that reads Claude Code's own rate-limit data so the Usage page can show Claude alongside Codex instead of only Codex. Each configured `[claude.accounts.<name>]` entry polls the unofficial `GET /api/oauth/usage` endpoint on an interval and writes what it finds into the same `rate_limit_snapshots` table Codex already populates, now generalized with a vendor column so both sources share one schema, one set of queries, and one Usage-page section.

The oauth/usage response's top-level `limits` array is the primary source: an account-wide entry's raw kind is canonicalized to `session` or `weekly`, and a model- or surface-scoped entry (the shape a Fable seat's per-model weekly cap takes) becomes `<kind>:<scope identity>`, with the scope rendered as a badge next to the window title rather than folded into the label itself. When `limits` is empty or absent, ingestion falls back to the older fixed-bucket fields. A separate `extra_usage_monthly` window tracks the account's monthly credit allowance against the dollar limit the API reports, when that feature is enabled for the account.

Identity keys a rate-limit window to a seat within an organization, not to the Claude account alone: the oauthAccount's accountUuid stays constant across every org a user belongs to, but logging into a different org only changes organizationUuid and organizationName. `AccountKey` combines both so each org gets its own group instead of overwriting the others whenever a login switch happens.

Credentials come from the macOS Keychain entry Claude Code itself writes, a `.credentials.json`-shaped file at an explicit path, or an environment variable holding the raw access token, aimed at CI. The token is read fresh on every poll and never written to the archive or logged. A 401 is treated as a hard error surfaced through poller status rather than an invitation to refresh the token itself, since only the `claude` CLI holds the refresh flow.

As a lower-latency, network-free complement to the poller, `agentsview claude statusline-sink` reads the JSON Claude Code pipes to a statusLine command and records the five_hour/seven_day windows it carries, converging on the same rows the poller would write for the same window.

The Settings > Connections > Claude accounts panel lists each configured account with its identity, tier, last poll time, and last error, plus a Test button that triggers an on-demand poll through the same scheduler the background job runs on.

A long review cycle against this shared scheduler and storage layer surfaced a series of real gaps beyond the initial implementation, each with its own regression test: the dedup key needed session_id and the per-event ordinal folded back in after both were dropped in an earlier revision, since two concurrent sessions or two same-second events could otherwise collide and silently discard one observation; a resync migration recomputing dedup keys needed to read the same fields instead of defaulting them; a deduped row needed an unconditional refresh of its mutable fields on every poll, guarded against replaying an older observation, so a window whose identity had not changed within the same minute still stayed visible; label resolution for plan_type and limit_name needed to stay scoped to the whole limit rather than to one window within it; a poll that reported an empty `limits` array after previously reporting a full one needed to stop writing the fixed-bucket fallback rather than resurrecting a second, stale window under a different key; that fallback-suppression state needed to key off the account identity rather than the polling job, since one Job instance follows whichever org a user is currently logged into; and retirement of a window that stopped appearing in a later poll needed to be driven by persisted database state rather than an in-memory flag, so it survives a daemon restart.

The last two review passes moved outward from Claude's own ingestion into the shared scheduler the Settings panel's Test button runs on. `TriggerNow` bypasses a job's steady-state cooldown by design, but it was also bypassing a pending Retry-After wait the same way, so a Test click right after an upstream 429 could immediately repeat the same failing request; a 429 with no usable Retry-After header was also treated as an immediate-retry instruction rather than falling back to ordinary backoff. Both are fixed at the scheduler level, with the wait deadline persisted as part of job status so a restart cannot bypass it either. Two Claude settings handlers also copied server configuration outside the mutex that guards a concurrent write to it, and `agentsview doctor pollers` never listed a configured Claude account at all; both are fixed here too.

Where to look: `internal/claude` for the client, identity, and poller job; `internal/db/rate_limit_snapshots.go` for the schema-level identity and dedup key work; `internal/poller/poller.go` for the Retry-After and cooldown fix; `internal/server/huma_routes_claude.go` and the ClaudeAccountsSettings panel for the settings surface; `docs/configuration.md` and `docs/agents/storage.md` for the fuller picture.

title: fix(appearance): unify zoom controls with a configurable default
body:
Appearance, the desktop status bar, and desktop shortcuts use one Zoom preference in place of the separate Text size and Desktop zoom controls. Existing local preferences migrate to it, and all controls use the same supported percentages.

The optional `zoom_level` in `config.toml` supplies a default for browsers and desktop webviews without a local preference. Interface changes stay in that client’s local storage, so clients with different displays keep independent choices. Manual config edits require a daemon restart and client reload; explicit settings API updates retain validated TOML persistence.

Fixed typeahead menus, context menus, and chart tooltips keep their viewport positioning while their contents scale with the interface. The date picker retains its existing scale because the pinned component fixes its panel width. The pinned kit-ui integration and browser coverage are documented in `DESIGN.md`.

Closes #1697

title: fix(command-palette): search two-character CJK queries on the server
body:
The command palette sent a query to the server only after it reached three characters, and shorter input fell back to a client-side filter over the loaded recent sessions. That threshold fits Latin text, but most Chinese, Japanese, and Korean words are one or two characters long. A two-character query such as "消融" therefore never reached full-text search, and the palette usually showed an empty recent-sessions list even though the archive had plenty of matches.

The palette now decides with one small check. Input that contains Han, Hiragana, Katakana, or Hangul text goes to the server once it has two characters, counted by code point. Everything else keeps the three-character minimum. A single CJK character still filters recent sessions locally, because one character matches too broadly to be a useful full-text query and would be expensive to rank.

The same check drives the recent-session filter, the choice between recent and server results, and whether typing triggers a search, so the three stay consistent. The search store and the backend already accept short queries, so no server change is needed. Mixed input such as "a消" counts as CJK. The component tests cover two-character Chinese, Japanese, Korean, and mixed queries alongside the unchanged Latin and single-character cases.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

title: feat(parser): support Cline CLI sessions
body:
Cline CLI task sessions were not previously surfaced in AgentsView. This adds discovery, synchronization, and parsing support for sessions stored in `~/.cline/data/sessions/`.

### What it does
- Discovers task sessions from `<sessionId>/<sessionId>.json` (metadata, exit code) and `<sessionId>/<sessionId>.messages.json` (transcript), skipping dot- and underscore-prefixed directories.
- Parses user messages, assistant text, extended thinking blocks, tool calls, and tool results (handling both string and array content blocks).
- Extracts per-message token metrics (`inputTokens`, `outputTokens`, `cacheReadTokens`, `cacheWriteTokens`) from assistant turns for multi-step breakdown and peak context tracking.
- Preserves authoritative `metadata.totalCost` (including explicit zero costs) via non-duplicating aggregate usage events.
- Normalizes Cline tools (e.g. `read_files`, `replace_in_file`) into canonical taxonomy categories.
- Coalesces continuation snapshots for the same Cline teammate/subagent into one stable session, so the UI does not show duplicate rows for every transcript snapshot; genuinely distinct runs remain separate.
- Adds Cline-specific HTTP and SSH sync resolvers that emit curated session files, preserving empty file lists when all sessions are deleted so client mirrors can evict stale files without recursive root archiving.
- Adds Cline provider configuration (`CLINE_DIR` env var, `cline_dirs` config key), UI metadata, and format provenance documentation in `docs/internal/session-format-sources.md`.

### Safety and correctness hardening
- **Safe SSH & HTTP remote sync**: Preserves empty file-scoped targets when all sessions are deleted so client mirrors can authorize eviction without triggering recursive archiving of the root.
- **Physical containment & symlink guards**: Enforces physical root containment on configured roots, direct sessions roots, `data`, and `data/sessions` ancestors across both HTTP remote sync and SSH resolvers (`curatedRoot` and `[ -L "$target" ]`), and rejects symlinked session directories or files escaping the configured Cline root.
- **Root scanning guard**: Eliminates fallback to scanning the configured root when `data/sessions` is absent in `clineResolveSessionsDir`, preventing non-session directories like `~/.cline/settings` from being traversed.
- **Tar injection protection**: Rejects backslashes (`*'\'*`) in SSH Cline session IDs to prevent GNU tar escape processing from introducing path traversal during remote archive creation.
- **Terminal tool completion**: Handles `attempt_completion` as an explicit terminal tool call in session classification, ensuring successful Cline tasks ending on completion are marked `TerminationClean` rather than `TerminationToolCallPending`.
- **Stable teammate identity and reconciliation**: Derives continuation-chain IDs from stable chain roots rather than winner order, reuses persisted identities from the continuation chain when an earlier snapshot disappears, and tombstones missing teammate sessions while allowing them to revive when files return.
- **Remote identity stability**: Normalizes stored Cline IDs before parsing so remote host prefixes are applied exactly once and teammate links remain unchanged across resyncs.
- **Multi-run link safety**: Keeps `team_run_task` links only when a teammate run can be identified unambiguously, avoiding links to the wrong session when multiple runs share an agent ID.
- **Path containment & traversal guards**: Added strict validation rejecting dot-prefixed directories (`.secret`), directory separators, and `..` traversal in session IDs, plus physical containment checks that reject symlinked session directories or files escaping the configured root.
- **Symlink and freshness handling**: Rejects unsafe Cline primary files, preserves provider-specific JSONL companion symlink behavior, and uses stable tool-call locations so later tool results are attached after parsed-message slice growth.
- **Content-block decoding**: Preserves raw JSON payloads in `ContentRaw` while normalizing array-shaped `tool_result` content blocks.

### Tradeoffs and Limits
- Session discovery targets Cline CLI task directories (`~/.cline/data/sessions/<id>/`). Cline VS Code extension sessions stored in extension `globalStorage` are not tracked by this provider.
- Teammate continuation snapshots are intentionally represented as one logical UI session. Independent runs for the same subagent are retained separately, but ambiguous `team_run_task` calls are left unlinked rather than guessed.
- Token metrics are recorded at the turn level when present; aggregate usage events carry authoritative total cost without duplicating tokens.

### Where to look
- `internal/parser/cline.go`: Session and message parsing, teammate continuation coalescing, stable identity recovery, token metrics extraction, authoritative cost preservation, and tool call pairing.
- `internal/parser/cline_provider.go`: Directory discovery, physical path classification, symlink rejection, and traversal guards.
- `internal/sync/engine.go`: Cline stored-identity hints and complete-source teammate reconciliation.
- `internal/remotesync/resolve.go`: Remote target resolution, ancestor symlink validation, and empty-root retention for stale eviction.
- `internal/ssh/resolve.go`: SSH resolution script emitting curated session files, ancestor symlink validation, and backslash rejection.
- `docs/internal/session-format-sources.md`: Format provenance and upstream Cline schema evidence.

title: Parse retention budget wastes 22% of full resync time serializing to one file at a time
body:
Full resync spends 81% of parse worker time blocked on the parse retention budget, because one large container source takes the whole budget and no second parse starts.

Capping the weight a single source can take, so eight parses fit, cut a 5.4 GB resync from 150.5s to 117.7s, **22% of wall time.**

`parseRetentionSourceBytes` (`internal/sync/parse_retention.go` line 159) returns the container file size for a multi-session container member, so each of the 204 `opencode.db` member sessions reports the entire 2.54 GB store as its own source size. `weight` (line 118) turns that into `min(64 KiB + 4 * sourceBytes, capacity)`, which saturates at the full 256 MiB `defaultBulkParseRetentionBytes`. A single member holds the whole semaphore, so one parse runs at a time while eight workers exist.

Charge a container member the bytes it actually parses instead of the container file size, and cap any single acquisition below the semaphore capacity so no one source can exclude every other. The second half matters on its own, since a 100 MB single-file transcript reaches the same saturation point through the `4 *` multiplier.

## Why the workers look busy

The lease is acquired before the provider parses (`internal/sync/engine.go` line 11766) and released when the collector dequeues the result (line 10283), not when the parse returns. The semaphore therefore bounds pipeline depth rather than parse concurrency, and a worker blocked in `acquire` is still inside `processFile`. Sampling in-flight worker count every 20 ms over a full pass gives a mean of 7.39 with 7383 of 8127 samples at all 8 workers, which reads as saturated parallelism. The time split inside those workers shows what they are doing.

| worker time | stock | weight capped at 32 MiB |
| --- | --- | --- |
| total in `processFile` | 20m11s | |
| blocked in `acquire` | 16m22s | 9m44s |
| blocked emitting to the collector | 1m34s | |
| collector blocked waiting for a result | 45s | 6.7s |

## Measurements

Archive of 5.4 GB, 6740 sessions, 6718 discovered files (1015 claude, 2669 codex, 2803 mimocode, 204 opencode). Windows 11, 8 cores, local NVMe, warm page cache. `agentsview sync --full`, interleaved A/B, four pairs.

| pair | stock | weight capped at 32 MiB | delta |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 169.6s | 124.5s | -26.6% |
| 2 | 152.7s | 121.4s | -20.5% |
| 3 | 139.3s | 114.0s | -18.2% |
| 4 | 140.3s | 111.0s | -20.9% |
| mean | 150.5s | 117.7s | **-21.8%** |

Background CPU load was sampled every 3s throughout every run. Pair 3 is the pair where both sides matched, at 19.3% and 19.1%, and it gives the smallest delta at 18.2%. The larger deltas come from pairs where the stock run drew more background load, and running one parse at a time amplifies external stalls because nothing else is in flight to absorb one. Read 18% as the floor and 22% as the mean over these four pairs.

Instrumenting one pass over the same archive: mean recorded source size 608 MB across 6740 results, `retainedBytes` saturating the 512 MiB pending budget for 3008 of them, and 3008 of 3136 write batches flushing on the retention bound against 10 flushing on the 100-session count cap.

## Adjacent

Raising `defaultBulkPendingRetentionBytes` from 512 MB to 2 GB, capping the per-result retention estimate, and capping the per-source size estimate each change batch counts by up to 6x and move wall time by less than the run-to-run spread. Transaction count is not the constraint here, so a fix aimed at batch size alone will measure as nothing.

Same resync path as #1717, independent cause. That one is `findGitRepoRoot` rescanning directories per session; this one is the retention budget.

title: feat(parser): add charm crush agent harness support
body:
## Summary

Adds Charm Crush (`charmbracelet/crush`) as a supported agent.

Crush keeps one SQLite store per project at `<project>/.crush/crush.db`, with a project registry (`projects.json`) in its global data directory. The provider expands registry entries into roots, parses the parts-based message JSON (`text`, `reasoning`, `tool_call`, `tool_result`, `finish`), pairs tool results into system messages keyed by call ID, links subagent sessions through `parent_session_id` and the `<uuid>$$<spawning-tool-call-id>` child-ID convention, and emits one aggregate usage event per session from cumulative token totals and the recorded provider cost.

Notable decisions:

- **Timestamps are Unix seconds.** Crush's schema comments claim milliseconds, but its own update triggers write seconds. Decoding uses seconds with a magnitude fallback for forward compatibility, covered by an era regression test.
- **Freshness hashes rows, not just mtimes.** Second-resolution timestamps make same-second edits invisible to stat-based freshness, so the provider fingerprints the session and message rows and requires the hash for freshness.
- **Watcher work is bounded.** Rowid cursors over `sessions` and `messages` mean a database event re-parses only sessions with new rows; a scheduled reconciliation pass covers metadata-only edits and deletes.
- **Format detection is schema-shape based.** The `messages.parts` column identifies a Crush store; the vendored goose migration table (`goose_db_version`) proves nothing and must not be mistaken for the Goose agent's format.

Limits: Crush stores no per-request usage, so there is no per-message token attribution or cache-token breakdown; projects registered after startup are picked up by scheduled reconciliation; unknown future `parts` types are skipped rather than failing the session.

Where to look: `internal/parser/crush.go` (parser), `internal/parser/crush_provider.go` (discovery, cursors, fingerprint), `internal/parser/crush_test.go` (16 tests incl. provider-path usage and watcher-bounds coverage), the wiring in `types.go`/`provider.go`/`taxonomy.go`, frontend color/label, and the pinned provenance entry in `docs/internal/session-format-sources.md`.

title: perf(sync): charge shared SQLite container members their share of the container
body:
Sessions in a shared OpenCode-family SQLite database are discovered as one virtual source per row, and each of them stats back to the same container file, so the parse retention budget charged every member the size of the whole database.

On a 2.5 GB opencode.db each of its 204 sessions weighed the full 256 MiB bulk budget and a sync admitted one parse at a time. This divides a container member's estimated source bytes by the sessions the current pass discovered in that container. Members partition the container's rows, so the shares still sum to the container file and the memory ceiling is unchanged.

The semaphore capacity, the four-times multiplier and the pending-results bound are untouched. A file that is not a container member keeps its stat size, and so does a member whose pass tracks no membership.

With a 64 MiB container holding 64 discovered sessions, bulk admission goes from one concurrent parse to the full worker pool. The estimate is read at the three parse seams in internal/sync/engine.go and internal/sync/s3.go.

Closes #1723

title: test(e2e): match the full image cleanup preview count
body: The image-cleanup preview test now matches `5 image payloads` exactly. This prevents temporary paths containing `5` in hidden provider settings from causing Playwright strict-mode failures.

title: test(timing): reject new sub-second polling budgets
body:
Lint and pre-commit checks now reject new sub-second literal budgets in `Eventually` and `Never`, completing the prevention step after the conversions in #1708, #1709, and #1710.

The Go checker evaluates budget expressions and preserves the remaining integration waits through explicit allowances tied to test names, durations, and occurrence counts. Named constants and polling intervals stay outside the rule.

Closes #1702

title: fix(sync): offload tool-result images at ingest
body:
When you set `tool_result_images = "offload"`, AgentsView moves supported tool-result images into its asset store during ingestion and keeps readable references in the archive. New sessions retain image access without storing image bytes inside tool-result text.

The setting applies to new and resynced sessions, incremental updates, and late tool results. AgentsView publishes each asset before saving its reference, and keeps the inline image if publication fails. The Settings control accepts `offload`, and existing inline images can be moved with `agentsview db migrate --images`.

Refs #1718 (slice 3b)

title: feat: derive hosted raw captures into PostgreSQL sessions
body:
Adds opt-in server-side derivation for hosted raw sync. Accepted captures now feed a bounded worker, an isolated Linux parser, and a transactional PostgreSQL projection. Hosted browsing no longer needs a local SQLite archive or `pg push` to turn raw captures into sessions. Local sync and hosted derivation share the preparation path; the existing artifact wire format stays unchanged.

The hosted store enforces tenant isolation and maps storage IDs to public session IDs. Copies with the same provider identity and content share a session. Curation survives matching copies, conflicting copies remain explicit, and deleting a source removes only its contribution. Publication is transactional; retries and pending-signal maintenance are bounded.

Deployment remains one tenant per server instance, with explicit owner provisioning and a restricted runtime role. Disabling derivation preserves hosted reads. Embedding work is queued durably; its consumer, device-enrollment UI, and broader lifecycle controls remain separate work.

Continues item 4 of #1352 after #1607. Operator setup and limits are in `docs/hosted-raw-sync.md` and `docs/pg-sync.md`.

title: fix(config): allow installation ID reads during Windows rename
body:
Concurrent AgentsView startup on Windows now reads the installation ID while another process finishes creating it, avoiding intermittent file-sharing errors. Read-only diagnostics use the same reader.

Windows briefly keeps a delete-access handle open after publishing the filename. The reader now permits delete sharing while requesting read access, preserving the lock-free read path. A Windows regression test holds that handle open to exercise the race deterministically.

title: feat(mcp): expose running HTTP listeners through status
body:
`agentsview mcp status --json` reports running HTTP MCP listeners, including their actual bound ports, backend targets, and private token-file paths. Clients can discover an existing listener instead of guessing its port. Status does not start a daemon or print bearer tokens.

Listeners publish after binding and remove their records on orderly shutdown. Status omits dead processes; stdio sessions do not appear in the list.

title: Draw Activity concurrency as one stacked bar chart
body:
## TL;DR

The Concurrency chart on the Activity page was designed as a stacked bar chart but shipped as three separate tracks, each with its own y-axis and peak label, so a reader could not see how much work ran at the same time. Each time bucket is now one bar with Interactive, Subagents, and Automated segments stacked on a shared axis.

## How

Segment heights come from the counts recorded at the bucket's combined peak, so the segments always sum to the bar. The independent class maxima are not stacked; they can occur at different instants inside the bucket and stacking them would overstate overlap. The tooltip shows both the stacked split and each class's own peak.

A legend and the combined peak label replace the three track titles and the "each track has its own scale" note, which is removed from every locale. The usage overlay draws over the single plot. Hover, drag and keyboard selection, future shading, and the activity strip are unchanged.

## Reviewer notes

- **Peak label gains a date on day and week ranges.** A bare clock time did not identify the peak there.
- **Focus area:** the stacking order and seam styling in the segment loop of `ConcurrencyTimeline.svelte`.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

title: feat(search): expand CJK full-text search to Japanese and Korean
body:
Japanese and Korean message searches now preserve character order and adjacency within each search term. Previously, the Chinese query segmenter could make `かな` match `なか`, or make Korean `검색` match separate occurrences of `검` and `색`.

Rename the optional SQLite feature to CJK full-text search, including `make install-cjk-fts`, its workflow, tables, triggers, and fingerprint identifiers. The feature has not shipped, so the schema definitions use the new names directly without migration code for the earlier names.

Queries containing kana or Hangul use character phrases. Han-only queries retain Chinese word segmentation; Japanese kanji-only searches can use explicit quoted phrases. This remains SQLite message search, without Japanese or Korean grammatical analysis. The query behavior lives in `internal/db/cjk_fts_search.go`.

title: Formatted tool output fails to render retained PNGs and creates a huge base64 text line
body: AgentsView's Formatted tool output leaves retained Codex PNG results as base64 text. Large payloads produce an extremely wide paragraph with partly blank text that reappears when selected. Reproduced on Windows with Chrome 153, after stopping the daemon, building and installing a fresh detached checkout of upstream `main` at `527df8fa6343af732aac88724eaff436a8e1d90e`, restarting the daemon, and reloading the browser. The same session exhibited the problem on release `v0.42.0`, commit `ff8fb4e8`. Tool-result images are set to Keep. ### Reproduction 1. Have Codex return a PNG through a tool result, for example an image-generation result. Use a PNG large enough to produce roughly 1.5 MB of base64 text. 2. Let AgentsView ingest the session with `tool_result_images = "keep"`. 3. Open the session and expand that tool's output. Raw is the default. 4. Select Formatted. The result in this case is a JSON array containing `input_text`, `input_image`, and `input_text`, in that order. The image block holds a `data:image/png;base64,...` string in `image_url`. Expected behavior is an image between the surrounding text blocks. Raw should retain access to the original output. ### Observed behavior Measurements from the rebuilt main, using the same image-generation result: | Measurement | Raw | Formatted | | --- | --- | --- | | Output width | 1,623 CSS pixels | 1,623 CSS pixels | | Horizontal scroll width | 1,617 CSS pixels | 10,812,829 CSS pixels | | Output height | 300 CSS pixels | 115 CSS pixels | | Image elements | 0 | 0 | The original result contains 1,502,431 characters. Chrome decodes its PNG as 1254 x 1254 pixels. Formatted creates one paragraph with `white-space: normal`, `overflow-wrap: normal`, and `word-break: normal`. A three-second steady-state profile on main recorded zero JavaScript execution time and zero layouts, with most CPU samples idle. The user-visible symptom includes apparent rendering contention and text that repaints when selected. The measurements establish the oversized text layout; they do not establish an infinite Svelte update loop. ### Cause and related behavior `displayToolResult` in `frontend/src/lib/utils/toolDisplay.ts` returns the original string unless it contains an `agentsview_image` placeholder. `ToolBlock.svelte` passes that string to `renderMarkdown` in Formatted mode. A retained `input_image` therefore reaches the Markdown renderer as JSON text. The formatted paragraph has no wrapping rule for the long base64 token. The working after screenshot in #1696 exercises a different representation. Migration writes the bytes to the asset store and replaces the inline image block with an `agentsview_image` placeholder containing a Markdown image reference. The frontend renders that reference. It still lacks equivalent rendering for retained inline image blocks. The fix should cover a retained PNG between text blocks, an image-only result, and a migrated asset reference. Large image payloads should render without creating an enormous text line. Related storage request: #1622.

title: feat: build hosted embeddings and activate complete search generations
body:
Hosted PostgreSQL can now build embeddings from projected sessions and serve semantic and hybrid search without a local SQLite archive. The server owns encoding, durable retries, and current-source coverage. Unchanged chunks can reuse vector values after a raw append replaces their physical session IDs.

Operators provision a versioned generation with an owner connection, then enable its worker on the restricted runtime target. A rebuild keeps the previous generation serving until the replacement has complete coverage. Each search uses one generation and its matching encoder throughout the request. Usage-only mode clears derived embedding content; keyword search remains available when the active embedding profile cannot be used.

This implements item 5 of #1352 and depends on #1730. While that parent is open, this PR against main includes its PostgreSQL projection changes as well. The embeddings feature itself is commit 5be5df10; the parent must land first, then this branch can be refreshed to leave only the embeddings diff. Generation storage, worker lifecycle, and configured-runtime acceptance tests are the main review areas. Retention and garbage collection remain part of roadmap item 6.

title: feat: retry failed hosted embeddings without rebuilding
body:
Operators can retry failed hosted embedding work after fixing an encoder or resource problem, without rebuilding the generation. `pg embeddings retry-failed` queues one capped batch for an explicitly selected active or desired generation. Existing workers process it with a fresh retry budget and lease fence; completed vectors and search activation stay in place.

The command uses the restricted PostgreSQL target and reports aggregate counts. It skips stale sources for normal reconciliation and does not call the encoder or open a local SQLite archive. Reprovisioning the current desired instance with the owner role adds the failure index on existing schemas (use the active instance if there is no desired generation); older status, worker and search paths continue to work before that upgrade. A manually altered failure index is rejected and requires owner repair; reprovisioning does not replace it.

This is the first recovery and operations slice of #1352 item 6. Raw-job recovery, retention, garbage collection, quotas and disaster rebuilds remain separate work. It depends on #1736 and #1730; while those are open, this PR against main includes their changes too. Review `d9acd068` for this feature's diff.

title: fix(frontend): render retained tool-result images
body:
Formatted tool output renders retained Codex PNG results between surrounding text and keeps large payloads within the output pane. Image-only results render as images, and Raw keeps retained inline results available for inspection.

The frontend projects retained input_image data URIs for PNG, JPEG, WebP, and GIF through the existing Markdown renderer and asset resolver. Migrated asset references keep their current behavior. Unsupported media, malformed blocks, and remote URLs remain stored text. The change stays in ToolBlock and its display helper, with no backend, storage, configuration, or locale changes.

PR #1729 covers ingest-time offload. This change covers retained inline images in Keep mode.

The reproduction came from #1735. It measured 10,812,829 pixels of horizontal scroll in a 1,623 pixel box, with zero image elements. Focused tests and Chromium proof cover the change and browser smoke tests confirm the fix.

Closes #1735

title: feat: allow session usage queries without source sync
body:
Add `session usage --no-sync` for consumers that need archived usage without triggering a source refresh on every lookup. The flag preserves authenticated session-ID resolution, full subagent attribution, breakdowns, and the existing missing-session and no-data exit codes. Default usage queries still refresh sources.

The local path uses the existing no-sync daemon policy; a newly started daemon has source synchronization disabled, and disabled autostart requires an existing compatible daemon. Recent usage becomes visible after a watcher or separate sync indexes it.

[T3 thread](https://kyber.tail950b36.ts.net:8443/4dc26984-7b97-484d-989a-6f51098dec27/8e601efe-8f1b-4cbd-99bd-290d1ab24ff8)

title: feat: build hosted embeddings in shadow before cutover
body:
Hosted embedding generations can now finish building without taking over search. Provision a generation with `--activation-mode manual`, inspect its coverage with `pg embeddings status`, then use `pg embeddings activate --generation ID` to cut over explicitly. Automatic activation remains the default for new generations.

The hold is stored with the generation and enforced in PostgreSQL, including against an older worker that is already running. Workers keep the active and desired generations current while search stays on the active one. Explicit activation checks the selected profile, then switches only after verifying complete, current coverage under the existing transaction fence; it does not call the encoder or rebuild vectors.

Existing schemas need an owner provisioning pass before using the new runtime. A generation's activation mode is fixed when it is created; reusing its instance key preserves that mode. Coverage readiness does not establish semantic parity. Returning to a retired generation still requires reselecting it and rebuilding current coverage.

This is the first migration and cutover slice of #1352 item7. Raw backfill, normalized parity, provider/device rollout and full local-work retirement remain separate work. This PR depends on #1737, #1736 and #1730 and includes their unmerged changes while it targets main. Review `2d3ef9d2` for this feature’s diff.

title: feat(raw-sync): add finite resumable backfills
body:
`raw-sync backfill --run-id ID --provider NAME` uploads existing local session sources as a finite, resumable run before an operator starts `raw-sync watch`. It saves progress and exits nonzero while discovery or uploads remain incomplete, without waiting through retry delays. Completion requires a full discovery pass and server receipts for every capture.

Runs retain their selected providers, root order, resolved folders, capture bindings, and Crush project attribution. Resumes drain captured work before scanning; completed runs return their saved result. New runs reject missing roots or unreadable Crush registries. Overlapping Codex roots keep the first eligible root as owner across batch boundaries.

Watch and backfill share a checkpoint bound to one server URL, including its path prefix. Another destination requires a separate data directory and device enrollment. Older checkpoints with uploads but no recorded destination also require a separate data directory; their original state remains intact.

Permanent rejection (`rejected`) or a lost local capture (`capture_lost`) requires a new run ID after addressing the cause. Start watch after completion for later changes and deletions. S3 sources, migration parity checks, rollout controls, and retiring local parsing remain outside this change. The durable completion logic is in `internal/rawcheckpoint` and `internal/rawwatch`.

title: Generated Insights: "Generate" button silently does nothing when [insights] endpoint mode is configured (v0.42.0)
body:
## Environment

- agentsview v0.42.0 (image `ghcr.io/kenn-io/agentsview:0.42.0`, commit ff8fb4e8)
- SQLite archive, `--require-auth`, behind a reverse proxy (Caddy) at a non-localhost origin
- **Endpoint mode configured** per the [Recall docs](https://www.agentsview.io/docs/recall/#current-surface):

  ```toml
  [insights]
  endpoint = "http://<bridge-gateway>:8081/v1"   # local Ollama behind a bearer-gated proxy
  model   = "gemma4:12b-it-q4_K_M"
  api_key_env = "OLLAMA_PROXY_KEY"
  allow_http = true
  ```

- Config verified against the docs: all documented `[insights]` requirements are met
  (both `endpoint` and `model` set, valid TOML, env var present at runtime, Bearer-only
  key, `allow_http` opt-in for non-loopback HTTP as documented, endpoint accepts
  non-streaming `POST /chat/completions` and returns string `message.content`).

## Why we consider this a bug

The docs state endpoint mode is a supported configuration:

> "Generated insights use the configured OpenAI-compatible endpoint when `[insights]`
> has both an `endpoint` and `model`; when `[insights]` is absent, they use the
> selected agent CLI on your machine."

and that the form "always shows … the generator … used for the next report". With
endpoint mode configured, the UI still renders the Generate flow (button **enabled**,
`title="Generate quality recommendation"`, `disabled=false`) — but clicking it does
**nothing**: no task card, no console error, and no request reaches the server.

## How we established no request is triggered

Every click attempt was monitored on both sides — in the browser and on the server:

1. **In-browser network capture** — instrumented `window.fetch` *and*
   `XMLHttpRequest.prototype.open` immediately before each click. Across multiple click
   attempts (synthetic `el.click()`, real CDP coordinate clicks, keyboard Enter), the
   log captured only the page's periodic polling calls (`/api/v1/sync/status`,
   `/api/v1/stats`, `/api/v1/projects`, …) — never `/insights/generate`.
2. **Server-side access log** — `grep insights/generate` on the reverse-proxy access
   log: **0 hits** from any click. The count incremented only when the request was sent
   directly via the API (workaround below).
3. **Control test on the same panel** — a real (CDP) coordinate click on the Template
   typeahead **did** open its dropdown, proving trusted click events land and are
   handled on this exact page while the Generate click produces nothing.
4. **Console errors** — global `error` + `unhandledrejection` listeners installed
   before clicking caught **nothing**; the handler isn't throwing, the request is
   simply never sent.

The click handler in the served bundle is
`N(l)||(Q2.setType('llm_canned'),Q2.generate())` and the guard `l` evaluates false
(the button title shows the enabled state) — so the likely causes are an event binding
that never fires, or `Q2.generate()` aborting before `fetch` without surfacing an error.

## The API works — the button is the only broken link

Sending the exact payload `insights.generate()` builds, from the same authenticated
browser origin (same localStorage bearer token), succeeds end-to-end through the
configured Ollama endpoint:

```
POST /api/v1/insights/generate
{"type":"llm_canned","kind":"prompt_maturity_review","llm_opt_in":true,
 "date_from":"2026-09-10","date_to":"2026-09-12","project":"",
 "timezone":"Europe/Berlin"}
```

→ SSE stream `building_payload → generating → validating → saving → done`; the report
is persisted (recorded `model: gemma4:12b-it-q4_K_M`, `agent: openai` — confirming the
server correctly selects endpoint mode over the dropdown's agent) and renders in the UI.

Reproduced independently in two browsers (a real desktop browser and an automated
Chromium session), same result.

## Workaround

Call the endpoint directly (curl, or the browser console on the app origin with the
bearer token) — generation succeeds; only the button appears non-functional with
endpoint mode configured.

title: fix(search): make in-session search reliable
body:
Fixes unreliable in-session search by rebuilding the complete path from a query to a visible match. Previously, pressing Previous or Next could move the transcript without revealing the text the user was trying to find. A result could be counted but remain inside a collapsed block, an unmounted row, or an inner scroll pane. Navigation, highlighting, and expansion used separate search paths, so a changing counter or scroll position did not reliably tell the user where the match was.

The underlined `ab` toggle enables whole-word matching while substring matching remains the default. Switching modes updates counts, results, navigation, and highlights together. Unicode letters, combining marks, numbers, and underscores are treated as word characters.

**The goal of this PR is to make search work as a coherent interaction: find the content, select the result, reveal it, bring it into view, and clearly highlight the current position.** It replaces the search architecture across indexing, state management, transcript components, and scrolling to make those steps agree.

![Before: navigation selects the tool message while its matching output remains hidden. After: the matching output is revealed, scrolled into view, and highlighted.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/dqtz5vpvj9-create/agentsview/1058d0b2cc51ca385f574456fdf94c3827a75576/docs/images/session-find-comparison.png)

*The screenshots show one concrete failure and its repair using the same synthetic English transcript and query. On upstream `ed20f62f`, navigation selects the tool message but leaves its matching output below the inner scroll position. With this PR, navigation opens the target block, scrolls that pane, and highlights the selected text. The result list and overview make the current location easier to understand.*

The rebuilt interaction addresses the problems together:

- **Navigation leads to visible text.** It loads the required history, waits for the virtual row to mount, reveals the current block and native `<details>` ancestors, and handles both inner and outer scrolling. Stale navigation is cancelled when the query or session changes. Previous/Next, result clicks, and overview clicks use the same cursor.
- **Search covers the transcript consistently.** Prose, thinking, code, skills, tool inputs, tool outputs, and result history share text extraction and matching rules. Folded or offscreen content remains searchable within the active scope. Counts, current highlighting, block badges, and result snippets describe the same results.
- **Filters remain meaningful during search.** Block filters and Focused mode define the scope. Changing them updates results immediately without retyping or unexpectedly revealing excluded content. Search restores its temporary disclosure changes while preserving manual choices.
- **Long and changing sessions remain usable.** A stable cursor preserves the selected match as history arrives. Cached text preparation avoids repeating character conversion on every query, while virtual rendering remains in place. Incomplete history is shown explicitly and can be retried in either pagination direction.

A shared occurrence index gives counting, selection, and rendering a common identity for each result. A stable cursor and one reveal pipeline carry that identity through history loading and layout changes to the text the user sees.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  subgraph before["Before: separate paths can leave the target hidden"]
    direction TB
    Q1["Query"] --> API["Server search"]
    API --> ORD["Matching message ordinals"]
    ORD --> SCROLL["Scroll to message"]
    Q1 --> DOM["Mounted DOM scan and mark elements"]
    Q1 --> FOLD["Component-local expansion checks"]
  end
  subgraph after["After: a coordinated path to visible matching text"]
    direction TB
    DATA["Session messages and active filters"] --> BLOCKS["Shared searchable text"]
    BLOCKS --> INDEX["Unified match index"]
    INDEX --> RESULTS["Count, results, badges and overview"]
    INDEX --> CURSOR["Stable current match"]
    CURSOR --> LOAD["Load history and mount the row"]
    LOAD --> REVEAL["Open target and scroll nested panes"]
    REVEAL --> VISIBLE["Matching text visible and highlighted"]
    INDEX --> PAINT["Block-owned CSS Highlight ranges"]
    PAINT --> VISIBLE
  end
  before ~~~ after
  style before fill:#f8fafc,stroke:#cbd5e1
  style after fill:#f8faff,stroke:#a5b4fc
  classDef old fill:#f2f4f8,stroke:#94a3b8,color:#334155
  classDef fresh fill:#eef2ff,stroke:#6366f1,color:#1e3a8a
  class Q1,API,ORD,SCROLL,DOM,FOLD old
  class DATA,BLOCKS,INDEX,RESULTS,CURSOR,LOAD,REVEAL,PAINT,VISIBLE fresh
```

The old DOM-rewriting highlight path is removed. Mounted blocks own their CSS Highlight ranges and clean them up as content changes; browsers without that API retain counts and navigation. Text extraction follows the upstream XML display preference and image-placeholder conversion. During search, tool output uses the plain-text display so the indexed text and visible text agree, then returns to the saved formatted-output preference. Unicode offsets and message-internal reading order are preserved.

Initial indexing remains synchronous and may include history loading and Markdown parsing; caching improves repeated queries without capping results. Inline subagent transcripts remain scoped to their own sessions. This frontend rebuild does not change the backend search API or database schema.

For review, `search/session-scope.ts`, `block-text.ts`, and `session-index.ts` establish the shared search model. `stores/inSessionSearch.svelte.ts` owns selection and history recovery; `search/reveal.ts` and the transcript attachments complete the path to visible text. `FindResultsList.svelte` and `FindOverviewRail.svelte` provide the new navigation context.

title: refactor(goose): reuse shared SQLite provider infrastructure
body:
Goose now uses the shared database provider directly, removing its duplicate factory, discovery, watcher routing, and fingerprint wrappers. SQLite cursor bookkeeping is reusable; Goose retains its producer schema, row identities, and content hash. The refactor removes 180 production lines overall while preserving archive handling and raw capture.

The factory retains cursors across short-lived providers. Watcher events return only sessions with newly inserted rows; edits and deletions remain reconciliation's job. Discovery reports through the shared scan observer and publishes cursors only after every root succeeds, without retreating progress from a concurrent watcher. Other database providers retain their existing event behavior.

title: refactor(parser): share SQLite source handling
body:
SQLite source readers now share read-only connection setup, so changes to that setup no longer need to be repeated across providers. Each reader keeps its existing busy timeout and live-WAL or immutable-snapshot behavior. Goose is excluded from this refactor.

The OpenCode family uses the shared provider factory and adapter. The adapter now forwards event relevance and reconciliation source state, preserving discovery digests across the sync spool. JSON precedence, per-session freshness, archive preservation, and the existing container trust gates remain unchanged; hybrid sources are not forced into whole-container replacement semantics.

Generic database/WAL mtime helpers and the WAL header constant move out of provider-specific files. Kiro reuses the shared event classifier while retaining its symlink containment checks, and ZCode reuses the shared mtime calculation. Most edits are connection substitutions; the main review points are `source_set.go`, `opencode_provider.go`, and `sqlite_dsn.go`.

title: Separate turn time spent on thinking, messages, and tool calls
body:
# Summary

Session and turn durations are currently derived from the gap between consecutive message timestamps, so a turn containing a bash call displays its entire elapsed time as bash run time.
This makes slow sessions look like slow tool executions even when most of the time was model thinking or response generation.
The viewer should attribute turn time to activity types: thinking, assistant message generation, and tool calls.
That way, someone diagnosing a slow session can see what actually consumed the time.

# Background

A turn's elapsed time is really a mix of activities: model thinking before visible output, assistant text generation, waiting for tool calls to execute, and unattributed gaps between entries.
Today the inter-message gap for a turn with tool calls gets reported as tool execution time, which misattributes the slowest and most common source of delay: thinking.

The messages table already stores per-message timestamps plus has_thinking, thinking_text, and has_tool_use, but durations are not stored per activity, and parsers collapse thinking, text, and tool_use blocks of one assistant message into a single row, so within-turn boundaries are lost at sync time.

Source formats differ in what is recoverable: Claude Code JSONL has per-entry timestamps for thinking, tool_use, and tool_result entries, while other agents may only report one timestamp per assistant message.
The breakdown should degrade gracefully: attribute what the source supports, and label the remainder as unattributed instead of guessing.

# Version

532fd65

# Acceptance Criteria

## Must

- [ ] Turn time is attributed across thinking, assistant message, and tool call activities instead of one gap assigned to a single activity
- [ ] The session detail view shows the per-turn activity time breakdown
- [ ] Time that cannot be attributed from source data is shown as unattributed rather than counted as tool time
- [ ] Unit tests cover attribution for a turn containing thinking followed by a tool call
- [ ] The per-turn activity breakdown is available with matching aggregation across all supported backends (SQLite, PostgreSQL, DuckDB)

## Should

- [ ] Claude Code sessions (per-entry JSONL timestamps) produce a fully attributed breakdown; other formats degrade to unattributed
- [ ] Session-level analytics (for example active duration) can report the same activity breakdown
- [ ] The breakdown names the specific tool that consumed the time within a turn

body:
Filtering out Code previously removed each fenced block without a trace. The transcript now keeps every filtered fence in place as a compact localized placeholder with its language when available. Readers can expand or collapse each fence independently.

Expanded fences retain code and Mermaid rendering and raw copy. Code-only messages remain visible, and in-session search continues to reveal source text.

title: test(parser): canonicalize temp paths in Codex fork capture tests
body:
## The issue

On macOS, the two Codex raw capture fork tests
(`TestCodexProviderPlansForkWithReplayParent` and
`TestCodexProviderPlansForkCaptureWithoutReplayParent` in
`internal/parser/raw_capture_test.go`) fail with path-mismatch assertion
errors. `/var` is a symlink to `/private/var` on macOS: `t.TempDir()`
returns the symlinked `/var/folders/...` form, but the Codex provider
resolves discovered session paths to their real `/private/var/folders/...`
form. The two tests built their expected paths straight from the temp dir,
so `require.Contains` and `assert.Equal` compared different strings for
the same file.

The other raw capture tests in the same file already avoid this by passing
paths through the `canonicalRawCaptureTestPath` helper; these two fork
tests never applied it.

## The resolution

Wrap the expected paths written by the test helpers with
`canonicalRawCaptureTestPath`, so both sides of the comparison use the
resolved real path. In the no-replay-parent test, the assertion now
compares `plan.Entries[0].LocalPath` against the canonicalized path of the
written transcript instead of `child.DisplayPath`.

Test-only change: no production code is touched, and on Linux (where
`/var` is not a symlink) the resolved paths are identical to the inputs,
so behavior is unchanged.

title: fix(usage): show preparation progress and preserve session freshness
body:
`agentsview usage daily` prints preparation phases and elapsed time while a cold report builds its cache. Summary, comparison, and top-sessions requests can finish beyond the normal server timeout, with caller cancellation preserved. Statusline has a separate 30-second deadline for startup and reporting.

Daily reports read committed archive data while routine startup ingestion is deferred. Session usage, token-use, and statusline complete pending startup ingestion even when reusing a daemon started by daily usage. Later queries do not repeat the startup sync. Run `agentsview sync` first when a daily report must include new source changes.

Foreground and background startup waits show active work and extend while progress advances. Canceling autostart reports that the child continues running. The server enforces required archive reparsing before readiness.

Usage progress reuses the existing stream parser and forwards phases directly. The API version requires an upgraded daemon with the progress endpoint; there is no fallback to an older daemon's JSON response.

title: feat(usage): show Codex rate limits and sparklines
body:
Codex rollout files already include rate-limit observations. This shows them
in Usage alongside token and cost totals.

Current windows, reset times, and credits are grouped by machine and limit.
Sparklines follow the selected dates, with at most 512 samples per limit;
current readings remain independent of that range. Observations use the
existing SQLite sync lifecycle. Missing values remain unknown. This is
Codex-only and unavailable in remote mode, with no additional polling or
account inference.

Review `internal/parser/codex.go`, `internal/db/rate_limits.go`, and
`frontend/src/lib/components/usage/RateLimitsSection.svelte`.

title: Include complete project identity in reporting exports
body:
Reporting exports now include project identity evidence alongside combined usage cells. An archive-scoped label key does not identify a repository: unrelated repositories can share a display name, and a separate catalog read can describe a different snapshot.

This completes the unreleased reporting schema 4 contract: joint cells and their identity evidence ship together. It does not extend a released schema-4 contract or introduce schema 5. Default schema 3 is unchanged. Development consumers must use the complete shape and refresh digests from earlier development builds.

The `joint.projects` catalog is keyed by the cell's project key and covered by the hour digest. A project resolves only when every session contributing activity or canonical usage has matching, consistent source identity. Missing evidence remains unknown; conflicting identities remain ambiguous. Neither borrows an identity from a known sibling. Identity-only changes therefore trigger ordinary digest-based correction discovery.

The exporter reuses stored session snapshots and the existing identity resolver, reading them in bounded batches once per export. It does not inspect live checkouts, expose raw paths or session identifiers, or change cell grouping and accounting. Consumers still own authorization; opaque machine-root keys alone cannot prove a configured path matches. The synthetic SQLite benchmark now includes resolved repository snapshots at its one- and five-minute precisions.

title: perf(parser): reuse git root resolution within sync passes
body:
Syncing Claude, Codex, OpenCode-family, Command Code, and Kiro CLI sessions now reuses Git-root lookups for repeated recorded working directories. Each sync operation owns the memo across worker batches and streamed reconciliation pages, and a new operation reads the filesystem afresh. Root results retain their linked-worktree attribution; sibling scans are shared by surviving ancestor while each deleted path is checked for its own worktree association.

OpenCode and its Kilo and MiMoCode forks, Command Code, and Kiro CLI also honor disabled filesystem discovery during remote imports and capture. Remote delta imports apply the same policy as full imports. Those sessions use recorded paths for project names instead of looking up a foreign working directory on the local machine, so project names can change on re-parse. Kiro SQLite carries the parse context through both bulk and single-session reads. Other providers using context-free extraction remain outside this change.

The memo uses separate standard-library caches for roots and sibling scans, with one calculation per key. Standalone parser calls continue to resolve without a memo.

Closes #1717

title: feat(frontend): copy resume commands for remote sessions (#1748)
body:
Remote sessions now expose "Copy command", so you can paste a usable resume command into a shell on the machine that owns the transcript.

The resume route strips the host namespace and carries the recorded working directory. Claude and Kiro include it in the response command. The client supports Kiro's command, and Cursor uses the response formatter. Fallback copying stays ID-only. Terminal, opener, directory, and editor actions stay local.

Reported by ruaridhw (https://github.com/kenn-io/agentsview/issues/1748). The current workaround is to remove the host prefix and assemble the command by hand.

Closes #1748

title: fix(claude): honor ai-title for Claude sessions
body:
Claude sessions in title-retaining archives now use Claude Code's latest non-empty `ai-title` when no `/rename` is present. Native Claude parsing previously fell back to the first message, while `/rename` let users choose a title.

The parser keeps `/rename` priority, including an empty clear, and gives every fork result the transcript title. The sync engine passes the stored name to the parser, which performs one replacing parse when a new title can fill an empty name. Repeated records stay incremental after the name is retained.

Usage-only archives keep their existing projection, so titles and transcript content remain absent and title records stay incremental. A session that stops changing is read again only by a later full parse. An empty `/rename` remains authoritative, so later title records can repeat the replacing parse while the stored name stays empty.

Title selection and the stored-name gate live in `internal/parser/claude.go`. The stored-name lookup lives in `internal/sync/engine.go`.

Closes #1749

### [`v2.25.1`](https://redirect.github.com/opral/paraglide-js/blob/HEAD/CHANGELOG.md#2251)

##### Patch Changes

- [`845e819`](https://redirect.github.com/opral/paraglide-js/commit/845e819): Upgrade the Inlang SDK to 3.0.4, including Lix 0.15.1 fixes for transaction-local message and variant reads.

### [`v2.25.0`](https://redirect.github.com/opral/paraglide-js/blob/HEAD/CHANGELOG.md#2250)

##### Minor Changes

- [`f719e1f`](https://redirect.github.com/opral/paraglide-js/commit/f719e1f): Expose `cleanOutdir`, `experimentalStaticLocale`, and `disableAsyncLocalStorage` as `paraglide-js compile` CLI flags.
- [`5ed1745`](https://redirect.github.com/opral/paraglide-js/commit/5ed1745): Add support for a `paraglide.config.js` (or `.mjs`, `.ts`, `.cjs`)
  configuration file inside the inlang project directory.

  The CLI and all bundler plugins now pick up compiler options from
  `<project>/paraglide.config.*`. The project directory comes from `--project`
  or the plugin's `project` option and defaults to the conventional
  `./project.inlang` — which means every bundler plugin can now be
  instantiated without arguments. Since the config lives inside the project it
  configures, it cannot set `project` itself. Explicit flags and plugin
  options win over the config file, which wins over the built-in defaults.
  Existing setups keep working unchanged.

  Also included:

  - A new `defineConfig` helper exported from `@inlang/paraglide-js` for type
    inference and autocompletion in config files.
  - Watch modes reload when the active config file changes, including renames
    between the supported file names. Deleting all config files falls back to
    the built-in defaults; an invalid config skips the compilation with an
    error — watch modes keep serving the previous output, production builds
    fail loudly. (esbuild does not support config watching.)
  - `cleanOutdir` is accepted but ignored: watch integrations always preserve
    the output directory for incremental compilation.

##### Patch Changes

- [`aa4ffd3`](https://redirect.github.com/opral/paraglide-js/commit/aa4ffd3): Resolve references to earlier local variables correctly in message declarations and formatter options.
- [`3634877`](https://redirect.github.com/opral/paraglide-js/commit/3634877): Fix `experimentalMiddlewareLocaleSplitting` corrupting the generated server file when a compiled message value contains a literal `$` (e.g. a price or currency symbol) that forms a `String.replace()` special replacement pattern such as `` $` ``.
- [`1bacc27`](https://redirect.github.com/opral/paraglide-js/commit/1bacc27): Fix `experimentalMiddlewareLocaleSplitting` keying `compiledBundles` by the raw bundle id instead of the safe module id, so every SSR message lookup missed and threw `globalThis.__paraglide.ssr.<id> is not a function` on hydration.

</details>

### [`v3.17.9`](https://redirect.github.com/TanStack/virtual/blob/HEAD/packages/virtual-core/CHANGELOG.md#3179)

[Compare Source](https://redirect.github.com/TanStack/virtual/compare/@tanstack/virtual-core@3.17.8...@tanstack/virtual-core@3.17.9)

##### Patch Changes

- [#​1260](https://redirect.github.com/TanStack/virtual/pull/1260) [`4a0adf3`](https://redirect.github.com/TanStack/virtual/commit/4a0adf3e3ba46968e0e6ba66471253e467babe55) - Recover the bottom pin when the browser clamps an end-anchored scroll compensation write. `resizeItem` compensates a size change by writing `scrollTop` before the consumer has committed the new total size, so when the grown item does not itself extend the scroll range the browser clamps the write to the old maximum and the viewport is left short of the end with no scroll event to correct it. Two cases hit this: `paddingEnd > 0` with a growing last item, where the overflowing item only extends `scrollHeight` to its own end and the clamp lands exactly `paddingEnd` short ([#​1258](https://redirect.github.com/TanStack/virtual/issues/1258)); and a row above the last one growing while the last row keeps its size, under `directDomUpdates` ([#​1266](https://redirect.github.com/TanStack/virtual/issues/1266)). A compensation write whose target exceeds the scroll maximum at write time is now recorded as clamped and re-issued once the sizer has grown — right after `notify` for consumers that size the container synchronously in `onChange`, and from `_willUpdate` for consumers that size it during a render. The clamped read-back keeps the retry pending; any other scroll event cancels it, so a user reading history is never yanked.
