title: feat(raw-sync): add hosted raw sync status endpoint
body:
GET /api/v1/raw-sync/status reports source heads, parse-job counts, active devices, and upload backlog for the authenticated tenant. Operators can inspect hosted pipeline state through the same scoped protocol that uploads raw data.

The route reads existing PostgreSQL metadata in one read-only transaction. It uses `ScopeStatus`, keeps tenant identity in the authenticated context, and leaves local `raw-sync status` and later health diagnostics unchanged. The source comes from the hosted-sync request in #1352.

Refs [#1352](https://github.com/kenn-io/agentsview/issues/1352#issuecomment-5723048552), slice 1 (server status endpoint)

title: feat(sync): add raw-sync clean-uploads maintenance command
body:
agentsview raw-sync clean-uploads gives server operators an on-demand pass that expires due upload sessions and removes orphaned spool files against the same PostgreSQL data directory used by pg serve.

The command reuses RawUploadStore and its batch, locking, and file ownership rules. It checks the configured target's raw-sync write capability before creating the upload spool. It reports completion of one bounded pass while the server's startup and 15-minute cleanup remain unchanged. Short-lived runs start a fresh spool cursor, so the running server remains the path for steady scan progress.

Operators currently start a writable pg serve or wait for its 15-minute pass. This adds maintenance without starting the server while reusing the existing PostgreSQL target and data directory configuration.

Refs [#1352](https://github.com/kenn-io/agentsview/issues/1352#issuecomment-5723048552), slice 4 (upload session maintenance slice)

title: feat(raw-sync): expose hosted parse-job health
body:
Hosted raw sync reports current parse-job problems through `GET /api/v1/raw-sync/health`. Status-scoped device tokens can read their tenant's health in both legacy raw-sync and explicitly configured hosted mode.

The report covers current manifests without parse jobs, expired leases, failures by error class, repeated retries, and parse lag. Jobs for older manifests and deselected parser versions are excluded. Parse lag means the current manifest was accepted before the caller's time window and still has no completed parse for a selected version; successfully parsed idle sessions do not count.

One PostgreSQL statement returns capped affected rows and exact totals. Timestamps use UTC, raw error messages are omitted, and the read leaves custody and worker state unchanged. Callers supply the attempt limit and lag window. Tenant-bound stores reject identities from another tenant before querying.

The SQL lives in `internal/postgres/raw_job_health.go`; authentication and responses use the existing raw-sync HTTP path.

Refs [#1352](https://github.com/kenn-io/agentsview/issues/1352#issuecomment-5723048552), slice 3.

title: fix(parser): support older Piebald app.db schemas
body:
Piebald chats from older app.db files now load when current_directory is absent, so existing worktree paths still reach the archive. The parser probes the chats schema before building its query and keeps current behavior when the column exists.

The sync engine remembers a failed Piebald source by database path, size, and modification time. Repeated ordinary passes keep the failure visible without repeating member parsing or duplicate parse-error logging. A database or WAL change or explicit resync retries it.

The report came from @colinmollenhour's issue (https://github.com/kenn-io/agentsview/issues/1819). Its private database wasn't attached, so the format inventory records that schema claim as unverified.

Closes #1819

title: feat(usage): add EUR cost display
body: Choose EUR in Settings and enter an exchange rate to see costs in euros throughout the UI. This replaces repeated manual conversion of totals, charts and session costs. The browser saves the currency and EUR-per-USD rate separately from language. All displayed dates use that rate, which you update yourself. Shared cost formatting converts the display; billing, API values and exports retain USD units. Refs #1824

title: test(insights): make log drain timeout coverage deterministic
body:
The insight log-drain test now uses a controlled clock to keep its simulated slow write between the drain and sender-stop deadlines. [Windows CI run #5213](https://github.com/kenn-io/agentsview/actions/runs/35300929889) failed when scheduling delayed the write past both stop windows, so the handler aborted before emitting the expected timeout error.

The test waits for the first write to block before filling the log buffer, then checks that all 299 remaining lines appear in the drop count. This covers both buffer overflow and the backlog discarded on timeout.

title: feat(mcp): expose content search inclusion filters
body:
MCP `search_content` now accepts `include_one_shot` and `include_automated`, so agents can search single-prompt runs and automated sessions in the same tool workflow. Both options default to false, preserving existing results.

The options map to fields already carried by the service and database search path. The tool description and MCP guide explain the exclusions and matching opt-ins, while the existing activity filtering and redaction stay in place.

Before this change, finding these sessions required the CLI's `--include-one-shot` or a separate `search_sessions` call. These MCP options keep the search in one tool call, where matches include the existing context and citations.

Closes #1832

title: chore: adopt shared Go lint policy
body:
Adopt kit's shared Go lint policy in AgentsView, with generated configuration and drift checks wired into lint targets and hooks. Thread caller contexts through storage and sync, preserve typed error identities, register native HTTP handlers through Huma, and replace timing-based tests with explicit synchronization or controlled timestamps. Current schemas omit CHECK constraints; historical migrations retain their original definitions.

The diff against `main` touches about **1,370 files**, with **30,300 additions and 27,700 deletions**: roughly **58,000 lines of churn**, but only **2,600 net added lines**. About 45,400 changed lines are in Go test files. The test-file total overlaps the categories below.

| Class of change | Approximate lines added + removed |
| --- | ---: |
| Context propagation through methods, callers, SQL operations, and tests | 36,900 |
| Assertion conversions and test helpers | 8,100 |
| Formatting and remaining Go/test lint fixes | 8,300 |
| Error classification, wrapping, and naming | 2,600 |
| SQL constraints and rows/statement cleanup | 1,300 |
| Synchronization and process/operation lifetimes | 500 |
| Documented lint exceptions | 300 |
| Linter configuration, dependency pins, and build hooks | 200 |
| HTTP registration and generated API changes | Under 100 |

These are rounded estimates from grouping diff hunks by their primary change. Mixed hunks include surrounding edits, and a replaced line counts once as a deletion and once as an addition. Context propagation accounts for roughly two-thirds of the churn; assertion changes are much smaller than the overall test diff.

Review attention should concentrate on cancellation and cleanup behavior: detached daemons and openers must outlive their launching requests, reused sync engines must use each operation's context, schema initialization must not retain an initial cancellation, and SQL rows must close at the correct ownership boundary. The rebased ClickHouse backend follows the same context-aware storage interfaces. Grok parent-discovery performance work is deferred to a separate change.

Uses kenn-io/kit#92 for SQL ownership analysis and canonical Testify naming. Requiring `assert.New` and `require.New` is optional and off by default; automatic JSON-equality rewriting is disabled.

title: fix(parser): nest Grok spawn_subagent children under their parent
body:
## TL;DR

Grok `spawn_subagent` children showed up as extra top-level conversations because the parser treated every summary `parent_session_id` as a fork. It now parents them from the parent session's `subagents/<id>/meta.json`, so the sidebar nests them and usage/activity count them as subagents.

## Why

Grok's summary `parent_session_id` is the source of a fork or restore, not a spawn. Spawned children sit beside the parent. The spawn link is `meta.json` under the parent.

## How

Child parse reads that metadata and sets relationship type `subagent` with parent id `grok:<parent-id>`. A summary that only has `parent_session_id` stays a fork. Resume-from summaries still point at the previous child; spawn metadata wins. Watch and fingerprint include `meta.json` so a later spawn re-parents without a full rescan.

## Reviewer notes

- **Resume-from is the easy mix-up.** The resumed child's summary still names the previous child as `parent_session_id`. `meta.json` names the spawning parent.
- **Format inventory wrap.** The markdown hook reflowed a few later list items in the Pi, DeepSeek Harness, and CodeBuddy sections. Those hunks are wrap-only.
- **Focus:** a worktree child in another cwd group is found only when `session_kind` starts with `subagent`.

title: OpenClaw 2026.9.x sessions not discovered: storage moved from sessions/*.jsonl to openclaw-agent.sqlite
body:
## Summary

AgentsView does not discover any OpenClaw sessions with OpenClaw 2026.9.4. The OpenClaw provider appears to scan `~/.openclaw/agents/*/sessions/` for per-session files, but current OpenClaw versions no longer write session files there — sessions are now stored in a per-agent SQLite database.

## Environment

- agentsview v0.43.0 (installed via `uv tool`), macOS 26 arm64
- OpenClaw 2026.9.4 (running as a gateway service)

## Expected

OpenClaw sessions show up as a project after sync.

## Actual

No `openclaw` project appears. Sync completes without errors, and the watcher reports 4 directories (the OpenClaw dir is watched), but nothing is imported. `~/.openclaw/agents/main/sessions/` exists but is **empty**.

## Root cause (from local inspection)

OpenClaw 2026.9.x stores all session data in SQLite:

```
~/.openclaw/agents/main/agent/openclaw-agent.sqlite
```

Relevant tables include: `session_conversations`, `session_nodes`, `session_windows`, `session_members`, `session_transcript_active_events`, `session_transcript_archives`, `session_transcript_fts`, `session_progress_cards`, `session_goal_operations`.

The legacy `~/.openclaw/agents/<id>/sessions/` directory (which the provider scans) remains but receives no files. OpenClaw's config (`~/.openclaw/openclaw.json`) exposes no option to write JSONL transcripts.

## Ask

Support the new SQLite-backed storage layout for OpenClaw (2026.9.x+), similar to the existing SQLite readers for other agents.

title: feat(parser): add Augure Code (Codex-based CLI) agent
body:
## What

Registers Augure Code, the Codex-based CLI from Augure (augureai.ca), as its
own agent in agentsview, independent from Codex.

- Sessions are Codex-format rollout JSONL under `~/.augure/sessions`, minted
  under the new `augure-code:` ID prefix and labeled "Augure Code".
- Reuses the shared Codex parser through the existing TraeX-style "fork
  relabel" pattern: an agent spec + relabel provider, no new parsing logic.
- Resume uses the vendor's own `augure resume <id>` CLI with the Codex-shaped
  `-m` model flag, on both the server and the frontend fallback.
- Sync's format-shaped branches (duplicate resolution, layout preference,
  reconciliation identity, parse-diff mtime) treat it as a Codex-format fork
  via `isCodexFormatAgent`; the Codex-only `session_index.jsonl` and S3
  branches stay Codex-only because Augure writes no index file and has no S3
  layout.
- Archive curation includes `augure-code` in the unmarked-user-row cleanup,
  since the fork shares the Codex unpaired-notification message shape.
- Configurable via `AUGURE_CODE_SESSIONS_DIR` (docs/configuration.md), with a
  format-provenance entry in docs/internal/session-format-sources.md.
- Models observed are proprietary Augure slugs (ossington-5, rosedale-1),
  which price as unpriced until catalog coverage appears.

## Why

Augure ships a Codex-based CLI (verified on CLI 1.0.2-1.0.6: rollout JSONL
with `originator: "codex-tui"`, `rate_limits.limit_id: "codex"`, Codex field
shapes throughout, plus Augure's own `legacy_migration.json` documenting a
one-time import from a stock `~/.codex` layout). Today agentsview attributes
that usage to Codex, so a user of both tools cannot see Augure usage separately
— filtering, colors, per-agent usage, and resume all route through the codex
agent. Registering the fork as its own agent gives accurate per-agent usage
while reusing the proven Codex parser, the same way TraeX already integrates.

## Scope

Parser registration and seams only. No schema changes, no migrations, no
session-model changes (PostgreSQL/DuckDB mirrors unaffected), no remap or
duplicate/canonical machinery. Historic-session handling (agent remap rules,
duplicate/canonical detection) is deliberately out of scope and planned as
separate proposals, since Augure's earlier clients mixed sessions into the
goose/codex stores before moving to their own stores.

title: feat(parser): add Augure Desktop (Hermes-based) agent
body:
## What

Registers Augure Desktop 3 (beta), the Hermes-based desktop client from Augure
(augureai.ca), as its own agent in agentsview.

- Sessions live in a Hermes-schema `state.db` at `~/.augure-desktop` (macOS/
  Linux) / `%LOCALAPPDATA%\augure-desktop` (Windows), minted under the new
  `augure-desktop:` ID prefix and labeled "Augure Desktop".
- Reuses the Hermes state-DB provider through a `hermesProviderSpec` seam; the
  provider claims only roots carrying the `.augure-desktop` fork marker (the
  store's own root name, never the schema shape), so a stock Hermes-shaped
  store stays with Hermes.
- Discovery is agent-keyed, so the fork's and Hermes's independently minted
  session IDs can't collide.
- Sync treats it like Hermes for fingerprint-hash freshness and provider
  fingerprint file info.
- `session export` dispatches the Hermes JSONL writer for both agents,
  deriving the raw session ID from the agent-aware prefix table and falling
  back across the same transcript layout.
- Remote sync is explicitly excluded for this agent until safe Hermes-schema
  snapshotting exists (live WAL-backed state.db + non-transcript application
  state), with a resolver test pinning the forbidden boundary.
- Configurable via `AUGURE_DESKTOP_SESSIONS_DIR` (docs/configuration.md), with
  a format-provenance entry and README agents row.

## Why

Augure Desktop 3.0.0-beta is a Hermes Agent fork (the app bundles a 340-file
`hermes_*` Python runtime and `hermes_constants.py` declaring
`DEFAULT_HERMES_HOME_DIRNAME = ".augure-desktop"`; its `schema_version` was 26
the same day stock Hermes measured 30 — same table family, independent version
lines). Without registration that usage is invisible to agentsview. Reusing
the Hermes provider through a narrow spec seam gives full support — parsing,
usage/cost, search, export — with a small, low-risk diff, and the fork-marker
root gate plus remote-sync exclusion keep the integration conservative until
snapshotting is proven.

## Scope

Parser registration and seams only. No schema changes, no migrations, no
session-model changes (PostgreSQL/DuckDB mirrors unaffected), no remap or
duplicate/canonical machinery. Historic-session handling (agent remap rules,
duplicate/canonical detection) is deliberately out of scope and planned as
separate proposals, since Augure's earlier clients mixed sessions into the
goose/codex stores before moving to their own stores.

title: Push sessions to ClickHouse and serve the dashboard from it
body:
## TL;DR

AgentsView could push the SQLite archive to PostgreSQL and serve the dashboard from that copy. ClickHouse had no equivalent. `agentsview clickhouse push` writes sessions into ClickHouse; `clickhouse serve` runs the same dashboard by querying that copy.

## Why

PostgreSQL already has that path. DuckDB is a local file, not a remote database.

## How

Push copies from SQLite into ClickHouse. Serve reads ClickHouse. The dashboard does not write ClickHouse: rename, trash, insights, stars, and pins stay on SQLite.

Push is a whole-session replace, not a PostgreSQL upsert. Each batch writes dependents, then `DELETE ... WHERE session_id IN (...) AND push_version < v`, then the session row. Cursors live in the mirror's `sync_metadata`. Readers open connections with `final=1` so they never write `FINAL` in SQL.

Query text is MergeTree-shaped (`toStartOfDay`, `IN (SELECT)`, `toInt64` on aggregates). Named-target parsing and OS service units are shared with PostgreSQL. The `clickhouse` command tree is its own cobra because the DSN, TLS check, and Sync types are not PostgreSQL's.

## Reviewer notes

- **Read-only serve.** Rename, trash, insights, stars, and pins stay on SQLite.
- **No vectors and no hosted raw-sync.** Those stay PostgreSQL-only.
- **Non-loopback URLs need verified TLS** unless `allow_insecure = true`. `skip_verify=true` is rejected on remote hosts.
- **Focus:** push order and the dialect hooks in `internal/db/query_dialect.go`. The CLI flags match `pg` on purpose.
- **Size.** Most of the added lines are ClickHouse SQL for the existing `db.Store` reads (analytics, usage, activity, search, sessions), not a new UI.

## Links

- [ClickHouse Sync](https://github.com/kenn-io/agentsview/blob/clickhouse-support-for-agentsview-server/docs/clickhouse-sync.md)
- [ClickHouse push and serve](https://github.com/kenn-io/agentsview/blob/clickhouse-support-for-agentsview-server/docs/internal/clickhouse-mirror.md)

title: feat(raw-sync): add server-status command with parse latency
body:
`agentsview raw-sync server-status` reads hosted status using a status-only device token. It prints source heads, parse jobs, devices, uploads, pipeline depth, and the most recent completed parse latency as one JSON object. Connection flags match `raw-sync watch`; the device credential comes from the environment.

The server reports `last_parse_completed_at` for each current source head. The CLI adds `last_parse_latency_seconds`, measured from that manifest's acceptance to completion. This includes waiting time and does not measure backlog age. It is `null` when no current head has completion evidence. Pipeline depth counts ready, leased, and retrying jobs, including historical generations.

Missing endpoints return an error that points operators to `raw-sync status` for local state. Request failures preserve their causes and HTTP error details, with the configured credential redacted from server diagnostics.

Refs #1352.

title: fix(parser): keep Codex exec automated and tag roborev
body:
Every `codex exec` session is automated. `originator=codex_exec` is stored as
`session_kind=non-interactive`.

Roborev reviews are a more specific kind of that work. When
`thread_source=roborev` (from `codex exec --thread-source roborev`), the
session is stored as `session_kind=roborev` so they are identifiable as code
review while remaining automated.

Interactive TUI and desktop sessions stay interactive. Native `spawn_agent`
children still use `source.subagent` plus `parent_thread_id`.

Companion roborev change: kenn-io/roborev#1205

## Evidence

- **Before:** exec sessions with a non-matching first message were
  interactive. `thread_source=roborev` was ignored.
- **After:** `originator=codex_exec` is automated. `thread_source=roborev`
  is automated and kind `roborev`.

```
go test -tags fts5 ./internal/parser -run 'TestParseCodexSession_ExecOriginator|TestParseCodexSession_RoborevThreadSource'
go test -tags fts5 ./internal/db -run 'TestIsAutomatedSessionMetadata|TestCurrentDataVersionCodexExecSessionKind'
```

Existing Codex-format rows reparse at data version 112.

## Merge danger

**Door:** two-way. Revert restores prompt-only classification for exec
sessions that do not match a built-in prefix.

**Blast radius:** every Codex exec session becomes automated, including
one-shot `codex exec` that is not roborev. Roborev-tagged sessions keep
the more specific kind.

title: Add a Go contract for replica and mirror storage backends
body:
## TL;DR

Adding a remote database meant copying the PostgreSQL CLI, config, push, watch, and serve code, and teaching the HTTP server about its push types. The ClickHouse backend on `main` was that copy. `internal/storage` now defines Go interfaces for the replica and mirror roles. PostgreSQL and ClickHouse implement them, and the CLI, daemon routes, and server drive every backend through the contract. ClickHouse vector push and search are a follow-up.

## How

The code already had three roles. The **archive** is SQLite and the only writable store. A **replica** is a remote database the archive pushes into and the UI reads from. PostgreSQL, CockroachDB, and ClickHouse are replicas. A **mirror** is a disposable local file, which today means DuckDB. A new remote SQL backend is a replica.

`postgres.Backend`, `clickhouse.Backend`, and `duckdb.Mirror` are thin structs over functions that already existed. `internal/backendcontract` asserts each one at compile time. `cmd/agentsview/backends.go` is the one registry. `pg` and `clickhouse` share `replica.go` and `replica_watch.go`, and `pg.go` keeps only the PostgreSQL-only serve extras. The server registers `/api/v1/push/<name>` per backend and imports no backend package.

I rejected one interface for all three roles, because DuckDB would have to fake push and status. I also rejected type aliases for the moved wire types. The repo forbids compatibility shims, so every call site changed instead.

## Reviewer notes

- **Operator behavior is unchanged** for `pg` and `duckdb`. ClickHouse `status` shifts a few lines by one space because values now align past the widest label.
- **Daemon push body changed.** One `replica` target replaces the per-backend blocks, so `server.APIVersion` is 10. The CLI already refuses a daemon on another version. In that target `push_vectors` is optional and omitted means enabled, the same default as the `[pg]` config key.
- **Status rows are backend-owned.** ClickHouse keeps its cursor in the mirror and prints different lines than PostgreSQL.
- **Moved types keep their JSON.** The OpenAPI document and both generated clients are regenerated.
- **Targets fail fast.** `storage.Replica` has `ValidateTarget`, called by the daemon handler and the CLI before any local sync. ClickHouse rejects plaintext remote URLs there and returns a 400 before the stream opens, as it did on `main`.
- **Focus area:** `internal/server/huma_routes_push.go` and `cmd/agentsview/daemon_push.go`, where the per-backend handlers collapsed into one path. The rest is renames.
- **Guide:** `docs/agents/storage.md` gains a "Backend Roles and Contract" section with the steps for adding a replica.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

title: feat(signals): extract observed tool sequences
body:
Adds `signals.ExtractToolSequences` for slice 1 of https://github.com/kenn-io/agentsview/issues/1852. Sequences start with an error or recognized empty result and record adjacent repeats and tool switches. Recovery requires content from a later message. Complete traces with uncertain final results end unknown; unfinished traces stay open.

Claude and Amp failure metadata survives parsing and storage. Amp retains explicit completion status, and Cline retains image markers so image-only results remain unknown. Shared failure detection counts `error` and `denied`, keeping health scores and failure streaks consistent. Version updates reparse sources and recompute quality signals.

Ingestion classifies image-only and staged evidence before display summaries are flattened. The source inventory distinguishes verified provider formats, contributor observations, and analyzer policy. API comments document index bounds, completion input, and the adjacent-call repeat limit. Sequence extraction is not yet exposed through storage, the API, or the UI.

title: Usage on model step-5-preview (StepFun) stays unpriced - missing from every pricing source
body:
**agentsview version:** agentsview bfc70de (commit bfc70de, built 2026-09-19T10:15:18Z)

**Install method:** Other / not sure (~/.local/bin, built 2026-09-19)

**OS / platform:** macOS

**Which agent and version:** n/a - any agent whose sessions carry the StepFun model name

Usage rows recorded with model `step-5-preview` are reported as unpriced:
the model appears under unpriced models and the session cost stays
unsettled (shown as $0 / no cost) even when token counts are complete.

Every other model in a session still prices normally, so only StepFun

title: feat(analytics): split activity timeline by role with absolute and percent views
body:
# What

- The "Activity by Day and Hour" timeline now splits each day's message bar into three stacked segments when the Messages metric is selected: user messages at the bottom in green, assistant messages in blue, and a gray Other segment on top for message rows that belong to neither role (tool-result carrier rows and system-injected rows), with a matching color legend in the header.
- Adds an Absolute/Percent toggle for the messages view. Percent normalizes every bar to the full plot height over the full message total, so the role mix per day stays comparable across days with very different volumes.
- Sessions view keeps a single bar per day; the toggle and legend only appear for Messages.
- Tooltips report the user/assistant/other split as counts in Absolute view and as percentages of the total in Percent view.

# Why

Messages were previously drawn as one indistinguishable bar, so there was no way to see the balance between user and assistant activity over time, and low-volume days flattened out entirely. The percent view makes the role-mix trend visible independently of daily volume. The Other segment keeps the painted stack consistent with the message total, since the backend counts tool-result carrier and system rows in the total but outside the user/assistant split.

# Design decisions

- Three `Bar` segments with array-valued `y` ranges (`[bottom, top]`) instead of layerchart's series/stack layout, because the chart renders one custom marks layer per date and this keeps the existing brush, selection, and keyboard machinery untouched.
- The Other segment reuses the existing `--chart-series-other` token and `shared_other` label, so no new color or locale keys were introduced beyond the tooltip's `other` parameter.
- Percent mode normalizes over the full message total, not the user/assistant split, so the three segments always sum to 100% and bars fill the plot.
- Only the user segment is focusable (`role="button"` with the existing arrow-key range selection); the assistant and other segments are `aria-hidden`, keeping one tab stop and one screen-reader label per day. Hovering any segment shows the shared tooltip.
- Kept the uniform 1px bar radius so segments render as `rect` elements: per-segment rounded caps switch layerchart to `path` output, which would change the DOM the component tests assert on.

# How to test

1. Open Analytics and find "Activity by Day and Hour" with Messages selected: bars are stacked green-blue-gray, the legend swatches match, and hovering a bar shows the total plus the user/assistant/other split.
2. Switch to Percent: every bar becomes full height and only the segment boundaries move, showing the day-by-day role trend.
3. Switch to Sessions: a single bar per day, and the toggle and legend hide.

# Visual proof

**Absolute (counts):**

![absolute view](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/TomzxForks/agentsview/assets/activity-timeline-role-split/activity-messages-absolute.png)

**Percent (share per day):**

![percent view](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/TomzxForks/agentsview/assets/activity-timeline-role-split/activity-messages-percent.png)

*Captured with Playwright against the built app with seeded fixture data.*

---

It accepts bare and attributed tags, removes repeated closed prefixes, preserves unclosed or envelope-only values, and keeps the original shell result when stripping would create an empty preview. Consumer routing, classification and stored content stay unchanged.

Sessions whose agent writes its own generated title are a separate path handled by the sibling parser change in this issue.

title: [vector.embeddings] max_batch_tokens is silently ignored — it belongs in [vector.embeddings.servers.<name>]
body:
### What is the issue?

Same root cause family as #1356 / #1379 (batch composition bounded by document count, not tokens) — but this report is about a **separate defect that made the obvious mitigation silently do nothing**: `max_batch_tokens` is accepted in `[vector.embeddings]` and has no effect. The key belongs in `[vector.embeddings.servers.<name>]`.

There is no error, no warning, and no log line. The daemon starts clean and the config looks correct.

### Environment

- agentsview v0.43.0 (commit 9be7745, build 2026-09-14)
- Apple M1, 16 GB, macOS
- Local provider: Ollama 0.34.2 on `http://127.0.0.1:11434/v1`
- Model: a `qwen3-embedding:0.6b` derived model pinned to `num_ctx 8192`, 1024 dims
- Corpus being embedded: ~34k documents / ~41k chunks / ~58M characters

### Config as written (key in the parent table — silently ignored)

```toml
[vector.embeddings]
model = "qwen3-embed-8k"
dimension = 1024
max_input_chars = 4000
model_context_tokens = 8192
max_batch_tokens = 32768          # accepted, never applied

[vector.embeddings.servers.local]
endpoint = "http://127.0.0.1:11434/v1"
timeout = "300s"
```

### Observed

With this config, `embeddings build --yes` submits batches of 32 inputs. Measured on the provider side (ollama's request log, single `POST /v1/embeddings` calls):

```
5m13s / 6m31s / 7m19s / 7m31s / 9m37s
```

The first full build died at 18.7% of the corpus:

```
fatal: encode batch beginning with document <doc_key>: encode batch at 0:
  [vector.embeddings] request: Post "http://127.0.0.1:11434/v1/embeddings":
  context deadline exceeded (Client.Timeout exceeded while awaiting headers)
```

The failing request exceeded the `300s` client timeout I had set.

### What actually fixes it

Moving the knob to the per-server table and using `batch_size`:

```toml
[vector.embeddings]
model = "qwen3-embed-8k"
dimension = 1024
max_input_chars = 4000
model_context_tokens = 8192

[vector.embeddings.servers.local]
endpoint = "http://127.0.0.1:11434/v1"
timeout = "1200s"
batch_size = 8
concurrency = 4
```

Same machine, same model, same corpus:

| `batch_size` | single-request duration |
|---|---|
| 32 (default) | 5m13s – 9m37s |
| 8 | 21s – 51s |

~10–15x shorter requests, no throughput regression. Confirmation that the value was actually read: the `done` counter in `GET /api/v1/embeddings/status` starts incrementing in steps of 8 instead of 32.

### Why this is worth fixing

Given that #1356 and #1379 already document that batch composition is bounded by document count, the natural first move for an operator hitting oversized batches is `max_batch_tokens`. Putting it in `[vector.embeddings]` is the reasonable guess — the key has the same prefix as the four keys above it, which do live there. It is silently discarded, so the symptom (multi-minute requests, timeouts on long builds) is unchanged and looks like the mitigation "did not work".

### Suggestions

1. Warn (or fail) on unrecognised keys anywhere under `[vector]`, or at least on keys that are valid in a different table of the same section.
2. Document, in the config reference and ideally in the settings-page snippet, which keys belong to `[vector.embeddings]` and which to `[vector.embeddings.servers.<name>]`.
3. Optionally: make the effective batch size (inputs and tokens) visible via `embeddings list` or `/api/v1/embeddings/status`, so a build can be checked before it runs rather than inferred from request durations.

Happy to test a build if a fix needs verification on M1 / local Ollama.

title: fix(config): reject unknown keys under [vector]
body:
Config loading now rejects unknown keys under `[vector]` and its subtables instead of silently ignoring them. This catches misplaced per-server settings such as `max_batch_tokens` under `[vector.embeddings]`, as well as misspellings such as `enabeld = true` that would otherwise leave semantic search off.

The check uses undecoded keys from the main TOML decode and runs whenever `[vector]` is present, including when `enabled = false`. The error reports the first unknown key. For a per-server setting in the parent embeddings table, it points to `[vector.embeddings.servers.<name>]`; that hint comes from the server struct's TOML tags.

Any command that loads the config, including `sync` and `embeddings build`, fails until the key is corrected or removed. Previously accepted configs can therefore require edits on upgrade. Unknown keys outside `[vector]` still load, and value validation for disabled vector search remains unchanged. The semantic-search guide and Unreleased changelog explain this behavior.

The terminal-cancellation regression test checks that the spawned terminal finishes after cancellation. It no longer requires a successful HTTP response from a canceled request, which caused intermittent CI failures.

Reviewer focus is `rejectUnknownVectorKeys` and its call in `applyConfigTOML` in `internal/config/config.go`.

Fixes #1866

title: Derive activity report candidate sessions and peer keys inside the database
body:
## TL;DR

An Activity day report served from a ClickHouse replica returned HTTP 500 once the day held about 3,800 Claude usage snapshots. The report inlined every `(message_id, request_id)` pair into the peer query and the statement crossed ClickHouse's 256 KiB `max_query_size`. Candidate sessions and their snapshot keys now come from subqueries inside the SQL on ClickHouse, SQLite, and PostgreSQL, so statement size no longer depends on how much usage a day holds.

## Why

clickhouse-go writes every bound argument into the statement text, so an `IN (?, ?)` list is a growing literal. The failing report inlined 841 session IDs twice (71 KB) and a pair list that hit the limit mid-request-ID. SQLite and PostgreSQL did not fail, but they chunked the same session list and pushed the same pair list back from Go.

## How

Each backend already had the predicate that selects the report's candidate sessions. That predicate now runs as a subquery inside the usage and interval queries, and the peer keys come from a CTE over the candidate rows, so one statement loads candidate rows plus cross-session peers. DuckDB already worked this way and was the reference. Survivor selection, attribution, web-search maximums, and ordering stay in Go with the same inputs.

I rejected raising `max_query_size` and truncating the pair list. Both keep a statement that grows with data.

## Reviewer notes

- **Candidate source filters by the loaded session list.** A push landing between the metadata query and the interval query could add a session the aggregator never saw, so candidates for unknown sessions are dropped.
- **Focus area:** `clickActivityReportUsageQuery` in `internal/clickhouse/activityreport.go`. The OR between candidate membership and key match replaces the old two-query load.
- **Chunked paths left alone.** `chQueryChunked` (900 IDs), mirror batches (500), and identity mutations (300) bound sets that arrive from outside the database. `docs/agents/storage.md` records the rule.
- **Regression test** pushes more pairs than the old literal list could carry and checks the ClickHouse report against SQLite, including peer snapshots that win the token row.

title: perf(clickhouse): persist usage prices and aggregate daily reads
body:
Daily usage reads from ClickHouse now aggregate stored request prices in SQL instead of transferring and pricing every event in Go. Push computes prices with the existing Go rules, preserving request rounding, historical rates, token tiers, provider adjustments, and pricing provenance.

Prices are keyed by their inputs and a digest of the pricing catalog, billing policy, and record format. Catalog changes take effect immediately through request-time pricing while the next push fills the new generation. Reader-specific overrides also use request-time pricing. Backfills use bounded batches, reads stream their results, and monetary sums preserve exact overflow checks and error identity.

This adds two derived tables in ClickHouse schema version 2. Run `agentsview clickhouse push` before using the updated reader against an existing mirror. The first push fills the price tables; older pricing generations remain available to concurrent readers. Serving stays read-only, and SQLite remains the archive. Review the pricing keys and contexts in `usage_prices.go` and the grouping and exception handling in `usage.go`.

The activity machine filter also keeps friendly labels visible and adds a short ID only when labels collide. The ClickHouse setup example documents native LZ4 compression.

<sup>generated by a clanker</sup>

title: fix(activity): avoid archive-wide SQLite usage scans
body:
Activity reports on SQLite now use indexed lookups for selected sessions and their Claude snapshot peers. The combined `OR` predicate introduced in #1869 scanned usage across the whole archive, making narrow reports slower as unrelated history grew.

Separate candidate and peer reads with `UNION ALL`, excluding candidate sessions from the peer branch so each usage row appears once. Snapshot keys remain inside SQL and parameter counts stay bounded. The existing working-set test now checks the executed query plan as well as its returned rows, catching the full-index scan that previously passed.

title: feat(skills): add proactive conversation recall

- Skill install and list now manage each generated artifact independently, preserving the existing protection for locally edited files and remote-target settings.

## Why

AgentsView already had the search and transcript primitives, but the installed skill left too much of the recall workflow implicit. Agents could miss relevant history, treat a snippet as evidence, or silently query the wrong archive after a remote failure.

## Usage

Run `agentsview skills install` to install or upgrade the recall package. Use `agentsview skills list` to see the state and path of each skill or search-agent artifact.

title: fix(pricing): price StepFun step-5-preview from the supplemental set
body:
Sessions that persist the model `step-5-preview` come back unpriced. The pinned LiteLLM snapshot (`litellm-6417938744b4`) has no `stepfun` entries, and the periodic refresh can't fix it until upstream lists the model, so I added a curated supplemental row in `internal/pricing/supplemental.go` following the existing `kimi-k3` rows. Both `step-5-preview` and `stepfun/step-5-preview` resolve to it through the canonical fallback. Like the other supplemental rows it's a fallback rather than a pin, so a later LiteLLM refresh replaces it once upstream publishes the model.

The rates are the published USD list prices from StepFun's Open Platform rate card, <https://platform.stepfun.ai/docs/en/guides/pricing/details>, which I read on 2026-09-21: input $1.00 per MTok on a cache miss, cache read $0.05, output $2.70. The same page notes the cache-miss input price includes writing new content to the cache, so cache creation uses the input rate instead of a separate number. StepFun also publishes a CNY card at `platform.stepfun.com`; I used the international USD card because the catalog is denominated in dollars.

A row added to `supplementalPricing` alone wouldn't reach archives that are already seeded, because `supplementalVersion` is folded into `pricing.SeedVersion` and the startup seed skips when the stored `_fallback_version` matches. I bumped it from 4 to 5 so the mismatch makes `SeedFallback` upsert the fallback set and pick up the new row without a resync.

The regression tests fail before the change: `Resolve` finds no pricing for either spelling, and a database holding `+supplemental-4` doesn't gain the row. Reviewer focus is the rate mapping in `supplemental.go` and the version bump.

Fixes #1862

title: feat(mcp): add bounded recall search contract
body:
Agents using MCP can now search for several literal terms within one user/assistant exchange and narrow recall by exact session, branch, project, agent, or date. An exchange is a user message plus its ensuing assistant run; assistant messages before a session's first user message anchor no exchange and never match. The response reports the effective mode, scope, and default exclusions, and next_cursor says whether another page exists; exact current-session exclusion happens before the limit so unrelated recent sessions remain eligible.

SQLite and PostgreSQL share the same exchange grouping, scope, ordering, and pagination behavior. The daemon HTTP path and generated clients carry the full contract, while unsupported stores reject `terms` explicitly.

Refs #1872

title: feat(mcp): add revision-bound evidence reads
body:
When an agent recalls something from past conversations over MCP, it makes two
calls: `search_content` finds a match, then `get_messages` opens it. A sync can
rewrite the session between those calls. Today `get_messages` then returns
different text at the same message number, and the agent quotes it as if the
search had found it.

This PR ties the two calls together with the session's transcript revision, a
counter that sync already bumps on every write:

- Search matches carry `transcript_revision` (SQLite and PostgreSQL). Passing
  it to `get_messages` as `expected_revision` fails with `source_changed` if
  the session has changed. The agent should then search again.
- `get_messages` returns the revision of the page it read. Every store reads
  the revision in the same query as the rows, so the two cannot disagree.
- A message cut at `max_chars_per_message` gets a `body_cursor` for reading
  the rest. Before this, text past 20,000 characters was unreachable over MCP.
  The cursor is bound to the revision, so a message cannot be stitched from
  two versions. It stops working after a server restart.

Reads without `expected_revision` behave as before. There are no new writes;
the counter already exists.

Limit: every append bumps the revision, so a citation into a session that is
still being written goes stale with each new message. Search skips recently
active sessions by default, so this shows up only with `include_active`.

Where to look: `internal/mcp/tools.go` for the cursor, `internal/service/direct.go`
for the revision checks, and `db.QueryMessagesWithRevision` plus each store's
`messages.go` for the same-query reads. The sync tests also switch to a locked
log buffer, because background signal retries wrote to it while tests reset it.

Refs #1872.

title: Add Spanish as an interface language
body:
## TL;DR

AgentsView had six interface languages and no Spanish. Español is now a choice in Settings, browsers that report `es` or any `es-*` variant get Spanish on first load, and the catalog covers every message key.

## How

Spanish plugs into the same places as the other locales: the inlang project settings, the supported-locale list, the language picker, and two new catalogs (`messages/es.json` and `messages/find/es.json`). The browser-language matcher maps `es` and every `es-*` tag to `es`.

The translation is neutral software Spanish. Instructions address the reader informally, buttons use the infinitive, and product names, model names, paths, commands, and raw API values stay in English, as in the French catalog. Search keywords for the Language setting list Spanish terms first and keep the English ones so both match.

A handful of user-facing strings still bypassed the catalogs: the empty state in the Trends line chart and the fallback error text in the usage, analytics, trends, activity, insights, and settings stores. Those now come from messages, so every language benefits.

## Reviewer notes

- **Zero is plural in Spanish.** CLDR puts 0 in `other` for Spanish but in `one` for French. The plural test asserts "0 llamadas a herramienta" so this cannot regress silently.
- **Key alignment is enforced.** The i18n tests fail if any catalog, including the new Spanish one, drifts from the English key set.
- **Playwright covers the real switch.** `e2e/spanish-locale.spec.ts` loads the app with an `es-MX` browser locale and also switches to Español from Settings, then checks the settings chrome and the Sessions view render Spanish.
- **Focus area:** the catalog is long. Spot checks on Recall (rendered as "Recordar"), Trash ("Papelera"), and Quality ("Calidad") wording are welcome.

title: Add local SessionStart memory refresh
body:
Conversation-memory lifecycle support, in four stacked parts:

- **Bounded recall search contract** (search_content): modes, scopes, and stable paging. Terms search matches user-anchored exchanges only and excludes assistant-only preamble groups, consistently in SQLite and PostgreSQL.
- **Revision-bound evidence reads** (get_messages): transcript revision pinning, plus body cursors that continue oversized messages. Cursors chain a page's truncated messages in order so no body is skipped, bind to the issuing page's session, revision, and role filter, and reapply system/role visibility before returning continuation content.
- **Focused memory profile**: an MCP tool surface exposing the memory tools with tuned defaults.
- **Local SessionStart refresh**: `agentsview memory session-start` ensures the writable local daemon is available and queues a coalesced background refresh within a 1.9-second deadline. The daemon route is hidden from the public API schema, protected by the existing auth and origin middleware, and unavailable on read-only or no-sync servers. `AGENTSVIEW_DISABLE_AUTO_SYNC=1` disables only the automatic lifecycle request.

This branch contains the stacked work also carried by #1875, #1877, and #1878; those pull requests resolve on merge. It covers the local archive-owner lifecycle; hosted contributor and reader roles follow separately.

Refs #1872.

title: Add hosted SessionStart lifecycle modes
body:
`agentsview memory session-start` now has explicit hosted-contributor and hosted-reader modes alongside the local archive-owner path. Contributors wake the identity-verified PostgreSQL push watcher for the selected target, so the existing owner keeps its debounce, credentials, embedding work, and push cadence; readers only probe their selected authenticated daemon or PostgreSQL target and never start a local archive.

The command keeps the 1.9-second lifecycle deadline and automatic-sync disable switch. Contributor wake delivery is available on macOS and Linux; Windows watchers continue on their normal filesystem-event and interval cadence.

title: Show query duration and a request timeline in the refresh control
body:
## TL;DR

The refresh control on the Activity, Analytics, Quality, Usage, and Recall pages said "Updated just now" with no hint of how long the refresh took, and its width tracked the text so the toolbar shifted on every tick. It now reads "Updated just now · 232 ms" at one fixed width, and hovering it opens a timeline of every query the page ran with server, transfer, and render segments per request.

## How

The wall clock runs from the first fetch a page starts to the moment it applies the last response. Each store records that as its query duration, so pages that fan out parallel panels report real elapsed time, not a sum of requests.

Per-request phases come from the shared API client. `orvalFetch` stamps when it sent the request, got headers, and finished the body, then attaches the stamps to the parsed response through a WeakMap. A store combines a stamp with its own apply time to build a step with Server, Transfer, and Render segments. The tooltip lays those steps on one axis with its origin at the first request, picks 1-2-5 tick intervals, and snaps any start within two pixels of zero onto the zero line so a burst of parallel requests shows one flush edge.

kit-ui #67 gave `RefreshControl` an `ageWidthSamples` prop that lays every candidate label into a hidden grid cell and sizes the box to the widest, plus an `ageTooltip` snippet slot. This branch pins that merge commit.

## Reviewer notes

- **Whole seconds only.** Under a second shows milliseconds, one second and up shows whole seconds, past a minute shows minutes and seconds. No decimals.
- **No placeholder without a duration.** The label drops back to the plain age string. The width samples still include the longest duration form so the box holds its size.
- **Activity maps SSE phases to steps.** The activity report streams phase markers. `ReportPhaseTimer` turns them into sessions, usage, scan, and finalize rows instead of one opaque bar.
- **Usage render starts at the later body.** Summary and the window summary arrive in parallel, so the render segment begins at the later of their body-complete stamps.
- **Focus area:** `querySegmentsFrom` and `queryStepFrom` in `frontend/src/lib/utils/refresh.ts`, and the tick and snap math in the shared `RefreshControl.svelte`. The jsdom tests read computed `left` and `width` styles because jsdom normalizes the raw style string.
- **Eight catalogs carry the 28 new keys,** including the Spanish and Azerbaijani ones that landed on main while this was in flight.

## Follow-up

The segments are client-observed. Splitting server time into database time versus the rest needs a `Server-Timing` header from the Go handlers and is a separate change.

title: Serve semantic search from ClickHouse behind a replica vector contract
body:
## TL;DR

A ClickHouse mirror could hold every session but answered semantic and hybrid search with "not supported", so a team serving the dashboard from ClickHouse lost the search mode the SQLite and PostgreSQL paths have. This adds a replica-neutral vector search contract, makes ClickHouse its second implementation behind PostgreSQL, and moves the local export of embeddings onto kit's new `sqlitevec.Snapshot` API.

## How

`storage.VectorSearchProvider` is what a replica backend implements to serve vectors: list pushed generations, and open a `db.VectorSearcher` for a config fingerprint or say why it cannot. `storage.VectorSearchStore` is the two setters a replica store exposes for the searcher and the unavailable reason. One gate in `cmd/agentsview/replica_vector_search.go` runs at serve startup for every replica and owns the config checks, encoder construction, and the operator-facing reason text. PostgreSQL moved onto that gate with no behavior change.

ClickHouse gets a vector phase inside `clickhouse push` and four `ReplacingMergeTree` tables keyed by the generation's config fingerprint and by the pushing archive. ClickHouse has no serial ids and no row-level upsert, so ownership follows the session tables' rule (a session's vectors live while its session row from this archive is resident) instead of PostgreSQL's owner markers. A change-scoped watch push widens to the whole generation until the archive records one clean generation-wide pass, and eviction never deletes rows another archive still records. Ranking is an exact `cosineDistance` scan in a shape the experimental `vector_similarity` index could later accelerate; the index itself is not created because it needs per-dimension tables and a result cap below the candidate pool.

The last commit replaces the raw SQL the export used to run against kit's sqlite-vec bookkeeping tables with kit's `Snapshot`, so the freshness rule lives in one place. It also swaps two private chunk rollups for `vector.RollupByDocument` and two hand-rolled single-text encoders for `vector.EncodeOne`.

## Reviewer notes

- **Behavior change for existing ClickHouse users.** A machine with `[vector]` enabled starts pushing embeddings on its next `clickhouse push`. `push_vectors = false` or `--no-vectors` opts out, matching PostgreSQL.
- **Schema version 1 to 2 only adds tables.** `EnsureSchema` upgrades an existing mirror in place. An older binary against an upgraded mirror ignores the new tables.
- **Focus area:** `internal/clickhouse/vector_push.go`. The completion marker, promotion rule, and ownership-aware eviction are where a wrong assumption would lose or leak vectors. `vector_push_chtest_test.go` covers interrupted passes, promoted exports that are not ready, and a two-archive handoff.
- **Semantic and hybrid `SearchContent` are still per backend.** PostgreSQL and ClickHouse each carry about 500 lines of the same orchestration around different SQL. A third backend is the point to lift it into `internal/db`; two did not justify it.
- **Setup runbook.** `docs/clickhouse-sync.md` gains a numbered sequence naming the output that confirms each step, written so an agent can run it unattended.

## Links

- kenn-io/kit#94 (the kit API this depends on)
- #1858 (the storage contract this builds on)

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

title: Expose conversation memory readiness over MCP
body:
Adds a shared, read-only conversation-memory status provider and exposes it through `GET /api/v1/memory/status` and the `get_memory_status` MCP tool. `search_content` responses carry the same compact lexical and semantic coverage snapshot, with bounded caching on the search path, explicit source-telemetry unknowns, vector generation coverage where available, and unsupported fallback for older remote servers.

SQLite reports active generation compatibility and embedded/missing counts, PostgreSQL preserves its negotiated availability reason, and DuckDB and ClickHouse report semantic search as unavailable. This is the server-readiness slice of the roadmap; local client installation diagnostics will follow separately. Depends on #1885.

title: Serve the ClickHouse Activity report from stored usage and event snapshots
body:
## TL;DR

The Activity report served from ClickHouse rebuilt candidate discovery in every query, parsed usage JSON per message, and paired tool events through a join that grew with the square of a session's size. On one private mirror a report took 5.5 seconds. The same report now takes about 1 second with identical output, for every agent harness.

## How

Discovery runs once and the selected session IDs ride along as a native external table, so later queries read `activity_candidate_ids` instead of repeating the predicate. Tool events pair per session in Go with a segment tree over message timestamps, which keeps the old ordinal and timestamp rules, including reversed clocks and the tail pairing after the last stamped message.

Two insert-maintained tables replace repeated scans. `usage_messages` stores token counters that its view computes from `token_usage` at insert time, keyed by the source message, so a retry that corrects a timestamp or removes usage still wins. The `messages` table keeps only the raw JSON. `terminal_event_snapshots` keeps the latest terminal tool event per session version, and discovery filters on it before version resolution.

## Reviewer notes

- **Revision ordering.** Both derived tables use `ReplacingMergeTree(revision)` with backfilled rows at `push_version * 2` and live rows at `push_version * 2 + 1`. A live insert beats a concurrent backfill of the same version, and readers join on `sessions.push_version` so superseded rows never surface.
- **Startup fill before serving.** The first push or serve after upgrading creates both tables and fills them from existing rows. Completion is recorded only after the work finishes, so an interrupted startup repeats it without touching source tables. A read-only serve role reports the pending fill until a capable push completes it.
- **Focus area:** `activitypairing.go` reimplements the SQL pairing rules in Go. The reversed-timestamp test covers the case I trust least.

title: Add conversation memory doctor diagnostics
body:
Adds `agentsview doctor memory` to report shared archive readiness alongside local client integration state. It supports read-only local SQLite, explicit daemon, and PostgreSQL targets; checks the native skill, focused MCP profile, SessionStart hook, and duplicate or differently targeted standalone skills; and emits human or JSON output without exposing paths, server URLs, or tokens.

title: [bug] Codex `apply_patch` calls record no file path, so Recent Edits never shows Codex edits
body:
### Summary

The Recent Edits feed (`/recent-edits`, `GET /api/v1/recent-edits`) never shows
an edit made by Codex CLI, so the feed appears to freeze on the last day a
non-Codex agent was the editor of record.

On a local archive where Claude Code was the main editor through 2026-09-10 and
everything after that is Codex CLI, the newest file in the feed is 2026-09-10,
even though Codex recorded 468 file edits after that date. Sync is healthy and
the rows exist; they just carry no `file_path`:

- `tool_calls` rows for `apply_patch` have `category = 'Edit'` and a non-empty
  `input_json`, so the calls are parsed and stored.
- `tool_calls.file_path` is NULL for 100% of them, and Recent Edits requires a
  path to group by.

### Environment

- agentsview v0.44.0 (commit 413a87f7, built 2026-09-21), binary install
- Linux x86_64, local daemon over SQLite, single machine
- Codex CLI 0.155.1 (sessions under `~/.codex/sessions`)
- Archive: a few thousand sessions across many agents, 527 `apply_patch` calls

### Evidence

Query 1 is exactly what the feed requires (Edit/Write with a path):

```sql
SELECT substr(m.timestamp,1,10) AS d, count(*)
FROM tool_calls tc
JOIN messages m ON m.id = tc.message_id
JOIN sessions s ON s.id = tc.session_id
WHERE tc.category IN ('Edit','Write')
  AND tc.file_path IS NOT NULL AND tc.file_path <> ''
  AND s.deleted_at IS NULL
GROUP BY d ORDER BY d DESC LIMIT 3;
```

```text
2026-09-10 | 58     <- newest day the feed can show
2026-09-09 | 33
2026-09-08 | 19
```

Query 2 is the same minus the `file_path` predicate:

```text
2026-09-21 | 22
2026-09-20 | 179
2026-09-18 | 96
```

The entire difference is Codex:

```sql
SELECT s.agent, tc.tool_name, count(*) AS calls,
       sum(CASE WHEN tc.file_path IS NULL OR tc.file_path = '' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS missing_path
FROM tool_calls tc
JOIN messages m ON m.id = tc.message_id
JOIN sessions s ON s.id = tc.session_id
WHERE tc.category IN ('Edit','Write') AND m.timestamp >= '2026-09-11'
GROUP BY 1, 2;
```

```text
codex | apply_patch | 468 | 468
```

That is 39 sessions and 468 calls since 2026-09-11, every one with a NULL
`file_path`. This is not a fresh regression: all 527 `apply_patch` calls in the
archive back to June have a NULL path. The feed only looked healthy before
because Claude Code was the editor of record; what changed is which agent is
doing the editing.

Tools whose arguments are JSON resolve normally, which makes the asymmetry
visible in the same archive: `view_image` calls (category `Other`) do carry a
path.

Timeline for the archive in question: the newest Claude Code session file on
disk is 2026-09-10T23:03 local, the newest `claude` Edit row is
2026-09-10T07:35Z, and after that only Codex (plus one read-only agent) produced
messages.

### Root cause

1. Recent Edits needs a structured path. `internal/db/recentedits.go` filters
   `tc.category IN ('Edit','Write') AND tc.file_path IS NOT NULL AND
   tc.file_path <> ''`, and groups by `(project, file_path)`.
2. The Codex parser never sets it. `handleFunctionCall` in
   `internal/parser/codex.go` builds `ParsedToolCall{ToolUseID, ToolName,
   Category, InputJSON, Rendering, SkillName}` with no `FilePath`
   (`internal/parser/types.go` documents `FilePath` as the "resolved edit/write
   target path, when known natively").
3. The generic fallback cannot recover it. `internal/sync/engine.go` fills an
   empty `FilePath` from `parser.ResolveFilePathFromJSON(tc.InputJSON)`, and
   `internal/parser/content.go` returns "" unless the input is valid JSON with a
   `file_path` / `path` / `filePath` / `file` key. A Codex `apply_patch` payload
   is raw patch text (`*** Begin Patch ...`), so it always fails that check.
4. The file names are already parsed, just not returned. `extractPatchedFiles`
   in `internal/parser/codex.go` (used by `formatCodexApplyPatchCall`) builds the
   summary, so a row renders as

   ```text
   [Edit: <path> (+1 more)]
   <path>
   <path>
   ```

   while `tool_calls.file_path` stays NULL.

The same gap applies to `custom_tool_call` items, which are the shape Codex exec
sessions use (see #1023 for the earlier fix that made these calls parse at all).

### Impact

- Recent Edits shows no Codex edit, for any project filter or date range: Codex
  is invisible in the one view dedicated to "what changed most recently".
- Anything else keyed on `tool_calls.file_path` inherits the same hole.

### Suggested fix

Set `ParsedToolCall.FilePath` for `apply_patch` from the patch text the parser
already walks for the summary (`extractPatchedFiles`):

- Single-file patch: use that file. This covers 391 of the 468 calls above.
- Multi-file patch: only one path can be stored today, so either keep it NULL and
  accept the 77 missing calls, or extend the model so one call can record several
  paths. The applied set is also available after the fact in
  `custom_tool_call_output` / `patch_apply_end`, which reads
  `Success. Updated the following files:` followed by `A`/`M`/`D` lines with one
  path each; 448 of those 468 calls carry such a result event in this archive.
  That source is only known once the result arrives, so it does not fit the
  current "resolve at call time" flow without a second pass.

No workaround exists in the UI. The edits are readable in the session timeline,
because the rendering text and the tool result keep the file names; only the
file-keyed feed is missing them.

Happy to send a PR once there is a preferred shape for the multi-file case.

title: fix(ui): clear the minimum prompt filter from the session filter menu
body:
The min-prompts row in the sidebar filter menu only ever sets a value. Clicking 2, 3, 5, or 10 again re-sent the same number, so once `min_user_messages` was set the widget had no way to drop it. The only remaining ways out were the active-filter chip or Clear filters, and the latter removes the rest of the filter set too.

Zero already means "no filter" everywhere else: `Filters.minUserMessages` defaults to 0, `filtersToParams` leaves `min_user_messages` out at 0, the sidebar index params drop it, and the query builders only add the `user_message_count >= N` clause when N is greater than 0. So this is a widget bug rather than a gap in the filter representation, and no new sentinel or query parameter is needed. I made the active pill toggle back to 0, matching the status pills in the same dropdown, which already clear on a second click.

The regression tests fail on `main` before the change: clicking 5 twice leaves the filter at 5, and an agent filter set alongside the minimum-prompt filter survives the clear untouched. Reviewer focus is the toggle in `SessionFilterControl.svelte`.

Fixes #1893

title: fix(parser): record Codex apply_patch file paths
body:
Recent Edits never shows a Codex edit because `tool_calls.file_path` is NULL for every `apply_patch` call. Codex names the edited files only inside the patch body (`*** Add File:`, `*** Update File:`, `*** Delete File:`, `*** Move to:`), so the generic `ResolveFilePathFromJSON` fallback can't find a path: the call carries either a JSON `patch` argument with no path key or, for `custom_tool_call`, raw patch text that isn't JSON at all. `formatCodexApplyPatchCall` already walked those markers to build the summary, so this reads the same markers into `ParsedToolCall.FilePath`.

One `apply_patch` can touch several files. Since `tool_calls` stores one `file_path` per row, the parser now emits one tool call per file, each carrying the same patch `input_json` and rendering and its own path. A multi-file patch therefore counts as several tool calls; sessions have no stored per-call aggregate, and the file-keyed views need the per-file rows. A patch with no recognizable file markers, or no patch body at all, keeps the previous single call with an empty `FilePath`, so a malformed patch can't fail a sync. Both Codex shapes are covered: a JSON `patch` argument and a `custom_tool_call` `input` string.

Existing archives won't pick this up from a normal sync, because unchanged source files are only reparsed when the data version moves, so I bumped `dataVersion` to 114 with the usual comment and `CurrentDataVersion` test. The regression tests fail before the change: the single-file patch reports no path, `codex/fc_args_2.jsonl` reports one tool call instead of two, and the `custom_tool_call` fixture reports an empty path.

Fixes #1899

title: fix(parser): index Pi subagent sessions in nested directories
body:
The `pi-subagents` extension doesn't keep child sessions beside interactive chats. For a parent transcript at `<project>/<parent>.jsonl` it writes the child to `<project>/<parent>/<runId>/run-N/session.jsonl`, and a child that delegates again repeats that shape below its own `session.jsonl`. Pi's `IncludePath` only admitted the sessions root and one project directory, so `agentsview sync` walked past those transcripts even though each one carries a normal Pi session header.

I replaced the predicate with `isPiSourcePathAtAnyDepth`, which keeps both existing layouts and accepts any deeper path under a configured root, rejecting only empty and traversal segments. The recursive walk was already in place, and `IsPiSessionFile` still filters file contents, so a nested `.jsonl` that isn't a Pi session stays out. That also picks up the forked children the extension writes under `<parent>/forks/`.

A fresh child's header records no `parentSession`, so the Pi parser now links it by path. A `session.jsonl` inside a `run-N` directory takes `<parent>.jsonl`, three levels up, as its parent and is marked as a subagent. This is the same way OMP subagents are linked, and it matches the path the parent's `subagent` tool result records in `details.results[].sessionFile`. The link only happens when `<parent>.jsonl` exists and is a Pi transcript. A run under an explicit `sessionDir` has no parent transcript above it, so it stays a standalone session instead of getting a guessed parent. Forked children keep the parent link from their header.

The regression test builds the extension's layout and fails on main because the child is never discovered. The other cases pin a nested child two levels down that links to the child above it, layouts that must stay unlinked, a run directory holding only companion files, and a project directory added as a second root so the same transcript isn't indexed twice. Reviewer focus is the predicate in `internal/parser/pi_provider.go`, the parent lookup in `internal/parser/pi.go`, and the fixture depths in `pi_provider_test.go`.

Fixes #1894

title: Reuse the ClickHouse Activity freshness probe and scan only the exact usage range
body:
## TL;DR

A repeated Activity report served from ClickHouse rescanned six tables to learn nothing had changed, then read a month of padded usage parts twice and sorted wide rows in Go. The report now reuses its freshness probe while the mirror's parts are unchanged, scans only the exact report range once, and sorts row indexes. Output is identical for every agent harness.

## How

**Freshness from part metadata.** Every request first asks whether the mirror changed. That probe scanned `sessions`, `messages`, `usage_events`, both pricing tables, and `sync_metadata` for counts and maxima. The store now hashes the active `system.parts` rows of those tables and returns the cached probe while the hash matches. A merge rewrites parts without changing data, so the hash is never the report token. On a miss the store recomputes the original probe and caches it under the new hash, so only a real data change moves the token or resets pagination. Errors are not cached.

**Exact usage bounds, one pass.** The usage scan padded the report range by 14 days on each side and truncated bounds to whole seconds. Survivor selection only compares rows inside the range, so the padding bought nothing. The query now uses the exact range with fractional seconds. Snapshot-key discovery reads the candidate sessions' pairs directly instead of building a bounded key list, joining it to `sessions`, and filtering the main read through it again.

**Obsolete usage rows.** A push deletes older versions of every dependent table, but a materialized view fills `usage_messages`, and views never see deletes. A shorter republished session left its removed ordinals behind at the old version. The push now deletes them in the same step. `terminal_event_snapshots` stays out because the session insert writes its row last and readers match that version exactly.

**Less Go work.** The usage sort orders a slice of indexes instead of moving wide scanned rows, and pricing resolves rates once per computed row instead of twice.

## Reviewer notes

> [!IMPORTANT]
> The serve role now needs `GRANT SELECT ON system.parts`. Under the default `select_from_system_db_requires_grant`, a role granted only `SELECT ON <db>.*` can read `system.columns` but not `system.parts`. Without the grant the Activity report fails with an access error that names it. There is no fallback.

- **The query depends on exact skip-index mode.** The exact time filter reaches the `usage_messages` minmax index under FINAL, so the query sets `use_skip_indexes_if_final_exact_mode`. Without it, a timestamp correction that moves a message out of range resurrects the older in-range version. Both 25.8 and 26.8 default the setting on, so the regression test forces it off on its connection and the query's own setting is what the test proves.
- **Integration pin moves to 26.8.** Compose, the testcontainers fallback, CI, and docs now use the 26.8 LTS line, which matches deployments. The 25.8 parser read an ISO `T...Z` literal in a `Nullable(DateTime64)` column as NULL, so the fixtures use the space-separated form.
- **Focus area:** `clickActivityReportUsageQuery` in `activityreport.go`. Key discovery may now return obsolete keys. The outer read still resolves version, eligibility, and time, and a peer-only group cannot be attributed to a candidate.

title: Refuse to open an archive whose fts5 index this build cannot load
body:
## TL;DR

An agentsview build whose SQLite lacks the fts5 module could open an archive that an fts5 build had already indexed, then fail every message write with `no such module: fts5` until someone read the sync log. Writable open now probes the existing `messages_fts` table and refuses the archive with the SQLite error and the build flags that fix the executable.

## Why

`CREATE VIRTUAL TABLE IF NOT EXISTS` skips the module lookup when the table already exists, so schema init reported success. The `messages_ai`, `messages_au`, and `messages_ad` triggers still reference fts5, so the first insert or delete on `messages` failed. In a packaged deployment this ran for hours: every incremental write and session rewrite errored, local sync reported processing incomplete, and mirror pushes were rejected while the process looked healthy. The binary recorded the fts5 build tag, so the tag alone was not proof that SQLite had fts5.

## Reviewer notes

- **Fresh archives are unchanged.** A build without fts5 still creates an archive without the index and runs with search fallback. The probe only runs when `messages_fts` already exists.
- **Read-only opens are unchanged.** They never write through the triggers, so a serve-only process can still read an fts5 archive.
- **The test rewrites the stored module name.** A process cannot drop its own fts5 module, so the test points `messages_fts` at a module nothing registers. SQLite reports the same failure mode.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

title: fix(sync): bound idle watcher and failed-source work
body:
Reduces idle sync work on large archives, following #1820. Watcher batches link
subagent relationships only for affected sessions. Unchanged polls skip global
linking unless earlier work left unfinished links. Metadata-only changes refresh
clients without requesting global linking.

Failed or canceled syncs retain unfinished links for later polls, even while an
unrelated source keeps failing. Workers pass repair counts and pending work to
the daemon. Startup adopts pending links before reconciling the worker-to-watcher
gap. Audit workers receive pending repairs even when sources are unchanged.
Workers confirm link state separately from source errors, so finished repairs
clear retries even when another source fails. Installed rebuilds also clear
finished retries; missing or invalid results preserve them. Committed repairs refresh clients even after
cancellation. Queued, scoped, and legacy repairs contribute to those counts, with transactions preserving counts across retries. Queued
repairs run even when discovery finds no files. Full resync counts restored
links and aborts replacement if relinking fails. Discarded replacements preserve
the live archive's pending retries and do not report repairs.

Grok fingerprints include companion files. Repeated watcher events preserve the
failure cache; actual companion edits still trigger sync.

Retry state lives in the running engine. Review scoped linking in
`changed_session_links.go`, polling eligibility in `engine.go`, and the worker
handoff in `cmd/agentsview`.

title: Count the refresh time up and show query steps live while a query runs
body:
## TL;DR

On a slow refresh, the label read "Updated 1m ago · 17 s" for the whole query. The time changed only when the query finished, and the popover listed only finished steps. Now the time counts up from the start of the query, and the popover shows each request or report phase as it starts, with running bars that grow along the time axis.

## How

Each page's store records its running query in a new `LiveQuery` object in `utils/liveQuery.svelte.ts`. The store marks each step when it starts and when it settles, and drops it if it fails or is cancelled. `RefreshControl` runs a 100 ms clock only while a query runs, draws running bars up to that time, and goes back to the last completed query when it ends. A running query gets at least one second of time axis, so bars start at zero width instead of filling the track in the first milliseconds. The axis now uses at most four tick intervals, so a one-second axis reads 0, 500 ms, 1 s instead of crowded labels. All timings come from the browser, and the Activity report already streams its phases, so the server is unchanged.

## Reviewer notes

- **Step handles, not names.** A cancelled request can finish cleaning up after its replacement starts. Each step start returns its own handle, so late cleanup cannot remove the new step.
- **Untracked reads in `LiveQuery`.** Recall loads its data inside a Svelte effect, which reruns when any state it reads changes. A tracked read made that effect loop.
- **Activity label width.** Activity passes its progress messages as `statusWidthSamples`, so "Loading sessions… · 3 s" fits without cutting off the time.
- **Focus area.** Check the `LiveQuery` calls in `stores/usage.svelte.ts`, where the summary request can retry after a project-scope error.
