title: fix(parser): add the Windows Hermes state root
body:
Hermes Agent sessions on Windows now load without directory configuration. The provider adds the Windows archive root beside the existing POSIX root, so a stock install reaches its sibling SQLite state.db through the parser's existing archive routing even when no sessions directory exists.

The change keeps database and sessions watches bounded, while preserving session identity, continuation links, profiles, explicit overrides, and remote consumers. Redirected LOCALAPPDATA and named Windows profiles remain explicit configuration cases.

The Windows location is documented from the pinned Hermes owner source in the format guide.

Closes #1880

title: fix(parser): support SQLite-backed OpenClaw sessions (#1845)
body:
OpenClaw sessions stored in `agent/openclaw-agent.sqlite` now appear alongside legacy JSONL sessions. This restores sync for current OpenClaw installs while keeping existing session IDs and using the shared OpenClaw event decoder. A broken agent database no longer blocks readable siblings. The reader covers the measured OpenClaw 2026.9.5 schema; QClaw behavior stays unchanged.

SQLite fingerprints belong to individual sessions, so one append reparses only the changed session. Discovery scans event payloads once and carries each fingerprint into sync. Quick sync compares these fingerprints even when event timestamps are old, so edits and deletions remain detectable. A write arriving after discovery can wait for the next sync. Unchanged sources skip duplicate-ranking lookups. An unavailable remote path mapping no longer turns that lookup into a sync error.

SQLite wins when both layouts contain the same session. While configured roots and remote-path mappings identify the stored SQLite source, JSONL cannot replace it even after the database disappears. Returning to a JSONL-writing OpenClaw version therefore keeps the last SQLite snapshot: later JSONL messages for those IDs are not imported. Removing a member from an existing database marks it unavailable while retaining its saved messages.

Legacy JSONL discovery streams candidates as directories are read. Discovery, session-ID lookup, and reconciliation prefer live files over archives, then the newer copy, with paths breaking ties. Explicit stored-source preferences remain supported, but hints cannot override a requested session ID. A shortened file keeps its archived messages; a newer, different copy can still replace the transcript.

The roborev guidance now states that missing source files leave sessions archived, and only an explicit user delete removes stored data.

Closes #1845

title: Skip repair passes for clean transcript text
body:
Syncing spends less CPU checking transcript text. `SanitizeUTF8` in `internal/db/messages.go` used to run every string through three passes (strip NUL bytes, repair invalid UTF-8, strip control characters), even though almost all transcript text is already clean. It now runs a single `isCleanText` check first. That check looks for NUL, invalid UTF-8 and C0/C1/DEL control characters in one pass, and skips printable ASCII 8 bytes at a time without decoding runes. Clean text is returned unchanged; anything else takes the old repair path, so output is identical by construction. Archive writes, fingerprints and the PostgreSQL push path still share this one helper.

Measured against main 66dd6e5dc on an Apple M5 Max. The machine was shared, so wall times are noisy.

| Case | main | This PR |
|---|---|---|
| ASCII transcript text (microbenchmark) | 20.8 µs | 3.05 µs (-85%) |
| JSON tool output | 30.2 µs | 4.22 µs (-86%) |
| Mixed Unicode | 22.8 µs | 12.4 µs (-46%) |
| CJK text | 27.1 µs | 22.4 µs (-17%) |
| Text that needs repair | 37.5 µs | no change |
| `sync --full`, 950 MB local corpus: user CPU | 14.50 s | 13.88 s (-4.3%, p=0.01) |
| `sync --full`: wall time | 15.6 s | 15.9 s (not significant) |

Allocations are unchanged: none for clean text. In a CPU profile of the full sync, `SanitizeUTF8` fell from 0.89 s to 0.15 s. Every fresh-sync archive had identical message, tool-call and session digests on main and on this branch. An earlier estimate of about 9% faster fresh-sync wall time did not reproduce on this machine, so this PR claims only the CPU saving.

Where to look:
- The block scan inside the `isCleanText` loop. It builds each 8-byte word from single byte loads, and the arm64 compiler turns that into one load. There is no `unsafe` or `encoding/binary`. A version with the block scan in a separate helper was measured and was 13-36% slower on clean text, so the check stays inline.

title: Hold less parsed data while bulk sync writes wait
body:
Full syncs and archive rebuilds now hold less parsed data in memory. During bulk passes (full sync, resync rebuild, contributor rebuild), finished parser results wait in a collector until the next database write. The collector was allowed to keep an estimated 512 MiB of them, on top of the 256 MiB budget for parses still running. On large archives that waiting data was most of the live heap. This PR lowers the pending-result budget to 128 MiB (`defaultBulkPendingRetentionBytes` in `internal/sync/parse_retention.go`). The collector writes smaller batches sooner and drops parsed content earlier. Worker admission and the 256 MiB active-parser budget do not change, so parse concurrency is the same. A source with an unknown or oversized estimate still counts as 256 MiB, which is at least the pending budget, so it is still written in a batch by itself.

Measured against main 66dd6e5dc on an Apple M5 Max. The machine was shared, so timing varied by ±12-17%. The memory effects are much larger than that noise.

| Measurement | main (512 MiB) | 256 MiB | This PR (128 MiB) |
|---|---|---|---|
| `sync --full`, 2.1 GB local corpus: peak RSS | 441 MiB | 373 MiB (-15%) | 342 MiB (-22%, p=0.008) |
| same corpus: wall time | 40.4 s | 43.0 s (n.s.) | 41.3 s (n.s.) |
| same corpus: write transactions | 19 | 36 | 73-76 |
| same corpus: max live heap | 131-209 MB | 98-193 MB | 78-97 MB |
| Synthetic rebuild benchmark: peak RSS | 520 MiB | 367 MiB (-30%) | 291 MiB (-44%) |
| Synthetic rebuild benchmark: write batches | 2 | 4 | 8 |

Allocation volume barely changes (+0.1% to +0.5%). Smaller batches shorten how long parsed data lives; they do not reduce how much is allocated. The tradeoff is more write transactions per rebuild. No throughput gain is claimed, and no throughput loss was measurable on this machine. Row-level digests of every non-FTS table matched across all three budgets.

Where to look:
- `bulkPendingRetentionBytes` is a package variable that defaults to the constant. Production code never writes it. It exists so `benchColdArchive` can set it from `AGENTSVIEW_BENCH_SYNC_PENDING_MIB`, because rebuild contributor engines build their own budgets through `NewEngine` and a per-engine field would not reach them. The benchmark restores it on cleanup.
- `BenchmarkResyncBulkContributorIngest*` now reports `batches/op`, one per write transaction. Bench-gate runs against older bases will not have this metric.
- Test expectations in `parse_retention_test.go` follow the new budget: saturated, unknown and negative sources now retain 256 MiB, and the batching fixture uses 12 MiB sources so two estimates still overflow the 64 MiB test budget but fit together under 128 MiB.

title: Pair activity events once per day in hourly reporting exports
body:
`export day` and `export digest` build their hourly reports faster. `reportingHoursFromSource` in `internal/db/reporting_export.go` used to call `activity.PairActivityEvents` once per hour, up to 24 times a day. Each call grouped, sorted and parsed every event of the day again. It now pairs the day's events once, over `[date - gapCap, end)`. For each hour it takes the subslice of paired candidates whose start falls in `[hourStart - gapCap, hourEnd)`, found with two binary searches on the start-ordered list.

The output matches per-hour pairing exactly. The prior model is computed over all events in order, independent of the pruning window, and every hour's window lies inside the day's window, including a partial current day. So each subslice is the same ordered candidate list that per-hour pairing produced. The subslice is capped with a full slice expression (`dayCandidates[first:last:last]`), and neither aggregator modifies it. The read snapshot, source loading and the reporting range contracts are unchanged.

| Day with 32 long sessions (720 messages each) | 68.1 ms to 25.4 ms (-63%) | 154 MiB to 35 MiB (-77%) | -4% |
| Joint day, 4 or 100 projects, schema v3 | -17% | -21% to -23% | -40% to -43% |
| Joint day, schema v4 (5m and 1m) | -7% to -11% (5m with 4 projects: n.s.) | -9% to -15% | -29% to -34% |

title: Profile spawned sync workers on request
body:
Background sync workers can now write their own CPU, heap and trace profiles. The server runs heavy passes (startup, sync, resync-build, audit) in a separate `sync-worker` process. The hidden `--cpuprofile`, `--memprofile` and `--trace` flags only profile the CLI process, so there was no way to see where a worker spent its time. Without that, later fresh-sync changes cannot be attributed.

`runSyncWorkerContext` now calls `startSyncWorkerProfile` first. It reads two environment variables that workers inherit from the server:

- `AGENTSVIEW_SYNC_PROFILE_DIR`: each worker creates a private `sync-worker-<mode>-<pid>-<random>` directory (mode 0700) there and writes `cpu.pprof` and `memory.pprof`. File names never include source identities.
- `AGENTSVIEW_SYNC_PROFILE_TRACE` (parsed as a bool): also writes `runtime.trace`.

Profiling is off by default and best-effort. An invalid trace value, an unknown mode, or a root that cannot be created writes one line to `debug.log`, and the pass runs without profiles. Worker stdout still carries only NDJSON progress and result lines. The server must be started with the variables set; a running server does not pick them up.

The shared profile closer in `sync_profile.go` also changes order. CPU and trace capture now stop before the forced GC and heap encoding, so that shutdown work no longer appears as sync work. This also affects the existing `sync` and `export` profiling flags.

With capture off, a `sync --full` and a worker startup pass on a local 274-session corpus showed no change in time or peak RSS against main 66dd6e5dc (n=10 per side, p>0.3). With capture on, the profiles and trace opened in `go tool pprof` and `go tool trace`. The trace contained no GC from the profiler's heap snapshot, which confirms the reordering. Every run produced the same archive digest as main.

Where to look:
- `startSyncWorkerProfile` and the closer ordering in `cmd/agentsview/sync_profile.go`.
- `TestSyncProfileTraceExcludesHeapSnapshotGC` runs `go tool trace -d=parsed` and depends on its text output (a tab before `runtime.GC @`). It needs `go` on PATH and is skipped under `-short`. The pinned `golang.org/x/exp/trace` cannot read traces from the Go 1.27 toolchain this repository uses, so the test does not use it.
- `docs/internal/performance-simulator.md` has a new section on profiling sync workers. `memory.pprof` is taken after a GC, so it is not peak memory: use `alloc_space` for allocation volume and OS tools for peak memory. Keep timing runs unprofiled, and profile only disposable archive copies.

title: Lowercase GenAI price match rules once per lookup
body:
GenAI price lookups are cheaper, and they still select the same price. Before this change, every `starts_with`, `ends_with` and `contains` rule lowercased both the rule text and the model ID on every check. A catalog of hundreds of rules therefore paid hundreds of lowercase conversions per lookup, and an uppercase model name allocated each time.

- Catalog (`internal/pricing/catalog/genai.go`): scalar match patterns are lowercased once when the catalog is parsed. `Resolve` lowercases the model ID once per call and passes it through provider lookup, model lookup, fallback providers and nested `or`/`and` clauses. Equality still uses `strings.EqualFold` on the original text, and regex rules still see the original case. Applying `strings.ToLower` twice gives the same result as applying it once, for every valid rune and for invalid UTF-8, so matching is unchanged.
- Resolver (`resolveGenAI` in `internal/export/pricing.go`): the alias list (canonical, reported, effort-tier base, flat fallback) and the provider candidate list are built in fixed-size arrays instead of growing slices. Alias order, provider precedence and the priced model name are unchanged.

Measured against main 66dd6e5dc (Apple M5 Max, n=12 per side, benchstat, all p=0.000):

| Lookup | Time | Bytes/op | Allocs/op |
|---|---|---|---|
| 256 scalar rules, lowercase model | 4.87 µs to 0.58 µs | 16 to 16 | 1 to 1 |
| 256 scalar rules, uppercase model | 11.2 µs to 0.64 µs | 4128 to 32 | 258 to 2 |
| Bundled catalog, direct | 1313 ns to 451 ns | 176 to 144 | 4 to 3 |
| Bundled catalog, uppercase | 2977 ns to 503 ns | 1328 to 168 | 52 to 4 |
| Bundled catalog, provider-qualified | 1499 ns to 452 ns | 272 to 144 | 5 to 3 |
| Bundled catalog, unmatched | 720 ns to 414 ns | 56 to 0 | 3 to 0 |

Most of the gain is from the catalog commit. On its own, the resolver commit removes one or two allocations per lookup; its time gain is significant only for provider-qualified lookups (-9%). It can be dropped separately if that is not worth the code. A differential run over every provider and model in the bundled catalog, in plain, uppercase, provider-qualified, dated, prefixed and invalid-byte forms, produced byte-identical results on main and on this branch, including patterns and provenance.

title: Aggregate PostgreSQL tools and skills analytics in SQL
body:
The PostgreSQL **Tool Usage** and **Top Skills** analytics panels now run one SQL query each. Before, each panel loaded every matching session into a Go map, queried `tool_calls` in chunks of 500 session IDs, and applied the local date, hour and weekday filters in Go. On a large archive, one year of tools analytics moved 73,000 rows and allocated 652 MiB in AgentsView.

Now a query in `internal/postgres/analytics.go` (`WITH analytics_sessions ... analytics_calls ...`) applies the existing session filters and tool-session window. It joins `tool_calls` to `messages` on `(session_id, ordinal)` as before, then applies the model filter and the padded UTC message window. Each call's time is the message timestamp, or the session start when that is missing. PostgreSQL converts it to local time with `AT TIME ZONE` and filters on local date, ISO weekday and hour.

- Tools returns one row per session, category, tool name, agent and local date. `BuildToolsAnalytics` still forms the weekly trend and the "Unknown" label.
- Skills returns one row per session, skill, agent, project and day/week/month bucket, with the latest use time. `BuildSkillsAnalytics` still does the final shaping.
- Session IDs stay in the grouping, so distinct session counts are exact.
- `analytics_sessions` is `MATERIALIZED`. Without that, pgx's per-connection prepared statements let PostgreSQL switch to a generic plan from the sixth execution on. For sparse filters that plan hash-joined all tool calls to all messages and was about 5x slower than main. With `MATERIALIZED`, all executions keep the session-first plan.

Measured against main 66dd6e5dc on PostgreSQL 16 with default settings (Apple M5 Max, n=10 per side, all p<=0.002). The large fixture has 4,380 sessions and about 219,000 tool calls.

| Case | main | This PR |
|---|---|---|
| large, tools, one year | 1.70 s, 652 MiB | 130 ms, 8.7 MiB |
| large, tools, all history | 5.33 s, 1.96 GiB | 334 ms, 29 MiB |
| large, skills, one year | 345 ms | 67 ms |
| large, tools, one project of 50 | 34.2 ms | 17.0 ms |
| large, skills, one project of 50 | 13.7 ms | 5.0 ms |
| geomean of all 12 cases | 79.3 ms | 13.1 ms (-84%) |

A differential dump of 64 responses (8 filters, tools plus three skills granularities) was byte-identical on main and on this branch.

Remaining differences from main:
- Time zone conversion uses PostgreSQL's time zone data instead of Go's. They agree for current zones; they could differ if the server's tzdata is older or newer.
- A malformed `From` or `To` returns an error from the `::date` cast. Main compared the local date to the raw bound as text. The HTTP handler rejects malformed dates first. Matching main's text comparison in SQL (`to_char(...) COLLATE "C"`) cost about 40 ms per 219,000 calls, so this PR does not do it.
- PostgreSQL needs a zone name, so `timezone=Local` resolves through `timeutil.LocalTimezoneOrUTC`, the shared helper AgentsView already uses to name the server's zone.

A call with no message timestamp and no session start or creation time keeps main's behavior: an upper bound alone keeps it with an empty date, and a lower bound drops it.

body:
### agentsview version

agentsview v0.44.0 (commit 413a87f7)

### Install method

install.sh / install.ps1

### OS / platform

arch (lates)

### Which agent and version

n/a

### Which model(s)

n/a

### What happened, and what did you expect



Several machines each run agentsview pg service install (i.e. pg push --watch) against the same PostgreSQL database. When two of them push at almost the same moment, one push fails:

pg watch: push (change) failed: installing raw ingest append-only guards: ERROR: tuple concurrently updated (SQLSTATE XX000)

The next trigger, about 30 seconds later, succeeds and sends the backlog (pushed 1 sessions, 247 messages (change)), because the watermark wasn't advanced. So nothing is lost, but every collision leaves a failed push in the log. The more machines push, the more often it happens.

Likely cause

Each push seems to re-run the DDL that installs the raw-ingest append-only guards: CREATE OR REPLACE on functions and triggers, or something similar. PostgreSQL doesn't serialize concurrent CREATE OR REPLACE on the same catalog row, so when two sessions run it at once, one gets tuple concurrently updated (XX000).



Suggested fixes (any one would do)

- Wrap the schema and guard setup in a transaction-level advisory lock (pg_advisory_xact_lock(<constant>)), so concurrent pushers take turns.
- Skip the guard installation when the guards already exist at the expected version, and do the DDL only on migration.
- Treat SQLSTATE XX000 "tuple concurrently updated" from this step as retryable: back off briefly and retry within the same push, instead of failing it.

Impact: low, because it heals itself. But it's noisy, and it makes real push failures harder to spot in pg-watch.log.


### Steps to reproduce

Repro

1. Point two machines at the same database with [pg].url.
2. Make a session change on both within about a second, so both watchers fire together, or run agentsview pg push on both at once.
3. One of them logs the error above.

title: fix(pg): serialize concurrent raw custody guard installation
body:
PostgreSQL schema setup re-runs the raw custody guard DDL, so two `pg push` processes hitting the same database at the same time both run `CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION raw_ingest_reject_accepted_mutation()`. That updates the same `pg_proc` row, PostgreSQL serializes the row, and one session waits and then fails with `SQLSTATE XX000` ("tuple concurrently updated"). The statement is identical in both sessions, so the collision doesn't need the definition to change.

I reproduced it on a local PG16 with two sessions replacing the same existing function: the second blocks, then errors once the first commits. The regression test drives the same race through `ensureRawIngestSchemaPG` by dropping the three triggers and holding `raw_manifests` in `ACCESS EXCLUSIVE`, which parks both installers inside the guard DDL. Before the change one installer fails with XX000; after it both finish and all three triggers are installed. That's the same catalog-row race as the report, not the reporter's exact production interleaving or timing.

The guard DDL now runs in one transaction that first takes the `raw_ingest_schema_lock` row in `sync_metadata`, the same kind of row lock that pricing syncs already take. Both now use one shared helper, `lockSyncMetadataRow`. A row lock is used instead of `pg_advisory_xact_lock` because supported CockroachDB versions don't implement advisory locks. I only locked the guard step: the `CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS` pass before it is a no-op on an existing schema, and putting it in the same transaction would roll back table creation when the guards hit `SQLSTATE 0A000` on a backend without PL/pgSQL. Provisioning a brand-new database concurrently still assumes one provisioner. The 0A000 fallback is otherwise unchanged, so those backends still log that immutability stays application-enforced.

Before taking the lock, the installer checks the catalog. When the guard function source matches `rawIngestAppendOnlyFunctionBody` and all three triggers exist, it returns without locking or running DDL. A provisioned schema therefore never waits on another installer, and a changed function body is still reinstalled. On CockroachDB the lock is released before DDL runs, because the server auto-commits the transaction before DDL (`autocommit_before_ddl`). CockroachDB stores normalized function source, so the check never matches there and setup reaches the same `0A000` fallback as before.

Fixes #1928.

title: feat(parser): add Junie CLI session ingestion
body:
Adds native ingestion for Junie CLI sessions in `~/.junie/sessions`: prompts, assistant messages, system notices, titles, project metadata, timestamps, and per-response model, token, and reported cost data. Tool calls, tool results, file edits, and IDE-only conversations are outside this provider's scope.

Index events select changed sessions once an in-memory baseline exists. Fresh planning engines, including remote delta imports, select and re-hash every listed transcript. Failed metadata-only updates recover on the next full sync, normally within 15 minutes, or transcript write.

Missing roots and corrupt index records do not block healthy roots. Corrupt indexes retain the last good cached metadata; without a cache, that root waits for a valid index and keeps its archived data. An absent index clears cached metadata. Malformed event lines are skipped; oversized records and invalid costs reject the import.

Results replace markdown under the same step ID, matching Junie's producer. Review `internal/parser/junie.go`, `internal/parser/junie_provider.go`, and the public-artifact reproduction details in `docs/internal/session-format-sources.md`. No schema change or new dependency.

title: feat(signals): expose friction spans and session input adapter
body:
Archived sessions can now be reviewed for corrections, tool errors, workarounds, deferrals, frustration, interruptions, and repeated health problems. Findings include the messages and tool calls behind retries, edit churn, runaway loops, compactions, and high context pressure, using the existing signal rules.

The adapter excludes system rows, thinking, and tool renderings, including OpenHands action summaries. Edit churn uses stored file paths and supported input keys, so Codex patches and other tool formats are counted consistently in full and incremental scans. Empty Bash failures and bare timeouts remain suppressed.

This adds in-memory review only; storing findings and displaying them remain follow-up work. Part 2 of the Friction Log series, building on merged #1924. Refs #1908.

title: feat(serve): support reverse-proxy base paths
body: This adds a new `--base-path` option to `agentsview serve`, which lets you mount agentsview behind a subpath of a reverse proxy. The frontend and backend already had all of the necessary infrastructure; we just need a config option to hook it all up. With this approach, `--public-url` should remain origin-only. The docs describe the appropriate setup: to serve this behind a reverse proxy at `https://example.com/agentsview/`, you would use `--public-url https://example.com --base-path /agentsview`. This mimics the existing available options for e.g. `agentsview pg serve`.

title: fix(clickhouse): check Activity metadata permissions at startup
body:
ClickHouse serve now refuses to start when its account cannot read `system.parts`, instead of accepting startup and returning an internal error on the Activity page. The startup error explains how an administrator can grant access through SQL or the XML user configuration.

This checks the actual metadata read. It does not grant permissions automatically: the application account cannot grant access it lacks, and SQL cannot modify XML-managed users. Deployments missing the grant must add it before starting the updated server.

title: perf(clickhouse): narrow usage source and single-session reads
body:
## TL;DR

A one-day usage read joined every message to its session before applying the date range, so almost every joined row was thrown away. Messages that have a timestamp are now filtered by it before the join; messages without one still fall back to the session start, so results do not change.

`GetSession` and `GetSessionFull` also put the session id in `PREWHERE`. The id is the table key, so ClickHouse reads only the matching granules instead of every selected column, which keeps peak memory down for sessions with large columns.

## Reviewer notes

- **Fallback path.** The test covers a message with no timestamp, both edges of a local day, and a timestamp that a later push replaced.

title: fix(clickhouse): keep a session's payload unchanged across push retries
body:
## TL;DR

When a batch insert failed, the push retried each session on its own and loaded it from the archive again. If the archive changed in between, the retry wrote a different payload under a push version the failed batch had already partly written, so one version could hold rows from two archive states. Each retry now reuses the first load of that session; the local change goes out with the next push under a new version.

title: perf(signals): skip the frustration pattern when no marker can match
body:
## TL;DR

The signals panel ran a case-insensitive regular expression over every user prompt in every matched session, and on one day of prompts that scan was most of the request. A case-folding substring check now skips the expression when none of its dozen required literals is present, and the ClickHouse server keeps each session's marker count per push version.

## Why

On a local copy of one workstation's archive, the signals panel dropped from 954 ms to 301 ms cold and 19 ms warm.

## Reviewer notes

- **Same matches.** Every alternative in the expression needs one of the literals, so the check never skips a prompt the expression would match. A scan that matches the old expression strips code fences.
- **Counts are stored only after a full read.** A canceled scan cannot leave a zero behind.

title: perf(clickhouse): cache the pricing catalog per set of pricing parts
body:
## TL;DR

Every report reloaded the pricing catalog: three queries, a 477 KB GenAI document parse, and a sort of about 4,000 rows for the digest. The server now keeps the catalog per set of active pricing parts, so only a push that changes pricing replaces it.

## Reviewer notes

- **Model match cache.** Row pricing also re-ran provider and model patterns for every usage row. The server now keeps the matched model per model name as reported, because regex rules match on its original case. Only the price version depends on the row's timestamp.

title: feat(clickhouse): publish complete usage snapshots and prepare usage rows
body:
## TL;DR

Every usage report recomputed its date-ordered rows from the raw message and usage event tables, and on a small ClickHouse host that work dominated the Activity and Usage reports. Pushes now publish one complete, versioned usage snapshot per session, and a refreshable materialized view turns those snapshots into prepared usage rows that the Activity report reads.

## How

Each push reads a session and its usage from the archive in one transaction, so a snapshot never mixes two archive states. The `prepare_usage` view rebuilds `prepared_usage` from the snapshots on a schedule and after each push. Report pagination fingerprints now come from row contents instead of part checksums, so a background merge no longer resets an open report.

## Reviewer notes

- **Projections are added only when missing.** Every refresh swaps in a new table, and an `ALTER` that meets the swap fails with "metadata file has different UUID". When a projection is missing, the schema step stops the refresh, waits for a running one, alters the table, and always starts the refresh again, reporting both errors if either step fails.

- **New grant.** Serve needs `SELECT ON system.view_refreshes` to tell whether the prepared rows are current. It checks at startup and names the grant if it is missing. #1953 removes this requirement.

title: perf(clickhouse): pair activity intervals while usage loads
body:
## TL;DR

The Activity report ran usage loading and interval pairing one after the other, although both depend only on the candidate sessions, and it checked snapshot coverage with a full sessions join twice per request. Pairing now runs while usage loads, and the server keeps coverage per set of table parts.

## Why

With the pricing cache and prepared usage rows below it in the stack, the one-day Activity report on a local copy of one workstation's archive dropped from 144 ms to 87 ms, and the all-data report from 1.5 s to 0.87 s.

title: perf(clickhouse): serve range usage from prepared rows priced at refresh
body:
## TL;DR

The usage summary, top sessions, and comparison panels still scanned every raw message row for a one-day range, and ClickHouse spent about 120 of the summary's 137 ms planning a 16 KB query built around a per-request price join. Range reads now use prepared rows that are sorted by time and priced when the refresh runs, and recent reads are kept in memory.

## Why

| Local copy of one workstation's archive | Before | First load | Repeat |
|---|---|---|---|
| One-day usage summary | 284 ms | 89 ms | 16 ms |
| Top sessions | 140 ms | 60 ms | 7 ms |

The day filter now reads 2 of 35 granules instead of all of them.

## How

Each prepared row stores its timestamp key, price model, price key, and price record, plus the snapshot set and pricing digest it came from. A read uses prepared rows only when that stamp matches the live snapshots, and otherwise falls back to the price join or the raw rows. The table comment names the query that built it; a table built by a different query is rebuilt in place, and a rebuild that stopped halfway finishes on the next start.

## Reviewer notes

- **Double count fixed.** Prepared reads apply project, agent, and model filters after Claude snapshot attribution, as the raw read does. Before, a session whose usage facts belong to another session in the same request was counted twice.
- **Kept reads.** One slot per read, versioned by the mirror's parts and keyed before any read, so a push that lands mid-read makes the next request miss. Reads filtered by `active`, `stale`, or `unclean` termination depend on the current time and are never kept.
- **Refresh interval** is now 15 minutes, because every push starts a refresh anyway.

- **Grant dropped.** Readiness now compares the stamp on the prepared rows with the live snapshots, so serve no longer needs `SELECT ON system.view_refreshes`.

title: perf(clickhouse): read each analytics page's session listing once
body:
## TL;DR

Every panel on the analytics page listed the same filtered sessions, so one page load ran that read eleven times. The server now keeps the listing in memory per predicate and arguments, versioned by the mirror's parts, so a page reads it once.

## Why

On a local copy of one workstation's archive: tools 136 ms to 46 ms, skills 78 ms to 27 ms, projects 22 ms to 2 ms, sessions 26 ms to 16 ms.

## Reviewer notes

- **Key format.** The key renders arguments in Go syntax, because `%v` made `["a b", "c"]` and `["a", "b c"]` the same key.
- **Timezone cache.** The tool and skill panels read the zone database from disk for every row. They now share the usage filter's location cache.
- **Session ids** travel as one external table instead of one statement per 900 placeholders.
- **Concurrent panels share one read.** The panels of a page ask at once, so the first request reads the listing and the others wait for its result. The read finishes even if the request that started it is cancelled, so the others still get it.

title: perf(clickhouse): serve prepared usage across pushes with a per-session delta
body:
## TL;DR

With pushes about every half minute, prepared usage was almost never current, so reads between refreshes fell back to raw rows and took seconds on a small host. Reads now keep the prepared rows of unchanged sessions and add rows prepared in Go for the sessions pushed since the last refresh.

## How

Prepared rows carry the revision of the snapshot they came from. For changed sessions, the server prepares and prices rows with the same resolver a push uses and sends them to the read as an external table, which replaces those sessions' stored rows. A refresh empties this delta. Pricing happens in Go because a join against the price records would scan every record to find a few keys.

Finding the changed sessions stays cheap. The server compares coverage in Go instead of with anti-joins under `FINAL`. Changed ids reach ClickHouse as an `Array(String)` parameter that the snapshot key can narrow. The server keeps prepared delta rows per snapshot, so it reads only new snapshots.

## Why

On a local copy of one workstation's archive, the first Usage reads after a push take 100-170 ms for a week and 60-100 ms for a day.

## Reviewer notes

- **Refresh mid-read.** A read skips the stored rows of every session the delta supplies, so a refresh that lands after the state was taken cannot count a new session twice.
- **Focus area:** readiness now requires every session to have a current snapshot. The parity test pushes a republished, an added, and a removed session between refreshes.

title: perf(clickhouse): keep activity report inputs and ended ranges' reports
body:
## TL;DR

The Activity report re-read every candidate session's messages, tool events, and usage on each request, and an ended day's report was rebuilt whenever any push landed. The report now keeps its inputs per session version and keeps the whole report of an ended range until a push touches the rows it read.

## Why

On a local copy of one workstation's archive, a repeat of the day's report dropped from about 52 ms to 28 ms, and a past day viewed again after an unrelated push to 14 ms, against 133 ms before this stack.

## How

Pairing inputs are kept per session and push version, so after a push only sessions whose version moved are read again. An ended range's report key names everything it reads: candidate sessions and their push versions, the snapshots behind each usage row in the range, the pricing catalog and digest, the project identity tables, the filter, and the range.

## Reviewer notes

- **One slot per selection.** Each kept read holds only its latest version, so pushes replace entries instead of adding copies.
- **One parts snapshot per request.** Every check in a request uses the same snapshot of table parts, and an ended range already checked against those parts is served without further reads.
- **Cancelled reports stop.** Pairing checks the request's context per session and before each sort, so a report a client abandons stops using CPU.
- **Interrupted pushes.** A push writes a session's messages and tool events before its session row. If it fails in between, kept pairing inputs and ended-range reports show the session as it was until its next successful push; the push retries it at once and the watch daemon within minutes. Uncached reads show the half-written messages instead.

title: perf(clickhouse): keep reports fast across pushes in bounded memory
body:
## TL;DR

Every push invalidated the kept reads, so the first report after a push, usually the one a person sees, paid for the full query, and a past day was fast only if someone had opened it since the last restart. Kept reads also grew without bound. Serve now saves each ended day a client opens to disk, re-reads only the sessions a push changed for ranges still in progress, bounds what it keeps in memory, and keeps prepared usage for every host whose snapshots are complete.

## Why

Local replica of one workstation's archive (15,686 sessions), ten past days nobody had opened:

| | Time |
|---|---|
| Before this stack | 37-126 ms |
| First open | 12-62 ms |
| Reopen from memory | 3-5 ms |
| Reopen from disk after restart | 6-11 ms |

On a 16,000-session mirror, a client that walked every Activity day, week, and month left about 850 MB of live heap before this change and about 90 MB after. The all-sessions report after a push went from 0.77 s to 0.55 s, and the server's peak heap from 800 MB to 530 MB.

With the whole stack on a 29,000-session mirror, a 12-week all-sessions Activity report takes 2.5 s warm, against 4.3-4.5 s on the same main without the stack.

## How

- **Opened days on disk.** Only days a client opens are written, under the service cache directory. Each open refreshes the file time, and a sweep at startup and about once a day removes reports nobody opened for 30 days.
- **Read keys that survive merges.** A prepared usage read keys on the prepared table's stamp and the small tables it joins or prices from. Merges rename the large tables' parts for a minute or more after a push, so a key over every table was usually stale before a client asked.
- **Ranges in progress.** Today, this month, or an all-time range keeps every session's usage rows in report order, compactly encoded, with the snapshot revision each was read at. After a push, a report reads only the sessions whose revision changed and merges them in. When more than a quarter of the sessions changed, one read of the range is used instead.
- **Bounded memory.** Each kept read has a byte cap as well as an entry cap and drops its oldest entries past it: 128 MiB for each of the two report memos, 256 MiB for ranges in progress, 64-128 MiB for the rest. A range in progress whose end has passed is dropped, and an ended range keeps only its report. Top sessions keep one total per session. Pairing keeps timestamps as microseconds, interns roles and models, and its memo holds up to two million messages and tool events, so a report over a large mirror reads only the sessions a push changed.
- **Per-host readiness.** Prepared usage used to turn off for the whole mirror while any session lacked a current snapshot, so one host running a client without snapshot publishing sent every report back to raw rows. A host is now ready once all its sessions have a current snapshot. The other hosts' sessions are read raw, shaped and priced like prepared rows. Serve logs readiness and each host's snapshot coverage when they change.
- **Message counts from pairing inputs.** The pairing read keeps one flag per message saying whether the Activity message counts include it, so the report counts from inputs it already holds instead of reading every message in the range again. On the same local replica, a warm 12-week report's counts went from 65 ms to 15 ms.

## Reviewer notes

- **No background rebuilds.** An earlier version of this PR reran recent reads after every push. On a small host that work competed with the requests it meant to speed up and pushed the server past 2 GB, while saving about 20 ms on the day view, so it is gone.
- **Disk use.** If the cache directory cannot be used, serve logs it and keeps reports in memory.
- **Custom pricing.** Serve reads the first prepared usage state and starts the sweep only after it installs custom model rates.
- **Interrupted pushes.** Ranges in progress and message counts also come from data kept per published session version, so they catch up at the session's next successful push; see #1956.

title: Incremental sync can store the parsed size with the pre-parse mtime, so a growing file gets a full re-parse on the next sync
body:
### agentsview version

agentsview v0.44.0 (commit 413a87f7bfbd67b2815b1119ac51abc1efbeeaba, built 2026-09-21T12:48:49Z)

### Install method

install.sh / install.ps1

### OS / platform

macOS 26.6.2 (arm64)

### Which agent and version

Claude Code 2.1.282

### Which model(s)

n/a (not model-specific)

### What happened, and what did you expect

Over 94 minutes of debug.log on v0.44.0, `file size unchanged at N but changed since last sync, full parse` appeared 53 times across 29 transcripts, and those full parses re-read 7.2 GB. They land on the transcripts being written most. 4.9 GB of it is five re-parses of one transcript, which grew from 0.3 GB to 1.5 GB during the window.

From reading the code at v0.44.0, I think this is a race inside the incremental path:

- `internal/sync/engine.go:15568` takes the mtime from the stat done before parsing (`incMtime := info.ModTime()`).
- The Claude parser then reads from the stored offset to whatever end of file exists at read time (`readJSONLFrom`, `internal/parser/linereader.go:220`, with no bound at the stat size).
- `engine.go:15767` stores `fileSize: newOffset` (offset plus consumed bytes) together with that earlier mtime.

If Claude Code appends between the stat and the read, the stored size describes the later state and the stored mtime the earlier one. On the next sync, if nothing more was written, the size matches, the mtime doesn't, and the branch at `engine.go:15553` forces a full parse.

I'd expect the stored size and mtime to describe the same moment. Bounding the read at the stat size would do that, or re-running the stat after the read and storing its mtime when the size still equals `newOffset`. I know this branch is what catches same-size in-place rewrites (the v0.36.1 fix), so I'm not suggesting it be skipped, only that this race stop reaching it.

I haven't ruled out that something else on my machine also changes transcript mtimes.

### Sample session file or snippet

I can't share the transcripts, but I can share the relevant debug.log lines or test a build.

### Steps to reproduce

1. Run agentsview serve v0.44.0 while a Claude Code session is writing a large transcript continuously.
2. `grep -c 'but changed since last sync, full parse' ~/.agentsview/debug.log`, and compare which files it names with the ones being written.

### Checklist

- [x] I searched existing issues
- [x] I removed secrets and private data from any attached session files

title: Claude incremental sync re-parses the whole transcript when a sync lands inside one response (shared message.id)
body:
### agentsview version

agentsview v0.44.0 (commit 413a87f7bfbd67b2815b1119ac51abc1efbeeaba, built 2026-09-21T12:48:49Z)

### Install method

install.sh / install.ps1

### OS / platform

macOS 26.6.2 (arm64)

### Which agent and version

Claude Code 2.1.282

### Which model(s)

n/a (not model-specific)

### What happened, and what did you expect

Thanks for v0.44.0. The 15-minute scheduled sync no longer re-reads unchanged transcripts, and on v0.37.4 that sweep was the largest single reader of the disk on my machine.

What's left is on transcripts that are still being written. I run many Claude Code sessions at once, and some transcripts are over 1 GB. Over 94 minutes of debug.log, `appended chunk shares message.id with stored tail, full parse` appeared 14 times, and each one re-parsed the whole transcript. Two of them were on the same transcript, when it was 0.3 GB and then 1.3 GB.

As I read the check against `LastClaudeMessageID` (`internal/sync/engine.go` around line 15807), it fires when the previous sync stored part of an assistant response and the new bytes continue the same `message.id`. Claude Code writes several JSONL records for one API response, all with the same `message.id`, so a sync boundary that falls inside a long response (thinking, text, several tool calls) takes this path. The comment there explains why a plain append would be wrong.

I'd expect a sync of a file that only grew to cost about as much as the new bytes. Two ideas, if either fits the design:

1. Don't advance the stored offset past an assistant response that could still be continuing, so the next sync reads that response from its first record as a normal append. The live view would then lag by one response.
2. Re-parse from the first record of the stored tail message and replace messages from that ordinal onward. That needs a stored byte offset for the message, the parser state from just before it, and recomputed totals for the replaced rows, so it's a bigger change than it sounds.

This is a different fallback from #1073, and the size-unchanged full parses in the same log are in #1962.

### Sample session file or snippet

I can't share the transcripts. I could share redacted record metadata around one boundary (record types, uuid/parentUuid, message.id, byte offsets, no content), or test a build.

### Steps to reproduce

1. Run agentsview serve v0.44.0 with a Claude Code session producing long responses (several tool calls each).
2. `grep -c 'shares message.id with stored tail, full parse' ~/.agentsview/debug.log`.

### Checklist

- [x] I searched existing issues
- [x] I removed secrets and private data from any attached session files

title: docs(roborev): define schema compatibility
body:
Roborev now expects migrations to upgrade databases from main and releases without data loss, and stops flagging missing migrations for schema that only existed on an unmerged branch.

Adds rule 20, Schema Compatibility, following the [review discussion on #1730](https://github.com/kenn-io/agentsview/pull/1730#issuecomment-5824098444).

title: perf(sync): read conversation export text from archived messages instead of a stored copy
body:
The archive from the corpus in #1968 is 694 MB instead of 782 MB, close to the 655 MB before #1782, with no change in sync time. The export index kept a second copy of every message body.

Text reads join the archived message at the projected position, hash it, and check the hash against the digest the index published, so a read pinned to a revision returns the same bytes or reports the revision as changed. Resync and archive copies read text the same way, and rewriting an older archive with nothing new publishes nothing.

The column stays in the schema and stays empty, so the table shape and data version are unchanged, and older archives shrink on their next full resync. An older exporter can't read text from an archive written this way.

Stacked on #1969.

Refs #1968

title: fix(sync): store the parsed size with its post-parse mtime
body:
Incremental sync reads a transcript from the stored offset to whatever end of file exists at read time, but the mtime it persists comes from the stat the caller did before that read. `tryIncrementalJSONL` takes `incMtime` from `info.ModTime()` and then computes `newOffset` from the parser's consumed bytes, so when a writer appends in between, `file_size` describes the later file and `file_mtime` the earlier one. On the next sync the size matches and the mtime doesn't, which is the `currentSize == inc.FileSize` branch in the same function, and it returns `forceReplace` for a full parse. That's the `file size unchanged at N but changed since last sync, full parse` line from the report: the whole transcript is re-read and its messages are replaced, so nothing is duplicated or skipped, it's just wasted work proportional to the file.

The fix re-stats after the read and, when the file still ends at `newOffset`, persists that stat's mtime and reuses it for the Codex checkpoint, which stores the same size and mtime pair. I re-stated rather than bounding the read at the stat size because bounding means threading a limit through every provider's `ParseIncremental`, while the re-stat stays in the engine. The refresh only happens when the read went past the pre-parse stat, so a same-size in-place rewrite still leaves its mtime change for the next sync to notice. There's no format change and no migration: a row already carrying the mismatched pair is exactly what makes the next sync re-parse once, and that full parse rewrites it with a consistent pair.

The regression test runs a real Claude sync and grows the transcript inside the stat-to-read window through the engine's path rewriter, then asserts the persisted offset and mtime and that the next sync skips. It fails on `main` on the mtime assertion and on the skip. What it doesn't do is race a real writer against a running sync, so it pins the persisted pair and the skip predicate rather than re-parse counts, and the window it injects is one append rather than the multi-gigabyte growth in the report. A second test covers the ordinary append, where size and mtime advance together and the unchanged file still skips.

Reviewer focus is the block after `newOffset` in `tryIncrementalJSONL`, the `os.Stat(file.Path)` it adds, and whether `newOffset > info.Size()` is the boundary you'd draw.

Fixes #1962

title: fix(sync): re-parse only the open Claude run when a sync splits one response
body:
A sync that stops partway through a Claude response stores the partial response as one message. The next sync saw the appended chunk share its `message.id` and re-parsed the whole transcript to finish that one response. In #1963 that meant reading up to 1.3 GB.

Now `parser.ClaudeSplitRunStart` scans back from the stored offset to the response's first record. The engine re-parses from there, and `IncrementalSessionUpdate.ReplaceFromOrdinal` replaces only the rows from that response onward. Earlier rows, tool calls, and pins stay as they are, and session totals are adjusted by the replaced range. Parallel tool calls, where a `tool_result` sits between records with the same id, now append normally instead of forcing a full parse.

Anything the re-parse can't prove matches a full parse still gets a full parse. That covers usage-only archives, malformed records, offset or ordinal mismatches, the session's first prompt, and the parser's existing fallbacks.

The main logic is in `tryClaudeSplitSuffixUpdate` (`internal/sync/engine.go`) and `replaceSessionIncrementalTx` (`internal/db/sessions.go`).

Fixes #1963.

title: fix(sync): apply session provider settings without a daemon restart
body:
Changing session providers on the Settings page now takes effect in the running daemon. Before this change, turning a provider on or off, or adding or removing an alternate agent home, saved the setting but did nothing until someone restarted the daemon. The panel told users to restart it by hand. The sync engine, file watchers, polling, and live activity poller all kept the provider set they were built with at startup.

**How it applies now.** After a settings save that touches `disabled_agents` or `agent_homes`, the daemon reloads its configuration the same way startup does: defaults, `config.toml`, environment, then the original `serve` flags. The sync worker processes already reload this way on every pass. The HTTP response returns right away with the new derived session roots. The daemon then applies the change in the background:

1. The engine swaps its provider set and session roots as one snapshot. It waits for any in-flight sync first, so a pass never changes providers partway through.
2. New watchers and polling start before the old ones stop, so a file change cannot fall in the gap. A change seen by both is synced twice, which is harmless.

A reload never starts a sync, so saving settings never waits on one. New files under newly enabled roots arrive through the new watchers. Sessions already on disk there arrive with the next sync, whether that's the Sync button, the daily audit, or a restart. Reloads are serialized by a mutex. Each one reads the saved configuration again under that mutex, so the last reload to run applies the latest settings, even when two saves race.

With `--no-sync` there is no background engine; the server reconfigures its on-demand engine instead, so manual syncs follow the new settings. If a reload fails, the server restores the previous provider settings, so `config.toml`, the response, and the running engine agree.

A provider that becomes disabled keeps its archived sessions, the same as when the daemon starts with it disabled. The Settings notice now confirms the change was applied. It only asks for a restart of any separate `push --watch` process.

**Limits.** Edits made directly to `config.toml` still apply at the next daemon start; only Settings saves trigger a reload. Separate `pg/clickhouse/duckdb push --watch` processes are unchanged.

**Where to look.** The core risk is in `internal/sync/engine_sources.go` and `cmd/agentsview/ingestion_reload.go`. The engine's `agentDirs`, `sourceMachines`, `providerFactories`, `preserveAgents`, and `providerStatHashers` moved behind an atomic snapshot (`e.sources()`). Most of the `internal/sync` churn is that mechanical rename plus test engines built with `withTestSources`. `runServe` now hands ownership of the watcher, poller, and live activity poller to `daemonIngestion`. The server reads its active disabled-provider list and config under one lock, so callers never mix two reloads.

These screenshots come from an isolated daemon with synthetic sessions. OpenClaude starts disabled in `config.toml`. Toggling it on in the UI applies the change without a restart:

![settings-before.png](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/9fcef97b-d73b-4dc6-b4bb-a1b34eb6ae11)

title: perf(sync): build the conversation export index on first export
body:
A fresh sync no longer pays for the conversation export index. On the corpus from #1968 it takes what it took before #1782, and the first `export conversations changes` on that archive takes about 2 s.

An archive is cold until its first export: sync writes no index rows, only per-session records for deletions, policy gaps and project changes. The first export builds the index from stored messages in one transaction and marks the archive active; later writes maintain it. The read-only export command asks the owning daemon through a new local route, or opens the writer itself when no daemon runs.

Only archives that have never exported get the faster sync. One that has exported stays active, and a full resync still maintains its index so message IDs carry across; building it once at the end of the rebuild is the follow-up.

Refs #1968
