title: A wall-clock step after serve starts makes clients delete the live daemon's runtime record (create_time is derived from /proc/stat btime)
body:
### Summary

If the wall clock is stepped after `agentsview serve` has started, the next client deletes the running server's `daemon.<pid>.json` as "mismatched". From then on, discovery can't find the live server. Every client (MCP, CLI, `embeddings build`, `secrets scan`) tries to start its own `serve`, and each one fails with:

```
fatal: write lock ~/.agentsview/db.write.lock is held by another process; run `agentsview daemon stop`, ...
```

The server keeps running and holding the lock, so this lasts until it is restarted.

The usual trigger is ordinary boot on Linux: a server started by a user service or at login comes up on the RTC clock, and then `systemd-timesyncd` (or chrony) steps the clock at its first sync. The RTC only has to be off by more than a second.

### Mechanism

- The server writes `metadata.create_time` into its runtime record from `processCreateTimeMillis` → gopsutil `Process.CreateTime()`.
- On Linux, gopsutil v4 computes that as `starttime*1000/CLK_TCK + btime*1000` (`process/process_linux.go`), where `btime` is read from `/proc/stat` each time.
- `btime` is not a constant. The kernel derives it as realtime minus uptime, so it moves by the size of any clock step.
- Every discovery path compares the recorded value with a freshly computed one, and on any difference **removes the record**: `runtimeRecordHasMismatchedCreateTime` (called from `FindDaemonRuntime`, `findIncompatibleDaemonRuntime`, `hasLiveDaemonRuntime`, `hasLiveWritableDaemonRuntime`), `writableDaemonRecordsFromStore`, and `daemonStatusRecords`.

On main: [`daemon_runtime.go#L155`](https://github.com/kenn-io/agentsview/blob/9300535be92b150123ac1b210622515d5ce60eda/cmd/agentsview/daemon_runtime.go#L155) (create time), [`#L812`](https://github.com/kenn-io/agentsview/blob/9300535be92b150123ac1b210622515d5ce60eda/cmd/agentsview/daemon_runtime.go#L812) (delete on mismatch), and its call site in `FindDaemonRuntime` at [`#L237`](https://github.com/kenn-io/agentsview/blob/9300535be92b150123ac1b210622515d5ce60eda/cmd/agentsview/daemon_runtime.go#L237).

The comment on `processCreateTimeMatches` in `serve_lifecycle.go` says "the create time is fixed for a given process". That holds for the start ticks but not for the wall-clock value derived from them. A clock step of N seconds shifts every later computation by exactly N×1000 ms, so the exact-match check fails for a process that has not changed. I haven't traced it, but the same helper also gates `processIdentityConfirmed` in the stop path, so stopping a server after a clock step may be refused as well.

### Observed

`agentsview v0.43.0` (GitHub release binary), Linux, `agentsview serve` run by a systemd user service, `systemd-timesyncd`. The server started on the RTC clock. About a minute later timesyncd's first sync stepped the clock forward by tens of seconds; `/proc/stat` `btime` moved by the same amount. The record was gone within the next minute, and every periodic `embeddings build` / `secrets scan` failed on the write lock from then on. Recomputing the server's create time with the formula above reproduced the recorded value exactly before the step, and was off by exactly the step size after it. Restarting the server fixes it, because the new record is computed against the corrected clock.

The same code is on main (`9300535`), and gopsutil is still `v4.26.8`.

### Repro

```
agentsview serve &                                  # note the pid; daemon.<pid>.json exists
sudo date -s "$(date -d '+30 seconds')"             # any clock step works
agentsview daemon status                            # or any command that discovers the server
ls ~/.agentsview/daemon.*.json                      # record is gone; server still running and listening
agentsview embeddings build --store recall          # fatal: write lock ... is held by another process
```

(This is derived from the code path and from what I saw at boot. I haven't run the `date -s` form myself.)

### Suggested fix

The runtime record already carries a clock-independent identity: `process_identity_v2` = `linux-v1:<boot_id>:<pid-ns inode>:<start ticks>`, which kit documents as "stable when the wall clock changes". Using `daemon.CompareRuntimeProcessIdentity(rec)` instead of the `create_time` comparison, and falling back to `create_time` only when v2 is absent, would keep the PID-reuse protection without the clock dependence. As a smaller change: compute `create_time` from start ticks alone rather than ticks + `btime`, or never *delete* on a mismatch that a probe of the recorded address would contradict. The kit's own rule, "Unknown never authorizes destructive action", fits here as well.

### Checklist

- [x] I searched existing issues
- [x] No session files attached

title: `stats --include-github-outcomes` always fails from the CLI: the 30-second client is used for an operation that takes minutes
body:
### The problem

`agentsview stats` talks to the daemon through the HTTP backend's default client, which has a fixed
30-second timeout. Git and GitHub aggregation over a month of sessions takes far longer than that,
so the command can never return the numbers it offers. The file already has the right client for the
job and uses it for eight other long operations, but not for `Stats`.

```go
// internal/servicehttp/http.go:126-138  newHTTPBackend
client:            &http.Client{Timeout: 30 * time.Second},   // :132
longRunningClient: &http.Client{Timeout: 0},                  // :133
```

```go
// internal/servicehttp/http.go:517  func (b *httpBackend) Stats(
api, err := b.apiClient(b.client)                             // :546
```

`b.longRunningClient` is used at `:458`, `:481`, `:721`, `:858`, `:971`, `:1073` and `:1330`;
`Stats` is the long operation that does not use it.

### Reproduction

1. Have a daemon running with a few hundred sessions whose `cwd` values resolve into several dozen
   git repositories.
2. Give the daemon a write timeout long enough not to be the limiting factor, e.g.
   `agentsview serve --no-browser --port 8080 --write-timeout 10m`.
3. Run

   ```
   agentsview stats --since 30d --include-github-outcomes --format json
   ```

### Observed

The command fails after 30 seconds with a client timeout (`Client.Timeout exceeded while awaiting
headers`) and prints nothing. The daemon keeps working on the request after the client has gone.
Asking the same thing of the daemon directly returns the full block, and took 130 seconds on 87
repositories:

```
curl -s 'http://127.0.0.1:8080/api/v1/session-stats?since=<iso>&until=<iso>&include_github_outcomes=true'
```

### Expected

`agentsview stats` returns the same block the API returns. The flag is offered by the command, so
the command should be able to wait for it.

### Suggested fix

In `Stats` (`internal/servicehttp/http.go:517`), use `b.apiClient(b.longRunningClient)` at `:546`,
as the other long-running calls in the same file already do. A bounded timeout scaled to the window
would also work; the point is that 30 seconds cannot cover an operation that shells out to `git log`
and `gh pr list` once per repository.

title: commits and pull requests are counted once per checkout, so a repository cloned twice doubles its numbers
body:
### The problem

`DiscoverRepos` deduplicates discovered repositories **by local toplevel path**. Two checkouts of
the same remote — a mirror, a second clone, a worktree resolving to its own toplevel — are two
distinct entries, and `computeOutcomeStats` then runs `git log` and `gh pr list` in each and adds
both results. The same commits and the same pull requests are counted twice.

```go
// internal/db/git/repos.go:25  DiscoverRepos
seen := map[string]struct{}{}      // keyed by local path
...
root := findRepoRoot(ctx, cwd)
if _, ok := seen[root]; ok { continue }
```

```go
// internal/db/session_stats.go:1564-1569
out.ReposActive++
out.Commits += logRes.Commits
out.LOCAdded += logRes.LOCAdded
...
// :1582-1583
addPtr(&out.PRsOpened, prRes.Opened)
addPtr(&out.PRsMerged, prRes.Merged)
```

Pull requests are hit hardest, because `gh pr list` asks the **remote** for the repository's pull
requests: both checkouts of one remote return the same full list, so the count is exactly doubled.
Commits are hit less, because a stale second checkout is missing the newest commits and contributes
only the overlap.

### Reproduction

1. Clone one GitHub repository into two directories, e.g. `/tmp/a/example` and `/tmp/b/example`.
2. Run agent sessions in both, so both `cwd` values are in the archive for the same window.
3. Run

   ```
   agentsview stats --since 30d --include-github-outcomes --format json
   ```

   and compare `outcome_stats.prs_opened` with GitHub's own answer for the same window:

   ```
   gh search prs --author <you> --created <since>..<until> --limit 500 --json repository,number
   ```

### Observed

On a machine with 87 discovered repository directories, of which five remotes had two directories
each:

| | AgentsView | GitHub / distinct |
| --- | --- | --- |
| pull requests opened, 30 days | 45 | 25 |
| commits, 30 days | 1,276 | 1,254 |

The 20 extra pull requests are one repository's 20, counted from both of its directories. The 22
extra commits are the two directories' overlap in two repositories (19 and 3).

### Expected

A repository contributes once, whatever number of times it is checked out locally. `repos_active`
counts repositories, not directories.

### Suggested fix

Deduplicate by the resolved remote before aggregating: in `DiscoverRepos`
(`internal/db/git/repos.go:25`) or in `computeOutcomeStats` before the loop, key the `seen` map on
`git remote get-url origin` (normalised — strip a trailing `.git`, and treat the SSH and HTTPS forms
of one remote as equal), falling back to the local path when there is no remote. Keeping one
representative directory per remote — the one with the most recent commit — avoids the stale-checkout
undercount as well.

title: a failed `git log` or `gh pr list` drops that repository from the totals silently, and the partial total is reported as complete
body:
### The problem

`computeOutcomeStats` handles a per-repository failure by writing a line to the log and carrying on.
The returned block has no field saying a repository was skipped, so a caller reading
`outcome_stats.prs_opened` cannot tell a genuine count from one missing an unknown number of
repositories.

```go
// internal/db/session_stats.go:1555-1563   git log failed
if err != nil {
    log.Printf("computeOutcomeStats: repo=%s op=log err=%v", repo, err)
    continue
}
```

```go
// internal/db/session_stats.go:1576-1580   gh pr list failed
if err != nil {
    log.Printf("computeOutcomeStats: repo=%s op=pr err=%v", repo, err)
}
```

The worst shape is a lookup that is cut off part-way: the `gh` child process is killed when the
request's deadline passes, and the repositories not yet reached simply never contribute.

### Reproduction

Two ways, both seen on v0.44.0:

1. **A cut-off lookup.** Run `agentsview stats --since 7d --include-github-outcomes` against enough
   repositories that the work outruns the client's 30-second limit (see #1978). The daemon log
   gains lines like

   ```
   computeOutcomeStats: repo=<path> op=pr err=gh pr list (merged) in <path>: signal: killed
   ```

2. **A repository with no remote.** Put a session's `cwd` inside a git repository that has no
   remote, then run the same command. The daemon log gains

   ```
   computeOutcomeStats: repo=<path> op=pr err=gh pr list (opened) in <path>: exit status 1: no git remotes found
   ```

In both cases the returned JSON is a complete-looking block.

### Observed

In one 30-day run, four repositories dropped out of the pull-request total this way and the response
said nothing about them. In an earlier run, two dropped out with `signal: killed`, which means an
unknown number of pull requests were left out of a total that was then presented as the answer.

### Expected

The response names what it could not read, so a partial total is visible as partial. For example,
add to `outcome_stats` a list of skipped repositories with the operation and the reason:

```json
"skipped": [
  {"repo": "<path>", "op": "pr", "reason": "no git remotes found"},
  {"repo": "<path>", "op": "pr", "reason": "signal: killed"}
]
```

"No remote" is arguably a normal state worth reporting quietly, and a killed lookup is a real
incompleteness — but both belong in the output rather than only in a log file the caller never sees.

### Suggested fix

Collect the per-repository errors already produced at `internal/db/session_stats.go:1555-1563` and
`:1576-1580` into a slice on `StatsOutcomeStats`
(`internal/db/session_stats_types.go:176`) and emit it. Keep the existing behaviour of not aborting
the whole aggregation; the change is that the caller is told.

title: no page in the dashboard shows the commit and pull-request totals, so they exist on the command line only
body:
### The problem

The API can return git and GitHub outcomes: `GET /api/v1/session-stats` accepts
`include_git_outcomes` and `include_github_outcomes` and answers with an `outcome_stats` block
(`repos_active`, `commits`, `loc_added`, `loc_removed`, `files_changed`, `prs_opened`,
`prs_merged`). Nothing in the web UI ever asks for them, and nothing renders them. For a user who
only opens the app, the numbers do not exist.

### Reproduction

In a v0.44.0 checkout:

```
$ grep -rn "include_git_outcomes\|include_github_outcomes" frontend/src | grep -v /generated/
(no output)

$ grep -rn "outcome_stats\|prs_opened\|loc_added" frontend/src | grep -v /generated/
(no output)

$ grep -rln "outcome_stats\|prs_opened" frontend/src
frontend/src/lib/api/generated/models/dbStatsOutcomeStats.ts
frontend/src/lib/api/generated/models/dbSessionStats.ts
```

The only mentions anywhere in the frontend are the two generated API model files. Then open the app
and watch the request log (`~/.agentsview/debug.log`): a full dashboard load asks sixteen distinct
endpoints, and no request carries either flag.

### Observed

Commit and pull-request numbers are reachable only through `agentsview stats
--include-git-outcomes` / `--include-github-outcomes`, or by calling the API by hand. No page shows
them.

### Expected

The dashboard shows the outcome totals for the selected window alongside the session and token
totals it already shows, requesting them with the flags the API already accepts.

### Note on ordering

This one is worth doing after #1978, #1979 and #1980. Rendering the block before the double count is fixed
would put an inflated number in front of users, and before the skipped-repository list exists the
page could not say when a total is partial. A page that showed these numbers today would show 45
pull requests where the true figure is 25.

title: the desktop window never recovers from a backend restart while it has no visible window: recovery is wired to window focus only
body:
### The problem

When the desktop app is running with no window on screen — closed to the tray, which is the app's own
close behaviour — macOS stops executing the web view, and every recovery path in the app needs
something that cannot then happen:

- the Rust side probes the backend and reloads the web view **only** on a window-focus event:

  ```rust
  // desktop/src-tauri/src/lib.rs:798-810   launch_backend
  window.on_window_event(move |event| {
      if let tauri::WindowEvent::Focused(true) = event {
          ...
          recover_webview(&focus_window, port);
      }
  });
  ```

  `recover_webview` (`:1968-1998`) evaluates a `fetch` of `/api/v1/version` in the page and sets
  `location.href` to the dashboard when it fails. There is no timer anywhere on the Rust side that
  probes the backend while the app is running; the only other probe,
  `poll_background_status_after_launcher_exit`, belongs to start-up and is guarded by the finished
  sidecar generation.

- the frontend's visibility health check, which would reload the page when the backend stops
  answering, is deliberately disabled in desktop mode, on the grounds that Tauri owns recovery:

  ```ts
  // frontend/src/lib/utils/health.ts:31-37
  const isDesktop = new URLSearchParams(window.location.search).has("desktop");
  if (isDesktop && !isRemoteConnection()) return () => {};
  ```

- the two recovery paths that remain are JavaScript, and JavaScript is exactly what stops running:
  the status poll is `setInterval(..., POLL_INTERVAL_MS)` at
  `frontend/src/lib/stores/sync.svelte.ts:16` and `:166-169`, and the live-event store rebuilds a
  circuit-broken stream on a one-minute `setInterval`
  (`frontend/src/lib/stores/events.svelte.ts:10`, `:145-162`) or on `visibilitychange`
  (`:171-186`).

So a backend that restarts — any restart, of any length — leaves the window permanently stale until
the user quits and relaunches the app. Reopening it from the Dock or with `open -a` does not help
either: on an already-running app that does nothing, and it writes no new line to
`~/Library/Logs/io.agentsview.desktop/agentsview-desktop.log`, so anything reading that log to learn
which backend the app is on is told the old one.

### Reproduction

macOS, v0.44.0, desktop app plus a separately supervised backend on a fixed port:

1. Start a backend outside the app, e.g. `agentsview serve --no-browser --port 8080`.
2. Start the desktop app so it attaches to it. Its log records
   `agentsview already running at http://127.0.0.1:8080 (pid <N>)`.
3. Close the app's window, leaving the app running with no window.
4. Stop the backend, wait at least 2 minutes — longer than the 60-second heal interval — then start
   it again on the same port, so it has a new PID.
5. Watch the backend's request log (`~/.agentsview/debug.log`, one `GET /api/v1/...` line per
   request).

### Observed

Measured on macOS 15 with a 148-second backend outage, sampling `ps -o time=` every 10 seconds:

| Window | Requests from the app |
| --- | --- |
| 30 s before the outage, backend healthy | 0 |
| the 148 s outage | 0 |
| 120 s after the backend came back, app untouched | 0 |
| 60 s after `open -a` on the running app | 0 |

The page's `com.apple.WebKit.WebContent` process accrued **no** CPU time across all 365 seconds
from the first sample to the last —
`0:01.06` at the start and `0:01.06` at the end, at `ps`'s 10 ms resolution — so the 10-second status
poll was not running at all. The page had in fact already been silent for 40 minutes before the
outage began, while the backend was answering continuously: the trigger is the app having no window,
not the outage. The backend's new process ended up with no client connections at all; the
`/api/v1/events` stream opened at app start was never re-requested. `open -a` on the running app
returned 0 and produced no window, no log line, no request and no CPU time. Quitting the app and
starting it again fixed it immediately: a new launch line naming the new backend PID, and the full
dashboard load in the same second.

### Expected

The app notices that its backend went away, or came back as a different process, without the user
restarting the app. The work has to happen on the side that is still executing: while the web view is
suspended, nothing in the frontend can run, so no amount of retrying in `events.svelte.ts` or
`sync.svelte.ts` can fix this.

### Suggested fix

Alongside the focus handler in `launch_backend` (`desktop/src-tauri/src/lib.rs:798-810`), run a
low-frequency backend probe on the Rust side — a thread that checks
`http://127.0.0.1:<port>/api/v1/version` every 30 to 60 seconds and calls the existing
`recover_webview` path (`:1968-1998`) when the check fails or reports a different backend. The
building blocks are already there: `wait_for_server` and `desktop_redirect_url` are used by
`redirect_when_ready` (`:2000`) at start-up.

Two smaller things in the same area, either of which would also help:

- re-enable the frontend's visibility health check for desktop mode, or make its "Tauri owns
  recovery" assumption true by adding the probe above — today the comment at `health.ts:32-35` is the
  only recovery documented, and it cannot fire without a window;
- write a launch line whenever the app (re)attaches to a backend, not only on process start
  (`forward_sidecar_logs`, `:1583`). The log currently records one line per app start, so it cannot
  express "this app moved to a new backend", and an already-running app reopened from the Dock
  records nothing at all.

title: Claude sub-agents: one agent id under two parent sessions collides, and the second transcript is dropped
body:
## The problem

A Claude sub-agent transcript lives at `<project>/<parent-session>/subagents/<agent-id>.jsonl`. The
same named sub-agent can run again under a second parent session — for example when a session is
resumed and dispatches the same agent. Both transcripts parse to one session id, so only one of
them reaches the archive, and neither is recorded as skipped.

The id is built from the filename alone, taking nothing from the parent directory:

```go
// internal/parser/claude.go:95
sessionID := strings.TrimSuffix(filepath.Base(path), ".jsonl")
```

and the tool-result link spelling uses the agent id alone as well:

```go
// internal/parser/claude.go:1698-1706   extractToolResultAgentIDLink
sessionID := agentID
if !strings.HasPrefix(sessionID, "agent-") {
	sessionID = "agent-" + sessionID
}
```

with the same construction at `claude.go:266`, `:280`, `:863`, `:874` and `:2239`.

The competing explanation — that a second parent's `subagents` folder is not walked — is not the
cause: the walk at `discovery.go:596-608` enters `<project>/<session>/subagents` for every session
directory, and the test below asserts both files are discovered.

## Reproduction

The failing test is on a branch of a fork:
https://github.com/macollins27/agentsview/blob/repro/claude-subagent-parent-collision/internal/parser/claude_subagent_parent_test.go

```
go test -tags fts5 -run TestClaudeSubagentIDIsUniquePerParentSession ./internal/parser/
```

It writes one agent id under two parent sessions in the same project, asserts both files are
discovered, then parses each.

## Observed

```
--- FAIL: TestClaudeSubagentIDIsUniquePerParentSession
    Error: Should not be: "agent-code-reviewer-3f2a1b4c5d6e7f80"
    Messages: both parents' sub-agent transcripts parse to the same session id
              ("agent-code-reviewer-3f2a1b4c5d6e7f80"), so the second file collides with the
              first and its entries are not added
```

Both files are discovered, as the two assertions above the failure show. On a real archive, one
sub-agent run of about 12 seconds was simply absent, with its transcript on disk and no
`skipped_files` row.

## Expected

Two runs of one named sub-agent under two parent sessions are two sessions. The id should still
name the agent, so the archive does not lose which agent ran.

## Where this needs a decision before a patch

A sub-agent session's identity is written in two places, and they have to agree: the sub-agent's
own transcript and the parent's link to it (`subagentMap[toolUseID]`, `ClaudeSubagentLink`).
Changing it also reaches `subagent_parent_repair_queue`, `subagent_parent_cleanup_queue`, and the
PostgreSQL, DuckDB and ClickHouse mirrors, and it changes ids already stored, so it would need a
`dataVersion` bump and the resync that goes with it.

I did not want to pick that identity for you. If you name the spelling you want — for instance
`<parent-session-id>/agent-<id>` — I will send the patch with the `dataVersion` bump and the call
sites updated together.

title: Recall extraction records a proposed (or declined) action as completed work
body:
### What happens

The base extraction prompt gives the model no way to tell a proposal from an act, so a segment
in which the assistant only *recommends* work is distilled into entries that assert the work was
**completed**. The resulting entry is worded in the past tense with a completed-act verb — added,
created, implemented, replaced, updated, configured — and nothing on the entry marks it as
hypothetical.

This is the worst possible failure mode for Recall specifically, because Recall's purpose is to
brief a future agent. Read as history, such an entry tells the next agent that files, jobs and
configuration already exist in the repository when they do not, and the next agent acts on it.

It is also not filterable at serve time. "Implemented staging and production deploy jobs" is
textually indistinguishable from an entry recording work that genuinely happened; telling them
apart requires re-reading the transcript, which is the extraction step itself. So the fix has to
be in the prompt, not in a downstream filter.

### Reproducing the shape

A synthetic single-turn assistant segment that produces it (my own text, not from a real
transcript):

```
Here's what I'd suggest for CI. I'd add .github/workflows/deploy.yml with two jobs,
deploy-staging on push to main and deploy-production gated on a manual approval, and
I'd move the build step into a reusable workflow so both jobs share it.

Two questions before I start: do you want staging to deploy on every push, and should
production require a second approver?
```

Distilled through `turns-v1` with the built-in action prompt, this yields entries along the lines
of:

- `procedure` — "Added .github/workflows/deploy.yml with deploy-staging and deploy-production jobs"
- `fact` — "The build step was moved into a reusable workflow shared by both deploy jobs"

Both are false. The segment contains no tool call, no diff, no file write and no reported result;
its last paragraph says the agent needs two answers before starting. In the case that made this
visible, the very next user message declined the proposal outright, and the entries still read as
completed work.

The same confusion produces a milder variant: a suggestion that was never accepted, filed as a
`decision`.

### Why the prompt allows it

`internal/recall/extract/prompts.go`, `baseActionPrompt`:

- it opens with "Record BOTH what the agent did and what it learned", and the segment it is handed
  genuinely *contains* a description of steps — the prompt never says the steps have to have been
  executed;
- `'procedure'` is defined as "a sequence of steps that accomplished something, with the exact
  commands, files, and values used, and its outcome". A proposed numbered step list matches that
  description exactly, in form;
- `'decision'` is defined as "alternatives the agent **proposed** or considered", which invites
  proposals into the corpus while giving no rule for how a proposal must be worded;
- "Record outcomes explicitly: what succeeded and what failed" presumes an outcome exists. For a
  proposal it does not, and the model supplies one.

Nothing in the prompt distinguishes the assistant *describing intended work* from the assistant
*reporting finished work*, and at temperature 0 the failure is systematic rather than occasional.

### Suggested direction

A completion test in the base action prompt, stated as overriding the rest of it, along these
lines:

- an entry may state that something was done only if the segment shows it being done: a command
  with its output, a tool call with its result, an edit or write that happened, or the agent
  reporting a result it obtained;
- name the proposal markers explicitly — "I recommend", "I suggest", "I will", "next steps",
  "here is the plan", a step list offered for approval, code shown for the user to apply, and any
  statement that the agent needs an answer before starting;
- for a proposal, forbid completed-act verbs and allow at most one `decision` entry whose title
  and body say in plain words that it was proposed and not applied;
- when the segment alone cannot settle whether something was executed, treat it as not executed.

Narrowing `'decision'` from "alternatives the agent proposed or considered" to choices actually
settled in the segment would remove the milder variant at the same time.

I have a working override of both role prompts along these lines, applied through
`[recall.extract.prompts] dir`, and I'm happy to open a PR against the base prompt if that shape
is welcome. Worth noting for anyone else hitting this: because prompt digests join the generation
fingerprint, changing the base prompt starts a new generation, so the fix cannot be retrofitted
onto an existing corpus — which is an argument for fixing it sooner rather than later.

### Version

v0.44.0.

title: Recall: first extracted corpus cannot serve until the whole archive is covered
body:
### Problem / motivation

Recall extraction is all-or-nothing on first activation. A generation cannot
start serving until *every* eligible session in the archive has been
extracted, so on a large archive the Recall page shows nothing at all — not a
partial corpus, nothing — for as long as the entire backlog takes to distill.

The gates live inside the activation transaction, in
`verifyExtractActivationCoverageTx`:

- any fully eligible session in `pending` or `partial` blocks
  ("has N sessions still being extracted");
- any eligible session with no progress row at all blocks
  ("has eligible sessions that were never extracted").

There is no route around them and no force option:

- `maybeActivate` probes the backlog and returns early on any hit;
- `Manager.Activate` checks only "some session done" and "some entry exists",
  then calls the same transaction, which applies the same gates;
- `Manager.Retire` deliberately withholds the database `force` flag, and the
  HTTP activate route takes no parameters.

Concretely, with a local model doing the distillation: an archive of roughly
twelve thousand eligible sessions, twelve of them extracted so far and 600-odd
entries produced. `/api/v1/recall/entries` returns `{"entries":[]}` and the
page is empty, while `?status=archived` shows the entries sitting staged. The
coverage panel is accurate and honest throughout — it reports sessions done,
units done and the backlog — so the information needed to present a partial
corpus truthfully is already there and already on screen.

Waiting is a real answer, and on an archive of this size it is a very long
one. Every faster alternative trades output quality: a smaller model, a
smaller segmenter window, a reduced output budget, or narrowing which sessions
count. None of those is acceptable when the point of the corpus is its
content.

### Proposed solution

Require coverage completeness only while a generation is active.

What those two gates protect is the *served* corpus: activation retires
whichever generation was active and archives its entries in the same
transaction, so promoting an incomplete generation would replace a complete
corpus with a fragment. That hazard is real. It does not exist when nothing is
serving — there is no corpus to protect, and the alternative to serving what
has been extracted is serving nothing.

So: a first corpus (no generation active) may activate on partial coverage;
any replacement generation keeps the full requirement exactly as it is today.
Reading "is anything active" inside the activation transaction keeps a racing
activation from seeing a stale answer.

Deliberately unchanged:

- the refusal to promote when nothing is servable, so an empty generation
  still cannot take over;
- the staleness gates — a done session written past its coverage stamp, or a
  failed session holding staged output made stale by a later write. Those
  describe output that no longer matches its transcript, which disqualifies a
  first corpus exactly as much as a replacement;
- the in-transaction cleanup that deletes the staged entries and progress rows
  of sessions that have become ineligible, so privacy retraction is untouched;
- the generation fingerprint. Activation semantics are not among its inputs,
  so an existing corpus carries over unchanged.

One consequence makes this smaller than it looks: entries are staged as
archived only while `generation.State != active`, so once a generation is
active every later pass writes straight to served. A single early activation
is the whole mechanism — no separate "serve while building" path is needed.

Two related points, separable if you prefer them apart:

1. **Automatic activation.** Leaving `maybeActivate`'s backlog probe strict
   means nothing switches itself on early; the first switch stays an explicit
   operator action. That seems the right default, but it is a judgement you may
   want the other way.
2. **Backlog order.** `extractCandidateSQL` ends `ORDER BY ended_at ASC, id
   ASC`, so the oldest corner of the archive is distilled first and the
   sessions someone is working on now come last. Reversing it is order only —
   same sessions, same entries — and it is safe against the discovery
   watermark, which advances from the pass start time and only on a pass that
   took everything it found, never from the last row processed. This matters
   much more with partial serving than without it: newest-first means the page
   fills with current work.

This is a behaviour change on an activation boundary, so it may well belong
behind an option (a config setting under `[recall.extract]`, or a parameter on
the activate route) rather than as the new unconditional default. Happy to
follow whichever shape you prefer — the pull request that follows implements it
unconditionally, which is the simplest thing to review and the easiest to put
behind a flag if you would rather have one.

### Alternatives considered

- **Waiting.** Correct, and on a large archive it means an empty page for a
  very long time.
- **Extraction concurrency.** There is none today: the pass loop walks
  sessions one at a time and the unit loop walks units one at a time. Adding it
  would be new machinery, and with one local GPU it divides the same compute
  rather than adding any — prefill is compute-bound, so two streams do not
  raise aggregate throughput.
- **Scoping eligibility to recent sessions.** The eligibility rule has no
  recency ceiling and no configuration hook. `quiet_period` is a floor, so
  raising it makes the served corpus older rather than usefully smaller. It
  would also mean deciding some sessions never get distilled, which is a
  different product.
- **A force flag on activate.** Possible, but it reads as an escape hatch for
  the dangerous case the gates exist to prevent. Scoping the allowance to "no
  corpus is serving" is narrower and needs no operator judgement about when it
  is safe.
- **A separate "serve while building" state.** Unnecessary, given entries are
  already written straight to served once a generation is active.

title: Antigravity: a conversation whose stream is encrypted is never stored, though a plaintext transcript sits beside it
body:
### What happens

An Antigravity conversation can end up in the archive as nothing at all, even
though a readable, complete transcript of it is sitting on disk.

The `antigravity` provider treats `conversations/<uuid>.db` as the only session
source (`antigravitySourceSet.discoverSessionPaths`). Older Antigravity builds
did not write that database: a conversation is stored as
`conversations/<uuid>.pb`, an AES-encrypted stream, and without
`ANTIGRAVITY_KEY` there is nothing in it the parser can read. Those
conversations are simply absent from the archive.

Antigravity's agent brain, though, writes a plaintext transcript of the same
conversation to

```
brain/<uuid>/.system_generated/logs/transcript.jsonl
```

one JSON object per logged step, carrying `source` (`USER_EXPLICIT`, `MODEL`,
`SYSTEM`), `type`, `status`, `step_index`, `created_at`, `content`, `thinking`
and `tool_calls`. That is the user's turns, the model's turns, its reasoning and
its tool calls, in the clear. Nothing reads it today:
`collectAntigravityBrainMessages` reads only the top-level `*.md` artifacts in
`brain/<uuid>/`, and `antigravityBrainID` classifies a brain path only when it
is exactly three segments (`brain/<uuid>/<file>`), so a transcript five
segments deep is never classified and never discovered.

### Second half of the same loss: the IDE build's directory

`.gemini/antigravity` is the only default root for the provider
(`internal/parser/types.go`). The IDE build writes to `.gemini/antigravity-ide`
in the same layout, so every conversation there — database, transcript or
otherwise — is outside discovery no matter what the parser can read.

### Why the obvious fix is the wrong one

Pointing the `antigravity-cli` provider at these directories, or adding them to
its default dirs, looks like it solves this and does not. That reader does
accept `conversations/<uuid>.pb` and `implicit/<uuid>.pb`, but with no key and
no sidecar the parse returns a session with **no messages and no error**
(`antigravity_cli.go`, the message-less branch). The result is one session row
per encrypted file, each pointing at a file whose contents were never
recovered: the loss stops being visible without anything being recovered. The
encrypted streams should stay undiscovered until there is a key or a plaintext
sidecar.

### Expected

- A brain transcript is a session source in its own right when the conversation
  has no `conversations/<uuid>.db`, and is folded into that database's session
  when it does — one conversation, one session either way.
- `.gemini/antigravity-ide` is a default root for the `antigravity` provider.
- An encrypted `conversations/<uuid>.pb` or `implicit/<uuid>.pb` with no key
  still yields no `antigravity` session, by discovery or by watch event.
- Two configured roots holding the same conversation id yield two sessions with
  distinct ids and distinct file paths, and which root the walk reaches first
  does not change the outcome.

### Reproducing

With a root containing only

```
brain/<uuid>/.system_generated/logs/transcript.jsonl
```

`Discover` on the `antigravity` provider returns no sources, so the
conversation is never stored.

title: feat(parser): link Antigravity IDE subagent sessions to parents
body:
## Summary

Antigravity IDE sessions spawned via `invoke_subagent` previously appeared as top-level sessions with no connection to their parent cascade, so the parent's children list and inline subagent panel stayed empty. This change links them.

Two independent mechanisms now establish parentage:

- **Descriptor indexing.** `brain/<parent>/.system_generated/subagents/<child>.json` files are scanned at discovery into a `childID -> parentID + role` map kept on the source set. Children parsed through it get `ParentSessionID`, `RelSubagent`, and `SessionName` from the descriptor role (falling back to `typeName`). The map is updated incrementally on watch events — the descriptor path itself carries both ids — and the descriptor is included in the child's fingerprint companions. Descriptors are linked regardless of `state` (killed subagents remain historical children); malformed JSON, invalid ids, filename/`conversationId` mismatches, and self-links are skipped. This covers batch spawns and arbitrarily deep nesting (grandchild cascades exist in live data).
- **Spawn edges.** During `.db` decode, an `invoke_subagent` tool call looks ahead at the following result step for the `Created the following subagents` marker and extracts `conversationId` values with whitespace-tolerant matching. The first id lands on `tool_calls.subagent_session_id` (the model stores one id per call), which the existing linker resolves into `parent_session_id` plus the inline panel. The marker gate is required: `manage_subagents` results also list real `conversationId`s and would create false edges. Failed invokes with no ids are tolerated. Since CLI sessions share the decode path, `antigravity-cli` gains spawn-edge linking too, without descriptor scanning (no CLI descriptors exist).

Additional changes:

- IDE `.trajectory.json` sidecars now propagate `parentCascadeId` as a fallback parent source when no descriptor exists (descriptor wins).
- `dataVersion` bumped 119 -> 120 so existing archives reparse on the next sync.

Limits: a batch spawn links inline only through its first `conversationId`; siblings are still sidebar-linked via descriptors. Agent-message steps (kind 101, e.g. "Message from <role>") render as plain assistant text — no per-message subagent attribution.

Verified end-to-end against a live `~/.gemini/antigravity` corpus on a scratch archive: 302 subagent relationships and 246 spawn edges materialize, including killed children, nested grandchildren, and a six-child batch.

Reviewers: start at `internal/parser/antigravity_subagents.go` (descriptor map + spawn-edge pass), then `internal/parser/antigravity_provider.go` (watch routing, fingerprint companions).

title: fix(sync): poll recently active Codex sources without history hints
body:
Codex Desktop sessions on macOS now update in AgentsView within about 30 seconds, so a session you're watching or searching shows what the agent just did. Before, it stayed frozen at an old point until Codex closed the file, AgentsView restarted, or you ran a full resync.

macOS reports a change to a file only when it's created or closed, and Codex keeps the active session file open. AgentsView already polls the sessions that Codex's `history.jsonl` marks as active, but Codex Desktop never writes that file. The poller now also checks up to 256 local Codex sessions active in the last 24 hours, and syncs the ones that changed.

A new index finds those recent sessions, so a poll's cost depends on recent activity instead of archive size. Building it takes a one-time scan of the archive on first launch.

title: ci: fall back to direct module fetch on proxy errors
body:
CI no longer fails when Google's module proxy drops a download partway through. Go now fetches that module from its source repo instead.

Since Sep 12, 2 Windows test runs failed this way. The default proxy setting only falls back when a module is missing, so a proxy error fails the job.

Every Go workflow and Docker build stage now sets `GOPROXY=https://proxy.golang.org|direct`, where the pipe means fall back on any error.

title: ci: lint Windows-only files on the Windows runner
body:
Lint problems in Windows-only code now fail CI. Before, they only showed up if someone happened to run the linter on a Windows machine.

The lint job runs on Linux, and Go skips files built only for Windows there, so the linter never looked at them. A handful of findings had piled up in that code as a result.

The Windows test job now builds the pinned custom linter and runs it, and this fixes every finding it reported without changing behavior.

title: cursor-ide: started_at comes from composerData.createdAt, which can be days or months away from the conversation
body:
### agentsview version

agentsview v0.44.0 (commit 413a87f7, built 2026-09-21T12:48:49Z); the parser code is unchanged on current `main`

### Install method

install.sh / install.ps1

### OS / platform

Windows 11 (x64)

### Which agent and version

Cursor IDE (`cursor-ide`) 3.22.7

### Which model(s)

n/a (session timing, independent of model)

### What happened, and what did you expect

For `cursor-ide` sessions, `started_at` comes from `composerData.createdAt`. It falls back to the first message timestamp only when that field is zero. On one real archive, `createdAt` differs from the earliest bubble timestamp by more than a day for 30 composers and by up to about 235 days. Date filters such as `--since` / `--date-from` and date-grouped session lists put these sessions on the wrong day.

Expected: a session starts at its earliest timestamped message, like other providers.

Read-only inspection of the Cursor IDE global `state.vscdb` (761 composers with headers):

| Measure | Composers |
|---|---:|
| Nonzero `createdAt` and at least one timestamped bubble | 735 |
| UTC date of `createdAt` differs from UTC date of earliest bubble | 43 |
| Absolute difference > 1 hour | 93 |
| Absolute difference > 1 day | 30 (25 with `createdAt` earlier, 5 later) |
| Absolute difference > 7 days | 7 |
| `createdAt` later than the composer's *last* bubble | 6 |
| Header order differs from chronological bubble order | 38 |
| No bubble timestamps at all | 26 |

The largest difference is about 5,643 hours. The same 43 / 93 / 30 / 7 counts appear in the AgentsView archive when `sessions.started_at` is compared with the earliest `messages.timestamp`. Because `createdAt` can fall *after* every bubble, it can't be read as "the composer was opened before the conversation started." The bubble timestamps are the only field that tracks when the conversation actually happened.

**Proposed fix:** start at the earliest timestamped message (the minimum, not `messages[0]`, because header order is not always chronological). Use `createdAt` only when no bubble has a timestamp. Bump the data version so unchanged `state.vscdb` containers are re-parsed. I have a PR ready.

**Related observation (not addressed by the PR):** 462 of 505 `cursor` (agent-transcripts) session IDs on the same machine also exist as `composerData:<id>` in the IDE's global `state.vscdb`, so the same conversation is archived once as `cursor` and once as `cursor-ide`. That doesn't match the current provenance note that the GUI writes no `agent-transcripts` files. Local data can't show which product wrote those transcripts. 175 of those `cursor` sessions have no message timestamps: their transcripts have no `<timestamp>` tags and there's no matching `store.db`, so `started_at`/`ended_at` fall back to file mtime. For 172 of them, the matching composer has bubble timestamps and the `cursor-ide` twin already shows the correct time. Enriching untimed `cursor` transcripts from the matching composer, or linking/deduplicating the pair, would cross the provider boundary, so I'd like maintainer input before attempting either.

### Sample session file or snippet

```text
Synthetic cursorDiskKV rows (no real session content):

composerData:<id>   {"createdAt": 1781427600000,            // 2026-06-14T09:00:00Z
                     "lastUpdatedAt": 1782026801522,
                     "fullConversationHeadersOnly": [
                       {"bubbleId": "b1", "type": 1},
                       {"bubbleId": "b2", "type": 2}]}
bubbleId:<id>:b1    {"type": 1, "text": "ask",   "createdAt": "2026-06-21T07:27:29.606Z"}
bubbleId:<id>:b2    {"type": 2, "text": "reply", "createdAt": "2026-06-21T07:27:31.522Z"}
```

### Steps to reproduce

1. Create a `state.vscdb` with a `cursorDiskKV` table holding the rows above.
2. Point the `cursor-ide` agent directory at it and run a sync.
3. Observe `started_at` = `2026-06-14T09:00:00Z`, a week before any message; expected `2026-06-21T07:27:29.606Z`.

### Checklist

- [x] I searched existing issues
- [x] I removed secrets and private data from any attached session files

title: fix(parser): start Cursor IDE sessions at the earliest bubble
body:
Cursor IDE sessions used `composerData.createdAt` as `started_at` unless that field was zero. On a real archive, the field differs from the earliest bubble timestamp by more than a day in 30 of 735 comparable composers, by up to about 235 days, and it lies after the last bubble in 6 composers. Those sessions appear on the wrong day in date filters and date-grouped views. Fixes #2003.

## What the parser does now

- `started_at` is the earliest nonzero message timestamp in the composer. It is a minimum, not the first message, because header order and chronological order differ in 38 of the inspected composers.
- `composerData.createdAt` is used only when no bubble carries a timestamp. A composer with no timestamps at all still gets a zero start, as before.
- `ended_at` is unchanged: the later of `lastUpdatedAt` and the latest message timestamp. Because the start now comes from the same messages, `ended_at` can no longer fall before `started_at` when bubbles are timestamped.

## Existing archives

`dataVersion` goes to 115. A `state.vscdb` container has no archive row of its own, and its skip-cache key includes the data version. The bump makes an upgraded binary re-parse unchanged containers and rewrite the members' `started_at`. The new sync test rewinds an archive to what the previous version persisted, including the container skip entry keyed to the old version, and checks that a fresh engine corrects the start. Marking one member stale without the version change isn't enough to force the re-parse. That matches how the container cache is keyed today.

## Tradeoffs and limits

- For typical composers, the start moves from the moment the composer was created to the first message, usually a difference of seconds to minutes. That fits how other providers define `started_at`. If maintainers would rather keep composer creation time, it could be stored as a separate field, but nothing in the schema or UI reads it today.
- Bubble timestamps that don't parse are ignored, the same way message timestamps are elsewhere.
- The related `cursor` / `cursor-ide` overlap described in the issue (untimed agent-transcripts that duplicate IDE composers) is out of scope here.

## Where to look

- `internal/parser/cursor_ide.go`: the session bounds block in `parseCursorIDEComposer`.
- `internal/sync/cursor_ide_integration_test.go`: the upgrade-path test, especially the skip-cache rewind that stands in for an older binary.
- `docs/internal/session-format-sources.md`: the new "Session bounds" evidence entry under Cursor IDE.

title: OpenCode: measure tool execution start to completion, not call creation to completion
body:
# Background

The session timing API already reports per-call durations from paired tool_result_events rows with source='tool_execution' and status started/completed.
The main OpenCode parser does not emit those events, so every OpenCode tool call reports an unknown duration and its turn time falls back to unattributed.

OpenCode's source records carry the execution boundaries: a tool part's state time marks when execution started and ended.
The parser currently decodes only the tool input and metadata, so both boundaries are dropped.

The measured value must be execution start to completion.
Call creation (the tool part creation time or the assistant message timestamp) includes the wait for a permission approval or queue scheduling, so using it as the start makes a blocked call look slow.
Where a real execution start is unavailable, the duration should stay unknown instead of falling back to creation to completion.

# Version

dc25258

# Acceptance Criteria

## Must

- [ ] The OpenCode parser emits paired tool_execution result events (started at execution start, completed/errored at execution end) for calls whose source records both boundaries
- [ ] An OpenCode call's measured duration is execution start to completion and never call creation to completion
- [ ] A call whose source lacks an execution start keeps an unknown duration instead of falling back to the assistant message timestamp
- [ ] Unit tests cover a call that waits before execution (duration excludes the wait) and a call missing the execution-start boundary (duration unknown)
- [ ] SQLite and PostgreSQL report the same OpenCode call durations, and the DuckDB mirror carries the events

## Should

- [ ] Formats that record only call creation and completion degrade to an unknown duration rather than an inflated one
- [ ] The session detail view shows the execution duration for OpenCode calls once the parser emits the events

title: Improve Codebuff and Freebuff session fidelity
body:
## What this does now

Codebuff and Freebuff sessions keep more of what happened, and their cost is
counted correctly.

- **`FREEBUFF_CONFIG_DIR` is honored for discovery**, locally and over SSH.
  Codebuff and Freebuff are one CLI that writes sessions under this directory
  when it is set, so it replaces the default root. `CODEBUFF_DIR` and
  `agents.codebuff.dirs` still override it.
- **Cost is recorded per prompt.** The CLI resets its credit counter at every
  user prompt, so before this change only the last prompt's spend survived. Each
  prompt's credits now become their own reported-cost row, under the model that
  turn ran: the bring-your-own-key model when set, otherwise the agent
  template's model. Archives from older CLIs without per-message credits keep
  the single run-state total.
- **Message content is preserved.** Attached images, pasted text, and files
  appear as labeled markers in their prompt. Runtime and validation errors,
  ask-user answers, sponsored-proposal notices, and agent lists stay in the
  transcript.
- **Subagents are their own sessions.** Each nested agent block becomes a
  subagent session linked to its parent, the same way Claude, Cline, and Pi
  subagents are stored. The parent's agent call keeps the final answer and links
  to the child session.
- **Transcripts decode one message at a time.** Peak memory during a parse is
  one message rather than the whole `chat-messages.json`. A malformed
  transcript is still a parse error, as before.
- Sessions also gain `git_branch` from run-state and a termination status.

Data version 119 re-parses existing Codebuff and Freebuff sources to backfill
these rows. There are no schema changes.

## Tradeoffs and limits

- A parent and its subagents share one `chat-messages.json`, so sync treats it
  as a multi-session source. The session ID prefix (`codebuff:` or `freebuff:`)
  comes from run-state and can change between syncs; sync moves the row to the
  new label and does not revive one the user trashed.
- `chat-meta.json` handling is unchanged from `main`.
- Per-turn input and output token counts are still unavailable, because the CLI
  does not persist them.

## Where reviewers should look

- `internal/parser/codebuff_decode.go`: message structs, the decoder, and the
  block walker that emits subagent sessions.
- `internal/parser/codebuff.go`: per-turn cost and model resolution.
- `internal/sync/engine.go`: Codebuff source-missing and relabel handling.

title: Recall extraction: let a pass distill several sessions at once against endpoints that can take them
body:
### Problem / motivation

Recall extraction runs one session at a time and one unit per model call, so
a pass is bound by the endpoint's round-trip latency. With a hosted model
reached through an OpenAI-compatible endpoint, the daemon completed about 16
sessions (roughly 200 units) in 40 minutes, while the endpoint sat mostly
idle between requests. The archive has more than 4,000 eligible sessions, so
the first corpus would take several days to build.

#1993 considers extraction concurrency and sets it aside because, with one
local GPU, prefill is compute-bound and two streams only share the same
compute. That holds for a single local model. It does not hold for hosted
endpoints or for local servers that batch concurrent requests (vLLM, SGLang,
llama.cpp with parallel slots). For those, parallel requests are the only way
to use the capacity. The two changes are independent: #1993 decides when a
partial corpus may serve, and this one decides how fast the corpus gets
built.

### Proposed solution

Add an optional per-server `concurrency` setting, next to `timeout` and
`api_key_env`:

```toml
[recall.extract.servers.hosted]
endpoint = "https://example.invalid/v1"
concurrency = 4
```

- **Default 1.** Behavior stays exactly as it is today unless someone opts in.
  An explicit `0` or a negative value is a config error, the same rule as
  `[vector.embeddings.servers.<name>] concurrency`.
- **Transport only.** Like the rest of the server entry, the setting is not
  part of the generation fingerprint, so changing it never starts a new
  corpus.
- **Parallel by session.** A pass hands its selected sessions, in selection
  order, to up to `concurrency` workers. Each session belongs to one worker
  for the whole pass, and that worker still distills and commits the
  session's units in cursor order.

How this keeps the invariants in `docs/internal/recall-extraction.md`:

- **Generation isolation.** The fingerprint and the staged/active handling are
  unchanged, and all workers in a pass write under the same generation.
- **Optimistic concurrency.** Progress rows are per (session, generation), and
  within a pass a session has exactly one writer. Cursor advances stay
  strictly monotonic from the unit's derived position, and the digest and
  cursor guards on commits and failure marks work as they do today. Cross-pass
  exclusion (`passMu`, drop-not-queue) does not change.
- **Write-lock hold time.** Model calls stay outside every transaction. Unit
  commits still go through the archive's single writer connection, so
  parallel sessions only interleave short commits and never hold the lock
  across a model call.
- **Failure backoff and pass aborts.** Session-scoped failures are marked and
  backed off exactly as now. An error that aborts a sequential pass (an
  endpoint-scoped rejection, an exhausted retry ladder, a storage error) stops
  handing out sessions and cancels the sessions still in flight. Cancellation
  leaves their rows resumable, the same contract as daemon shutdown, so an
  outage cannot burn every in-flight session's retry ladder or backoff.
- **Response size bounds.** They apply per call, as now. Memory grows by at
  most `concurrency` loaded transcripts, so the default keeps today's
  footprint.
- **Reconciliation, activation, and watermarks.** These stay outside the
  parallel section and run before and after it exactly as today. Watermarks
  still advance only after a pass covers everything it selected.

I have an implementation with tests and would open a pull request if this
direction is acceptable.

### Alternatives considered

- **Parallel units within one session, with commits kept in order.** This
  gives more parallelism for a few very long sessions. The cost is buffering
  out-of-order results and a new "committed up to here" rule, which touches
  the cursor contract (commits advance from exactly the derived position,
  and a same-digest reset must not let a stale worker skip units). Session
  parallelism gets most of the throughput without changing that contract.
- **A global `[recall.extract] concurrency`.** Capacity belongs to the
  endpoint, and `[vector.embeddings]` already puts `concurrency` on the
  server entry, so the per-server placement keeps the two consistent.
- **Running several daemons or manual passes side by side.** This is not
  possible: manual write commands refuse while a daemon owns the archive, and
  passes are mutually exclusive by design.

title: feat(recall): distill several sessions at once with per-server extraction concurrency
body:
Recall can now distill several sessions at once against a hosted or batching model endpoint, so a large archive's first corpus isn't held to one round trip at a time. On an archive of more than 4,000 sessions, distilling one at a time got through about 16 sessions in 40 minutes while the endpoint sat mostly idle, which put the first corpus days away.

Set `concurrency` on a recall extraction server to choose how many sessions run at once. The default of 1 keeps today's behavior. Each session stays with one worker, so its units still run and save in order, and its saved progress works as before. An error that would stop a one-at-a-time pass stops the parallel one too and cancels the sessions in flight, which resume on the next pass instead of spending their retries on an outage.

Parallelism is per session, so one very long session still runs one unit at a time. Running a session's units in parallel would let them finish out of order and change what its saved progress point means. A single local model gains nothing from parallel requests, since they only split its compute, so the default stays 1.

Closes #2007.

title: feat(parser): index OMO sessions as their own agent
body:
AgentsView now finds OMO (oh-my-openagent) sessions on its own and lists them under OMO, so you can search them and see their usage and cost next to your other agents. Before, OMO sessions were missing unless you pointed `PI_DIR` at `~/.omo`, and then they were counted as Pi.

OMO runs senpi, a Pi fork, and writes Pi's session format under `~/.omo/agent/sessions`, so the Pi parser reads it unchanged. The new agent gets its own default directory, an `OMO_DIR` override, and its own session IDs.

Sessions already indexed through the Pi override keep the Pi label, because AgentsView can't yet move a session to another agent. The changelog tells those users to drop the override so new OMO sessions aren't indexed twice.

title: ci: move macOS jobs to GitHub-hosted runners
body:
Move the focused FSEvents tests and both macOS desktop builds to GitHub-hosted runners so they no longer depend on self-hosted macOS machines. Use `macos-26` for ARM64 and `macos-26-intel` for Intel, preserving the macOS generation, main-push triggers, build targets, and artifacts.

Remove the obsolete runner-group guidance and persistent-host cache condition. Linux and Windows retain their existing runners and cache behavior.

title: fix(frontend): keep password managers off every typeahead search
body:
Password managers no longer open their autofill menus over typeahead search boxes. The reported case was Bitwarden covering the project picker with saved identities (#2011). It ignores `autocomplete="off"` and the `data-1p-ignore` attribute that #1465 added.

The fix lives in Kit UI ([kenn-io/kit-ui#71](https://github.com/kenn-io/kit-ui/pull/71)). Its `Typeahead` search input now always sets the documented opt-out attribute for 1Password (`data-1p-ignore`), Bitwarden (`data-bwignore`), LastPass (`data-lpignore`), and Dashlane (`data-form-type="other"`). This PR moves the `@kenn-io/kit-ui` pin to Kit UI `main` (`cfcfcd6`), so every picker in agentsview gets the opt-out, not only the project picker.

`ProjectTypeahead` no longer passes these attributes itself through `inputAttributes`, and its test for them is removed. Kit UI now sets them and has its own browser test.

The bump also brings in the other Kit UI changes since the old pin:

- Menus are positioned correctly inside CSS-zoomed containers (#70).
- `svelte-check --tsgo` sees real component types (#69).
- Typeaheads support optional icons (#72).

Fixes #2011.

title: fix(import): append new messages to existing ChatGPT conversations
body:
Re-importing a ChatGPT export now appends new messages when the archived conversation matches the beginning of the export. Previously, every existing conversation was skipped.

The importer compares messages after applying database sanitization and the archive's content policy. It inserts only the new tail rows, preserving existing message IDs, pins, metadata, and custom display names. Unchanged conversations are skipped and their imported titles are refreshed.

Shorter exports, changed history, and session IDs belonging to another agent are reported as errors without replacing the archived transcript. Existing conversations in usage-only archives are skipped because their discarded text cannot be checked. Excluded and trashed sessions are also skipped.

Appends clear derived quality signals and secret findings in the same transaction, leaving the conversation eligible for signal backfill. Edited conversation branches remain unsupported: they continue to report an error instead of overwriting saved history.

The main changes are in `internal/importer/importer.go`; `docs/chat-import.md` explains re-import behavior.

title: High CPU during Cursor IDE sync, increasing GOMEMLIMIT helped
body:

agentsview v0.44.0 (commit 413a87f7bfbd67b2815b1119ac51abc1efbeeaba, built 2026-09-21T12:48:49Z)

title: fix(desktop): accept authenticated daemon readiness (#2000)
body:
When a local daemon requires authentication, the desktop treats its 401 health response as ready so startup can reach the interface instead of timing out.

The probe sends no token and still checks version fields on 200 responses. Update shutdown also recognizes the authenticated daemon as running.

Refs #2000

title: fix(daemon): keep live runtime records across clock steps
body:
After Linux corrects its clock, AgentsView still finds a running server through its runtime record. It holds the archive write lock, so losing that record makes replacement attempts fail and stalls scheduled work until someone restarts it.

Linux reports a different creation time for the same process after a clock step, so clients discarded the live server's record. As proposed in https://github.com/kenn-io/agentsview/issues/1977, they now use its clock-stable process identity to verify both discovery and shutdown. Older records keep the creation-time check.

Closes #1977

title: fix(import): refuse shorter Claude.ai exports and compare in stored form
body:
Claude.ai re-imports now refuse exports with fewer messages than the archive, preventing stale exports from deleting saved turns. Unchanged conversations are compared after sanitization and archive-content projection so they are skipped reliably. Equal-length or longer exports still refresh earlier content, including attachment text; Claude.ai does not require the archived turns to match the start of the export.

## Details

- `upsertConversation` rejects an export whose message count is below the archived session's `message_count`, before the session row is touched. It uses the session count rather than `GetAllMessages`, so the check holds under reduced `archive_content` policies.
- The unchanged-skip comparison canonicalizes incoming messages with `ValidateAndSanitize` + `ProjectSessionForStoragePolicy` (via `storeArchiveContent`), matching what the write path stores.
- Appends still go through `ReplaceSessionMessages`, whose in-place diff keeps archived message IDs and pins; a test locks that in.
- Docs: the Claude.ai entry in the Chat Import re-import section.

The ChatGPT comparison and image-publishing follow-ups that accumulated here during review have moved to #2031, so this PR is scoped to Claude.ai only.

## Tests

`go test -tags fts5 ./internal/importer/` passes. `TestImportClaudeAIRejectsShorterExport` and `TestImportClaudeAIReimportComparesStoredForm` fail on `main` without this change.

title: feat(desktop): log the backend port decision at startup
body:
The desktop startup log records the selected backend port, whether it came from sidecar stdout or `serve status`, and whether the readiness check succeeded or timed out. Navigation failures also reach this log in packaged builds.

Launch records include the desktop version and PID plus the sidecar PID. Status probes preserve redacted daemon output, including its PID, so a port mismatch can be traced to the process the desktop discovered. All records use the existing nonblocking background log writer.

Refs #2000

title: fix(sync): keep only changed Cursor IDE chats in memory during a container reparse
body:
When Cursor IDE writes to state.vscdb, the daemon's reparse now keeps only the chats that changed in memory, so its memory no longer grows with the size of the Cursor archive under the daemon's 256 MiB soft limit.

The shared container parser now hands each chat to sync as soon as it is parsed. Sync checks it against the archive at once, keeps it only if it will be written, and records its ID so chats deleted in Cursor are still retired once the whole set is in. Only Cursor IDE streams this way, and the other container providers pass through the same per-chat checks.

The 256 MiB limit stays, because raising it lets one reparse grow the daemon to the size of the whole archive. A pass where every chat changed still holds them all, and those are mostly full syncs, which run in a worker without the limit.

Refs #2014

title: fix(parser): retain opencode dispatch-to-completion timing
body:
OpenCode session details now show the time from a tool call's dispatch to its result, so you can see the full delay before the result arrives. A 20-second permission wait followed by two seconds of work shows 22 seconds. OpenCode never records when a permission is granted, so a duration that leaves out the wait can't be measured.

OpenCode records dispatch and completion, so the parser carries those timestamps into the existing timing views and reparses saved sessions. Calls without a dispatch timestamp keep an unknown duration. Tool outputs remain stored once when a timing event accompanies them, and timing marks with no output stay out of a tool's History list.

Closes #2005

title: fix(desktop): discard superseded startup results
body:
Accepting an in-app update while the backend is still starting no longer leaves the window showing errors from the backend the updater just stopped, such as "AgentsView backend stopped" or "interface did not respond" for the old port.

Nothing told the old launch it had been replaced, so its status poll, readiness wait, and exit handler kept writing to the window during the stop and install. Each launch already has a number. A finished update stop now retires the current one, and that leftover work checks the number before acting. A stop that times out leaves the old launch in charge, as before.

Refs #2000

title: perf(sync): skip unchanged Cursor IDE chats when state.vscdb changes
body:
When Cursor IDE writes to state.vscdb, the watcher now parses only the chats whose saved document changed, so one edited chat costs one parse however many chats the archive holds.

On each watcher event, one SQLite query reads every chat's composerData document, and each document's hash is compared with the archived one. Only chats whose hash differs, or that the archive lacks, get parsed, and trashed or deleted chats are skipped. The stored hash gains that document digest, so a data-version bump reparses the archive once on upgrade.

The document's header list changes with every new message, while some chats lack a current lastUpdatedAt. Reply text written after the document waits for the next change or the 15-minute reconciliation Cursor IDE joins here. This builds on #2019.

Closes #2014

title: Configure the default insight agent in config.toml
body:
### Problem / motivation

Generated insights start from an agent CLI that is hardcoded to `claude`. There
is no `config.toml` key for it, so an operator cannot make another generator the
starting choice.

On a machine where the default CLI is not installed, every generation action
that does not name an agent fails immediately:

```
claude CLI not found: exec: "claude": executable file not found in $PATH
```

That covers "agent analysis" on a session and the Activity insights panel, and
the failure surfaces as a generation error in the UI. Operators who generate
with `codex`, `copilot`, `gemini`, or `kiro` have to change the picker for every
report, because the selection is not remembered.

### Proposed solution

Add `[insights] default_agent` to `config.toml`:

```toml
[insights]
default_agent = "codex"
```

- Generation requests that name no agent use this value. Leaving it unset keeps
  today's `claude` default.
- The Web UI picker starts from the same value, reported as
  `insight_default_agent` by `GET /api/v1/settings`.
- An unknown name fails configuration validation at startup instead of failing a
  generation later.

### Alternatives considered

- Choosing the agent in the picker for each report. It works, but the first
  attempt on a machine without `claude` still fails.
- Pointing `[agent.claude] binary` at another CLI. The generator passes
  Claude-specific flags, so another CLI does not run.
- Falling back to another installed CLI when the selected one is missing. It
  hides configuration mistakes and runs an agent the operator did not choose.

title: feat(insights): configure the default generation agent
body:
Adds `[insights] default_agent` so an install can choose the agent CLI used for new generated insights. Requests without an agent use this setting; leaving it unset keeps Claude as the default. Config loading normalizes the name and rejects unsupported values.

The web UI reads the default from `GET /api/v1/settings` and leaves the request's agent unspecified until the user chooses one. This also honors the server default while settings are loading. Switching servers clears that choice. The frontend pickers share one agent list.

Endpoint mode still applies only when both `endpoint` and `model` are configured. The settings API preserves `default_agent` when saving other settings. The docs clarify both behaviors and keep the default-agent guidance in one section.

Closes #2025.

title: feat(activity): show user and assistant message frequency
body:
Activity now switches between **Concurrency**, **User messages**, and **Assistant messages** in the existing timeline. Each view keeps the same time buckets and filters, with its own scale and total, so sparse prompts remain visible during busy agent runs.

User counts cover interactive conversations only. Assistant counts include all selected sessions. Both exclude system entries and tool results, and count timestamped transcript messages, including lone prompts. The counts and time-range drilldown work across all four storage backends.

The compact control supports keyboard navigation and shorter labels on narrow screens. All screenshots below use synthetic sessions.

title: feat(analytics): split activity timeline by role with absolute and percent views
body:
The Messages view of the Analytics activity timeline now stacks each day's user, assistant, and other messages in separate colors, with an Absolute/Percent toggle, so you can see how the split between you and your agents changes over time, even on quiet days.

Other covers system-injected and tool-result rows, which count toward a day's total but belong to neither role. PostgreSQL counted system-injected rows as user messages while SQLite, DuckDB, and ClickHouse did not, so it now matches them, with tests for assistant-only, system-only, and mixed days on each backend. Each day is one keyboard target that spans the full column and reads out its counts, so days without user messages stay reachable. The Sessions view keeps one bar per day.
