Replaces #1863, whose fork branch maintainers can't push to. Keeps Tom Rochette's commits and authorship, rebased onto main.

title: fix(recall): scope tool evidence to each action window (#1992)
body:
Recall restricts procedure entries to action windows with stored tool evidence, reducing false records of work an agent only suggested. A tool call in an earlier window supplies no evidence for a later proposal.

Each window checks stored tool calls, flags, and output rows. A tool row with no visible text marks the assistant block before it and the block after it, so a packing boundary cannot split one call from the narration that reports its result. A window without evidence gets a schema that omits procedure and a completion instruction prepended to its resolved prompt. The manager chooses each unit's prompt and allowed types; the client builds the schema from them.

If a server ignores the narrowed enum and returns procedure anyway, only that session fails, behind the normal backoff, and the pass continues. A type outside every enum still aborts the pass as a protocol violation. Changed extraction output starts a new generation, so upgrading re-extracts every session.

Completion wording in other entry types still depends on the model. A stored call counts as evidence even when it was denied or failed, and mixed tool use and proposals within one window share that window's classification.

Closes #1992

title: fix(parser): stop Antigravity sessions from re-syncing on their own -shm writes
body:
Antigravity IDE and Antigravity CLI sessions no longer re-sync in a loop. Before this change, every sync pass re-read every Antigravity session and pushed it to PostgreSQL again, even when nothing had changed. On one reported Windows archive, that meant about 640 sessions every 1-2 minutes.

**Cause.** Each Antigravity session is a SQLite database in WAL mode. Opening one to read it makes SQLite rewrite the database's `-shm` file, a shared-memory index that holds no session data. Both Antigravity providers included `-shm` in the fingerprint AgentsView uses to decide whether a session changed. Both also treated a `-shm` file event as a session change. So each read changed the fingerprint and scheduled the next read. #1580 fixed the same problem for the other SQLite-backed providers but did not cover Antigravity.

**Fix.**

- The fingerprint and effective file info for both providers now use only the database and its `-wal` file. New messages always land in one of those two files, so real changes still trigger a sync.
- A `-shm` file event no longer maps to a session.
- The `conversations/` watch globs narrow from `*.db-*` to `*.db-wal`. The sync engine currently ignores watch globs, so this only keeps the watch plan accurate.

**After upgrading.** There is no migration or data-version bump. Sessions that have a `-shm` file today get a new fingerprint, so the first sync re-parses each of them once with the same output. After that they stay idle.

**Where to look.** The fingerprint inputs are in `antigravityIDECompanionPaths` and `antigravityCLICompanionPaths`. The event mapping is in `antigravityConversationDBForPath` and `antigravityCLISourcePathForEvent`. `TestAntigravityProvidersParseLeavesFingerprintStable` reproduces the loop: it leaves a WAL-mode database with `-wal` and `-shm` on disk, then parses it twice and checks that the fingerprint does not move.

**Not fixed here.**

- After Antigravity closes a database cleanly, the next read-only open can create an empty `-wal` file. That causes one extra parse per app close, not a loop.
- The recursive `brain/` watch spans about 16,000 directories, which is over the 8,192-directory watch budget. The Antigravity root therefore falls back to polling.
- Each re-parse fully decodes every `executor_metadata` snapshot in the session, even though it needs only the newest one. This costs much less now that the loop is gone.

title: fix(import): fill ChatGPT tool results that were empty when archived
body:
Re-importing a ChatGPT export now fills in tool results that were empty at the first import, like an unfinished code run, and adds the newer messages. Before, that output never appeared, and re-importing a trashed conversation counted as an import error.

The history check now also compares each archived tool call's name and category and whether its result is empty. The archive_content and tool_result_images settings change none of those, so switching them between imports is safe. One transaction sets only the empty results and adds the new messages, so message IDs, pins and other archived rows stay as stored.

A result that was already filled stays as stored, even if the new export shows something different.

title: fix(sync): show progress during subagent relationship repair
body:
Full resync now reports checked/total queued sessions while repairing subagent relationships, so users can see whether a long repair is advancing. Progress updates after each batch, including repairs copied from the old archive, and a separate saving stage identifies the final commit. Startup status and terminal output show the counts; redirected output is limited to one update every five seconds plus the first and last counts.

Repair changes and queue removal still commit together, preserving retries after cancellation. This PR improves visibility; the reported multi-minute repair time remains under investigation.

title: fix(db): speed up long-session preservation during resync
body:
Full resync now seeks conversation records by session and ordinal when preserving archived sessions. The missing index made every copied message scan its session's retained history, producing quadratic work for long sessions and accumulated tombstones.

A partial index excludes removed records and is built on the next writable open, without a parser resync. Fresh-archive and upgrade regressions check the actual refresh query plan and preservation of message identities and tombstones. A synthetic full resync with 8,192 live messages and 8,192 tombstones in one orphaned session fell from 7.1 seconds to 0.3–0.5 seconds locally; larger archive preservation still includes the cost of copying stored content.

title: fix(daemon): restart when the CLI version differs
body:
CLI commands now restart the local writable daemon when its version differs from the CLI, including development builds and switches between releases. Previously, development builds skipped automatic replacement and release builds only replaced older releases, leaving commands attached to a different build.

Replacement uses the existing launch lock and preserves daemon launch options. A newer archive data version still blocks replacement before the running daemon stops. Startup failures now show the archive compatibility error directly or include the current launch's output, bounded to 8 KiB.

title: fix(watcher): watch Antigravity brain folders one level deep
body:
## Summary

On a large Antigravity install, the recursive watch on `~/.gemini/antigravity/brain` used up the whole 8192-directory recursive-watch budget. After that, every remaining root (Claude projects, Codebuff, and others) fell back to 2-minute polling, and each poll took tens of seconds.

The Antigravity providers only parse `brain/<id>/*.md`, their `.metadata.json` sidecars, and the IDE's plaintext transcript at `brain/<id>/.system_generated/logs/transcript.jsonl`. Antigravity also keeps large generated trees inside every `brain/<id>` (`.git`, `scratch`, `.user_uploaded`, and the rest of `.system_generated`), and AgentsView never reads them. On one real install, 372 session folders held about 16,000 subdirectories, and watching the root recursively exhausted the budget. With this change, each session folder needs at most three watches: the folder itself, plus `.system_generated` and `logs` when they exist.

## What changed

- `parser.WatchRoot` and `sync.WatchRoot` gain two optional fields:
  - `MaxDepth` limits how many directory levels below the root are watched. Zero means no limit, so existing providers are unaffected.
  - `ExtraDirectories` lists deeper directories to watch anyway, as `/`-separated patterns where `*` matches one directory name. Directories on the way to a listed one are watched, but their own files stay ignored.
- Both Antigravity providers set `MaxDepth: 1` on their `brain` root. The IDE provider also lists `*/.system_generated/logs`.
- `collectWatchRoots` and the raw-sync root planner carry both fields through. When several plans share a path, `sync.MergeWatchDepth` keeps the widest coverage (an unlimited plan wins, otherwise the deeper limit), and `sync.MergeExtraDirectories` keeps every listed directory.
- The fsnotify backend applies the limits where it already applies exclude patterns: the initial `AddRecursive` walk, runtime-created directories, event translation, and the walk of a newly created subtree. The subtree walk is told whether each path is a file or a directory, so it never reads directories below the limit. Only files directly inside the deepest watched directory get the extra level.
- The limits are stored under their own leaf `RWMutex` because the exclude checks run while `rootsMu` or `watchMu` is held.

## Tradeoffs and limits

- The macOS FSEvents backend is unchanged. It watches a whole tree with one stream and has no per-directory budget.
- Changes in the unwatched generated trees were already ignored by `SourcesForChangedPath`, which only resolves the paths listed above. No parsed content loses coverage.
- This is a per-provider limit. It does not change how the watcher behaves when some other root exhausts the budget.

## Where to look

- `internal/sync/watch_backend_fsnotify.go`: `beyondRootDepth`, `filesVisibleIn`, `shouldExcludeForRoot`, `includeCreatedSubtreePath`, `shouldExclude`
- `internal/sync/watch_backend.go`: `MergeWatchDepth`, `MergeExtraDirectories`
- `internal/parser/antigravity_provider.go` and `antigravity_cli_provider.go`: the `brain` roots

title: fix(sync): speed up upgrade imports and show accurate progress
body:
Data-version upgrades could spend minutes showing “repairing subagent relationships” after that work had finished, then leave `agentsview sync` silent while it waited for startup reconciliation. Imports also performed repeated broad scans and rebuilt conversation records that had already been copied.

This PR addresses each problem:

- **Report the actual startup stage.** Publish phase and detail together whenever the stage changes, including transitions into archive copying and index rebuilding. The counter throttle previously dropped these one-shot notifications permanently. Repeated session counters remain throttled, while their first update appears immediately.
- **Explain queued sync requests.** Both coordinated sync entry points now emit “Waiting for the current sync to finish” when another operation holds the sync lock. The requesting client receives the notice without replacing the active operation’s progress.
- **Bound source-file trash checks by file path.** Use the existing path index instead of scanning every session for an agent. This shared query serves local and remote imports. In a controlled replay of 5,534 cached remote files, import processing fell from 169 to 99 seconds and profiled CPU time fell by 70%; database opening is excluded.
- **Keep unchanged copied conversation records.** Full-content archive copies no longer reread, hash, and rewrite conversation records copied alongside already-sanitized messages. That redundant refresh took 53 seconds in the measured archive replay. Legacy sanitization and content policies that change messages still refresh the records while preserving their message IDs.
- **Use indexed conversation lookups during reconciliation.** Check whether each session has old conversation records through an indexed existence lookup instead of materializing session IDs from millions of message rows.

Archive comparisons preserved all 78 table counts and retained archived-message identities. Data-version upgrades still reparse cached remote sources even when few files were downloaded, and metadata audits, search rebuilding, and deferred indexes still take time. This change introduces no schema migration or data-version bump.

title: refactor(sync): remove SSH remote sync support
body:
AgentsView now syncs remote hosts over HTTP only. This removes the deprecated SSH transport, its CLI flags, shell discovery and transfer code, and SSH test infrastructure.

Each `[[remote_hosts]]` entry requires a remote daemon URL and token; omitted `transport` defaults to HTTP. `sync --host NAME` selects a configured remote in both daemon and direct mode, and unknown names fail before sync starts. Existing archived sessions are preserved. The docs and generated API clients reflect the change.

PR CI uses the workflow from the same revision, so changes to test steps stay aligned with the code under test.

title: Show the session names users set in Claude Code, Qwen Code, Copilot CLI, and OpenClaw
body:
## TL;DR

A Claude Code session renamed with `/rename` still showed its generated title or first message in AgentsView. Current Claude Code stores the rename as a `custom-title` record, and the parser ignored it. The parsers for Claude Code, Qwen Code, Copilot CLI, and OpenClaw now put the name the user chose into the existing session name field.

## How

| Agent | Where the user's name lives | Generated titles |
|---|---|---|
| Claude Code | `custom-title` transcript record | `ai-title` stays the fallback |
| Qwen Code | `custom_title` system record unless `titleSource` is `auto` | not shown |
| Copilot CLI | `workspace.yaml` `name` when `user_named: true` | still replace the first message |
| OpenClaw | SQLite `session_nodes.label` | `display_name` is not shown |

Storage, the API, and the UI already show `session_name`, so the schema does not change.

## Reviewer notes

- **Claude sync stays incremental.** Claude Code writes `custom-title` again after every turn. An appended record forces a full parse only when its name differs from the stored one.
- **OpenClaw renames change the hash.** A rename touches only `session_nodes`, so a non-empty label now feeds the session hash. Unlabeled sessions keep their old hash.
- **Data version 118** reparses unchanged sources once, so sessions renamed before the upgrade get their names.
- **Docs.** `session-format-sources.md` pins upstream evidence for each agent. It also corrects the Codex `session_index.jsonl` entry and fixes dead Kilo (legacy) links.
- **Not covered.** OpenCode, Kilo, VS Code Copilot, and Kimi keep renames and generated titles in one field with no flag to tell them apart. OpenClaw's older JSONL layout is also out.

title: fix(ci): run macOS capture checks on Intel runners
body:
macOS raw capture checks use Intel runners so CI can run independently of GitHub's constrained arm64 pool. In the [failed run](https://github.com/kenn-io/agentsview/actions/runs/36729955348/job/109936611499), GitHub cancelled the job after 15 minutes without assigning a runner or starting a step.

The job uses `macos-26-intel` with the same tests and CGO setup. The separate macOS FSEvents workflow retains its arm64 runner. PR checks call the workflow pinned to `main`; this [branch dispatch](https://github.com/kenn-io/agentsview/actions/runs/36733844164) runs the changed workflow.

title: Usage page "Input tokens" card is misleading under heavy prompt-cache usage (cache reads are ~98% of real input) — suggest labeling + a total-input aggregate
body:
## Summary

The usage page's "Input tokens" card shows **pure `input_tokens` only**. Under heavy prompt-cache usage this is ~2% of the actual prompt volume, and nothing on the card signals that cache reads are excluded — so the number reads as "the tracker is missing data" rather than "this is the non-cached slice."

I spent a full reconciliation session convincing myself nothing was lost. Other heavy-cache users will hit the same misreading.

## Environment

- AgentsView v0.44.0 (commit 413a87f7), macOS, brew cask install
- Data sources: Claude Code JSONL (primary), plus hermes/openclaw sessions
- Usage pattern: long Chinese-context sessions, aggressive prompt caching

## What I measured

Re-parsed my local `~/.claude/projects/**/*.jsonl` from scratch, deduped by `message.id` (streaming appends multiple snapshots per message), filtered to a 30-day window by message timestamp, and compared against `/api/v1/usage/summary?window_days=30`:

| Metric | API (AgentsView) | Local deduped truth | 
|---|---|---|
| input_tokens | 248.6M | 176.7M (Claude Code only) |
| cache_read_tokens | 7.65B | 7.09B (Claude Code only) |
| full input (in + cache_read + cache_creation) | 7.9B | 7.27B |

(API is slightly higher because it also includes my other agents — coverage is fine.)

So the pipeline is accurate. The problem is presentation: the "Input tokens" card showed ~238M while my actual prompt volume for the window was ~7.3B — **cache reads are 97.6% of real input**, and the card has no hint of that.

## Suggested changes

Ordered by effort:

1. **Label the metric** (one-line fix): subtitle or tooltip on the "Input tokens" card — "excludes cached prompt tokens" — and make sure a "Cache read" card/series is visible at the same level, not buried in chart breakdowns.
2. **Add a "Total input" aggregate**: `input_tokens + cache_creation_input_tokens + cache_read_tokens`, matching what most usage tools (e.g. ccusage-style reporting) treat as "prompt tokens". Either as its own card or as a toggle on the existing one.
3. **Optional**: a settings preference for the default input convention (pure vs. total), for users who bill against one or the other.

## Two related observations (may be by design)

- `usage_dedup_key` in my usage-cache DB has **1 distinct value across ~95K rows** — dedup doesn't appear to be discriminating anything. If it's intentional (e.g. keys only set for remote/hosted sources), feel free to ignore.
- `totals.inputTokens` from the summary API (248M) differs from the raw eligible `usage_facts` sum for the same window (~1.65B for 365d) by roughly the streaming-snapshot factor — the API's internal per-request aggregation is doing the right thing, but it's undocumented; a note in the API docs would help anyone auditing the numbers like I did.

Happy to provide more data from my install if useful.

title: Show each agent's own session title as the session name
body:
## TL;DR

After #2039, agents still handled session titles in different ways. Some put the title in the first-message field, some ignored generated titles, and Gemini CLI and Kimi CLI titles were never read. Every agent now follows one rule: the agent's own title is the session name, a name the user chose wins over a generated one, and the first message is what the user typed.

## Why

The project already settled this in #601: show agent-provided names by default, with no toggle. #2039 then hid generated titles for Qwen, Copilot, and OpenClaw, which broke that rule. Older parsers for OpenCode, Amp, Copilot, and VS Code predate the session-name field, so they put titles in the first message instead. That hid the user's first prompt from previews and search.

## How

| Agent | Title source | Change |
|---|---|---|
| Qwen Code | `custom_title` records | a generated title shows when there is no rename |
| OpenClaw | `session_nodes.label`, else `display_name` | a generated title shows when there is no `/name` |
| Copilot CLI | `workspace.yaml` `name` | always the session name |
| OpenCode, Kilo, MiMo Code | `session.title` (placeholders skipped) | moved out of the first message |
| Amp | thread `title` | moved out of the first message |
| VS Code Copilot, Positron, Windsurf | `customTitle` | now the session name |
| Kimi CLI | `state.json` `custom_title`, legacy `metadata.json` `title` | new |
| Gemini CLI | generated `summary` | new |
| Kiro CLI (legacy JSONL) | sidecar `title` | now the session name, matching the current layout |

A title still fills in the first message when a session has no user message, which is what most parsers already did.

## Reviewer notes

- **Kimi watches two more files.** `state.json` and `metadata.json` become companions of `wire.jsonl`, so a rename triggers a resync even though the transcript doesn't change.
- **Data version 120.** Main already uses 118 and 119, so this bump re-reads unchanged sessions once more.
- **Not covered.** Kimi Work, the `.kimi-code` agents layout, and OpenClaw's legacy JSONL store have no title source that AgentsView reads. Cursor CLI's store `name` has no local sample or producer source to verify against.
- **Docs.** `session-format-sources.md` pins the upstream writer for each agent. The usage guide and changelog describe the rule.

title: fix(deps): update dependency dompurify to v3.4.16 [security]
body:
This PR contains the following updates: | Package | Change | [Age](https://docs.renovatebot.com/merge-confidence/) | [Confidence](https://docs.renovatebot.com/merge-confidence/) | |---|---|---|---| | [dompurify](https://redirect.github.com/cure53/DOMPurify) | [`3.4.15` → `3.4.16`](https://renovatebot.com/diffs/npm/dompurify/3.4.15/3.4.16) | ![age](https://developer.mend.io/api/mc/badges/age/npm/dompurify/3.4.16?slim=true) | ![confidence](https://developer.mend.io/api/mc/badges/confidence/npm/dompurify/3.4.15/3.4.16?slim=true) | --- ### DOMPurify: IN_PLACE: node-removing afterSanitize hook leaves detached subtree event handlers armed, causing DOM XSS [GHSA-p98j-92pf-mc4p](https://redirect.github.com/advisories/GHSA-p98j-92pf-mc4p)
More information #### Details ##### Summary In `IN_PLACE` mode DOMPurify sanitizes the caller's live DOM subtree directly. To close a known hazard (GHSA-55q2-fjhq-7xh7), the library neutralizes any node a hook detaches during sanitization by stripping its subtree's non-allow-listed attributes, but this neutralization is wired only into the `beforeSanitizeElements` and `uponSanitizeElement` hook sites. An `afterSanitizeElements` or `afterSanitizeAttributes` hook that removes a non-root element (a documented, supported pattern) detaches that element's subtree with no neutralization, so descendant `on*` handlers remain armed on the caller's live tree after `sanitize()` returns, yielding DOM XSS. No special privilege is required beyond supplying markup to an application that uses `IN_PLACE` together with a node-removing afterSanitize hook. ##### Root Cause `IN_PLACE` sanitization mutates the caller's live document, so any element a hook detaches from that tree must have its subtree neutralized before `sanitize()` returns; otherwise a queued resource-event handler (for example an `` that began loading when the caller built the tree) fires in page scope even though the handler never reached the sanitized output. The guard helper `_handleHookDetachedNode` (which calls `_neutralizeSubtree` in `IN_PLACE`) is invoked only after `beforeSanitizeElements` and after `uponSanitizeElement`. It is never invoked from the afterSanitize return paths, and `_sanitizeAttributes` never calls it at all. The post-walk `IN_PLACE` neutralization pass iterates only `DOMPurify.removed`, and hook-detached nodes are intentionally not recorded there, so that pass cannot reach them either. ```text src/purify.ts _sanitizeElements: _handleHookDetachedNode present at lines 2142 and 2175 (before/upon), absent after afterSanitizeElements at lines 2208 and 2249. _sanitizeAttributes: afterSanitizeAttributes fires at line 2670 with no detach re-check; the function never calls _handleHookDetachedNode. Post-walk IN_PLACE pass (lines 3081-3090) iterates DOMPurify.removed only, which by design (comment at lines 2096-2099) excludes hook-detached nodes. ``` ##### Impact An attacker who supplies markup processed by a victim application that runs `DOMPurify.sanitize(node, { IN_PLACE: true })` and registers a node-removing `afterSanitizeElements` or `afterSanitizeAttributes` hook can retain arbitrary `on*` event handlers on descendants of a removed non-root element. Because `IN_PLACE` operates on the caller's live document, a queued resource-event handler on such a descendant fires in the page origin after the synchronous `sanitize()` call returns, giving script execution in the victim's session (DOM XSS). This defeats DOMPurify's `IN_PLACE` contract to neutralize handlers on subtrees removed from the live tree. The capability is script execution in the victim origin; exact confidentiality and integrity effects depend on the hosting application's session. ##### Proof of Concept ```text Dependencies: Node.js and jsdom. The harness builds a live tree, registers a removal hook, runs IN_PLACE sanitize(), then inspects whether the attacker onerror handler survives on the detached descendant. jsdom does not perform real image loads, so the retained handler (rather than an actual fired event) is the observed hazard; the retained on* attribute on a live detached node after a synchronous sanitize() return is the neutralization failure. ``` Reproduction steps: 1. Build a live subtree `#root > section#wrap > img[onerror]` where `#root` is the walk root and `section#wrap` is a non-root wrapper. 2. Register an `afterSanitizeElements` (or `afterSanitizeAttributes`) hook that calls `node.remove()` on the wrapper. 3. Call `DOMPurify.sanitize(root, { IN_PLACE: true })`. 4. Observe that the descendant `` retains its `onerror` handler, whereas the same removal performed in a `beforeSanitizeElements`/`uponSanitizeElement` hook strips it. ```javascript const { JSDOM } = require('jsdom'); const createDOMPurify = require('dompurify'); const { window } = new JSDOM(''); const DOMPurify = createDOMPurify(window); const root = window.document.createElement('div'); root.id = 'root'; root.innerHTML = '
'; window.document.body.appendChild(root); DOMPurify.addHook('afterSanitizeElements', (node) => { if (node.id === 'wrap') node.remove(); }); DOMPurify.sanitize(root, { IN_PLACE: true }); // The detached still carries its onerror handler: console.log(root.querySelector('#wrap') === null, // true (removed from live tree) !!window.document.querySelector('img[onerror]') || // handler survives on the detached node root.innerHTML); ``` ```text PASS: beforeSanitizeElements detach neutralizes descendant onerror (control) PASS: uponSanitizeElement detach neutralizes descendant onerror (control) PASS: without a removal hook the descendant onerror is stripped normally PASS: afterSanitizeElements detach LEAVES descendant onerror armed (GAP) PASS: afterSanitizeAttributes detach LEAVES descendant onerror armed (GAP) PASS: kept custom element removed in afterSanitizeElements leaves descendant onerror armed (GAP) ``` ##### Attack Chain 1. **Exposure:** The victim application calls `DOMPurify.sanitize(liveNode, { IN_PLACE: true })` on attacker-influenced markup and has registered a node-removing `afterSanitizeElements` or `afterSanitizeAttributes` hook per an application policy (`src/purify.ts:3026` walk, `2136` element pass, `2522` attribute pass). 2. **Control:** The attacker controls the markup, including a non-root wrapper element and, inside it, a descendant carrying an `on*` resource-event handler such as ``. 3. **Path:** The pre-order walk visits the wrapper before its descendants. During the wrapper's element or attribute pass the application hook detaches the wrapper from the live tree. 4. **Guard:** The detach-neutralization guard `_handleHookDetachedNode` runs only after `beforeSanitizeElements` (`2142`) and `uponSanitizeElement` (`2175`); it is absent after `afterSanitizeElements` (`2208`, `2249`) and is never called by `_sanitizeAttributes` (afterSanitizeAttributes at `2670`). The NodeIterator advances past the detached subtree, so the descendants are never revisited, and the post-walk pass iterates only `DOMPurify.removed`, which excludes hook-detached nodes. 5. **Primitive:** The descendant retains its `on*` handler on the caller's live document after `sanitize()` returns. 6. **Result:** The queued resource event fires the attacker handler in the victim page origin, achieving DOM XSS despite `IN_PLACE` sanitization. ##### Bypass Evidence The relevant prior fix is GHSA-55q2-fjhq-7xh7 ("IN_PLACE hook removal leaves a detached subtree executable, causing XSS"), whose change (`#1557`) added `_neutralizeSubtree` at the `beforeSanitizeElements` and `uponSanitizeElement` detach sites. Inspection of that change shows it touches no afterSanitize site: the diff adds the neutralization only at the before/upon locations, later refactored into `_handleHookDetachedNode` at `src/purify.ts:2142` and `2175`. A subsequent hardening change (`#1616`) added a `rootWasRemoved` throw and a neutralization sweep over `DOMPurify.removed`, but that sweep still iterates only `DOMPurify.removed`, which by design excludes hook-detached non-root nodes, so it does not close this gap. The `afterSanitizeElements`-on-kept-custom-element site at `2208` was itself introduced by the fix for GHSA-c2j3-45gr-mqc4 (`#1527`), adding another uncovered hook site. Disproof attempts, all failed: (a) that a later release closed the afterSanitize gap, refuted by inspecting the published 3.4.13, 3.4.14, and 3.4.15 artifacts; (b) that detached descendants are revisited or re-sanitized, refuted at runtime (the `onerror` is retained only at the afterSanitize sites and stripped at the before/upon sites and with no removal hook); (c) that the post-walk pass catches hook-detached nodes, refuted by the design that excludes them from `DOMPurify.removed`; (d) that the precondition is contrived, refuted by parity with the accepted GHSA-55q2 threat model and the library's own supported pattern of removing a node inside `afterSanitizeElements`. The only edge not directly executed is the browser resource-event dispatch (jsdom performs no real image load); it is established by the proven retention of the live handler after a synchronous return, the library's own comments describing exactly this hazard, and parity with the accepted GHSA-55q2 mechanism. ##### Affected Versions - `Ecosystem: npm` - `Package: dompurify` - `Confirmed affected range: >= 3.4.13, <= 3.4.15` - `Latest release checked: 3.4.15 (npm registry)` - `Fix status: fixed in 3.4.16` The before/upon detach neutralization introduced for GHSA-55q2-fjhq-7xh7 first shipped in 3.4.13; the residual afterSanitize gap was verified by reproducing it against the published npm artifacts for 3.4.13, 3.4.14, and 3.4.15. The 3.4.12 artifact predates that neutralization and behaves differently at the before/upon sites, so it is outside this specific incomplete-fix range. No release through 3.4.15 neutralizes detached subtrees at the afterSanitize sites, so no fixed version is established. ##### Suggested Fix Enforce the same `IN_PLACE` detach-neutralization invariant at every hook site that can detach a node, not only the before/upon sites. Concretely, apply a `_handleHookDetachedNode(currentNode, root)` re-check after `afterSanitizeElements` at both `src/purify.ts:2208` and `2249` (returning as removed when the node was detached), and add an equivalent `IN_PLACE` detach check plus `_neutralizeSubtree` after `afterSanitizeAttributes` at `2670`. As an interim mitigation without a code change, applications using `IN_PLACE` can avoid removing nodes inside `afterSanitizeElements`/`afterSanitizeAttributes` hooks and instead perform such removals in `beforeSanitizeElements`/`uponSanitizeElement`, or avoid `IN_PLACE` for attacker-influenced content. title: fix(ci): run macOS raw capture checks on Namespace
body:
macOS raw capture checks run on Namespace's Apple Silicon runners, so pull requests stop waiting on GitHub's arm64 queue. In a [failed run](https://github.com/kenn-io/agentsview/actions/runs/36729955348/job/109936611499), GitHub cancelled the job after 15 minutes without assigning a runner.

The macOS leg of the Go test matrix uses `namespace-profile-mac-6cpu` and the Namespace Go cache, matching the Linux and Windows legs. It keeps Apple Silicon coverage, which moving to GitHub's Intel runners (#2040) would have dropped. The FSEvents tests and macOS desktop builds keep their GitHub-hosted runners.

PR checks call the workflow pinned to `main`; in this [branch dispatch](https://github.com/kenn-io/agentsview/actions/runs/36765877789) of the changed workflow, the macOS job got an arm64 Namespace runner right away and finished in 49 seconds.

title: test(sync): wait for the provider reload to finish before writing sessions
body:
The provider settings reload test stops failing intermittently on Windows CI, where it timed out after 20 seconds waiting for the watcher to import a new session ([failed run](https://github.com/kenn-io/agentsview/actions/runs/36766083622/job/110060492067)).

A reload switches the sync engine to the new folders before it starts the file watcher that covers them. The test waited only for the engine switch, then wrote a session file, which could land before the new watcher was listening, so nothing imported it. The test now waits for the whole reload to finish. Delaying watcher startup by 500 ms reproduced the CI failure every time before the fix and passes after it.

Production keeps its current behavior. A reload already promises only that sessions on disk arrive with the next sync.

title: Load Activity sessions as you scroll instead of with a button
body:
## TL;DR

The Sessions table on the Activity page had a "Next sessions" button that people could not explain, and clicking it replaced the 200 rows on screen with the next 200. The table now adds the next page as you scroll. If a page takes longer than half a second, a thin loading bar like the one on the Analytics and Quality pages appears on the table edge.

## How

- **Row-based trigger.** The next page starts when 15 rows or fewer are left below the view. The table measures a row instead of using a pixel distance, so the lead stays the same at any interface zoom or text size.
- **Add or replace.** A next page is added to the list. A new sort, time range, date, filter, or refresh replaces the list and scrolls back to the top. Sorting stays on the server and covers the whole report.
- **Errors.** A failed load stops loading on scroll, so an error cannot repeat in a loop. Retry sends the failed request again: the sort, time range, or next page. The Activity page tracks that request because it owns the time-range badge.

## Reviewer notes

- **Effect order in `SessionsTable.svelte`.** The scroll reset runs before the near-end check. In the other order, a user at the bottom of the list who changed the sort got page 2 of the new sort at once.
- **Paged API unchanged.** Same endpoint, cursor, and 200-row page size.
- `SessionsTable.test.ts` is now `SessionsTable.svelte.test.ts`, so tests can change props with `$state`.

title: fix(sync): show remote failure details without false completion messages
body:
`agentsview sync` now preserves the daemon’s actionable failure messages, including DNS and authentication errors, instead of collapsing them to “HTTP remote sync failed.” This applies to both JSON and streamed responses; direct sync errors still use the existing sanitization.

Phase timers now report elapsed time instead of saying “completed,” because they also run when a step fails.

title: fix(ci): give NilAway an independent lint job budget
body:
CI runs NilAway alongside the other Go linters, giving each analysis its own 10-minute job budget. This prevents the earlier checks from consuming the time NilAway needs to finish.

In the [failed run](https://github.com/kenn-io/agentsview/actions/runs/36786692547/job/110129696757), ordinary lint finished after nearly seven minutes including setup, then the job timed out during NilAway. The two matrix jobs preserve every check from `make lint-ci` and run the Huma contract check once. Both jobs finish independently even if one fails.

title: fix(daemon): prevent restarts from stale clients
body:
Long-lived MCP and push-watch clients now reconnect without replacing a running daemon. A client that survives an executable upgrade keeps its old in-memory version while launching the new file, so replacing on every version mismatch could repeatedly restart the same new daemon. These clients can still start a missing daemon and receive client-restart guidance when compatibility prevents reconnection. The launch lock enforces the same rule when a daemon appears during startup.

Automatic replacement between releases now only moves to a newer release. An older installed release reuses a compatible newer daemon, preventing separate installations from downgrading each other. Explicit replacement still permits intentional downgrades when the archive is compatible. Ordinary commands retain replacement for different development versions; the command guide explains unchanged dirty-build versions and separate development installations sharing one archive.

Follow-up to #2034.

title: ci: move focused macOS and CJK tests to Namespace
body:
Run the focused macOS FSEvents suite on `namespace-profile-mac-6cpu` and the CJK full-text-search suite on `namespace-profile-linux-8cpu`, with Namespace Go caching. Both use the existing Restricted public profiles.

The macOS workflow still runs only on pushes to `main`, so its first run on the new runner will follow the merge. The CJK workflow runs on this PR.

title: refactor(vector): move embedding transport and generation lifecycle onto kit
body:
Moves AgentsView's semantic search onto the shared Kit embedding stack and deletes the local code Kit replaces.

Builds on Kit v0.29.2. v0.29.1 stops `embedclient` from sending `"dimensions": 0` when `request_dimensions` is off (kenn-io/kit#137). v0.29.2 classifies failed responses with a `Reason` (kenn-io/kit#138).

## What changes

- **Transport.** `internal/vector/encoder.go` now wraps `embedclient` and is about 1,000 lines shorter. Config maps onto `embedconfig` Model, Roles, Deployment and Transport. The public `[vector.embeddings]` TOML, including `api_key_env`, is unchanged. Kit's `OllamaMetalRecovery` replaces the local Metal gate. AgentsView keeps one retry loop for document builds: they wait out HTTP 429 without limit, while 408, 5xx and transport failures share one `max_retries` budget.
- **Error classification.** Kit's `APIError.Reason` decides skip versus abort. Only an input that is too long or refused by policy skips the document. A 400 Kit cannot attribute to the input (wrong model, unsupported field), credential failures, rate limits and server failures abort the build, so documents stay pending and a later build retries.
- **Generation lifecycle.** Auto-activation uses sqlitevec `Activate`, which refuses while documents are pending. Generation listing and coverage use `Coverage`, `ActiveGeneration` and `Generations`. Additive covering indexes on `(doc_key, content_hash, embed_gen)` keep `Coverage` an index scan.
- **No re-embed on upgrade.** `vectorSpace` builds an `embedmodel.Descriptor` whose `Legacy` entry is the existing fingerprint. Builds and the staleness gate use `Descriptor.Matches`, so stored generations stay current. A change to the model, recipe or prefix still cuts a new generation. Generation keys are still the AgentsView fingerprint, so replica push and serve paths are unchanged.
- **Lexical.** Literal FTS quoting uses `lexical.Literal().PrepareLiteral`. CJK detection uses `lexical.EnableCharacterPhrase().IndexFor`.

## Kept local, and why

- **Retired-generation revival and `embeddings activate --force`.** Kit makes retirement terminal because `Reclaim` may have dropped vectors. AgentsView never reclaims, so a retired generation still holds usable vectors.
- **`db.RRFMerge`.** Subordinate hits (sidechain runs, subagent sessions) are ranked 5 places lower before fusion. `search/rrf` only supports per-leg weights, so it cannot apply that penalty.
- **Jieba Han tokenization, SQLite FTS query shapes, recall OR queries, and ILIKE substring search on PostgreSQL, ClickHouse and DuckDB.** Kit's lexical builders don't produce these shapes.
- **PostgreSQL halfvec and `ef_search`.** Kit has no equivalent.
- **`countPending` and `resetGeneration`.** Kit has no equivalent.

## Behavior changes (in the changelog)

- Requests use float JSON instead of base64.
- An invalid vector is retried only during Ollama recovery.
- Ordinary Ollama requests are no longer paused while recovery runs.
- Endpoints may not contain query strings.
- Public IP endpoints require https.

## Where to look

- `cmd/agentsview/kit_migration_test.go` pins the pre-migration fingerprints. It also reopens an existing `vectors.db` through the Kit client and checks four things: no document re-embeds, search serves the stored vectors, an edited document is the only one re-embedded, and a deleted document stops matching.
- `internal/vector/index.go`: `reviveRetiredGeneration` and `fillGenerationInfo`.
- `internal/vector/build.go`: `resolveBuildTarget` matching and `maybeActivate`.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

title: Cursor IDE: an empty state.vscdb-wal created by the daemon's own reads re-triggers full container reparses
body:
### Summary

On Windows, the daemon keeps re-parsing the whole Cursor IDE `state.vscdb` while Cursor is not even running. Opening the database creates an empty `state.vscdb-wal` and closing it removes it again, and that flips the container's state hash, so each parse schedules the next one. This is the same class of bug as #1580 (`-shm`) and #2030 (Antigravity `-shm`), but for an empty `-wal`.

On my machine (Windows 11, `state.vscdb` is 5.1 GB with 543 composers, Cursor closed) this kept about 0.7–0.9 of a core busy on `cursorIDEParseContainer` and held 220–270 MB of parse results live. Together with the watch buffers below, that pushed the heap past the 256 MiB serve memory limit, and the garbage collector ran nonstop.

### Evidence

- With Cursor closed and `state.vscdb` unmodified for a day, a `FileSystemWatcher` on `state.vscdb*` saw 11 create/delete cycles of `state.vscdb-wal` and `state.vscdb-shm` in 90 seconds, each right after the daemon opened the database. The `-wal` is always 0 bytes.
- `cursorIDESQLiteStateHash` (`internal/parser/cursor_ide_provider.go`, still the same on current `main`) folds `|wal:<size>|` plus the WAL header into the hash whenever a `-wal` file exists. An empty WAL holds no transactions, but its presence or absence still changes the hash, so the skip cache misses and the whole container is parsed again.
- CPU profile, 60 s, no `GOMEMLIMIT` (binary built from `main` at the end of September, before #2019/#2024): 5.57 cores in total, `gcDrain` 44%, `cursorIDEParseContainer` 17%. The heap profile shows `parseCursorIDEComposer` holding about 266 MB, plus 539 MB of fsnotify watch buffers (see below).

### Partial fix I tested

Skipping an empty WAL in the hash:

```go
if info, err := os.Stat(walPath); err == nil && info.Size() > 0 {
```

This dropped the self-triggered cycles from about 7 per minute to about 2 per minute. It did not eliminate them, so there is at least one more trigger I haven't found yet. #2019 and #2024 make each reparse cheaper but don't remove the trigger. I'll keep digging; I'm filing this now so the pattern is on record.

### Related: watch buffer memory on Windows

fsnotify allocates a 64 KiB `ReadDirectoryChangesW` buffer per watched directory. With the full 8192-directory recursive-watch budget that is about 512 MiB, already twice the daemon's default soft memory limit. In my measurements 16 KiB buffers (`fsnotify.WithBufferSize`) cut that part from 539 MB to 122 MB. That alone did not stop the GC churn while the Cursor loop was running, but it is a separate, independent improvement. I can send a PR for it if you agree.

title: fix(sync): keep both files when two sources share a session id
body:
When two Gemini CLI or Cursor files record the same session ID, AgentsView keeps both transcripts. Previously, the file synced last could replace a longer archive (#2067, #2058, #2057). Other providers keep their existing behavior.

The stored file keeps its ID; another file becomes a linked session with a derived ID. When the stored file is gone, a new file with at least as many messages can take over the original ID. Complete remote mirrors can establish the same ownership. Partial imports, excluded paths, and paths outside exported roots stay separate.

Provider-recognized moves, including Cursor replacing `.txt` with `.jsonl`, preserve IDs, names, stars, and pins locally and in complete remote mirrors. The replacement supplies the complete transcript, even when shorter. Data version 125 reprocesses the archive once after upgrading, including unchanged HTTP mirrors, to recover previously collapsed conversations. Rebuilds snapshot ownership only for providers with participating local or remote source roots.

Batch exclusion bookkeeping tracks each write by position. Resume commands resolve collision IDs on the server through the provider capability. Review the ownership and relocation rules in `internal/sync/source_collision.go`.

Remaining limits:

- On a first sync, parallel parse order decides which file gets the original ID; the earliest segment is not guaranteed to become the base.
- Already derived sessions retain their IDs at recorded paths or provider-recognized moves. Arbitrary moves can create another derived session.
- Trashing the base hides linked sessions from the sidebar without trashing their transcripts. Permanent deletion promotes them.
- Cursor copies retain their shared prefix, so search and usage count those turns twice pending #2057. Copied subagents link to the session sharing their ID, replacing their original parent link.
